units.title: Period 1: 1491–1607
units.blurb: Maize, the Pueblo and Iroquois, Columbus, the Columbian Exchange, encomienda, the Pueblo Revolt and the first enslaved Africans. Questions compare Native societies by environment and trace the effects of contact.
keys: Maize farming spread north from Mexico and let peoples such as the Pueblo build permanent, irrigated, socially stratified towns.
Native societies fit their environments, from Pueblo irrigation farmers to mobile Plains bison hunters and salmon-rich Chinook villages.
Cahokia's mounds and the Iroquois Confederacy prove North America held cities and complex governments long before 1492.
God, gold and glory, backed by the caravel, compass and astrolabe, carried Columbus to the Caribbean for Spain in 1492.
The Columbian Exchange moved crops, animals and disease both ways and collapsed Native populations through epidemic disease.
Spain ruled through encomienda labor, the casta hierarchy and missions, a system Las Casas denounced at Valladolid in 1550.
As Native labor collapsed, Spain and Portugal imported enslaved Africans on the sugar plantation model built at Madeira and Sao Tome.
Native peoples resisted as well as adapted, most successfully in the 1680 Pueblo Revolt that expelled Spain from New Mexico.

topics.t: Native American societies before European contact
Columbian Exchange, Spanish exploration, and conquest
Labor, slavery, and caste in the Spanish colonial system
Cultural interactions between Europeans, Native Americans, and Africans

excl.s: Optional Sources pages offer examples of sources appropriate for a college-level course. None of the AP Exam questions require students to have studied these specific sources.

units.check: Progress check · 15 multiple choice · 2 short answer (primary source (partial), primary source (partial)) · 1 free response (long essay (partial))

frq.title: SAQ 1 · Who conquered Mexico? (secondary source)
frq.stem:
Answer (a), (b), and (c) using the excerpt below.

"For five centuries the fall of Tenochtitlan has been told as the triumph of a few hundred Spaniards over an empire of millions. That story mistakes the flag for the army. The warriors who besieged the Mexica capital in 1521 were overwhelmingly Tlaxcalans, Texcocans, and other Native peoples who saw in the strangers a chance to end the tribute and captive-taking the Triple Alliance imposed on them. Smallpox, arriving in 1520, did the rest, killing the Mexica ruler Cuitlahuac and thousands of defenders. The conquest of Mexico was, in large part, a Mesoamerican war whose winners soon discovered they had exchanged one overlord for another."

Elena Ruiz-Hartley, historian, The Allied Conquest, 2019. (The historian and the book are fictional, written for this exercise.)

parts.q: Describe the historian's argument about the Spanish conquest of the Aztec (Mexica) Empire.
parts.a: The historian argues that the fall of Tenochtitlan was mainly the work of Native peoples and disease rather than of Spanish power: Tlaxcalans, Texcocans and other subject peoples, resentful of Mexica tribute and captive-taking, made up most of the besieging army, and the smallpox epidemic of 1520 killed the ruler Cuitlahuac and many defenders, so the Spaniards were a small part of the victory.
parts.n: Quoting the excerpt, or writing 'the historian talks about the conquest', earns nothing; describe the claim (allies and disease, not Spanish strength, won) in your own words.

parts.q: Explain how ONE historical development from the period 1492 to 1607, not directly mentioned in the excerpt, supports the historian's argument.
parts.a: Pizarro's conquest of the Inca Empire (1532-1533) supports it. Fewer than 200 Spaniards succeeded because smallpox had already killed the Inca ruler Huayna Capac and set off a civil war between his sons Atahualpa and Huascar, so Andean divisions and disease, not Spanish numbers, decided the outcome, the same pattern the historian finds in Mexico. (Also accepted: Malintzin's translation making the Tlaxcalan alliance possible; Spain's later reliance on Tlaxcalan colonists to end the Chichimeca War.)
parts.n: Reusing the excerpt's own evidence (the Tlaxcalans, the 1520 epidemic) earns nothing; the development must be new and tied to the argument.

parts.q: Explain how ONE historical development from the period 1492 to 1607 could be used to challenge or modify the historian's argument.
parts.a: Tlaxcala had fought the Mexica for decades without taking Tenochtitlan, so the new element in 1519-1521 was Spanish: Cortes organized the coalition, and Spaniards built thirteen brigantines that cut the island city off by water during the 1521 siege. The Spanish role was therefore decisive even if Spaniards were few. (Also accepted: the conquest of the Caribbean islands, where Spaniards subdued the Taino without large Native allied armies.)
parts.n: Simply disagreeing ('the Spanish did win') earns nothing; the point needs a specific development and an explanation of how it limits the historian's claim.

frq.title: SAQ 2 · A town petitions the king (primary source)
frq.stem:
Answer (a), (b), and (c) using the excerpt below.

"To our lord the King: We, the governors and nobles of this town, kiss your royal hands. When the Marques [Cortes] came, we received him in peace, gave him food and warriors, and our men died in the war against Mexico in your service. Now the encomendero to whom we have been given demands tribute in cloth, maize, and gold beyond what our fathers paid to Moctezuma, and he sends our people to the mines, where many die. Our fields go unplanted and our children go hungry. We ask that you command that we pay only what is just, as your laws declare, and that our town be placed under your royal crown."

Described period document: a petition from the council of an Indigenous town in central Mexico to the king of Spain, 1560. It was composed for this exercise on the model of the petitions, written in Nahuatl or Spanish, that Indigenous town councils sent to the Spanish crown in the mid-1500s.

parts.q: Describe the historical situation in which the petition was written.
parts.a: By 1560 Spain ruled central Mexico, which it had conquered in 1519-1521 with the help of Native allies, and had granted Native towns in encomienda to Spanish colonists who collected tribute and labor for mines and farms. Epidemics were shrinking Native populations, so the same demands fell on fewer people, and the New Laws of 1542 had given the crown a legal basis to limit encomenderos, which Native towns invoked in petitions like this one.
parts.n: Summarizing the document ('they are complaining about tribute') describes its content, not its historical situation; the point needs the conquest, the encomienda and the crown's reforms around it.

parts.q: Explain how the purpose or the audience of the petition shaped its content.
parts.a: Written to persuade the king to relieve the town, the petition stresses the town's loyalty and its warriors' service in the conquest, contrasts the encomendero's excessive demands with the lighter tribute paid under Moctezuma, and appeals to the king's own laws. The leaders present themselves as faithful vassals wronged by a subordinate, the framing most likely to move a monarch who was already trying to rein in encomenderos.
parts.n: Identifying the audience ('it is written to the king') without explaining how that audience shaped what the town chose to say earns nothing.

parts.q: Explain ONE way the Spanish colonial labor system changed in the period 1492 to 1607.
parts.a: Spain shifted from private encomienda grants toward crown-controlled labor drafts and enslaved African labor. After the Caribbean population collapsed and the New Laws of 1542 barred new encomiendas and the enslavement of Native people, the crown channeled Native labor through state drafts such as the repartimiento in New Spain and the Potosi mita (1573), while planters and mine owners imported growing numbers of enslaved Africans.
parts.n: Saying labor 'got worse' or 'changed' without naming the specific shift and why it happened earns nothing.

frq.title: SAQ 3 · The population of central Mexico, 1518-1605 (non-text source)
frq.stem:
Answer (a), (b), and (c) using the graph described below.

Described line graph, titled 'Estimated Native Population of Central Mexico, 1518-1605'. Horizontal axis: year, 1518 to 1605. Vertical axis: population in millions, 0 to 30. Seven points joined by a line:
Year · Estimated population (millions)
1518 · 25.2
1532 · 16.8
1548 · 6.3
1568 · 2.65
1580 · 1.9
1595 · 1.375
1605 · 1.075
The line drops steeply from 1518 to 1548, then falls more slowly and flattens just above 1 million after 1595.

Source: data from estimates published by the historians Sherburne F. Cook and Woodrow Borah (1960s-1970s); graph described for this exercise.

parts.q: Identify ONE pattern shown in the graph.
parts.a: The Native population of central Mexico fell by roughly 96 percent, from about 25.2 million in 1518 to about 1.1 million in 1605, and the fall was steepest in the first three decades (to 6.3 million by 1548) before slowing after 1568.
parts.n: 'The population went down' is too vague; state the direction with the scale or the timing the graph shows.

parts.q: Explain ONE cause of the pattern shown in the graph.
parts.a: Epidemics of diseases from Europe and Africa, to which Native peoples had no acquired immunity, were the main cause: smallpox struck during the conquest in 1520, and later great epidemics, including the cocoliztli outbreaks of 1545-1548 and the late 1570s, line up with the graph's steepest drops. Forced labor, tribute and famine under the encomienda weakened survivors and made each outbreak deadlier.
parts.n: 'Disease' with no mechanism or example earns little; the point needs the lack of immunity or a named epidemic linked to the decline. What cocoliztli was is still debated.

parts.q: Explain ONE effect of the pattern shown in the graph on Spanish colonial society in the period 1519 to 1607.
parts.a: The collapse shrank the tribute and labor base on which the encomienda depended, so the crown restricted encomiendas (New Laws, 1542), organized the survivors' labor through state drafts (the repartimiento), and forcibly resettled scattered survivors into compact towns (congregaciones, around 1600), while colonists turned increasingly to enslaved Africans for labor.
parts.n: An effect asserted without a link to the population loss ('Spain needed workers') earns nothing; connect the decline to a specific Spanish response.

frq.title: DBQ · Religion and the European conquest of the Americas, 1492-1607
frq.stem:
Practice. The exam draws its DBQ from 1754 to 1980, so none comes from Period 1; this one practises the same seven-point skills on Period 1 content.

Evaluate the extent to which religious motives shaped European conquest and colonization in the Americas from 1492 to 1607.

The documents are paraphrased for this exercise from the sources named in each source line; the wording is not a direct quotation.

Document 1
Source: Christopher Columbus, letter announcing his first voyage, addressed to Luis de Santangel, a financial official of the Spanish crown, 1493.
"The islands are fertile beyond description, with fine harbors, many spices, and great mines of gold. The people go unarmed, are timid, and give whatever they have for trifles. They know no sect or idolatry, and I believe they would readily become Christians. Their Highnesses may have as much gold as they need, spices and cotton, and slaves, as many as they order, taken from the idolaters."

Document 2
Source: The Requerimiento, a statement drafted for the Spanish crown by the jurist Juan Lopez de Palacios Rubios in 1513, to be read aloud by Spanish commanders to Native peoples before fighting began.
"We ask that you acknowledge the Church as ruler of the whole world, and the pope, and in his name the king and queen of Spain, and that you allow the faith to be preached to you. If you do so, we will receive you with love. If you do not, or maliciously delay, with the help of God we shall make war on you, enslave you, your wives, and your children, and take your goods; and the deaths and losses that follow will be your fault, not ours."

Document 3
Source: Hernan Cortes, second letter to Emperor Charles V, 1520, reporting on his entry into Tenochtitlan.
"The city is as large as Seville or Cordoba. It has a square where more than sixty thousand people come each day to buy and sell every kind of goods: gold, silver, precious stones, and feathers. In the principal temple I had the idols thrown down the steps and the chapels cleansed of the blood of sacrifices, and I set up images of Our Lady and the saints there, which grieved Moctezuma and his people."

Document 4
Source: Bartolome de las Casas, Dominican friar and former encomendero, A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies, written in 1542 for Emperor Charles V and printed in 1552.
"The reason the Christians have killed and destroyed such an infinite number of souls is solely that they have made gold their ultimate aim, seeking to grow rich in a very short time. They have cared no more for the souls of these peoples, the humblest and most peaceful in the world, than for beasts, and have killed them before they could hear of the faith."

Document 5
Source: Juan Gines de Sepulveda, Spanish scholar and royal chronicler, Democrates Alter, a dialogue written about 1544 defending the justice of war against Native peoples; he argued the same case at Valladolid in 1550.
"Compare the prudence and virtue of the Spaniards with these barbarians, who are as inferior to the Spaniards as children are to adults. They worship idols and offer human sacrifice. It is therefore just that they be ruled by the Spaniards, and war to subject them is lawful, for it ends their crimes against nature and opens the way for the preaching of the Christian religion."

Document 6
Source: Account of the conquest by Nahua elders, recorded in Nahuatl in the Florentine Codex, compiled from the 1550s to about 1577 under the direction of the Franciscan friar Bernardino de Sahagun.
"When the Spaniards were given the gold banners and necklaces, they rejoiced. They seized the gold like monkeys; it satisfied and gladdened their hearts. They hungered for it like pigs. Later they went into Moctezuma's treasure house and took everything, the gold and the jewels, as if it were their own."

Document 7
Source: Richard Hakluyt, English clergyman and geographer, Discourse of Western Planting, written in 1584 for Queen Elizabeth I to urge support for English colonies in North America.
"This western voyage will greatly enlarge the gospel of Christ, a duty that falls chiefly on the princes of the reformed religion, since the Spaniards have converted the people only in name and with cruelty. Planting there will also supply the commodities we now buy from our enemies, give a market for our woolen cloth, set our idle poor to work, and give us a base from which to trouble the King of Spain and cut off his treasure."

rows.earns: A defensible claim about extent that sets up a line of reasoning, in one place, e.g.: religion shaped conquest mainly as a justification and partner of the pursuit of wealth: Spain's crown made conversion the legal key to war, land and labor (Docs 2, 5), conquerors pursued gold under a religious banner (Docs 1, 3, 4, 6), and by the 1580s English promoters fused Protestant mission with commerce and rivalry (Doc 7).
rows.loses: Restating the prompt ('religion shaped colonization to some extent'), a claim with no line of reasoning, or a thesis split between introduction and conclusion.

rows.earns: Describes a broader development relevant to the prompt, beyond a phrase: e.g., the Reconquista's crusading tradition, completed at Granada in 1492, which fused conquest, reward and conversion; or the Protestant Reformation after 1517, which split Europe and turned imperial rivalry into religious rivalry.
rows.loses: A phrase such as 'during the Age of Exploration' or 'Europeans wanted God, gold, and glory'; context unconnected to the prompt.

rows.r: Row C · Evidence from the documents
rows.earns: 2 points: uses the content of at least four documents to support an argument (e.g., Doc 2's demand to accept the Church on pain of war and slavery; Doc 3's destruction of idols beside the gold of the market; Docs 4 and 6 on greed for gold; Doc 7's mix of Protestant, commercial and anti-Spanish aims). 1 point: accurately describes the content of three documents that address the topic.
rows.loses: Quoting or listing documents without describing their content; describing fewer than three; misreading a document (e.g., treating Doc 4 as a defense of conquest).

rows.r: Row C · Evidence beyond the documents
rows.earns: One specific, described piece of evidence not in the documents and different from the context, e.g.: the encomienda, which granted Native labor on condition that the holder Christianize the workers; Potosi silver (from 1545) and the mita; Franciscan missions in Florida and New Mexico (from 1598); the New Laws of 1542.
rows.loses: A name dropped without description ('the encomienda'), evidence already in a document, or the same evidence used for contextualization.

rows.earns: For two documents, explains how or why point of view, purpose, historical situation or audience is relevant to the argument, e.g.: Doc 1's purpose, winning a larger second voyage, explains why converts are paired with gold and slaves; Doc 5 was written to defend conquest by a scholar who never went to the Americas; Doc 6 records Nahua memory decades later under a Franciscan's direction, which may sharpen its criticism of lay Spaniards' greed; Doc 7's audience, the queen and investors, explains the Protestant appeal tied to profit.
rows.loses: Identifying the author or date ('Doc 4 was written by Las Casas in 1542') without explaining why that matters to the argument.

rows.earns: A complex understanding woven into the argument, e.g.: explains that religious and economic motives reinforced each other (the Requerimiento made refusing conversion the legal ground for seizing land and labor); distinguishes Spanish Catholic and English Protestant uses of religion; or uses Docs 4-6 to show Europeans themselves disputing whether faith justified conquest.
rows.loses: A single sentence noting 'there were many motives', or a counterargument that is stated but not explained or tied to the thesis.

parts.q: Row A · Thesis: write a thesis for this prompt.
parts.a: Religious motives shaped European conquest mainly as a justification for, and partner of, the pursuit of wealth: Spain made conversion the legal key that unlocked war, land and Native labor, conquerors sought gold under a Christian banner, and English promoters by the 1580s fused Protestant mission with commerce and rivalry with Spain.
parts.n: A thesis that says only 'religion and wealth both mattered' does not establish a line of reasoning; say how the two were related.

parts.q: Row B · Contextualization: plan the context paragraph.
parts.a: Open with the Reconquista: seven centuries of Christian war against Muslim Iberia ended at Granada in January 1492, leaving Spain's monarchs with a crusading ideal and a practice of rewarding conquerors with land and the labor of the defeated. Add that Portugal's African voyages and the search for Asian trade made wealth a parallel motive, and that after 1517 the Reformation made religion a line of rivalry among European states.
parts.n: Two or three sentences that describe developments and connect them to the prompt; a single phrase earns nothing.

parts.q: Row C · Evidence from the documents: plan which documents support which part of the argument.
parts.a: Paragraph 1, religion as legal justification: Doc 2 (accept the Church or face war and slavery), Doc 5 (idolatry and sacrifice make war just), Doc 3 (idols thrown down and replaced). Paragraph 2, wealth as the driving motive: Doc 1 (gold and slaves promised beside converts), Doc 4 (gold the 'ultimate aim'), Doc 6 (Nahua memory of Spaniards seizing gold 'like monkeys'), Doc 3 (the market's gold and silver). Paragraph 3, a Protestant variation: Doc 7 (gospel, cloth markets, idle poor, attacks on Spain). Using six or seven documents also supports complexity.
parts.n: Describe each document's content in your own words and tie it to the claim; a list of document numbers earns nothing.

parts.q: Row C · Evidence beyond the documents: choose one piece and say where it goes.
parts.a: In paragraph 1: the encomienda, which gave a colonist the tribute and labor of a Native district on condition that he protect and Christianize its people, shows religion written into the labor system that produced wealth. Alternative for paragraph 2: Potosi silver (opened 1545), worked by drafted Native laborers under the mita from 1573.
parts.n: It must be described, not named, and must differ from the contextualization evidence.

parts.q: Row D · Sourcing: plan two sourcing explanations.
parts.a: Doc 1: because Columbus was writing to a crown financier to win a larger second voyage, he promised converts and gold and slaves together, so the letter shows that religion and profit were sold as one package from the start. Doc 6: recorded decades after the conquest by Nahua elders working under a Franciscan, it condemns Spanish greed, a theme friars shared, so its picture of gold-hungry conquerors fits both Nahua memory and missionary criticism of lay Spaniards.
parts.n: Each explanation must say how the sourcing affects the argument, not just identify the author, date or audience.

parts.q: Row D · Complexity: plan how the essay shows a complex understanding.
parts.a: Argue that religious and economic motives were not rivals but reinforced each other: the Requerimiento (Doc 2) made refusing the faith the legal trigger for seizing people and land, and Sepulveda (Doc 5) turned idolatry into grounds for rule; then qualify by showing Europeans disputed this (Doc 4) and that the English version (Doc 7) used Protestantism against Spain while pursuing trade.
parts.n: Complexity must run through the argument with evidence; a closing sentence that 'it was complicated' earns nothing.

frq.title: LEQ · Contact and change in Native American societies, 1492-1607
frq.stem: Evaluate the extent to which contact with Europeans changed Native American societies in the Americas from 1492 to 1607.

rows.earns: A defensible claim about extent that sets up a line of reasoning, e.g.: contact transformed Native societies where Spain conquered (the Caribbean, central Mexico, the Andes) through epidemics, the encomienda and mita, and missions, but most Native nations north of Mexico kept their land, government and economies to 1607, changed mainly by disease and trade goods.
rows.loses: Restating the prompt ('contact changed Native societies in many ways') or a claim that sets up no line of reasoning.

rows.earns: Describes the broader situation, beyond a phrase: e.g., before 1492 Native societies had adapted to diverse environments, from maize-based Pueblo and Mississippian towns to mobile Great Basin and Plains bands and salmon-rich Northwest villages, and the Aztec and Inca empires had recently built tribute states; or the Iberian background of Reconquista and Atlantic expansion.
rows.loses: A phrase such as 'Native Americans lived here first' or context unconnected to the question of change.

rows.earns: 2 points: uses at least two specific pieces of evidence to support an argument about extent (e.g., the 1520 smallpox epidemic and central Mexico's population collapse; the encomienda and the Potosi mita; Catholic missions and reducciones; continuity of three-sisters farming and self-government among the Iroquois and Algonquians; Chichimeca resistance). 1 point: identifies two specific, relevant examples without using them to support an argument.
rows.loses: General statements ('many Natives died', 'the Spanish were cruel') with no specific example.

rows.earns: 1 point: uses continuity and change to frame the argument (what changed, what persisted, and why). 2 points: demonstrates a complex understanding, e.g., explains both change and continuity with regional contrast, shows Native agency (alliances, syncretism, resistance) shaping how contact changed societies, or connects the period to later developments such as the Pueblo Revolt of 1680.
rows.loses: Listing changes with no explanation of why they happened or how far they reached; a one-line nod to complexity.

parts.q: Row A · Thesis: write a thesis for this prompt.
parts.a: Contact with Europeans transformed Native societies in the regions Spain conquered, where epidemics killed most people and the encomienda, silver mining and missions remade labor, religion and social order, but to 1607 it changed most Native nations north of Mexico only at the edges, through disease and trade goods, while their land, self-government and ways of making a living persisted.
parts.n: 'To a great extent' with no categories does not establish a line of reasoning.

parts.q: Row B · Contextualization: plan the context paragraph.
parts.a: Describe the Americas in 1491: tens of millions of people in societies adapted to their environments, including maize-irrigating Pueblo towns, Mississippian chiefdoms, Eastern Woodland farming villages, mobile Great Basin and Plains bands, and Northwest villages built on salmon, alongside the young Aztec and Inca tribute empires. This baseline is what contact changed, or did not.
parts.n: Must describe, in a few sentences, the situation the essay measures change against.

parts.q: Row C · Evidence: plan the body paragraphs and their evidence.
parts.a: Change, demographic: the Taino collapse on Hispaniola within a generation and central Mexico's fall from roughly 25 million to about 1 million by 1605 (a contested high estimate). Change, economic and social: the encomienda, the Potosi mita (1573), and the casta hierarchy. Change, religious: missions and reducciones, with syncretism blending Catholic and Native practice. Continuity: Iroquois and Algonquian three-sisters farming and council government, mobile Plains and Great Basin life, and forty years of Chichimeca resistance ending in Spanish gifts.
parts.n: Each piece must be specific and explicitly tied to the claim about extent.

parts.q: Row D · Analysis and reasoning: plan the reasoning and the complexity.
parts.a: Frame every paragraph as change or continuity and explain why: change was deepest where Spain found dense populations and silver, and continuity lasted where it found neither. For complexity, show Native agency shaping the outcome (Tlaxcalan alliance, syncretic religion, Chichimeca resistance) and connect forward: New Mexico's missions and labor demands led to the Pueblo Revolt of 1680, and Spanish horses would later transform Plains societies.
parts.n: The complexity must be explained with evidence; a final sentence that 'there was both change and continuity' earns nothing.

units.ced: AP United States History Course and Exam Description, Effective Fall 2026

units.title: Period 2: 1607–1754
units.blurb: Jamestown tobacco, Puritan New England, Quaker Pennsylvania, the Navigation Acts, Bacon's and Stono rebellions, and the Great Awakening. Questions contrast the regions and trace the shift from servants to slavery.
keys: The Virginia Company founded Jamestown in 1607 for profit, and Rolfe's tobacco after 1612 drove land hunger and demand for labor.
Winthrop's Puritans built Massachusetts Bay in 1630 as a city upon a hill and banished dissenters Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson.
Regions diverged, from Puritan family farms to Penn's tolerant Quaker Pennsylvania and the Black-majority rice and sugar plantations.
English land hunger sparked the Pequot War (1637) and King Philip's War (1675-76), which ended Native power in southern New England.
Bacon's Rebellion in 1676 pushed Chesapeake planters from indentured servants to enslaved Africans under the 1705 slave codes.
Enslaved people resisted daily and openly, as in the 1739 Stono Rebellion that provoked South Carolina's Negro Act of 1740.
Mercantilism and the Navigation Acts bound colonial trade to England, but salutary neglect let elected assemblies run local affairs.
Whitefield's Great Awakening and Locke's Enlightenment both taught colonists to judge established authority for themselves.

units.title: Period 3: 1754–1800
units.blurb: The French and Indian War, the Stamp Act, the Declaration, the Articles, the Constitutional Convention and Hamilton's plan, ending in 1800. Causation questions dominate, plus Federalist and Anti-Federalist contrasts.
keys: Britain's win in the French and Indian War (1754-1763) doubled its debt, ended salutary neglect and drew the Proclamation Line of 1763.
From the Stamp Act of 1765 to the Coercive Acts of 1774, colonists denied that a Parliament they did not elect could tax them.
Paine's Common Sense and Jefferson's Declaration of 1776 turned a tax quarrel into a Lockean rejection of monarchy itself.
Saratoga in 1777 won the French alliance whose fleet sealed Yorktown in 1781, and the 1783 Treaty of Paris recognized independence.
The Revolution brought republican motherhood and northern gradual emancipation but left southern slavery intact and women without the vote.
The Articles of Confederation passed the Northwest Ordinance yet could not tax or answer Shays' Rebellion, prompting the 1787 Convention.
The Constitution balanced large and small states, counted enslaved people as three-fifths, and won ratification by promising a Bill of Rights.
Hamilton's plan split Federalists from Jeffersonian Republicans, whose feud peaked in the Alien and Sedition Acts and the Revolution of 1800.

units.title: Period 4: 1800–1848
units.blurb: Jefferson and the Marshall Court, the War of 1812, the Missouri Compromise, the Market Revolution, the Second Great Awakening, abolition, Seneca Falls and Jackson. Many cards ask for a case holding or a definition.
keys: Jefferson preached strict construction yet bought Louisiana in 1803, doubling the nation through a loose reading of the treaty power.
Marshall's Court claimed judicial review in Marbury (1803) and expanded federal power in McCulloch (1819) and Gibbons v. Ogden (1824).
Impressment and War Hawks brought the War of 1812, whose nationalist aftermath killed the Federalists and produced the 1823 Monroe Doctrine.
The Missouri Compromise of 1820 admitted Missouri and Maine together and banned slavery north of 36°30', a fire bell in the night.
The Market Revolution's canals, Lowell mills and cotton gin tied North to West while cotton pushed slavery into the Deep South.
Jacksonian democracy widened white male suffrage, and Jackson's Bank veto, Force Bill and Indian Removal set Democrats against Whigs.
The Second Great Awakening's faith in human perfectibility powered temperance, Mann's schools, Dix's asylums and Seneca Falls in 1848.
Garrison's Liberator, Douglass's Narrative and Nat Turner's 1831 revolt pushed the South from necessary evil to positive good.

units.title: Period 5: 1844–1877
units.blurb: Manifest destiny, the Compromise of 1850, Kansas-Nebraska, Dred Scott, secession, emancipation, then the Reconstruction Amendments, sharecropping and the Klan. Causation from the Mexican Cession to Fort Sumter recurs.
keys: Manifest destiny's Mexican Cession of 1848 reopened the slavery question that the Wilmot Proviso and Compromise of 1850 could not settle.
The Fugitive Slave Act and Uncle Tom's Cabin radicalized the North, and the 1854 Kansas-Nebraska Act wrecked the Whigs and created the Republicans.
Bleeding Kansas, Dred Scott in 1857 and John Brown's raid on Harpers Ferry convinced each section that the other threatened its survival.
Lincoln's 1860 victory without a single southern electoral vote triggered secession, and Sumter in April 1861 united the North for war.
Antietam let Lincoln issue the Emancipation Proclamation, which blocked European intervention and put 180,000 Black soldiers in the Union army.
Union industry, the Anaconda Plan, Gettysburg and Vicksburg in July 1863 and Sherman's total war forced Lee's surrender at Appomattox in 1865.
Johnson's lenient plan and the black codes led Congress to impose military Reconstruction in 1867 and to pass the 14th and 15th Amendments.
Sharecropping, Klan terror, Court rulings like Cruikshank and the Compromise of 1877 left Reconstruction an unfinished revolution.

units.title: Period 6: 1865–1898
units.blurb: Railroads, Carnegie and the trusts, the Knights of Labor and the AFL, Haymarket and Pullman, new immigration, Populists and Bryan, the Dawes Act, Plessy and Jim Crow. Contrast pairs such as Washington and Du Bois recur.
keys: Federally subsidized railroads, joined at Promontory Summit in 1869, created a national market and the first big businesses.
Carnegie's vertical integration, Rockefeller's Standard Oil trust and Morgan's U.S. Steel concentrated industry in a few hands.
Social Darwinism and the Gospel of Wealth defended laissez-faire even as the 1887 ICC and 1890 Sherman Act began weak federal regulation.
The Knights of Labor died after Haymarket in 1886 while Gompers's craft AFL survived, and troops and injunctions crushed Homestead and Pullman.
New immigrants from southern and eastern Europe filled tenements and machine wards, met by Hull House and by Chinese Exclusion in 1882.
The Dawes Act of 1887, Wounded Knee in 1890 and Turner's frontier thesis marked the conquest and closing of the West.
Debt-ridden farmers built the Grange, the Alliance and the Populist Party, whose free silver crusade died with Bryan's 1896 loss to McKinley.
Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), disfranchisement and lynching built Jim Crow, which Washington accommodated and Du Bois and Wells attacked.

units.title: Period 7: 1890–1945
units.blurb: The Spanish-American War, muckrakers and the Square Deal, the Fourteen Points, the Harlem Renaissance, the New Deal agencies, Pearl Harbor, Korematsu and the atomic bomb. Contrasts and contextualization openers recur.
keys: Mahan's sea power and the hunt for markets produced the 1898 war with Spain, the Platt Amendment, the Philippine war and the Roosevelt Corollary.
Muckrakers spurred Progressive reforms from the 1906 Meat Inspection Act to the Federal Reserve and the 16th through 19th Amendments.
Submarine warfare and the Zimmermann Telegram brought U.S. entry in 1917, but Lodge's Senate rejected Wilson's League of Nations.
War brought the Espionage and Sedition Acts, Schenck's clear and present danger test, the Great Migration and the 1919 Red Scare.
The 1920s set installment-plan consumerism, the Harlem Renaissance and flappers against nativist quotas, Scopes and Prohibition.
Margin speculation, weak banks and unequal incomes turned the 1929 crash into a Depression that Hoover's voluntarism could not stop.
FDR's New Deal, from the CCC and AAA to Social Security and the Wagner Act, built the modern welfare state and the Democratic coalition.
Pearl Harbor ended neutrality, and wartime mobilization ended the Depression, interned Japanese Americans (Korematsu) and built the atomic bomb.

units.title: Period 8: 1945–1980
units.blurb: Containment from the Truman Doctrine to detente, Korea and Vietnam, McCarthyism, Levittown, Brown through the Voting Rights Act, the Great Society, Friedan and Roe, Watergate and stagflation. Comparisons recur.
keys: Kennan's containment produced the Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan and NATO, and NSC-68 and Korea turned it into a global military commitment.
After the 1949 loss of China and the Soviet bomb, McCarthyism and HUAC hunted subversives until the 1954 Army-McCarthy hearings.
The GI Bill, Levittown and the 1956 Interstate Highway Act built a white suburban middle class and left cities segregated.
Brown v. Board (1954), the Montgomery boycott and Birmingham's televised violence forced the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and Voting Rights Act of 1965.
Johnson's Great Society added Medicare, Medicaid and the War on Poverty while the Warren Court expanded rights from Gideon to Griswold.
Domino theory and the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution escalated Vietnam until Tet in 1968 broke public trust and Johnson's presidency.
After 1965 Black Power, the Chicano movement, AIM, Stonewall and second-wave feminists (NOW, Roe v. Wade) widened the rights revolution.
Watergate, stagflation and the 1973 oil embargo shattered trust in government, while Nixon's detente and Carter's Iran crisis closed the era.

units.title: Period 9: 1980–Present
units.blurb: Reagan's New Right and supply-side economics, the end of the Cold War, NAFTA, September 11 and Iraq, the 2008 crisis, immigration and marriage debates, and polarization. Comparisons with earlier eras recur.
keys: Stagflation, Watergate and backlash against Roe and busing built the New Right coalition that elected Reagan in 1980.
Reagan's supply-side tax cuts, deregulation and PATCO firings brought growth with a tripled debt, weaker unions and wider inequality.
Reagan's rearmament and SDI plus Gorbachev's glasnost and perestroika ended the Cold War with the Wall's fall in 1989 and the USSR's in 1991.
NAFTA in 1994, the WTO and the internet drove globalization, boosting growth while hollowing out Rust Belt manufacturing.
Clinton's welfare reform and impeachment, then Bush v. Gore in 2000, showed partisan polarization hardening before September 11.
September 11 brought the Afghanistan and Iraq wars, the PATRIOT Act and DHS, and reopened the security-versus-liberty debate.
Subprime mortgages and deregulation caused the 2008 crisis, answered by TARP, stimulus, Dodd-Frank and Obama's Affordable Care Act.
Post-1965 immigration, the marriage fight from DOMA to Obergefell and the culture wars deepened polarization in a more diverse nation.

units.title: Exam Craft
units.blurb: Exam format and timing, the SAQ, DBQ and LEQ rubrics point by point, causation, comparison and continuity essays, then practice theses, sourcing sentences and contextualization openers. Includes the May 2027 changes.
keys: The 3-hour-15-minute Bluebook exam weighs 55 multiple-choice questions (40%), three SAQs (20%), the DBQ (25%) and the LEQ (15%).
From May 2027 all three SAQs are required, each with a source, and everyone answers one LEQ prompt, while the rubrics are unchanged.
A multiple-choice answer must trace back to the stimulus, so read the whole set first and skip any question you cannot narrow.
Each SAQ part scores independently, and briefly explain demands one specific fact plus a sentence tying it to the question.
A thesis earns its point only by taking a defensible position with a line of reasoning, never by restating the prompt.
Contextualization needs two or three sentences describing broader developments before, during or after the prompt's time frame.
The DBQ rewards using six documents to support an argument, one piece of outside evidence and HIPP sourcing on three documents.
Complexity is earned across the essay by qualifying, corroborating or linking periods, and the LEQ must run on causation, comparison or CCOT.

cards.q: Date the boundary years of AP Period 1 and name the event that marks each end.
cards.a: 1491 to 1607. The period opens in 1491, the last year before Columbus's 1492 voyage began sustained contact, so that it starts with Native societies on their own terms rather than as a prologue to Europe; it closes in 1607 with the founding of Jamestown, England's first permanent colony, which opens Period 2 (1607-1754).
cards.h: → two years, each tied to one event
cards.n: Writing 1492 as the start earns nothing on a periodization question: the CED deliberately begins one year before contact.

cards.q: State the three developments the College Board identifies as defining Period 1.
cards.a: (1) Native populations migrated across North America and built distinct, increasingly complex societies by adapting to and transforming diverse environments (KC-1.1). (2) Contact among Europeans, Native Americans, and Africans produced the Columbian Exchange and social, cultural, and political change on both sides of the Atlantic (KC-1.2). (3) Within that contact, Europeans and Native Americans asserted divergent worldviews on religion, gender, family, land use, and power.
cards.h: → three key concepts, one sentence each
cards.n: 'Columbus discovered America' as the defining development earns nothing; the CED frames the period around Native adaptation, exchange, and divergent worldviews.

cards.q: Place these early colonial events in order: Treaty of Tordesillas, Columbus's first voyage, founding of Jamestown, Pueblo Revolt.
cards.a: Columbus's first voyage (1492) → Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) → founding of Jamestown (1607) → Pueblo Revolt (1680). The first two fall in Period 1; Jamestown closes it; the Pueblo Revolt is a Period 2 event that grew out of Period 1 Spanish colonization of New Mexico.
cards.h: → four events, earliest first, with years
cards.n: Borrows from u2: Jamestown and the Pueblo Revolt sit in Period 2. Placing Tordesillas before Columbus earns nothing; the treaty divided lands his voyage had just claimed.

cards.q: Describe the historical context of the Americas in 1491 that a contextualization paragraph for a Period 1 prompt should establish.
cards.a: The Americas in 1491 were densely and diversely peopled, not empty. Tens of millions of Native people lived in societies ranging from the Aztec and Inca empires to Pueblo irrigation towns, Mississippian mound cities, Eastern Woodland farming villages, mobile Great Basin bands, and salmon-rich Northwest villages. These societies had adapted to and transformed their environments through maize agriculture, irrigation, trade networks, and varied social structures.
cards.h: → population + range of societies + tie to environment
cards.n: 'Before Columbus the land was untouched wilderness' earns nothing and is historically wrong; the point requires describing settled, varied, environment-shaping societies.

cards.q: Describe the developments within Europe before 1492 that set the context for its expansion into the Western Hemisphere.
cards.a: Late-medieval Europe was recovering population and trade after the Black Death, and its monarchs were centralizing power. Renaissance curiosity and the Crusades fed demand for Asian spices and silks; Italian and Muslim middlemen controlled the overland routes, so Atlantic states sought sea routes. Portugal had pushed down Africa's coast (Dias rounded the Cape in 1488), and Spain completed the Reconquista in 1492 with a crusading, conversion-minded monarchy.
cards.h: → four European developments, each tied to expansion
cards.n: Naming 'the Renaissance' as a phrase earns nothing; contextualization must describe how these developments pushed Europeans outward.

cards.q: Describe the West African context that shaped the Atlantic world before and after 1492.
cards.a: West Africa held powerful, commercially connected states. Trans-Saharan caravans had long carried gold, salt, and captives between empires such as Mali and Songhai and the Mediterranean, and slavery existed as an African institution. From the 1440s Portuguese ships traded on the coast for gold and enslaved people, building forts such as Elmina (1482) and sugar colonies on Atlantic islands. That existing trade is what European merchants later redirected toward the Americas.
cards.h: → African states + trade before and after the Portuguese
cards.n: Describing Africa only as a source of slaves earns nothing for context; the point requires the pre-existing states, trade, and Portuguese partnership that KC-1.2.II.C builds on.

cards.q: Explain how a response earns the contextualization point on a Period 1 prompt about the Columbian Exchange, and what falls short.
cards.a: The point requires describing a broader development before, during, or after 1492-1607 that is relevant to the topic, in more than a phrase. For example: two sentences on Portugal's fifteenth-century Atlantic voyages, its sugar-and-slave plantations on Madeira and Sao Tome, and the search for a sea route to Asia, then a link to the exchange of crops, animals, disease and people after 1492. Restating the prompt's dates or dropping the phrase 'Age of Exploration' earns nothing.
cards.h: → describe a broader development + link it to the prompt
cards.n: Contextualization that only restates the prompt's period ('in the 1500s Europeans explored') is the classic zero; the rubric says a phrase or reference is not enough.

cards.q: Describe the continuities in Native American life across North America that persisted through the first century of European contact.
cards.a: Across most of North America Native societies kept their basic patterns to 1607. Maize-beans-squash farming with seasonal hunting continued in the Eastern Woodlands, mobile bison hunting and foraging on the western Plains and Great Basin, and salmon-based villages in the Northwest. Native nations still controlled almost all land north of Mexico, governed themselves, and traded along existing networks; Europeans held only Spanish Florida, New Mexico and coastal contacts.
cards.h: → three kinds of continuity, with where
cards.n: 'Everything changed after 1492' earns nothing on a continuity task; the answer must name specific patterns that lasted and where.

cards.q: Compare the Americas of 1491 with the Americas of 1607 in population, political control, and economy.
cards.a: Change: Native population fell by an estimated 50-90 percent in contacted regions from epidemics, warfare and forced labor; Spain ruled the Caribbean, Mexico, Peru, Florida and New Mexico, and silver mining, encomienda and enslaved African labor tied the Americas to a global economy. Continuity: outside Spanish zones, Native nations still governed themselves by the same maize, hunting and fishing economies, and European settlement north of Mexico was a few outposts.
cards.h: → change on three axes, then the continuity
cards.n: A comparison that lists 1491 and 1607 facts without stating what changed and what stayed the same earns nothing; the similarity or difference must be stated.

cards.q: Identify the pattern of migration and settlement that produced the diversity of Native societies Europeans met after 1492.
cards.a: Ancestors of Native Americans entered the continent from Asia, most likely across the Bering land bridge and along the Pacific coast during the last Ice Age (commonly dated to at least 15,000 years ago), then spread south and east over millennia. As groups settled deserts, grasslands, woodlands, river valleys and coasts, they developed distinct languages, subsistence systems and social structures adapted to each environment, so 1491 America held hundreds of nations.
cards.n: The migration dating is approximate and debated among archaeologists; the CED tests the adaptation-to-environment pattern, not a date.

cards.q: Classify each development in the Americas across 1491-1607 as a CONTINUITY or a CHANGE, with one phrase of reasoning: maize-beans-squash farming in the Eastern Woodlands · Native control of the North American interior · population of the Caribbean islands · labor system on Hispaniola · animals used on the Great Plains · religion in central Mexico · trade networks of the Mississippi and Great Lakes · political rule in Peru · European settlement north of Mexico · the Atlantic as a highway for people, crops and disease · social structure of Spanish colonial towns · subsistence in the Great Basin
cards.a:
Eastern Woodlands farming → continuity (same crops and seasonal round to 1607)
Native control of the interior → continuity (Europeans held only coastal and Southwest outposts)
Caribbean population → change (Taino collapse from disease and forced labor)
Hispaniola labor → change (encomienda, then enslaved Africans)
Plains animals → change beginning (horses spread after Spanish arrival, mostly after 1607)
Religion in central Mexico → change (Catholic missions, syncretism with Native practice)
Mississippi and Great Lakes trade → continuity (networks persisted, now carrying some European goods)
Rule in Peru → change (Inca replaced by Spanish viceroyalty after 1533)
European settlement north of Mexico → change but small (St. Augustine 1565, New Mexico 1598)
The Atlantic → change (Columbian Exchange makes it a two-way route)
Spanish colonial society → change (casta hierarchy created)
Great Basin subsistence → continuity (mobile foraging unchanged)
cards.h: → label each, then the one-phrase reason
cards.n: Labeling without the reason earns nothing on a continuity-and-change task; the reasoning phrase is the scored move.

cards.q: Explain why historians treat 1491 as a meaningful starting point for United States history rather than 1492.
cards.a: Starting in 1491 makes Native societies the baseline rather than a prologue to Europe. The story then begins with tens of millions of people in complex, environment-adapted societies, so change after 1492 is measured against what existed and Native peoples appear as actors, not as an empty stage.
cards.h: → Native baseline first → contact measured as change to existing societies → Natives as actors
cards.n: 'Because that is the year before Columbus' restates the date and earns nothing; the point is what the baseline does for the analysis.
o: A 1492 start would define Native peoples by European arrival, while 1491 lets their own migrations, adaptations and political systems count as history.
Beginning before contact turns the Columbian Exchange into a measurable transformation of existing societies rather than a discovery of new land.

w.a: Historians start in 1491 because that is the last year before Columbus sailed.
w.why: restates the date without saying why a pre-contact baseline matters

w.a: Historians start in 1491 because nothing important happened in the Americas before Europeans arrived.
w.why: false and the opposite of the CED's point about complex Native societies

w.a: Historians start in 1491 because the Aztec Empire was founded that year.
w.why: invented fact; Tenochtitlan dates to about 1325 and the Triple Alliance to 1428

cards.q: Explain why Europe, rather than a Native American or West African power, initiated sustained transatlantic contact in the 1490s.
cards.a: Europeans combined means and motive. Portugal and Spain had a generation of Atlantic sailing experience, caravels, compasses and charts, and monarchs willing to fund voyages. They had reasons to sail: a sea route to Asian wealth around Muslim and Italian middlemen, rivalry, and a crusading drive to spread Christianity.
cards.h: → Atlantic experience + ships and instruments + royal funding → plus wealth, rivalry, religion motives → voyages
cards.n: 'Because Europeans were more advanced' earns nothing; the answer must name the specific maritime means and the specific motives.
o: Iberian states had spent the fifteenth century learning Atlantic winds and currents on the African coast, so the westward crossing was an extension of an existing enterprise.
West African and Native American states were oriented toward land-based or coastal trade networks and had no comparable incentive to seek an ocean route to Asia.

w.a: Europe initiated contact because Columbus was the first person brave enough to sail into the unknown.
w.why: individual bravery explains nothing about why Iberian states funded and repeated such voyages

w.a: Europe initiated contact because Native Americans had no boats.
w.why: false; coastal and river peoples used sophisticated canoes, and it ignores Europe's means and motives

w.a: Europe initiated contact because the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople in 1453 completely cut off all trade with Asia.
w.why: overstated; Asian goods still reached Europe, and the claim omits ships, funding and religion

cards.q: Explain why the century after 1492 brought far greater change to the Caribbean, Mexico, and Peru than to the interior of North America.
cards.a: Spain went where dense populations and silver promised wealth and labor. Taino, Aztec and Inca lands were conquered, emptied by epidemics, and reorganized under encomienda, mining and missions. The North American interior held no such prize, so Europeans touched it only by disease, trade goods and expeditions.
cards.h: → wealth and labor draw Spain south → conquest, disease, encomienda there → interior untouched except indirectly
cards.n: 'Spain just did not get there yet' earns nothing; the point requires the pull of silver and dense populations and the resulting uneven change.
o: Change followed conquest, and conquest followed wealth: where there was silver and tribute-paying populations, Spanish institutions were built; elsewhere Spanish expeditions such as Coronado's found nothing worth holding.
Epidemics spread ahead of settlers, so even the interior changed demographically, but its political and economic structures survived because no colonial state replaced them.

w.a: The interior changed less because its Native peoples were stronger warriors than the Aztecs.
w.why: ignores that Spain chose targets by wealth and population, not by weakness

w.a: The interior changed less because Europeans did not know it existed until the 1700s.
w.why: false; Coronado and de Soto crossed it in the 1540s

w.a: The interior did not change at all because no Europeans settled there.
w.why: overstates the continuity; disease and trade goods reached the interior before settlers

cards.q: Explain why the Columbian Exchange is a turning point in world history rather than only in the history of the Americas.
cards.a: The exchange ran both ways, worldwide. American maize and potatoes fed population growth in Europe, Africa and Asia; American silver flowed via Spain and Manila to China; Eurasian animals, crops and diseases remade American populations; and demand for labor redirected the African slave trade across the Atlantic.
cards.h: → two-way flows → Old World crops and silver effects, American disease and animal effects, slave trade redirected
cards.n: 'The Columbian Exchange changed everything' with no specific exchange named earns nothing; each direction needs a named item and its effect.
o: European societies shifted from feudalism toward capitalism partly on American mineral wealth, so the exchange changed Europe's economic structure, not just its diet.
The demographic effects alone were global: the Americas lost most of their people while Old World populations grew on American crops.

w.a: The Columbian Exchange was a world turning point because Columbus proved the earth was round.
w.why: myth; educated Europeans already knew the earth was round, and it names no exchange

w.a: The Columbian Exchange mattered to the world because Europeans brought civilization to the Americas.
w.why: a value judgment, not a described exchange, and it ignores the flows toward Europe, Africa and Asia

w.a: The Columbian Exchange was mainly about Native Americans catching smallpox.
w.why: one effect in one direction; it misses crops, silver, animals and the slave trade

cards.q: Explain why most Native nations north of Mexico still governed themselves in 1607 despite a century of European contact.
cards.a: European presence north of Mexico was tiny and coastal. Spain held only St. Augustine (1565) and a few New Mexico settlements (1598); French and English efforts were voyages, fishing stations and the failed Roanoke colony. With no settlers, soldiers or missions inland, Native nations kept land, leaders and economies.
cards.h: → few Europeans, only coastal outposts → no colonial state inland → Native sovereignty persists
cards.n: 'Native Americans resisted successfully' alone earns nothing here; the continuity came mostly from the absence of a colonial presence, which the answer must describe.
o: Spanish colonization followed silver and dense populations, and North America offered neither, so the interior was left to Native control by default.
The tools that later broke Native sovereignty, permanent settler colonies and sustained warfare, only began with Jamestown and its successors after 1607.

w.a: Native nations still governed themselves in 1607 because Europeans respected their sovereignty.
w.why: false; Spain claimed everything by papal grant and conquered wherever it chose

w.a: Native nations still governed themselves because no European had yet reached North America.
w.why: false; Spain had Florida and New Mexico, and French and English ships had visited for a century

w.a: Native nations still governed themselves in 1607 because the Pueblo Revolt had driven the Spanish out.
w.why: wrong period; the revolt came in 1680, seventy-three years later

cards.q: Identify the Pueblo peoples and how they adapted to the arid Southwest.
cards.a: Pueblo peoples (Hopi, Zuni, Acoma, Rio Grande towns) were sedentary maize farmers of the arid Southwest. They met aridity with irrigation canals, terraces, check dams and dry-farming, and built permanent multi-story adobe and stone towns. Maize surpluses supported dense settlement, craft specialization and religious hierarchy, the KC-1.1.I.A chain from maize to economic development, settlement and social diversification.
cards.n: 'They lived in adobe houses' describes without connecting to aridity; the point requires the adaptation (irrigation) and its social result.

cards.q: Identify the subsistence pattern of Great Plains and Great Basin peoples before contact.
cards.a: Largely mobile hunting and gathering. Great Basin peoples (Ute, Shoshone, Paiute) moved in small bands through a seasonal round of pine nuts, seeds, roots and small game because the desert could not feed large settled groups. Western Plains peoples (such as the Apache) followed bison herds on foot, using dogs to haul goods; some eastern Plains groups (Mandan, Pawnee) also farmed maize in river valleys. Mobility was the adaptation to aridity and grassland (KC-1.1.I.B).
cards.n: Describing Plains peoples as horse-mounted buffalo hunters earns nothing for 1491: horses arrived with the Spanish and spread mostly after 1600.

cards.q: Identify the Iroquois (Haudenosaunee) and their form of political organization.
cards.a: An Iroquoian-speaking people of present-day New York who combined maize-beans-squash farming with hunting and lived in palisaded longhouse villages. Five nations (Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, Seneca; the Tuscarora joined in the 1720s) formed the Iroquois Confederacy, a council of chiefs chosen by clan mothers in a matrilineal society where women controlled fields and households. It illustrates complex social structure among mixed-economy villages (KC-1.1.I.C).
cards.n: The founding date of the Confederacy is debated (before 1600, possibly as early as the 1100s); do not invent one. Illustrative example, not a required name.

cards.q: Identify the Algonquian peoples of the Atlantic seaboard.
cards.a: A large family of Algonquian-language peoples of the Eastern Woodlands and coast (Powhatan, Wampanoag, Narragansett, Pequot, Lenape). They mixed maize, beans and squash farming with hunting, fishing and shellfish gathering, moving seasonally between villages, fields and hunting grounds; this mixed economy favored semi-permanent villages under sachems (KC-1.1.I.C). They were the first peoples the English met at Roanoke, Jamestown and Plymouth.
cards.h: → what the name covers + economy + settlement
cards.n: Illustrative example. 'Algonquian' names a language family, not one nation; treating Powhatan and Wampanoag as one people earns nothing on a comparison task.

cards.q: Identify Cahokia and the Mississippian culture.
cards.a: The Mississippian culture (roughly 800-1500 CE) of the Mississippi and Ohio valleys built maize-based chiefdoms with earthen platform mounds, ranked societies and long-distance trade. Its largest center, Cahokia near present-day St. Louis, peaked around 1050-1150 CE at a population commonly estimated at 10,000-20,000, the largest settlement north of Mexico, and was largely abandoned by about 1350-1400: farming producing complex settlement (KC-1.1.I.C).
cards.n: Population estimates vary (some run to 30,000) and the decline's causes are debated; give a range, not a single confident number.

cards.q: Identify the Chinook and other Pacific Northwest peoples.
cards.a: Peoples of the Northwest coast and Columbia River (Chinook, Kwakwaka'wakw, Haida, Tlingit) who did not farm but lived in permanent cedar plank-house villages on the ocean's wealth: salmon runs, shellfish, sea mammals and timber. Stored surpluses supported dense populations, craft specialization (canoes, totem poles), hereditary rank and the potlatch gift-feast. They show settled, stratified society built on ocean resources rather than agriculture (KC-1.1.I.D).
cards.n: Saying they were 'simple hunter-gatherers' earns nothing; the KC's point is settled communities supported by ocean resources.

cards.q: Identify the Chumash and other Native peoples of present-day California before contact.
cards.a: California peoples (Chumash, Pomo, Miwok, Yokuts and many others) lived by hunting and gathering, above all acorns ground into meal, plus fish, shellfish and game. Mild climate and varied resources let them live in relatively dense, semi-permanent villages with great linguistic diversity; the coastal Chumash built plank canoes, used shell-bead money and traded with the Channel Islands. Like the Northwest, California shows settled life without farming (KC-1.1.I.D).
cards.h: → staple food + other resources → settlement type
cards.n: Specific nation names are illustrative; the scored idea is hunting and gathering supporting settled communities, which contradicts 'no farming means nomadic'.

cards.q: Describe how the Ancestral Puebloans and the Hohokam transformed the Southwest environment before 1491.
cards.a: They engineered water. The Hohokam of the Salt and Gila valleys (present-day Arizona) dug hundreds of miles of irrigation canals to grow maize, beans, squash and cotton in the desert. Ancestral Puebloans at Chaco Canyon built multi-story great houses, roads and water-control systems around 850-1150 CE, then dispersed during drought to the Rio Grande and Hopi mesas. Both cases show societies transforming, not merely enduring, an arid environment (KC-1.1.I.A).
cards.h: → each society's technique + what it built + the outcome
cards.n: Illustrative examples. Chaco's decline is usually linked to drought and is debated; 'they mysteriously vanished' earns nothing because Pueblo peoples are their descendants.

cards.q: Describe the mixed agricultural and hunter-gatherer economy of the Eastern Woodlands and the settlement pattern it produced.
cards.a: Eastern Woodland peoples farmed maize, beans and squash in cleared fields, then supplemented crops with deer hunting, fishing, shellfish and gathered nuts and berries. Because fields fixed people in place for the growing season while game and fish drew them out seasonally, they built permanent or semi-permanent villages (longhouses, wigwams, palisades) near fields and rivers, moving when soils and firewood were exhausted. Mixed economies favored villages (KC-1.1.I.C).
cards.n: Listing foods without connecting them to the village pattern is description; the KC asks why mixed economies favored permanent villages.

cards.q: Describe the division of labor by gender in Eastern Woodland farming societies before contact.
cards.a: Women did most of the farming: planting, tending and harvesting maize, beans and squash, gathering wild plants, and controlling fields and household goods; men hunted, fished, cleared land, traded and fought. In matrilineal societies such as the Iroquois, descent passed through mothers and clan mothers chose chiefs. Europeans, who saw farming as men's work, read this as Native men being idle and women overworked, one of the misunderstandings in KC-1.2.III.
cards.h: → who did which work → resulting power → European view
cards.n: Describing Native women as powerless earns nothing; the Woodland pattern gave women control of food production and, among the Iroquois, of political succession.

cards.q: Identify evidence that Native societies before contact were linked by long-distance trade networks.
cards.a: Archaeology shows goods moving hundreds of miles. Cahokia's mounds held Gulf Coast shells, Great Lakes copper and Appalachian mica; obsidian and turquoise moved across the Southwest; Chumash shell beads circulated in California; Northwest peoples traded dentalium shells inland. Rivers such as the Mississippi and Missouri were the highways. These networks are why European trade goods and epidemics later spread ahead of Europeans themselves.
cards.h: → named goods far from source + river routes
cards.n: 'They traded with each other' is a phrase, not evidence; name a good found far from its source.

cards.q: Identify the Great Law of Peace and the two legendary founders credited with uniting the Iroquois nations.
cards.a: The Great Law of Peace (Gayanashagowa) is the oral constitution of the Iroquois Confederacy, establishing a Grand Council of chiefs from the five nations chosen by clan mothers and requiring consensus. Tradition credits the Peacemaker (Deganawida) and Hiawatha with persuading the warring nations to end blood feuds and unite. It is illustrative evidence of complex political structure among Northeastern villages (KC-1.1.I.C), not a name the exam requires.
cards.h: → what it is + what it set up + two founders
cards.n: Illustrative. The claim that the Confederacy inspired the U.S. Constitution is contested; do not present it as settled fact.

cards.q: Define the 'three sisters' agricultural system.
cards.a: The intercropping of maize, beans and squash in the same mounds, practiced across the Southwest, Mississippi Valley and Eastern Woodlands. Cornstalks support the bean vines, beans return nitrogen to the soil, and squash leaves shade out weeds and hold moisture, giving high yields without plows or draft animals and a nutritionally complete diet. It is the concrete form of the maize-based agriculture that supported settled villages (KC-1.1.I.A, I.C).
cards.h: → three crops + why they are grown together
cards.n: Naming the three crops alone is identification; the point on an explain task is how the combination raised yields and supported settlement.

cards.q: Contrast Pueblo and Great Plains societies in settlement and subsistence.
cards.a: Difference: Pueblo peoples were sedentary irrigation farmers in permanent adobe towns because maize and canals could turn a desert river valley into a food surplus; western Plains peoples were mobile bison hunters in small bands with portable dwellings because the dry grassland offered no reliable farming but abundant migrating game. Similarity: both were rational adaptations to scarce water, not different stages of advancement (KC-1.1.I.A vs I.B).
cards.h: → difference stated + reason for each + similarity
cards.n: A comparison that lists two descriptions without stating the difference and tying it to environment earns nothing.

cards.q: Contrast Northeast woodland and Pacific Northwest societies.
cards.a: Difference: Northeastern Iroquoian and Algonquian peoples farmed the three sisters and moved seasonally between fields and hunting grounds, so their villages were semi-permanent; Northwest peoples did not farm but harvested salmon and sea resources so rich that they lived in permanent, hereditary-ranked plank-house villages. Similarity: both produced surpluses that supported settled, complex communities, so surplus, not farming itself, produced complexity (KC-1.1.I.C vs I.D).
cards.n: Stating only that one farmed and one did not earns nothing; say what that difference meant for settlement and rank.

cards.q: Classify each Native society by its environment, main subsistence, and settlement type (mobile bands, semi-permanent villages, permanent towns): Hopi and Zuni · Ute · Shoshone · Apache (pre-horse) · Mandan · Cahokia (Mississippian) · Natchez · Iroquois · Powhatan · Chinook · Chumash · Kwakwaka'wakw (Kwakiutl)
cards.a:
Hopi and Zuni → arid Southwest; irrigated maize; permanent adobe towns
Ute → Great Basin desert; foraging seeds, pine nuts, small game; mobile bands
Shoshone → Great Basin and Rockies; foraging and hunting; mobile bands
Apache (pre-horse) → southern Plains; bison hunting on foot with dog travois; mobile bands
Mandan → upper Missouri valley; maize plus seasonal bison hunts; permanent earth-lodge villages
Cahokia → Mississippi floodplain; intensive maize; permanent mound city, ranked chiefdom
Natchez → lower Mississippi; maize and hunting; permanent towns under a hereditary chief
Iroquois → Northeast woodlands; three-sisters farming plus hunting; semi-permanent longhouse villages
Powhatan → Chesapeake tidewater; farming plus fishing and hunting; semi-permanent villages
Chinook → Columbia River and Northwest coast; salmon and trade, no farming; permanent plank-house villages
Chumash → southern California coast; acorns, fishing, shellfish, no farming; dense semi-permanent villages
Kwakwaka'wakw → Northwest coast; salmon and sea mammals, no farming; permanent ranked villages, potlatch
cards.n: Nation names are illustrative; the exam tests the region-to-adaptation match, and pairing a Plains group with farming towns or the Northwest with agriculture earns nothing.

cards.q: Explain how the spread of maize cultivation reshaped Native societies in the Southwest and Mesoamerica.
cards.a: Maize spread north from Mexico and produced storable surpluses. Surplus let people stay in one place, so populations grew, villages became towns, irrigation and terracing were built to secure the crop, and labor was freed for crafts, trade and chiefly or priestly elites, the social diversification the CED names.
cards.h: → maize → surplus → settlement and irrigation → population growth → specialization and hierarchy
cards.n: 'Maize let them have more food' stops before the point; the scored chain runs from surplus to settlement, irrigation and social diversification.
o: A storable staple removed the need to move for food, and permanence made investment in canals, terraces and stone towns worthwhile.
Once fewer people were needed to grow food, societies could support specialists and leaders, so status differences and trade grew with the crop.

w.a: Maize reshaped Native societies because it was a healthier food than hunting.
w.why: health is not the mechanism; surplus and permanence are

w.a: Maize reshaped Native societies because Europeans taught the Pueblo to farm it.
w.why: false; maize moved north from Mexico thousands of years before contact

w.a: Maize allowed Native societies in the Southwest to become nomadic hunters.
w.why: backwards; farming fixed people in place

cards.q: Explain why Great Basin and western Great Plains peoples developed mobile lifestyles while Southwest peoples built permanent towns.
cards.a: The difference came from water and food. The Great Basin and western Plains were too dry for reliable farming, and their food (scattered seeds, pine nuts, migrating bison) had to be followed, so small mobile bands were the efficient adaptation. Southwest river valleys could be irrigated for maize, so staying put paid.
cards.h: → aridity and scattered food → mobility pays → river valleys and irrigation → permanence pays
cards.n: Explaining the difference as 'some tribes were more advanced' earns nothing; the KC's explanation is environmental.
o: Both were rational choices: mobility spread a thin resource base across a large territory, while irrigation concentrated a rich one in a small area.
Settlement follows the food: where the food moved, people moved; where the food could be grown and stored, people built towns.

w.a: Plains peoples were mobile because they had horses to follow the buffalo.
w.why: anachronism; horses reached the Plains only after the Spanish arrived

w.a: Great Basin peoples stayed mobile because they did not know how to farm.
w.why: ignores that the environment, not knowledge, made farming unreliable

w.a: Southwest peoples built towns because they had more people.
w.why: reverses cause and effect; population grew because irrigated maize allowed permanence

cards.q: Explain why Pacific Northwest peoples developed permanent, socially stratified villages without agriculture.
cards.a: Salmon runs, shellfish, sea mammals and cedar gave the Northwest coast a surplus as reliable as a harvest. Dried fish could be stored, so people stayed in one place all year, and control of the best fishing sites and stored wealth produced hereditary rank and potlatch displays; the ocean did what maize did elsewhere.
cards.h: → storable ocean surplus → year-round permanence → control of sites and wealth → rank
cards.n: 'They had lots of fish' earns nothing unless the answer links storage and site control to permanence and rank.
o: Complexity depended on surplus, not on farming, and the ocean supplied the surplus.
Because prime fishing and hunting sites were fixed and limited, families that controlled them accumulated wealth and status across generations.

w.a: Northwest peoples had permanent villages because they secretly farmed maize as well.
w.why: false; the KC's point is that ocean resources replaced farming

w.a: Northwest peoples built permanent villages because the climate was too cold to travel.
w.why: invented; the mild coast was easy to travel by canoe

w.a: Northwest societies were stratified because they copied the Aztecs.
w.why: no such contact; rank grew from local control of fishing sites and surplus

cards.q: Explain why Eastern Woodland societies built semi-permanent villages rather than fully mobile camps or large permanent cities.
cards.a: Their economy was mixed. Maize, beans and squash fixed people near fields for the growing season and fed villages of hundreds, but hunting, fishing and gathering still supplied much of the diet, so groups moved seasonally and shifted villages when soil and firewood ran out. The result was villages, not camps or cities.
cards.h: → crops fix location → wild foods still needed → seasonal movement and village relocation → villages
cards.n: Saying they 'settled down because they farmed' earns nothing without the hunter-gatherer half that kept villages semi-permanent.
o: Villages were the compromise between the crop that demanded staying and the game that demanded moving.
Where maize alone could feed a large population, as at Cahokia, permanent cities did appear, which shows the balance of crops to wild foods set the settlement type.

w.a: Eastern Woodland peoples lived in villages because they were too few to build cities.
w.why: population size followed the economy; it did not cause the settlement type

w.a: Eastern Woodland peoples lived in villages because they lacked the stone to build cities.
w.why: materials are irrelevant; the mixed economy explains the pattern

w.a: Eastern Woodland peoples were nomadic hunters who never farmed.
w.why: false; maize, beans and squash were central to their economy

cards.q: Explain why environment, rather than a ladder of 'advancement', is the better explanation for differences among Native societies before contact.
cards.a: Each society's subsistence, settlement and structure tracked its resources. Where surplus could be grown or harvested (irrigated Southwest valleys, the Mississippi floodplain, salmon coasts) people built towns and ranked societies; where food was thin and scattered (Great Basin, western Plains) they stayed mobile.
cards.h: → surplus available → towns and rank; scarce and scattered → mobility → same people shift with environment
cards.n: Ranking societies as 'primitive' or 'civilized' earns nothing and contradicts the KC; the scored move is adaptation to and transformation of environment.
o: The Northwest had no farming yet had rank and permanent villages, which breaks any ladder that puts agriculture before complexity.
Ancestral Puebloans left Chaco's great houses for smaller villages when drought came, so complexity rose and fell with the environment, not with time.

w.a: Native societies differed because some had progressed further toward civilization than others.
w.why: the ladder the KC rejects; it explains nothing about resources

w.a: Native societies differed because each tribe simply had different customs.
w.why: restates difference without a cause

w.a: Native societies differed because Europeans influenced some regions before 1491.
w.why: false; there was no sustained European contact before 1492

cards.q: Explain why Southwest societies developed far more elaborate irrigation than Northeastern farming societies.
cards.a: Need drove the engineering. In the arid Southwest maize could not survive on rainfall, so Hohokam canals, Pueblo check dams and terraces were the price of farming at all. The Northeast had rain and rivers enough for rain-fed fields, so its farmers put labor into clearing forest and rotating fields, not moving water.
cards.h: → aridity → farming impossible without water control → canals and terraces; rain-fed Northeast → no need
cards.n: 'The Southwest peoples were better engineers' earns nothing; the comparison must be grounded in rainfall and the need for water control.
o: Both regions transformed their environments; the Southwest moved water while the Northeast cleared and burned forest, each solving its own limiting factor.
Where water was the scarce input, societies organized labor around it, which is also why Southwest towns were more permanent than Northeast villages.

w.a: Southwest peoples irrigated because the Aztecs taught them.
w.why: invented transmission; the techniques developed locally over centuries

w.a: Northeast peoples did not irrigate because they did not farm.
w.why: false; maize, beans and squash were central to the Northeast economy

w.a: Southwest peoples irrigated because they had more rivers than the Northeast.
w.why: backwards; the Southwest had fewer water sources, which is why each had to be engineered

cards.q: Explain why California supported one of the densest Native populations in North America without agriculture.
cards.a: California's mild climate and varied landscapes offered many reliable wild foods at once. Acorns from oak groves could be gathered in bulk, ground and stored like a grain crop, and coast, rivers and valleys added fish, shellfish, game and seeds. A storable staple plus year-round variety supported settled villages.
cards.h: → storable acorn staple + ocean and valley foods + mild climate → dense settled population without farming
cards.n: 'California had good weather' alone earns nothing; the point is a storable staple (acorns) that functioned like a crop.
o: Acorn processing did the work of farming: a predictable, storable harvest that freed people from constant movement.
Because resources were spread across many small ecological zones, California was divided into hundreds of small, linguistically distinct groups rather than one large society.

w.a: California was densely populated because its peoples farmed maize like the Pueblo.
w.why: false; California peoples did not farm before contact

w.a: California was densely populated because Spanish missions attracted people there.
w.why: missions came in 1769, long after the period

w.a: California was densely populated because there were no wars.
w.why: invented; conflict existed, and it does not explain subsistence

cards.q: Explain why Cahokia had declined before any European reached the Mississippi Valley.
cards.a: Cahokia's success strained its environment and politics. Feeding a dense population deforested the uplands, worsening floods and soil loss, and drought in the 1200s cut maize yields; a chiefdom whose authority rested on feasts and surplus lost legitimacy when the surplus failed. By about 1350-1400 the city was empty.
