cards.h: → dense population → deforestation, flooding, drought → surplus fails → chiefly authority erodes → dispersal
cards.n: The causes are debated among archaeologists (environment, climate, politics, warfare); an answer that names one cause as certain overstates the evidence.
o: Cahokia shows that Native societies transformed their environments so thoroughly that the transformation could undermine them.
Its decline before 1492 warns against reading every change in Native America as a European effect.

w.a: Cahokia declined because Spanish diseases killed its people.
w.why: the city was abandoned more than a century before Columbus

w.a: Cahokia declined because its people were nomads who never stayed anywhere long.
w.why: false; it was a permanent maize-fed city for centuries

w.a: Cahokia was destroyed by de Soto's expedition in 1541.
w.why: the city was empty by about 1400, and de Soto's route never reached it

cards.q: Explain what motivated and enabled European overseas exploration after 1450.
cards.a: Three motives drove it and new means made it possible. Motives (KC-1.2.I.A): new sources of wealth, above all a sea route to Asian spices and silks that bypassed Venetian and Muslim middlemen, plus gold; economic and military competition among newly centralized monarchies; and a desire to spread Christianity, sharpened in Spain by the Reconquista. Means: caravels with lateen sails, the magnetic compass and astrolabe, better charts, and royal funding.
cards.n: 'God, gold, and glory' as a slogan earns nothing; each motive needs a specific example, and ships and instruments are means, not motives.

cards.q: Date Columbus's first voyage and name his sponsor.
cards.a: 1492, sponsored by Queen Isabella of Castile and King Ferdinand of Aragon. Columbus sailed from Palos in August and reached the Bahamas on 12 October. The monarchs backed him months after taking Granada in January 1492, which completed the Reconquista, so the voyage joined a search for an Asian route with a crusading, conversion-minded mission.
cards.n: 'The king of Spain' is too thin; Columbus was Genoese, Portugal had already turned him down, and the sponsors were Isabella and Ferdinand.

cards.q: Define the Treaty of Tordesillas and give its year.
cards.a: The 1494 treaty between Spain and Portugal that divided newly claimed lands outside Europe along a north-south line 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands: Spain took lands to the west, Portugal lands to the east, which gave Portugal the African route to India and later Brazil. It revised Pope Alexander VI's 1493 line and assumed two Catholic crowns could partition lands Native peoples already held.
cards.h: → year + parties + the line + who got what
cards.n: It bound only Spain and Portugal; saying it divided the Americas among all European powers earns nothing, and France and England never accepted it.

cards.q: Date the founding of St. Augustine and Santa Fe and say why each matters.
cards.a: St. Augustine, Florida, 1565: founded by Pedro Menendez de Aviles, who then destroyed the nearby French Huguenot Fort Caroline, it is the oldest continuously occupied European-founded city in the present-day United States and shows Spain guarding its treasure-fleet route against rivals. Santa Fe, about 1610: capital of Spanish New Mexico, which Juan de Onate had begun colonizing in 1598, and the town Pueblo rebels took in 1680.
cards.h: → two settlements, a year and a reason each
cards.n: Borrows from u2: Santa Fe (1610; some sources say 1607-1608) and the 1680 revolt fall in Period 2. Both predate or match Jamestown.

cards.q: Identify the Roanoke Colony and give the years it was founded and found abandoned.
cards.a: England's first attempt at a permanent American colony, on Roanoke Island off present-day North Carolina, under Sir Walter Raleigh's royal patent. A 1585 military outpost was abandoned; a settler colony led by John White landed in 1587, and when White returned in 1590, delayed by the war with Spain, the colonists were gone, leaving 'CROATOAN' carved on a post. It shows England entering the competition late and underfunded.
cards.n: Illustrative example. The colonists' fate is unknown; 'they were killed by the Croatoan' states a guess as fact.

cards.q: Contrast the Spanish and early English models of American colonization.
cards.a: Difference: Spain colonized through crown-licensed conquest of dense Native populations and silver, ruling them through encomienda, mining labor drafts and Catholic missions under royal and Church authority. England before 1607 relied on privateers and privately funded ventures (Gilbert's Newfoundland claim in 1583, Raleigh's Roanoke) that sought profit and a base against Spain and planted no lasting colony. Similarity: both justified expansion by religion and rivalry.
cards.h: → difference in method and funding + one similarity
cards.n: Listing Spanish facts then English facts without stating the difference earns nothing; the English joint-stock colony at Jamestown belongs to Period 2.

cards.q: Contrast the Spanish economic model of mining and tribute with the French economic model of the fur trade in early colonization.
cards.a: Difference: Spain extracted silver and tribute with coerced Native and later African labor, so it built towns, missions, mines and a large administrative presence over conquered peoples. France, trading furs with Native hunters along the St. Lawrence from the late 1500s, needed Native partners to supply the pelts, so it relied on alliance, gift exchange and intermarriage and sent few settlers. Each model followed the kind of wealth available.
cards.h: → extraction by coerced labor vs trade by alliance, and why
cards.n: Borrows from u2: New France grew after Quebec (1608). Calling the French 'kinder' earns nothing; the difference came from what each economy needed from Native people.

cards.q: Identify Giovanni da Verrazzano's and Jacques Cartier's voyages and what they established for France.
cards.a: Verrazzano, an Italian sailing for Francis I in 1524, charted the Atlantic coast from the Carolinas to Newfoundland looking for a passage to Asia. Cartier made three voyages (1534, 1535-1536, 1541-1542) into the Gulf of St. Lawrence and up the St. Lawrence River to Stadacona and Hochelaga, sites of later Quebec and Montreal. Together they gave France its claim to the St. Lawrence region, the base of later New France.
cards.h: → two explorers, dates, one French claim
cards.n: Illustrative names. The scored idea is competition: France ignored Tordesillas, but no lasting French colony existed until Quebec in 1608.

cards.q: Identify Francisco Vasquez de Coronado's 1540-1542 expedition.
cards.a: A large Spanish expedition from New Spain that searched the present-day Southwest for the rumored golden Seven Cities of Cibola. It found Zuni pueblos instead of gold, fought Pueblo towns on the Rio Grande (the Tiguex War of 1540-1541), and reached present-day Kansas before returning in 1542 with no wealth, so Spain left the region alone until Juan de Onate colonized New Mexico in 1598.
cards.n: Illustrative. It shows the wealth motive of KC-1.2.I.A: when no gold turned up, Spain lost interest; 'Coronado discovered the Southwest' ignores its Pueblo inhabitants.

cards.q: Identify Richard Hakluyt and his 'Discourse on Western Planting' (1584).
cards.a: Richard Hakluyt the younger, an English clergyman and geographer, wrote the Discourse (usually titled Discourse of Western Planting) for Elizabeth I in 1584 to argue for North American colonies: they would spread Protestant Christianity, check Spain's power and treasure, supply raw materials and markets for English cloth, and employ England's poor. It backed Raleigh's Roanoke venture and states all three KC motives at once.
cards.n: Illustrative. Sourcing: written to persuade the queen and investors, it lists benefits and omits costs and Native claims, so it shows motives, not results.

cards.q: State what English 'Sea Dogs' like Francis Drake and John Hawkins contributed to England's colonial ambitions before 1607.
cards.a: They made war on Spain's empire profitable. Hawkins ran illegal slaving voyages to Spanish America in the 1560s; Drake raided Spanish ports and treasure ships and sailed around the world (1577-1580), with the queen among his investors. Their privateering exposed Spain's weakness, enriched English backers, trained seamen, and helped defeat the Armada in 1588, building the confidence and capital behind later colonies.
cards.h: → what they did → effect on Spain → effect on England
cards.n: Illustrative names. 'They were pirates' with no link to colonization earns nothing; the point is economic and military competition with Spain.

cards.q: Identify Vasco Nunez de Balboa and his 1513 expedition.
cards.a: A Spanish conquistador who in 1513 crossed the Isthmus of Panama with Native guides and became the first European to see the Pacific from the Americas, claiming it and its shores for Spain. The crossing showed that another ocean lay beyond the new lands, so they were not Asia, and it opened the Pacific route by which Spain later reached Peru.
cards.h: → route + what he saw + what he claimed
cards.n: Illustrative name. He did not 'discover' the Pacific, which Native peoples knew; his act was a European claim of possession, the competition the KC names.

cards.q: Identify the source of the name 'America.'
cards.a: Martin Waldseemuller's 1507 world map, made at Saint-Die in Lorraine, labeled the southern continent 'America' after the Florentine navigator Amerigo Vespucci, whose published accounts described the lands as a New World rather than part of Asia. Later mapmakers extended the name to the northern continent. The name reflects Europeans naming and claiming lands by their own reference points.
cards.n: Illustrative. Saying the name honors Columbus earns nothing; Columbus died in 1506 still insisting he had reached Asia.

cards.q: Identify the sponsoring nation and the main goal of each voyage or expedition: Columbus 1492 · John Cabot 1497 · Vasco da Gama 1497-1499 · Pedro Alvares Cabral 1500 · Juan Ponce de Leon 1513 · Ferdinand Magellan 1519-1522 · Giovanni da Verrazzano 1524 · Jacques Cartier 1534 · Hernando de Soto 1539-1542 · Francisco Vasquez de Coronado 1540-1542 · Francis Drake 1577-1580 · Raleigh's Roanoke colonies 1585-1587 · Juan de Onate 1598
cards.a:
Columbus 1492 → Spain; western sea route to Asia, gold, converts
John Cabot 1497 → England; northern route to Asia; reached Newfoundland, basis of English claims
Vasco da Gama 1497-1499 → Portugal; sea route around Africa to India's spices
Cabral 1500 → Portugal; bound for India, landed in Brazil and claimed it under Tordesillas
Ponce de Leon 1513 → Spain; land, gold and captives; named Florida
Magellan 1519-1522 → Spain; western route to the Spice Islands; first circumnavigation, finished by Elcano after Magellan died in 1521
Verrazzano 1524 → France; a passage to Asia along the North American coast
Cartier 1534 → France; passage to Asia and gold; St. Lawrence claim
De Soto 1539-1542 → Spain; gold and conquest across the Southeast
Coronado 1540-1542 → Spain; the golden Seven Cities of Cibola
Drake 1577-1580 → England; raiding Spanish Pacific ports and treasure ships
Roanoke 1585-1587 → England (Raleigh's patent); profit and a base against Spain
Onate 1598 → Spain; colonize New Mexico for silver hopes and missions
cards.n: Names are illustrative; the exam tests motives. Writing 'to explore' as the goal earns nothing: name the wealth, route, rivalry or conversion aim.

cards.q: Explain how the purpose and audience of Columbus's 1493 letter announcing his first voyage shaped its description of the Caribbean. (The letter, printed across Europe in 1493, says the islands are fertile and full of gold, spices and cotton; calls the inhabitants timid, generous and unarmed people who would readily become Christians; and promises the monarchs as much gold as they need and as many slaves, taken from the idolaters, as they order.)
cards.a: The letter was a sales document. Written to Luis de Santangel, the court official who had helped finance the voyage, for Ferdinand and Isabella, it had to justify the cost and win a larger second expedition, so it inflated the gold and spices and cast the Taino as docile converts and potential laborers. It is better evidence of Spanish motives, wealth and conversion, than of Taino society.
cards.h: → audience + purpose → how each shaped the content
cards.n: Naming the audience ('the king and queen') without explaining how it shaped the description earns nothing; the sourcing point needs the how.

cards.q: Explain why England lagged nearly a century behind Spain in founding permanent American colonies.
cards.a: England lacked the means and the opening. Through most of the 1500s it was absorbed by the Reformation, religious conflict and dynastic instability, the crown had no money for conquest, and Spain ruled the Atlantic. Only after privateering enriched investors and the Armada failed in 1588 did private ventures try again.
cards.h: → Reformation turmoil + poor crown + Spanish sea power → no funding → privateering and 1588 → private ventures
cards.n: 'England was busy' earns nothing; name the religious turmoil, the lack of crown money and Spain's naval power.
o: England had no Mexico or Peru within reach, so a colony had to pay through trade or farming, which needed private capital that only built up late in the century.
Religious swings at home, from Henry VIII's break with Rome through Mary's Catholic restoration to Elizabeth's settlement, kept English energy inward until the 1580s.

w.a: England lagged because English sailors did not know how to cross the Atlantic.
w.why: false; John Cabot crossed for England in 1497

w.a: England lagged because the Treaty of Tordesillas legally banned English colonies.
w.why: England never recognized the treaty; it lacked means, not permission

w.a: England was not interested in America at all until Jamestown.
w.why: ignores Gilbert, Raleigh, Hakluyt and Roanoke

cards.q: Explain why the Spanish crown, rather than Portugal, sponsored Columbus's westward voyage.
cards.a: Portugal already had a better route. Its captains were closing on India around Africa (Dias rounded the Cape in 1488), and its experts judged Columbus's distance to Asia too short. Castile, barred from the African coast by a 1479 treaty and freed by Granada's fall in 1492, gambled on a western route of its own.
cards.h: → Portugal near India via Africa, doubts Columbus → Spain barred from Africa, Granada won → funds the western gamble
cards.n: 'Spain was richer' earns nothing; the causal point is Portugal's African route against Spain's need for its own.
o: Rivalry drove the choice: Spain needed its own route to Asian wealth because Portugal controlled the African one.
Finishing the Reconquista freed the monarchs' money and attention, and its crusading spirit made a voyage promising converts attractive.

w.a: Spain sponsored Columbus because he was Spanish.
w.why: false; he was Genoese and had asked Portugal first

w.a: Portugal turned Columbus down because it did not care about Asian trade.
w.why: backwards; Portugal was pursuing that trade by the African route

w.a: Spain funded Columbus to prove that the earth was round.
w.why: myth; educated Europeans knew it, and the aim was a trade route

cards.q: Explain why a search for a sea route to Asia ended in the conquest and colonization of the Americas.
cards.a: The voyages hit unknown continents, and the motives found new targets. Caribbean gold, then Aztec and Inca treasure and Potosi silver, paid better than spices; rival crowns raced to claim land and people; and missionaries saw millions of possible converts. Wealth, rivalry and faith turned exploration into conquest.
cards.h: → Asia route blocked by continents → gold, silver and converts found → rivals race to claim → conquest
cards.n: Listing 'God, gold, glory' without showing how the goal shifted from a trade route to land and labor earns nothing.
o: The same three motives persisted but changed objects: wealth became American silver, competition became territorial claims, and conversion targeted Native peoples.
Explorers kept hunting for a passage (Verrazzano, Cartier), and each failure turned attention to the resources of the land itself.

w.a: Europeans colonized the Americas because they had always planned to settle there.
w.why: false; the first voyages sought Asia

w.a: Europeans turned to the Americas because the Asian trade had become worthless.
w.why: false; Portugal profited from Asian trade all century

w.a: Europeans conquered the Americas because Native peoples asked them to rule.
w.why: invented; conquest was resisted and driven by European motives

cards.q: Explain why the Protestant Reformation intensified European competition for the Americas.
cards.a: It made rivalry religious. After 1517 Catholic Spain cast its empire as a defense of the faith, while Protestant England, the Dutch and French Huguenots rejected papal grants such as the 1493 line and raided Spanish shipping. Spain answered by fortifying Florida, founding St. Augustine in 1565 against a Huguenot fort.
cards.h: → Reformation splits Europe → Protestants reject papal grants → raids and rival colonies → Spain fortifies
cards.n: Naming the Reformation as a phrase earns nothing; say how it undercut papal authority over land and made rivalry religious.
o: Religious difference gave rulers a reason to challenge Spain: Hakluyt urged English colonies to spread Protestantism and check Catholic Spain.
Catholic reform also sharpened Spanish missionary effort, so converting Native peoples became a weapon in the rivalry on both sides.

w.a: The Reformation mattered because Protestants wanted to find the Fountain of Youth.
w.why: invented and unrelated to religious rivalry

w.a: The Reformation had nothing to do with the Americas because it happened only in Europe.
w.why: ignores Huguenot Florida, English privateers and Hakluyt

w.a: The Reformation united every European power against Spain.
w.why: overstated; Catholic France and the Protestant powers were also rivals

cards.q: Explain why France and England refused to accept the division of the world in the Treaty of Tordesillas.
cards.a: The division served only Spain and Portugal. It rested on papal grants that Protestant England rejected after the 1530s and Catholic France refused to read as excluding it, and it shut every other crown out of unseen lands. Competing for wealth and prestige, both claimed land by exploration and occupation instead.
cards.h: → papal grant + excludes them → rivals want wealth and prestige → claims by discovery and occupation
cards.n: Treating the treaty as international law binding all Europe earns nothing; it bound only its two signers.
o: Francis I of France reportedly asked to see the clause in Adam's will that divided the world between Spain and Portugal, rejecting the pope's power to give away lands.
Both crowns sponsored voyages (Cabot 1497, Verrazzano 1524, Cartier 1534) to build claims on discovery rather than grant.

w.a: France and England rejected it because they had signed a different treaty with Spain.
w.why: invented; no such treaty existed

w.a: France and England refused the treaty because both were Protestant.
w.why: France stayed Catholic; its objection was exclusion

w.a: France and England obeyed the treaty until Jamestown was founded.
w.why: false; both sent voyages that ignored it from 1497 on

cards.q: Explain why Spanish expeditions into the North American interior in the 1540s did not lead to lasting settlement.
cards.a: They were hunts for another Mexico, and there was none. Coronado and de Soto found farming towns but no gold, silver or tribute empire to seize, while battles, disease and supply costs mounted. With no wealth to justify a colony, Spain pulled back until Onate's New Mexico venture of 1598.
cards.h: → goal is gold and tribute → none found, costly resistance → no profit → withdrawal until 1598
cards.n: 'They got lost' earns nothing; tie the withdrawal to the wealth motive of KC-1.2.I.A.
o: Spanish colonization followed extractable wealth and dense tribute-paying populations, and the Southeast and Southwest offered neither in a form Spain could use.
The violence of both expeditions turned Native towns hostile, raising the cost of any return.

w.a: The expeditions failed because the Spanish never found the Mississippi River.
w.why: false; de Soto's men crossed it in 1541

w.a: Spain did not settle because Native peoples welcomed the expeditions peacefully.
w.why: false; both fought Native towns

w.a: Spain did not settle the interior because the pope forbade it.
w.why: invented; the papal line assigned it to Spain

cards.q: Explain why the Reconquista shaped the way Spain conquered the Americas.
cards.a: Centuries of war against Muslim Iberia, ending at Granada in 1492, gave Spain a model: conquer for faith and crown, reward fighters with land and the labor of the defeated, and convert the conquered. Conquistadors carried that model across the Atlantic, where encomienda grants and forced conversion followed conquest.
cards.h: → crusading tradition + rewards for conquerors → conquistadors seek land, labor, converts → encomienda and missions
cards.n: Mentioning 1492 as a coincidence earns nothing; explain which practices moved from Iberian war to American conquest.
o: The crown had learned to license private conquerors for a share of the spoils, which is how Cortes and Pizarro operated.
Victory at Granada freed soldiers and money and seemed to confirm that conquest served God, binding the religious and wealth motives together.

w.a: The Reconquista mattered because Muslim sailors guided Columbus to America.
w.why: invented; the link is Spanish crusading and reward practices

w.a: The Reconquista had no effect because it ended before Columbus sailed.
w.why: it ended months earlier, and its practices carried straight over

cards.q: Define the Columbian Exchange.
cards.a: The transfer of plants, animals, microbes, people, precious metals and ideas between the Eastern and Western Hemispheres after Columbus's 1492 voyage (historian Alfred Crosby named it in 1972). It ran both ways: Eurasian and African diseases, livestock and grains to the Americas; maize, potatoes, cacao, tobacco and silver to Europe, Africa and Asia; and enslaved Africans across the Atlantic. It reshaped populations, diets and economies on both sides.
cards.h: → what moved, between where, from when + both directions
cards.n: 'The exchange of goods between Europe and America' earns nothing: name items flowing each way, including disease and people.

cards.q: Contrast what crossed the Atlantic eastward with what crossed westward in the Columbian Exchange.
cards.a: Westward to the Americas: horses, cattle, pigs, sheep, wheat, sugarcane, rice, smallpox, measles, influenza and malaria, and enslaved Africans. Eastward to Europe, Africa and Asia: maize, potatoes, cassava, tomatoes, beans, cacao, tobacco, and silver and gold. The difference in effect: westward flows brought epidemics and livestock that devastated Native populations and landscapes; eastward flows brought calories and bullion that fed population and economic growth.
cards.h: → two lists + the difference in their effects
cards.n: Two lists with no stated difference is description, not contrast. Syphilis may have gone east, but its origin is still debated.

cards.q: Explain how the horse changed Great Plains Native societies.
cards.a: It turned Plains peoples into mounted bison hunters and regional powers. Horses brought by the Spanish spread north through trade and raiding mostly after 1600, and especially after the 1680 Pueblo Revolt scattered Spanish herds. Mounted hunting was more productive, bands could travel and carry more, some farming peoples such as the Cheyenne left villages for full-time nomadism, and horse-rich nations such as the Comanche and Lakota dominated the southern and northern Plains.
cards.h: → how and when horses arrived → three changes
cards.n: Borrows from u2: the mounted Plains culture took shape after 1680. Picturing pre-contact Plains peoples on horseback is the classic anachronism.

cards.q: Identify the Aztec (Mexica) Empire and its capital.
cards.a: A tribute empire in central Mexico led by the Mexica from their island capital, Tenochtitlan (founded about 1325 on the site of modern Mexico City), which formed the Triple Alliance with Texcoco and Tlacopan in 1428. By 1519 it drew tribute from hundreds of subject towns and millions of people under the ruler Moctezuma II, and Tenochtitlan, with perhaps 200,000 people, was larger than any city in Spain.
cards.h: → people + capital + tribute empire + ruler in 1519
cards.n: Illustrative: the CED names no Mesoamerican empire. Tenochtitlan's population is an estimate (commonly 150,000-250,000).

cards.q: Identify the Inca Empire and how it governed its vast Andean territory.
cards.a: The Andean empire ruled from Cusco that by the early 1500s stretched some 2,500 miles from present-day Ecuador to Chile. The Inca governed directly: roughly 25,000 miles of roads with relay runners and storehouses, appointed provincial governors, knotted-cord khipu records for census and tribute, Quechua as a common language, and the mita, a rotating labor draft. Spain later adapted the mita to work its silver mines.
cards.h: → region + capital + tools of direct rule
cards.n: Illustrative. 'They had no writing, so they were primitive' earns nothing; khipu kept census and tribute records for a centralized state.

cards.q: Identify Hernan Cortes and give the dates of his conquest of the Aztec Empire.
cards.a: A Spanish conquistador who landed on Mexico's Gulf coast in 1519 with about 500 soldiers, allied with Tlaxcala and other enemies of the Mexica, and entered Tenochtitlan that November. Driven out in mid-1520, he returned with tens of thousands of Native allies while smallpox ravaged the city, and took Tenochtitlan after a long siege in August 1521.
cards.h: → who + start and end dates + how he won
cards.n: Illustrative name. Crediting guns and horses alone earns nothing; Native allies and smallpox decided the outcome.

cards.q: Identify Francisco Pizarro and give the dates of his conquest of the Inca Empire.
cards.a: A Spanish conquistador who, with fewer than 200 men, reached the Inca Empire just after a smallpox epidemic and a civil war between the brothers Atahualpa and Huascar. He seized Atahualpa at Cajamarca in November 1532, collected a room of gold and silver as ransom, executed him in 1533, and took Cusco late that year, though Inca resistance continued from Vilcabamba until 1572.
cards.h: → who + key dates + what he exploited
cards.n: Illustrative name. 'The Inca fell in a day' overstates it; Neo-Inca resistance lasted nearly forty years.

cards.q: Explain how silver from Potosi created the first truly global trade network.
cards.a: Potosi (in present-day Bolivia), opened in 1545 and worked by Native laborers, drafted under the mita from 1573, produced silver on an unprecedented scale. Treasure fleets carried it to Seville, where it paid Spain's debts and wars and spread through European trade; from 1571 the Manila galleons carried it across the Pacific to buy Chinese silk and porcelain, since China's economy demanded silver. One commodity now linked the Americas, Europe and Asia in continuous exchange.
cards.h: → mine + labor + two routes + the demand behind it
cards.n: 'Spain got rich' earns nothing; the point is the two routes and Chinese demand. Mexican mines such as Zacatecas (1546) fed the same flows.

cards.q: Define a joint-stock company and explain why it enabled English colonization.
cards.a: A business owned by many investors who bought shares, pooling capital for a venture too large and risky for one person and splitting profits or losses by share. Chartered companies such as the Muscovy Company (1555) and East India Company (1600) let England, whose crown could not fund conquest, raise private capital and spread the risk of long-distance trade; the Virginia Company used the model to found Jamestown in 1607.
cards.h: → definition + why it suited a cash-poor crown
cards.n: Borrows from u2: the Virginia Company and Jamestown open Period 2. 'A company that owned a colony' misses the pooling of capital and risk.

cards.q: Define the tribute system that funded the Aztec capital of Tenochtitlan.
cards.a: Conquered city-states kept their own rulers but owed the Triple Alliance regular tribute on a fixed schedule: maize, beans, cotton cloth, cacao, feathers, gold and other goods, plus labor and war captives for sacrifice, as recorded in lists such as the Codex Mendoza. It fed and enriched Tenochtitlan without direct rule, but its burdens bred resentment that Cortes turned into Native alliances against the Mexica.
cards.h: → who paid what to whom + purpose + consequence
cards.n: Illustrative. 'Taxes' with no purpose (feeding the capital while leaving local rulers in place) and no link to the conquest earns nothing.

cards.q: Contrast how the Aztec and Inca empires governed their conquered territories.
cards.a: Difference: the Aztec Triple Alliance ruled indirectly, leaving local rulers in place so long as they paid tribute in goods and captives, so subject peoples kept their own armies, identities and grievances. The Inca ruled directly through appointed governors, roads, khipu records, a common language and the mita labor draft, and even resettled whole communities. Similarity: both were young conquest empires with restless subjects, which Spain exploited.
cards.n: Illustrative. 'One was in Mexico and one in Peru' is not a difference in governing; say how each controlled subject peoples.

cards.q: State the approximate scale of Native population loss in the century after contact.
cards.a: Most estimates hold that contacted regions lost roughly 50 to 90 percent of their Native population within about a century, chiefly to smallpox, measles, influenza and other introduced diseases, compounded by war, forced labor and famine. One widely cited estimate for central Mexico runs from about 25 million in 1519 to about 1 million by 1605; the Taino of Hispaniola nearly vanished within fifty years.
cards.h: → percentage range + time span + main cause
cards.n: Figures are contested estimates (the central Mexico series, from Cook and Borah, is at the high end); give a range and name disease as the main cause.

cards.q: Date the founding of the Aztec Triple Alliance and the height of Inca expansion under Pachacuti.
cards.a: The Triple Alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan formed in 1428. Inca expansion took off after Pachacuti came to power in 1438 and continued under Topa Inca and Huayna Capac into the 1520s. Both empires were less than a century old when the Spanish arrived, which helps explain why recently conquered subjects joined the invaders.
cards.n: Illustrative dates the CED does not require; they matter only for the argument that young empires had restless, recently conquered subjects.

cards.q: Identify the improvements in maritime technology that made regular transatlantic voyages possible after 1450.
cards.a: The caravel, a small, fast ship whose lateen (triangular) sails let it sail closer to the wind, and larger carracks for cargo; the magnetic compass; the astrolabe and quadrant for finding latitude from the sun or stars; better charts; and Portuguese knowledge of Atlantic wind and current systems. Together they let ships sail out and reliably return, turning one-time voyages into regular transatlantic traffic (KC-1.2.I.C).
cards.h: → ship design + instruments + charts and wind knowledge
cards.n: 'Better ships' is a phrase, not an identification; name the device and what it allowed. The compass and lateen sail came to Europe through Asian and Arab contact.

cards.q: Classify each item of the Columbian Exchange by direction (to the Americas or from the Americas) and name one effect: horses · smallpox · maize · potatoes · sugarcane · cattle and pigs · silver · cacao · wheat · tobacco · malaria · cassava · enslaved Africans
cards.a:
Horses → to the Americas; later remade Plains hunting, trade and war
Smallpox → to the Americas; epidemics killed a majority of many Native peoples
Maize → from the Americas; became a staple in Africa, southern Europe and China
Potatoes → from the Americas; fed population growth in northern Europe
Sugarcane → to the Americas; Caribbean and Brazilian plantations worked by enslaved Africans
Cattle and pigs → to the Americas; ranching, and herds trampled Native fields and spread onto Native land
Silver → from the Americas; flooded Europe and China, fueling trade and inflation
Cacao → from the Americas; chocolate became a European luxury
Wheat → to the Americas; staple of Spanish settlers and their estates
Tobacco → from the Americas; a European habit, later a Chesapeake cash crop
Malaria → to the Americas (from Africa); made lowland plantation zones deadly
Cassava → from the Americas; a drought-tolerant staple in Africa
Enslaved Africans → to the Americas; forced labor for plantations and mines
cards.n: 'The Columbian Exchange changed everything' names nothing; the scored move is the specific item, its direction and its effect.

cards.q: Identify the argument of the following excerpt and one piece of evidence it uses. (Excerpt written for this deck in the voice of an economic historian: 'The silver of Potosi and Zacatecas did more than enrich Spain's kings. Flowing through Seville to Genoese and German bankers, it multiplied the money in circulation, helped push prices up several times over across the sixteenth century, and rewarded merchants and investors at the expense of landlords living on fixed rents. American bullion thus helped dissolve the feudal order and build a commercial Europe.')
cards.a: Argument: American silver helped move Europe from feudalism toward a commercial, capitalist economy (KC-1.2.I.B). Evidence the excerpt uses: silver flowing through Seville to Genoese and German bankers; the sixteenth-century price rise it fed; and the resulting shift of wealth from landlords on fixed rents to merchants and investors.
cards.h: → the claim in one sentence + one piece of evidence
cards.n: Naming the topic ('silver came to Europe') instead of the claim ('silver helped dissolve feudalism') earns nothing; historians also credit population growth for the price rise.

cards.q: Explain why Native American populations collapsed after European contact.
cards.a: Native Americans had no acquired immunity to Eurasian and African diseases such as smallpox, measles, influenza and malaria, since the Americas had long been isolated from them. Epidemics struck again and again, and war, forced labor, famine and disrupted farming made each outbreak deadlier.
cards.h: → isolation → no immunity → repeated epidemics → worsened by war, forced labor, famine → collapse
cards.n: 'Disease' alone earns little; the point needs the lack of prior exposure and the compounding role of war and forced labor.
o: Epidemics hit all ages at once, so no one was left to farm, nurse or bury, which turned disease into famine and social breakdown.
Spanish labor systems concentrated and overworked survivors, so colonial policy multiplied the effect of disease.

w.a: Native populations collapsed because Europeans deliberately spread smallpox everywhere.
w.why: the early epidemics were not a policy; spread was mostly unintended

w.a: Native peoples died because they were physically weaker than Europeans.
w.why: the cause was lack of prior exposure, not weakness

w.a: Native populations collapsed mainly from Spanish swords and guns.
w.why: violence mattered, but disease killed far more

cards.q: Explain why a few hundred Spanish soldiers were able to conquer the much larger Aztec Empire.
cards.a: The conquest was largely a Native war. Cortes recruited tens of thousands of Tlaxcalan and other allies who resented Mexica tribute, and smallpox swept Tenochtitlan in 1520, killing the ruler Cuitlahuac and many defenders. Steel, guns and horses mattered less than allies and disease.
cards.h: → tribute resentment → Native allies + smallpox epidemic → Mexica weakened → Spanish-led victory
cards.n: 'Superior weapons' as the main cause earns nothing; the scored causes are Native allies and epidemic disease.
o: The Triple Alliance ruled indirectly through tribute, so subject city-states kept their own rulers and armies, ready to change sides.
Malintzin's translation let Cortes negotiate those alliances, turning local divisions into a coalition against Tenochtitlan.

w.a: The Spanish won because their guns and armor made them unbeatable.
w.why: a minor factor next to allies and smallpox

w.a: The Aztecs surrendered because they thought Cortes was the god Quetzalcoatl.
w.why: a later legend historians doubt; the Mexica fought a long siege

w.a: The Spanish won because the Aztec Empire had no real army.
w.why: false; the Mexica drove Cortes out in 1520

cards.q: Explain how epidemic disease weakened Native capacity for armed resistance to European colonization.
cards.a: Epidemics killed warriors, leaders and the farmers who fed them, often before Europeans arrived in force. Smallpox killed the Mexica ruler Cuitlahuac in 1520 and the Inca ruler Huayna Capac in the 1520s, setting off the civil war Pizarro exploited. Depleted, leaderless societies could not field armies.
cards.h: → disease precedes invaders → kills leaders, fighters, farmers → succession crises and hunger → weak resistance
cards.n: Saying disease 'killed a lot of people' without linking the deaths to lost leaders, fighters and food earns nothing.
o: Disease created political crises as well as losses in numbers: disputed successions split both empires just as the Spanish arrived.
Where epidemics struck less hard, as among the mobile Chichimeca, armed resistance lasted for decades.

w.a: Disease weakened resistance because sick Native people surrendered to be cured by Spanish doctors.
w.why: invented; European medicine had no cure

w.a: Disease had little military effect because it killed Spaniards as often as Native people.
w.why: false; most Spaniards had survived these diseases in childhood

cards.q: Explain why American food crops stimulated population growth in Europe and beyond.
cards.a: American crops raised the food a field could yield. Maize and potatoes produce more calories per acre than wheat or rye and grow in poorer soils and harsher climates, so they enlarged the food supply of Europe, Africa and China, reduced famine, and let populations grow (KC-1.2.I.B).
cards.h: → high-yield crops + marginal land → more calories per acre → less famine → population growth
cards.n: 'More food' alone stops short; the scored link is higher yield on land the old crops could not use. Much of the growth came after 1650.
o: Potatoes let northern European peasants feed families from small plots, and maize and cassava became African staples.
A new crop cushioned the failure of old ones, so harvest disasters became less deadly.

w.a: American crops made Europe grow because they tasted better than European food.
w.why: taste is not the mechanism; yield per acre is

w.a: Europe's population grew because Europeans moved to the Americas.
w.why: emigration would shrink, not grow, Europe's population

w.a: American crops only mattered inside the Americas.
w.why: ignores their spread to Europe, Africa and Asia

cards.q: Explain why American silver facilitated Europe's shift from feudalism to capitalism.
cards.a: Silver multiplied Europe's money supply. It fed inflation that eroded landlords' fixed rents, enriched the merchants and bankers who lent to the Spanish crown, and paid for Asian trade, so wealth and power shifted from land toward commerce and capital (KC-1.2.I.B).
cards.h: → bullion floods in → inflation, credit, trade grow → landlords lose, merchants gain → commercial capitalism
cards.n: 'Spain got rich' earns nothing; historians debate how much silver, versus population growth, drove the price rise.
o: Spain spent its silver on wars and imports, so it flowed to Genoese, German and Dutch financiers and manufacturers, building capitalist centers outside Spain.
Plentiful coin made wages and market exchange easier than payment in labor services, loosening feudal obligations.

w.a: Silver ended feudalism because Spanish kings handed it out to peasants.
w.why: invented; silver went to crowns, merchants and bankers

w.a: Silver made Spain the most prosperous capitalist country in Europe.
w.why: Spain spent it abroad and suffered inflation and bankruptcies

w.a: American silver had no effect because Europe already had enough gold.
w.why: ignores the documented inflow and price rise

cards.q: Explain why joint-stock companies and improved maritime technology changed economies on both sides of the Atlantic.
cards.a: They made long-distance trade regular and financeable. Better ships made round trips reliable; Spain's Casa de Contratacion (1503) and convoyed fleets organized the silver trade; joint-stock companies pooled capital and spread risk. Europe gained commercial wealth, and American economies were rebuilt to export to it.
cards.h: → reliable ships + organized trade + pooled capital → regular trade → Europe commercializes, Americas export
cards.n: Naming 'the caravel' or 'joint-stock companies' without saying what each made possible earns nothing.
o: Pooling capital let merchants survive a lost ship or failed colony, so investors kept funding risky Atlantic ventures no single person could afford.
Regular shipping tied American mines and plantations to European demand, so colonial labor systems grew to serve export markets.

w.a: Joint-stock companies changed the economy because the government ran them.
w.why: they were private ventures under royal charters

w.a: Better ships changed economies because they let Columbus find America by accident.
w.why: one voyage is not the regular trade the KC describes

cards.q: Explain why Eurasian livestock transformed American landscapes and Native life after conquest.
cards.a: Pigs, cattle, sheep and horses met few predators or diseases suited to them, so they multiplied fast, roamed unfenced, and grazed and trampled Native fields and wild plants. Spanish ranches claimed land, and livestock damage and overgrazing pushed Native farmers off it, as in central Mexico's 1500s sheep boom.
cards.h: → few natural checks → herds explode → graze and trample Native crops → ranching displaces farmers
cards.n: 'Europeans brought animals' is identification; the scored effect is on land use, crops and Native displacement.
o: Livestock were agents of conquest: herds extended Spanish property claims and damaged the maize fields that fed Native towns.
The same animals gave Native peoples new resources, from wool to horses, so the effect was not only destructive.

w.a: Livestock changed the Americas because Native peoples had never kept any animals.
w.why: false; they kept dogs, turkeys and llamas

w.a: European animals had little effect because they died in the new climate.
w.why: false; the herds multiplied rapidly

cards.q: Define the encomienda system.
cards.a: A Spanish crown grant that gave a colonist (encomendero) the right to demand tribute and labor from the Native people of a district, in return for protecting them and teaching them Christianity. Its purpose was to marshal Native labor for mines, farms and plantations and to reward conquerors cheaply (KC-1.2.II.B); in practice it was coerced labor that, together with disease, devastated the peoples of the Caribbean.
cards.h: → who gets what from whom + purpose + result
cards.n: Describing the encomienda without its purpose, marshaling Native labor for mining and agriculture, earns nothing; it granted labor and tribute, not land.

cards.q: Define the casta system.
cards.a: The Spanish colonial hierarchy that ranked people by birthplace and ancestry: peninsulares (born in Spain) at the top, then criollos (American-born Spaniards), then mixed groups such as mestizos (Spanish and Native) and mulattoes (Spanish and African), with Native peoples and Africans, above all the enslaved, at the bottom. Its purpose was to fit a diverse population into one order that defined each group's status, tribute, labor duties and access to office (KC-1.2.II.D).
cards.n: Listing the ranks without the purpose (fixing status, duties and privilege in a mixed society) earns nothing; the elaborate categories multiplied mostly after 1600.

cards.q: Identify the earliest form of plantation slavery in the Americas.
cards.a: Sugar plantations worked by enslaved Africans, begun on Hispaniola in the 1510s-1520s and expanded on a much larger scale in Portuguese Brazil from the mid-1500s. Planters brought the system from Atlantic islands such as Madeira and Sao Tome: a large estate, a sugar mill (ingenio), and gangs of enslaved workers under brutal discipline producing one export crop. It became the model for later Caribbean and mainland plantation slavery.
cards.h: → crop + first places + what it modeled
cards.n: Naming cotton or the Chesapeake earns nothing; American plantation slavery began with sugar in the Caribbean and Brazil.

cards.q: Define the asiento system.
cards.a: A contract or license by which the Spanish crown granted a merchant, company or foreign state the right to supply a set number of enslaved Africans to Spanish America in exchange for fees. Because the papal and Tordesillas lines left the African coast to Portugal, Spain had no trading posts there; licenses began around 1518, and formal asiento contracts from 1595 went mainly to Portuguese merchants.
cards.h: → license + who supplied whom + why Spain needed it
cards.n: It licensed the supply of captives, not their ownership. Britain's asiento of 1713 is a later, Period 2 episode.

cards.q: Identify the Portuguese sugar-and-slave complex that became the model for later plantation slavery.
cards.a: Sugar estates on Portugal's Atlantic islands, first Madeira (from the mid-1400s) and then Sao Tome (settled in the 1490s), worked increasingly by enslaved Africans bought from West and West-Central African traders. Sao Tome in particular joined large estates, sugar mills and an enslaved African workforce, the combination that moved to Brazil and the Caribbean in the 1500s.
cards.h: → crop + islands + what it became a model for
cards.n: 'Slavery began in Virginia in 1619' misses a century and a half of Atlantic island and Brazilian plantations; Madeira also used free and Canary Islander labor.

cards.q: Identify the Taino people and their experience as the first Native population to meet Spanish colonizers.
cards.a: Arawak-speaking farmers and fishers of the Greater Antilles (Hispaniola, Cuba, Puerto Rico, Jamaica) who met Columbus in 1492. Settlers forced them into gold mining and farming under the encomienda; forced labor, famine, war and then smallpox (from 1518) cut Hispaniola's Taino population to a few thousand within a generation, which pushed the Spanish to seek other workers, including enslaved Africans.
cards.n: Hispaniola's 1492 population is disputed (estimates run from about 100,000 to several million); Taino ancestry survived through intermarriage.

cards.q: Identify the Kingdom of Kongo's conversion to Christianity under King Afonso I and its connection to the early slave trade.
cards.a: Kongo's ruler Nzinga Mbemba, baptized Afonso, reigned about 1509-1542, made Catholicism the court religion and traded with Portugal for goods, priests and advisers. Portuguese demand for captives, much of it from Sao Tome planters, drew Kongo into supplying enslaved people; in letters of 1526 Afonso complained to Portugal's king that traders were seizing free subjects and even nobles. Kongo shows the partnership, and tension, the KC describes.
cards.n: Illustrative. Africa as passive victim earns nothing; Kongo's rulers bargained with Portugal and sold captives themselves while protesting abuses.

cards.q: Define the 'seasoning' period newly arrived enslaved Africans endured on Caribbean sugar plantations.
cards.a: The first one to three years after arrival, during which newly enslaved Africans were forced to adjust to plantation labor, a new disease environment, a new language and harsh discipline. Deaths during seasoning were very high, commonly estimated at a quarter to a third of new arrivals on sugar islands, so planters kept buying new captives rather than relying on natural increase.
cards.h: → length + what captives endured + mortality + consequence
cards.n: Borrows from u2: seasoning is documented mainly for 1600s-1700s sugar colonies. The mortality figures are estimates.

cards.q: Explain how Hispaniola's early sugar-and-slave economy became the template later exported to Barbados and Carolina.
cards.a: Hispaniola first showed that sugar plus enslaved African labor could replace a destroyed Native workforce: by the 1520s-1540s its mills ran on enslaved Africans. Portugal scaled the model up in Brazil, English planters copied Brazilian methods in Barbados in the 1640s, and Barbadian migrants carried plantation slavery and their slave code to Carolina after 1670, which is why South Carolina developed a Black majority.
cards.h: → the model, then each step of its transfer
cards.n: Borrows from u2: Barbados and Carolina are Period 2. The direct link to Barbados ran through Brazil and Dutch traders more than through Hispaniola.

cards.q: Explain how West African agricultural knowledge crossed the Atlantic as part of the Columbian Exchange.
cards.a: Enslaved West Africans, many from the rice-growing Upper Guinea coast, carried knowledge of planting, flooding and processing rice, along with crops such as okra, yams, black-eyed peas and sesame. Planters in coastal South Carolina and later Georgia relied on that expertise to build the rice economy of the 1700s, so the exchange moved skills as well as plants and germs.
cards.h: → what knowledge moved → the economy it built
cards.n: Borrows from u2: Carolina rice began in the 1690s. How far planters depended on African expertise (the 'black rice' thesis) is debated.

cards.q: Date the first documented direct shipment of enslaved Africans to Spanish America.
cards.a: 1518: King Charles I licensed the shipment of enslaved Africans directly from Africa to the Spanish Caribbean instead of by way of Iberia, and the first documented direct voyages arrived in the mid-1520s. Before that, enslaved Africans had reached Hispaniola from Spain since about 1502.
cards.h: → year of the license + when direct voyages followed
cards.n: Sources differ on the 'first' (the 1518 license or a voyage of about 1525); give the license date and say direct voyages followed in the 1520s.

cards.q: State the approximate total scale of the transatlantic slave trade.
cards.a: About 12.5 million Africans were forced aboard slave ships between the early 1500s and the 1860s, and about 10.7 million survived the Middle Passage to land in the Americas (Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database estimates). Only a small share, roughly a quarter-million, embarked before 1600; the trade Portugal and Spain opened in Period 1 peaked in the 1700s.
cards.n: Most of the trade falls after 1607, and Brazil and the Caribbean, not mainland North America (under 400,000 landed), took the great majority.

cards.q: Identify the mita labor draft Spain used at the silver mines of Potosi.
cards.a: A rotating forced-labor draft that Viceroy Francisco de Toledo adapted from the Inca mit'a in 1573: Andean communities had to send about one-seventh of their adult men each year to work the Potosi silver mines (and the Huancavelica mercury mines) for token wages. It marshaled Native labor to extract precious metals (KC-1.2.II.B), killed and uprooted many thousands, and lasted until 1812.
cards.h: → origin + how it worked + purpose + result
cards.n: Illustrative. Calling it slavery misses the point: it was a state labor draft adapted from Inca practice, which is how Spain justified and staffed it.

cards.q: Identify the New Laws of 1542 and what they tried to change.
cards.a: Laws issued by Charles I in 1542, pushed by Las Casas and other reformers, that banned the enslavement of Native Americans, barred new encomiendas and ordered existing ones to lapse at the holder's death. Encomenderos resisted (in Peru they rebelled), and the crown withdrew the inheritance ban in 1545, but the laws marked a shift from private encomiendas toward crown-run labor drafts and, indirectly, toward enslaved African labor.
cards.h: → who + what they banned + resistance + long-run shift
cards.n: Illustrative. The laws protected Native vassals, not Africans; saying they 'ended forced labor' earns nothing.

cards.q: Classify each person into the category Spanish colonial officials would assign, and rank the categories from highest to lowest status: a man born in Seville · his son born in Mexico City · the child of a Spanish father and a Nahua mother · the child of a Spanish father and an African mother · the child of an African father and a Native mother · a Nahua farmer · a man enslaved in Angola and sold in Veracruz
cards.a:
Man born in Seville → peninsular (rank 1)
His son born in Mexico City → criollo (rank 2)
Spanish father, Nahua mother → mestizo (rank 3)
Spanish father, African mother → mulato (rank 4)
African father, Native mother → zambo, or lobo in some lists (rank 5)
Nahua farmer → indio, a tribute-paying royal vassal (rank 6, legally protected but subordinate)
Man enslaved in Angola → negro esclavo, legally property (rank 7)
cards.n: Labels varied by place and time, and Native and mixed ranks were debated; the scored idea is that birthplace and ancestry fixed status, duties and privilege.

cards.q: Compare the encomienda with African chattel slavery in Spanish America.
cards.a: Similarity: both were coerced labor that Spanish colonial economies used for plantations and mines. Difference: encomienda Indians were legally free royal vassals whose tribute and labor were granted to an encomendero who did not own them, and the crown could limit the grant (as in 1542); enslaved Africans were property, bought and sold for life, their children inherited the status, and reform laws did not protect them.
cards.h: → one similarity + the key legal difference
cards.n: Listing features of each without stating the similarity and the difference earns nothing; the legal status, vassal versus property, is the scored difference.

cards.q: Explain why the Spanish and Portuguese turned to enslaved Africans for colonial labor.
cards.a: Native labor was dying out and gaining legal protection. Epidemics and overwork destroyed Caribbean and coastal peoples, and the New Laws of 1542 banned Native enslavement. Portugal already bought captives from West African states, and sugar and mines needed permanent workers, so planters imported enslaved Africans.
cards.h: → Native collapse + legal limits → existing Portuguese-African trade → demand for permanent labor → African slavery
cards.n: A one-cause answer ('the Natives died') earns less than the demographic, legal and commercial causes together.
o: Enslaved Africans, far from home, could not easily escape into known terrain or appeal to royal protection as Native vassals could.
Many West Africans had survived malaria and smallpox and brought farming and mining skills that planters valued.

w.a: The Spanish turned to Africans because Africans volunteered to work in the Americas.
w.why: false; they were captured and sold

w.a: The Spanish used Africans because Native Americans refused to work.
w.why: Native people were forced to work; the problem was death and legal protection

w.a: The Spanish chose African labor because the pope ordered it.
w.why: invented; the causes were demographic, legal and economic

cards.q: Explain why the Spanish developed a caste system in their American empire.
cards.a: Conquest created a society of Spaniards, Native peoples, Africans and their mixed descendants, ruled by a small Spanish minority. Ranking people by birthplace and ancestry kept office and wealth with Spaniards, fixed who owed tribute and labor, and gave mixed groups a stake above Native and enslaved people.
cards.h: → mixed population + small Spanish elite → need to rule and extract labor → rank by ancestry → duties fixed
cards.n: Describing the ranks without their purpose (control, labor and privilege) earns nothing.
o: Few Spanish women emigrated early, so unions of Spanish men with Native and African women produced children whom the law had to place.
Iberian 'purity of blood' rules, first used against converted Jews and Muslims, gave Spain a ready model for ranking by descent.

w.a: The Spanish made the caste system so that everyone would be treated equally.
w.why: the opposite; it defined inequality

w.a: The caste system existed because Native Americans already used it before contact.
w.why: it was a Spanish colonial creation

w.a: The Spanish created castes only to decide who could marry whom.
w.why: status, tribute, labor and office were the purpose

cards.q: Explain why the Spanish crown moved to limit the encomienda in the 1500s.
cards.a: The crown feared both the loss of its Native vassals and the power of encomenderos. Reformers such as Las Casas exposed the destruction of Caribbean peoples, and hereditary grants threatened to create an American nobility beyond royal control. The New Laws of 1542 restricted grants, shifting labor toward crown drafts.
cards.h: → Native deaths + reformers' protests + fear of an independent elite → New Laws 1542 → crown-controlled labor
cards.n: Citing only Las Casas misses the crown's political interest in curbing the encomenderos.
o: Tribute-paying Native subjects were the crown's own revenue base, so their disappearance was a fiscal problem as well as a moral one.
Where the crown could not end grants at once, as in Peru after the 1544 revolt, it let them lapse and built the repartimiento and mita instead.

w.a: The crown limited the encomienda because Native peoples voted to abolish it.
w.why: invented; the decision was royal, pressed by reformers

w.a: The crown limited the encomienda only because it stopped making money.
w.why: misses the moral debate and the fear of an independent elite

cards.q: Explain why European traders partnered with West African states rather than conquering them to obtain enslaved laborers.
cards.a: West African states were strong and the coast was deadly to Europeans. Kingdoms such as Benin and Kongo fielded large armies, malaria killed most Europeans who stayed, and slavery and slave trading already existed there. Buying captives from African rulers and merchants at coastal forts was cheaper and safer than war.
cards.h: → strong African states + deadly disease environment + existing slave trade → partnership at coastal forts
cards.n: Treating Africans as passive victims earns nothing; the KC stresses partnership with African groups who practiced slavery.
o: African rulers controlled the supply of captives through war and tribute, so Europeans traded on African terms, paying in cloth, metal and later guns.
Portugal's model was the fortified trading post, such as Elmina (1482), not territorial conquest.

w.a: Europeans did not conquer West Africa because they did not know it existed.
w.why: false; Portugal traded on the coast from the 1440s

w.a: Europeans partnered with Africans because African rulers had no slaves of their own.
w.why: backwards; existing slavery made the trade possible

cards.q: Explain why sugar cultivation created an especially heavy demand for enslaved labor.
cards.a: Sugar was labor-hungry and deadly. Cut cane had to be ground and boiled within hours, mills ran around the clock, and heat and disease made the work brutal; planters found it cheaper to work people to death and buy replacements. High profits and high mortality together meant constant demand for new captives.
cards.h: → perishable cane + nonstop mill work + tropical disease → high mortality → constant replacement → demand
cards.n: 'Sugar was popular' explains demand for sugar, not for enslaved labor; link the crop's work regime to mortality and replacement.
o: Sugar needed large workforces on a single estate, and its profits were high enough to pay for imported captives.
Seasoning deaths and low birth rates meant plantation populations could not sustain themselves without new arrivals.

w.a: Sugar needed slaves because it was grown in very small gardens.
w.why: backwards; it was grown on large estates

w.a: Sugar needed enslaved labor because Europeans could not eat it without African cooks.
w.why: invented; demand came from production, not consumption

cards.q: Explain why Spanish colonial society developed large mixed-ancestry populations within a few generations of conquest.
cards.a: Spanish migration was mostly male. Conquistadors, soldiers and settlers formed unions, by marriage or by force, with Native and African women, and some marriages to Native noblewomen were encouraged to secure land and alliances. Their mestizo and mulatto children soon formed large groups the casta system had to place.
cards.h: → mostly male migrants → unions with Native and African women, many forced → mixed children → casta categories
cards.n: Leaving out coercion misdescribes the process; the answer must connect male migration to the mixed population and to the need to rank it.
o: Marriage to Native noblewomen, such as Moctezuma's daughter Isabel, gave Spaniards access to land, tribute and legitimacy.
Because Spaniards were a small minority among millions, mixing was unavoidable, so Spain regulated status rather than preventing unions.

w.a: Spanish society was mixed because Spain wanted everyone to be equal.
w.why: the casta system ranked people unequally

w.a: Spanish society became mixed because Native people moved to Spain.
w.why: the mixing happened in the Americas

cards.q: Explain why silver mining in Spanish America depended on coerced Native labor.
cards.a: Mines needed thousands of workers in remote, deadly conditions that few would accept at the wages owners wanted to pay. The crown and mine owners filled the gap by drafting Native communities, first through encomiendas and then the repartimiento and the Potosi mita, marshaling Native labor for silver (KC-1.2.II.B).
cards.h: → remote, deadly mines + mass labor need + low wages → drafts of Native communities → silver
cards.n: 'The Spanish forced people to work' is description; explain why the mines' needs led to state labor drafts.
o: Spain adapted existing Native institutions such as the Inca mit'a, which made coercion easy to organize.
Where drafts fell short, as at Zacatecas in northern Mexico, owners relied more on wage labor, showing that labor systems followed available workers.

w.a: Silver mining used Native labor because Native peoples owned the mines and ran them for profit.
w.why: Spaniards owned the mines; Native workers were drafted

w.a: Silver was mined mainly by enslaved Africans in the 1500s.
w.why: in the Andes most miners were drafted Native workers

cards.q: Define the Requerimiento.
cards.a: A 1513 Spanish legal text that conquistadors had to read to Native peoples, usually in Spanish and sometimes out of earshot, demanding that they accept the authority of the Church, the pope and the Spanish monarchs and allow preaching. If they refused or delayed, the Spanish declared a just war and blamed the victims for the deaths and enslavement that followed. Its purpose was to give conquest a religious and legal justification (KC-1.2.III.C).
cards.h: → what it demanded + what refusal triggered + purpose
cards.n: Calling it an invitation to convert misses its purpose: a legal pretext that made resistance, or simple incomprehension, grounds for war and enslavement.

cards.q: Identify Bartolome de las Casas and his argument.
cards.a: A Spanish colonist and former encomendero on Hispaniola who became a Dominican friar and the leading critic of Spanish treatment of Native Americans. In A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies (written 1542, printed 1552) and at the Valladolid debate (1550-1551) he argued that Native peoples were rational human beings with legitimate rulers, who must be converted by peaceful persuasion, not by conquest, forced labor or enslavement.
cards.n: He once proposed importing enslaved Africans to spare Native people and later repented it; calling him an opponent of all slavery from the start is wrong.

cards.q: Identify Juan Gines de Sepulveda and his argument.
cards.a: A Spanish humanist scholar and royal chronicler who, drawing on Aristotle's idea of natural slavery, argued in Democrates Alter (about 1544) and at Valladolid (1550-1551) that Native Americans were barbarous, idolatrous and incapable of self-rule. War against them was therefore just: it would end human sacrifice and idolatry, protect innocents, and open the way to Christian rule and conversion.
cards.h: → who + source of his idea + argument
cards.n: Illustrative name. He never visited the Americas, a sourcing point; his case is the cultural and religious justification for subjugation that KC-1.2.III.C names.

cards.q: Explain the significance of the Valladolid debate of 1550-1551.
cards.a: It was the first formal European debate over whether conquering Native peoples was just. Charles I suspended new conquests while theologians and jurists heard Las Casas argue that Native peoples were rational humans to be converted peacefully and Sepulveda argue that they were natural slaves whom war could rightly subject. No clear verdict followed and conquest resumed, but the debate shows Europeans contesting the humanity and rights of non-Europeans (KC-1.2.III.C).
cards.h: → issue + who argued what + outcome + why it matters
cards.n: 'Las Casas won and Native people were freed' is false: the panel issued no clear verdict, and forced labor continued in new forms.

cards.q: Identify the goals of the Spanish mission system in North America.
cards.a: Jesuit and then Franciscan missions in Florida (from the late 1560s) and Franciscan missions in New Mexico (from 1598) aimed to convert Native peoples to Catholicism, gather them into mission communities under friars, teach Spanish customs and farming, suppress Native religious practice, and draw on Native labor, securing Spain's frontier cheaply. They reflected the Spanish belief that conversion justified and completed conquest.
cards.n: 'To convert Native people' alone leaves out the labor and frontier-control purposes that made missions a grievance behind the 1680 Pueblo Revolt.

cards.q: Define the Pueblo Revolt and give its year and leader.
cards.a: The 1680 uprising in which Pueblo towns of New Mexico, coordinated by the Tewa religious leader Pope (Po'pay) of Ohkay Owingeh (San Juan), rose against Spanish rule, killed about 400 colonists including 21 Franciscan friars, destroyed churches, and drove some 2,000 survivors from Santa Fe south to El Paso. The Pueblos held New Mexico for about twelve years, until Diego de Vargas's reconquest began in 1692.
cards.h: → year + leader + what happened + how long
cards.n: Borrows from u2: 1680 falls in Period 2. It is KC-1.2.III.B's military resistance to demands on land, labor and religion at its peak.

cards.q: Explain the long-term significance of the Pueblo Revolt.
cards.a: It was the most successful Native revolt against a European power in North America, and it changed Spanish rule. After reconquest in 1692-1696 Spain did not restore the encomienda in New Mexico, tolerated more Pueblo religious practice alongside Catholicism, and relied on Pueblo allies against Apache and Comanche raiders, producing a more negotiated colonial order. The revolt also helped spread Spanish horses to the Plains.
cards.h: → outcome + changes in Spanish policy + wider effect
cards.n: Borrows from u2. Use it against a thesis that Native peoples were passive victims; the scored effect is the changed Spanish policy, not the revolt itself.

cards.q: Explain the range of Native responses to European colonization in Period 1.
cards.a: Native peoples chose strategies to fit their strength and interests. Some allied with Europeans against rivals (Tlaxcala with Cortes); many traded and adopted useful goods while keeping their own beliefs; some accepted baptism while blending Catholic and traditional practice; others moved away from colonized zones; and some fought, as the Chichimeca did for four decades. Each response aimed to defend sovereignty, land, belief and livelihood (KC-1.2.III.B).
cards.h: → a spectrum of responses + the shared purpose
cards.n: A thesis that Native peoples only resisted, or only submitted, earns less than one that shows the range and the purpose behind it.

cards.q: Define the two-spirit gender role recognized in many pre-contact Native societies.
cards.a: A recognized social and often ceremonial role, in many Native societies such as the Zuni, Lakota and Navajo, for people who took on work, dress or roles associated with another gender or with both, and who were often respected as healers, mediators or ceremonial leaders. Europeans, whose Christian worldview allowed only two fixed genders, condemned the role, one of the clashes over gender roles that KC-1.2.III names.
cards.h: → what the role was + its status + European reaction
cards.n: 'Two-spirit' is a pan-Indian term adopted in 1990; Europeans used the slur 'berdache'. Roles and names varied widely by nation.

cards.q: Identify La Malinche (Malintzin) and her role in the Spanish conquest of Mexico.
cards.a: A Nahua woman, earlier sold into slavery among the Maya, who was given to Cortes in 1519 and, speaking both Nahuatl and a Maya language, became his interpreter, adviser and intermediary, and later the mother of his son Martin. Her translation let Cortes negotiate with Moctezuma's envoys and recruit Native allies, making her central to the conquest and an example of a Native person navigating contact between two worlds.
cards.n: Illustrative. Later nationalists cast her as a traitor (malinchismo); historians stress she was enslaved and had few choices, so 'traitor' earns nothing.

cards.q: Define the Black Legend (Leyenda Negra).
cards.a: The portrayal of Spanish colonization as uniquely cruel, greedy and fanatical, spread from the late 1500s by Spain's Protestant rivals, England and the Netherlands, who translated and illustrated Las Casas's accounts (as in Theodor de Bry's engravings of the 1590s) to justify their own challenge to Spain. The name itself dates from 1914. It shows European debates over treating Native peoples becoming weapons in imperial rivalry.
cards.h: → the portrayal + who spread it + why
cards.n: Taking the Legend at face value earns nothing: English and French colonizers also used violence, and the portrayal served rivals' propaganda.

cards.q: Identify the first printing press in the Americas.
cards.a: The press set up in Mexico City in 1539 by the printer Juan Pablos, agent of a Seville printing house, with the backing of Bishop Juan de Zumarraga and Viceroy Antonio de Mendoza. It printed catechisms, grammars and religious works in Spanish and in Native languages such as Nahuatl for missionary use, a century before the first press in English North America (Cambridge, Massachusetts, 1638-1639).
cards.h: → place + year + who + what it printed and why
cards.n: Illustrative. Its purpose, conversion in Native languages, is the scored link to KC-1.2.III.A; the date alone earns nothing.

cards.q: Define the policy of reduccion (congregacion) in Spanish mission colonization.
cards.a: The forced resettlement of scattered Native communities into compact, grid-planned towns around a church, where friars and officials could supervise conversion, collect tribute and organize labor drafts. Carried out in Peru under Viceroy Toledo in the 1570s and in New Spain especially around 1600, it disrupted Native land use and subsistence and crowded people together, helping epidemics spread.
cards.n: 'Building towns' without the purpose (conversion, tribute and labor control) earns nothing; the policy imposed European ideas of settlement and land use.

cards.q: Identify the Chichimeca War (1550-1590).
cards.a: A four-decade war between mobile Chichimeca peoples of north-central Mexico and Spaniards pushing into the silver country around Zacatecas after 1546. Chichimeca raiders attacked mining towns and silver roads and Spanish campaigns failed, so Spain ended the war with 'peace by purchase': food, clothing and land for the Chichimeca, Tlaxcalan colonists settled among them, and missionaries. It shows military resistance forcing diplomacy (KC-1.2.III.B).
cards.h: → who + where + why + how it ended
cards.n: Illustrative. It shows Spanish conquest failing where there was no empire to capture; 'the Spanish always won' earns nothing.

cards.q: Contrast the typical European view with a common Native American view on each issue named in KC-1.2.III: religion · land · gender roles · family and descent · political authority · trade and gift exchange
cards.a:
Religion → Europeans: one true Christian faith to be spread, other beliefs idolatry; Native peoples: many traditions tied to place and nature, often open to adding new spiritual powers
Land → Europeans: exclusive private or crown property that could be fenced and sold; Native peoples: shared rights to use land for farming, hunting and gathering
Gender roles → Europeans: men farm and govern; many Woodland peoples: women farm and control fields, men hunt, trade and fight
Family and descent → Europeans: patrilineal households headed by fathers; many Native peoples (e.g., the Iroquois): matrilineal clans traced through mothers
Political authority → Europeans: monarchs claiming sovereignty by grant or discovery; many Native peoples: councils and chiefs who led by persuasion and generosity
Trade and gifts → Europeans: exchange for profit that ends with the deal; Native peoples: gifts that create alliances and ongoing obligations
cards.h: → European view; Native view, each issue
cards.n: These are generalizations: Native nations differed (the Aztec and Inca had rulers and tribute). Pair both views on each issue, or the comparison earns nothing.

cards.q: Identify the evidence the author uses to support his argument in the following paraphrase, and explain one limitation of that evidence. (Paraphrase of Bartolome de las Casas, A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies, printed in 1552 and dedicated to Prince Philip of Spain: the Native peoples of the islands were gentle, humble and peaceful; the Spaniards fell on them like starving wolves and lions on lambs, killing and torturing them to get gold; where Hispaniola once held more than three million people, scarcely two hundred remain.)
cards.a: Evidence: accounts of Spanish killing and torture for gold, and a claimed population collapse on Hispaniola from over three million to about two hundred, used to argue that the conquest was unjust and must be reformed. Limitation: written to move the crown toward reform, it inflates the numbers, credits killing rather than disease with most deaths, and portrays Native peoples as passive innocents, so it is stronger evidence of the European debate than of the death toll.
cards.h: → the evidence he cites + one limitation from purpose
cards.n: Summarizing the passage ('the Spanish were cruel') restates his claim; the point asks for the evidence he uses and a limitation tied to his purpose or audience.

cards.q: Explain why Europeans and Native Americans often misunderstood each other's claims to land.
cards.a: They held different ideas of what a land claim was. Europeans claimed land by grant, discovery or purchase as exclusive property that could be fenced and sold; many Native peoples held land communally as rights to farm, hunt and gather on it, so a 'sale' could mean sharing use, not giving the land up.
cards.h: → European exclusive, sellable property vs Native shared use rights → same deal read two ways → conflict
cards.n: Describing each view separately without saying how the difference produced conflict earns nothing.
o: Europeans often read seasonally unused hunting grounds as empty land open to claim, while their Native owners saw them as part of a planned yearly round.
The difference was one of legal tradition, not intelligence: each side applied its own rules of property to the other.

w.a: Native Americans had no idea of owning or controlling land.
w.why: overstated; they held clear territorial and use rights

w.a: They misunderstood each other only because they spoke different languages.
w.why: language mattered, but the deeper difference was the idea of property

cards.q: Explain why Europeans misread Native American gender roles.
cards.a: Europeans judged by their own norms. There men farmed and headed households; in many Woodland societies women farmed and controlled fields and, in matrilineal clans, helped choose leaders, while men hunted and fought. Europeans saw Native men as idle and Native women as drudges, missing the balance of work and power.
cards.h: → European norm: men farm and rule → Woodland women farm, clans matrilineal → Europeans see idle men, overworked women
cards.n: Saying only that roles differed, without the European norm that produced the misreading, earns nothing.
o: Hunting was aristocratic leisure in Europe but essential labor in Native economies, so the same activity carried opposite meanings.
Missionaries tried to push Native men into farming and women into the household, showing that gender was part of what they meant by conversion.

w.a: Europeans understood Native gender roles because they matched European ones.
w.why: false; the KC stresses divergent gender roles

w.a: Native women had no power in any Native society.
w.why: false; Iroquois clan mothers chose chiefs and controlled fields

cards.q: Explain why Las Casas and Sepulveda reached opposite conclusions about the Spanish conquest.
cards.a: Both wanted Native peoples as Christian subjects of Spain but disagreed about Native nature. Sepulveda, reasoning from Aristotle, judged them barbarous natural slaves open to just war; Las Casas, drawing on decades in the Indies, judged them rational peoples with legitimate rulers, convertible only by persuasion.
cards.h: → shared goal of conversion → opposite views of Native capacity → just war vs peaceful persuasion
cards.n: Describing each man's view without the shared premise and the point of disagreement earns nothing on a comparison.
o: Their evidence differed: Sepulveda argued from classical philosophy without visiting America, while Las Casas argued from experience as a colonist and friar.
Both served Spanish interests: Sepulveda defended conquest as the crown's right, Las Casas defended the crown's Native vassals against encomenderos.

w.a: They disagreed because one was Spanish and the other was Native American.
w.why: both were Spaniards

w.a: Las Casas wanted Spain to leave the Americas, while Sepulveda wanted it to stay.
w.why: Las Casas wanted Spanish rule and conversion by peaceful means

cards.q: Explain why European justifications for enslaving Africans differed from those for subjugating Native Americans in the 1500s.
cards.a: Native Americans were the crown's vassals and potential converts, so Spain debated their rights and in 1542 banned enslaving them. Africans were bought as captives from outside the empire, allegedly taken in just wars, so their enslavement drew little debate; religious, then racial, justifications attached to them.
cards.h: → Natives = crown vassals and converts → protected by law; Africans = bought captives → enslavement accepted
