cards.n: Describing the treatment of both groups without stating the difference in justification earns nothing.
o: The Valladolid debate asked whether Native peoples could rightly be subjugated; no comparable official debate asked it about Africans, whom Las Casas at first proposed as substitute laborers.
African slavery already existed in Iberia and Africa, so Europeans treated it as established, while Native subjugation was new and demanded justification.

w.a: Europeans justified enslaving Africans and Native Americans in exactly the same way.
w.why: ignores the laws protecting Native vassals

w.a: Europeans believed Africans had no souls, so they never baptized them.
w.why: false; enslaved Africans were baptized

cards.q: Explain why Europeans and Native Americans each adopted parts of the other's culture over time.
cards.a: Each side took what served its own purposes. Europeans adopted maize, potatoes, tobacco, canoes and Native knowledge of the land to survive and profit; Native peoples adopted metal tools, cloth, guns, livestock and horses, and some Catholic practices, to strengthen farming, hunting, war and spiritual power.
cards.h: → both seek advantage → Europeans take crops, canoes, local knowledge → Natives take metal, animals, some beliefs
cards.n: Listing borrowed items earns nothing; explain why each side chose them (usefulness) and that borrowing was selective.
o: Adoption was selective: Native peoples often fitted European goods and saints into their own beliefs rather than abandoning them.
Survival drove European borrowing: colonists who ignored Native crops and techniques often starved.

w.a: Native Americans adopted European culture because they wanted to become European.
w.why: adoption was selective and served Native goals

w.a: Europeans adopted nothing from Native Americans.
w.why: false; maize, potatoes and tobacco spread worldwide

cards.q: Explain why gift exchange and trade meant different things to Native and European participants in early encounters.
cards.a: For many Native peoples, exchange created relationships: gifts sealed alliances and obligations, and a partner who stopped giving became an enemy. Europeans usually saw trade as a transaction for profit that ended with the deal, so each side often read the other's behavior as naivety, greed or betrayal.
cards.h: → Native gifts build alliances and obligations vs European profit deals → each misreads the other → mistrust
cards.n: Describing only one side's view earns nothing on a comparison; state both meanings and the misunderstanding they produced.
o: French traders later prospered partly by learning to give gifts and take Native partners, following Native rules of exchange.
Columbus read Taino gift-giving as simplicity rather than diplomacy, an early case of the misunderstanding the KC describes.

w.a: Native people gave gifts because they did not understand what their goods were worth.
w.why: misreads diplomacy as ignorance

w.a: Europeans and Native Americans traded in exactly the same way.
w.why: the KC stresses mutual misunderstanding

cards.q: Explain why Native resistance took different forms among settled peoples such as the Pueblos and mobile peoples such as the Chichimeca.
cards.a: Resistance followed each society's way of life. Mobile Chichimeca bands had no towns to capture, so they waged long raiding wars Spain could not win and ended only with gifts and diplomacy; settled Pueblo towns, occupied under missions and labor demands, endured until they could coordinate one great uprising in 1680.
cards.h: → mobile bands → raids, no target → Spain buys peace; settled towns → occupied → coordinated revolt
cards.n: Borrows from u2 for the 1680 revolt. Describing each resistance without the difference and its cause earns nothing.
o: Settled farming peoples were easier to conquer and tax, which is why encomiendas and missions reached the Pueblos but not the Chichimeca.
Both forms pursued the same goals in KC-1.2.III.B: defending sovereignty, land, religion and livelihood.

w.a: The Pueblos resisted later because the Spanish never bothered them.
w.why: false; missions and labor demands weighed heavily on them

w.a: All Native peoples resisted Spain in exactly the same way.
w.why: ignores how settlement and mobility shaped resistance

cards.q: State the historiographical debate over how many people lived in the Americas before 1492.
cards.a: Low counts from early-1900s scholars such as James Mooney and Alfred Kroeber put North America north of Mexico near 1 million and the hemisphere under 10 million. From the 1960s Henry Dobyns argued for 90-112 million in the hemisphere (later about 18 million north of Mexico). Most scholars now accept middle figures, roughly 40-60 million for the hemisphere. Higher counts make the post-contact collapse larger and disease more central.
cards.h: → low estimates vs high estimates + why the number matters
cards.n: All figures are estimates from scarce evidence; the scored move is the low-versus-high debate and how the number changes the story of contact.

cards.q: Write a historically defensible thesis that establishes a line of reasoning for the prompt: 'Evaluate the extent to which transatlantic voyages from 1492 to 1607 changed societies in the Americas.'
cards.a: Transatlantic voyages transformed societies in the Caribbean, Mexico and Peru, where epidemics, the encomienda, silver mining and missions destroyed populations and rebuilt labor, religion and social order around a casta hierarchy; but most Native nations north of Mexico kept their land, government and economies to 1607, changed mainly by disease and new trade goods.
cards.h: → a position on extent + the categories that organize it
cards.n: 'Transatlantic voyages changed the Americas in many ways' restates the prompt and earns nothing; the thesis needs a position and a line of reasoning.

cards.q: Evaluate whether this thesis earns the thesis point, and revise it if it does not: 'The Columbian Exchange had many effects on both Europe and the Americas.'
cards.a: It does not earn the point: it restates the topic without a claim about which effects, how large, or why, so it sets up no line of reasoning. Revision: 'The Columbian Exchange devastated Native American societies through epidemic disease and the forced labor that followed, while it enriched Europe with silver and high-yield crops that fed population growth and commercial capitalism.' The revision makes a defensible claim with two lines of argument.
cards.n: Adding 'significant' or 'important' to a restated prompt still earns nothing; the thesis must say what the effects were and how the essay will argue them.

cards.q: Classify each cause of Spanish success against the Aztec and Inca empires as primary or secondary, with one phrase of reasoning: epidemic disease · Native allies · internal divisions of the empires · steel weapons and armor · horses · guns · Spanish religious zeal · interpreters such as Malintzin
cards.a:
Epidemic disease → primary; killed rulers, soldiers and farmers before and during the fighting
Native allies → primary; supplied most of the fighters, porters and food
Internal divisions (tribute resentment, the Inca civil war) → primary; created the allies and the openings Spain used
Steel weapons and armor → secondary; decisive only in close combat by small forces
Horses → secondary; frightening at first, limited in cities and mountains
Guns → secondary; few, slow and less important than steel
Religious zeal → secondary; drove the conquerors but did not win battles
Interpreters such as Malintzin → secondary but enabling; made the alliances possible
cards.h: → primary or secondary; reason, each case
cards.n: Rankings are arguable and earn credit only with the reason; making guns the primary cause is the classic error.

cards.q: Classify each effect of transatlantic voyages as short-term (clear within a generation of first contact) or long-term (unfolding over a century or more), and name the group most affected: smallpox in central Mexico · the Taino collapse · the fall of Tenochtitlan · Potosi silver reaching China · the Atlantic slave trade · horses on the Great Plains · American crops in European and Chinese diets · the casta hierarchy · the European price revolution · Catholic missions in New Mexico
cards.a:
Smallpox in central Mexico → short-term (1520); the Mexica and their neighbors
Taino collapse → short-term (1490s-1520s); the Taino of the Caribbean
Fall of Tenochtitlan → short-term (1521); the Mexica
Potosi silver in China → long-term (from the 1570s); Chinese merchants and the Ming economy
Atlantic slave trade → long-term (peaked in the 1700s); West and West-Central Africans
Horses on the Plains → long-term (mostly after 1680); Plains nations such as the Comanche
American crops in diets → long-term (1600s-1700s); peasants in Europe, Africa and China
Casta hierarchy → long-term (elaborated through the 1700s); mixed-ancestry and Native peoples
Price revolution → long-term (across the 1500s); Spanish and European wage earners and landlords
Missions in New Mexico → long-term (from 1598); the Pueblo peoples
cards.h: → short or long term; group affected, each case
cards.n: The label alone earns nothing; the scored reasoning (2.iii) is when the effect unfolded and on whom. Horses and the slave trade's peak borrow from later periods.

cards.q: Support the claim that epidemic disease was the most significant effect of transatlantic voyages on Native American societies from 1492 to 1607 with two pieces of specific evidence.
cards.a: The claim holds because disease shaped nearly every other outcome. Evidence 1: smallpox struck Tenochtitlan in 1520, killing the ruler Cuitlahuac and many defenders and enabling the Spanish-Tlaxcalan victory of 1521. Evidence 2: central Mexico's Native population fell by roughly 90 percent by about 1600 (estimates vary), and the resulting labor shortage pushed Spain toward labor drafts and enslaved Africans.
cards.h: → claim + two specific pieces, each tied back to it
cards.n: 'Many Native people died of disease' is not specific evidence; name a place, a date or figure, and the consequence that ties it to the claim.

cards.q: Explain the difference between a primary cause and a secondary cause, using the decline of the Native population of Hispaniola as the example.
cards.a: A primary cause does most of the work in producing an outcome; a secondary cause contributes to it or worsens it. On Hispaniola the ranking is debated: before smallpox arrived in 1518, forced labor under the encomienda, war and famine drove the Taino decline, so some historians rank exploitation primary; others rank disease primary because epidemics did the most killing overall. Either ranking earns credit if it is argued.
cards.h: → define both + apply to Hispaniola + justify a ranking
cards.n: Calling every cause 'important' avoids the task; the answer must rank the causes and justify the ranking.

cards.q: Explain how the development of transatlantic voyages affected West and West-Central African societies from the 1440s to 1607.
cards.a: The voyages tied African coastal states to an Atlantic economy. Portuguese traders from the 1440s exchanged cloth, metal goods and later guns for gold and captives; states such as Kongo gained trade and Christianity but were drawn into supplying enslaved people; after about 1518 the trade turned toward the Americas, where sugar and mines created steady demand; and American crops such as maize and cassava began entering African farming.
cards.h: → three effects, each with an example
cards.n: 'Africans were enslaved' alone earns nothing; the effects include African states' role in the trade, its redirection to the Americas, and new crops.

cards.q: Explain why the demographic collapse of Native peoples, rather than military conquest alone, is often judged the most significant effect of contact in Period 1.
cards.a: Disease reached further and cut deeper than any army. Epidemics killed most of the population in contacted regions, often ahead of Europeans, and nearly every other change followed from it: rapid conquest, the labor shortage behind the encomienda and African slavery, and emptied lands Europeans later claimed.
cards.h: → disease outruns armies → most people die → enables conquest, labor shortage, slavery, land claims
cards.n: Asserting significance without tying the collapse to later effects earns nothing; relative significance needs a comparison with conquest.
o: Conquest changed who ruled a region; demographic collapse changed who lived there at all, which shaped every later period.
Many Native societies that never met a Spanish soldier were reshaped by epidemics traveling along trade routes.

w.a: The collapse mattered most because it made Europeans feel sorry for Native peoples.
w.why: sentiment is not a causal effect

w.a: Military conquest was the only effect of contact that really mattered.
w.why: ignores the epidemics that did most of the killing

cards.q: Explain why transatlantic voyages led to the rise of the Atlantic slave trade.
cards.a: The voyages opened American mines and sugar lands needing more labor than collapsing Native populations could supply. Portugal already bought captives on the West African coast, so ships joined that supply to American demand; by about 1600 enslaved Africans were the main labor on Brazilian and Caribbean plantations.
cards.h: → American mines and sugar + Native collapse → labor demand → existing Portuguese-African trade → Atlantic slave trade
cards.n: 'Demand for labor' alone earns little; connect it to the Native collapse and the existing Portuguese-African trade.
o: Legal limits on enslaving Native peoples, such as the New Laws of 1542, steered colonial demand toward Africans.
Better ships and organized trade made regular ocean crossings possible, turning a coastal trade into an Atlantic one.

w.a: The slave trade began because Africans wanted to move to the Americas.
w.why: false; it was forced migration

w.a: The Atlantic slave trade started in 1619 when Africans reached Virginia.
w.why: it began a century earlier in the Caribbean and Brazil

cards.q: Explain why American silver had different long-term effects on Spain than on the rest of Europe.
cards.a: Spain received the silver but spent it on wars, debts to foreign bankers and imports, so it fed inflation at home and repeated royal bankruptcies (1557, 1575 and 1596, among others). The coin flowed on to Genoese, German and Dutch financiers and manufacturers, building commercial wealth elsewhere in Europe.
cards.h: → silver to Spain → spent on wars, debts, imports → inflation and bankruptcy → wealth grows in rival economies
cards.n: The contrast is the task: Spain's wealth described without the effects elsewhere earns nothing.
o: While bullion paid the crown's bills, Spain had little incentive to build its own industry, so silver produced dependence rather than development.
The same flow financed European purchases of Asian goods, so much of the silver ended up in China.

w.a: American silver made Spain permanently the richest country in Europe.
w.why: ignores the bankruptcies and relative decline

w.a: American silver had the same effect everywhere in Europe.
w.why: misses the contrast the question asks for

cards.q: Explain why the thesis that 'the Columbian Exchange benefited Europe and harmed the Americas' needs qualification to show a complex understanding.
cards.a: It holds broadly but hides exceptions on both sides. Some Native peoples gained, as Tlaxcala did at first from alliance and Plains nations later did from horses, and Europe's gains were uneven, with Spain's silver ending in inflation and bankruptcy. It also leaves out Africa, which lost millions to the slave trade.
cards.h: → pattern holds → exceptions: Native gains, uneven European gains, Africa's losses → qualified thesis
cards.n: Tacking 'however, it was complicated' onto the thesis earns nothing; complexity must be explained with specific evidence.
o: Explaining gains and costs within one society, such as maize feeding Europe while silver inflation hurt its wage earners, is another route to complexity.
Adding Asia, where American crops and silver reshaped Chinese diets and currency, connects the argument across regions.

w.a: The Columbian Exchange helped everyone equally, so the thesis is wrong.
w.why: replaces one oversimplification with another

w.a: The thesis is complex already because it mentions two continents.
w.why: naming two places is not nuance

cards.q: Explain why European goods and diseases affected Native societies in the North American interior before Europeans settled there.
cards.a: Native trade networks carried both ahead of the colonists. Metal tools, beads and cloth passed inland from coastal exchanges along existing routes, and epidemics spread through the same contacts, so interior peoples felt contact through new goods, trade rivalries and population loss decades before meeting settlers.
cards.h: → existing Native trade networks → goods and germs travel inland → new rivalries and losses before settlement
cards.n: How far early epidemics reached the interior is debated; an answer claiming total collapse everywhere overstates the evidence.
o: De Soto's expedition (1539-1542) spread disease and disruption along its route, and several Southeast chiefdoms it met had shrunk or vanished when later Spaniards arrived.
Control of European goods could shift power among Native nations, so contact reshaped relations among Native peoples as well as with Europeans.

w.a: Interior peoples were unaffected until Europeans settled among them.
w.why: ignores goods and epidemics moving along Native routes

w.a: European goods reached the interior because Europeans built roads there.
w.why: Native trade networks carried them

cards.q: Date the founding of Jamestown and name the company that financed it.
cards.a: 1607, founded by the Virginia Company of London, a joint-stock company seeking profit for its investors.
cards.n: Profit motive, not religion, launched the Chesapeake - the standard opening contrast with New England.

cards.q: Explain how tobacco saved and shaped the Virginia colony.
cards.a: John Rolfe's 1612 cultivation of a sweeter West Indian tobacco strain gave Virginia a profitable export. Tobacco's heavy labor demands and soil exhaustion drove constant expansion inland onto Native land and created an insatiable appetite for indentured and later enslaved labor.
cards.n: Theme WXT. The cash crop explains land hunger, Native conflict, and the labor shift in one causal chain.

cards.q: Define the headright system.
cards.a: A Virginia policy granting about 50 acres of land to anyone who paid the Atlantic passage of a settler, including for each indentured servant imported. It rewarded wealthy planters who imported many servants, concentrating land in few hands.
cards.n: Explains why Chesapeake landholding was unequal and why freed servants found no good land - the root of Bacon's Rebellion.

cards.q: Identify the House of Burgesses and give its founding year.
cards.a: Established in 1619 in Virginia, it was the first representative legislative assembly in English North America, elected by landowning colonists to make local laws alongside the company or royal governor.
cards.n: 1619 is a triple date: House of Burgesses, first Africans at Point Comfort, and arrival of women settlers.

cards.q: Define indentured servitude.
cards.a: A labor contract in which a poor English migrant traded four to seven years of unpaid labor for Atlantic passage, food, and shelter, plus 'freedom dues' at the end. Servants were legally temporary, could sue in court, and were overwhelmingly young single men.
cards.n: Key contrast: indenture was a status one exited; slavery became lifelong, hereditary, and racial.

cards.q: Identify Bacon's Rebellion and give its year.
cards.a: In 1676 Nathaniel Bacon led frontier farmers, former indentured servants, and some enslaved and free Black Virginians against Governor William Berkeley, attacking Native villages and burning Jamestown after Berkeley refused to wage war on Natives to open more land.
cards.n: Note the biracial coalition of poor laborers - that is exactly what terrified the planter elite.

cards.q: Explain the long-term consequences of Bacon's Rebellion.
cards.a: Elite planters, alarmed by an armed alliance of poor whites and Black laborers, shifted decisively from indentured servants to enslaved Africans and hardened racial law. Granting poor whites racial privilege split the lower classes and stabilized planter rule.
cards.n: Among the highest-yield causation arguments in P2; pairs directly with the 1705 slave codes.

cards.q: Identify the Virginia slave codes of 1705.
cards.a: A consolidated body of law defining enslaved people as chattel property, making slave status hereditary through the mother, stripping enslaved people of legal rights, barring interracial marriage, and granting poor whites legal privileges over all Black people.
cards.h: → what the law fixed in place
cards.n: Theme SOC. Shows race was constructed by law over decades, not present at the first Africans' arrival in 1619.

cards.q: Identify the Pilgrims and the Mayflower Compact.
cards.a: Separatists who broke entirely from the Church of England, landed at Plymouth in 1620, and, lacking a charter for that site, signed the Mayflower Compact - an agreement to form a civil body politic and obey laws made by the majority.
cards.n: Early self-government by consent; often paired with the House of Burgesses on 'colonial democracy' questions.

cards.q: Identify the founding of Massachusetts Bay Colony.
cards.a: Founded in 1630 when roughly 1,000 Puritans led by John Winthrop migrated during the Great Migration. Unlike Plymouth's Separatists, they sought to purify the Church of England from within and built a Bible commonwealth centered on Boston.
cards.n: Family-based migration gave New England balanced sex ratios and rapid natural population growth.

cards.q: Explain what John Winthrop meant by a 'city upon a hill.'
cards.a: In his 1630 sermon A Model of Christian Charity, Winthrop told Puritan settlers their covenanted community would be watched by the world as a model of godly society - so failure would disgrace the reform cause. It was a warning of obligation, not a boast.
cards.n: Classic sourcing trap: modern politicians use it as triumphalism; Winthrop meant scrutiny and duty.

cards.q: Contrast Separatists and non-separating Puritans.
cards.a: Separatists (the Pilgrims at Plymouth) considered the Church of England beyond saving and withdrew from it completely. Non-separating Puritans (Massachusetts Bay) remained formally within the Anglican Church, intending to reform it and offer a purified model.
cards.n: A small distinction that shows precision; both were Calvinists seeking their own community, not toleration.

cards.q: Identify Roger Williams and what he founded.
cards.a: A Puritan minister banished from Massachusetts in 1635 for arguing that church and state must be separated and that the king could not grant land already owned by Native peoples. He founded Providence, Rhode Island, in 1636 with religious liberty and purchased Native land.
cards.n: Rhode Island becomes the standard example of dissent producing religious toleration.

cards.q: Identify Anne Hutchinson and the charges against her.
cards.a: A Boston woman who held religious meetings in her home and taught that believers could receive grace directly from God without clergy mediation (antinomianism). Tried and sentenced to banishment in 1637 and expelled in 1638, she challenged both Puritan orthodoxy and women's prescribed role.
cards.n: Serves both the religion and SOC/gender themes; strongest P2 evidence of women challenging authority.

cards.q: Define the Halfway Covenant and give its year.
cards.a: A 1662 compromise letting the baptized but unconverted children of church members have their own children baptized, granting them partial, non-voting membership. It kept declining congregations attached to the church.
cards.n: Direct evidence of waning Puritan zeal by the second and third generations.

cards.q: Identify the Pequot War.
cards.a: A 1636-1637 conflict in which Massachusetts Bay and Connecticut settlers, allied with the Narragansett and Mohegan, destroyed the Pequot as a power in southern New England - including the burning of a fortified village at Mystic that killed hundreds of non-combatants.
cards.n: Shows English use of Native alliances and the early pattern of total war over land.

cards.q: Identify King Philip's War (Metacom's War).
cards.a: A 1675-1676 uprising in which Metacom, called King Philip, united Wampanoag, Nipmuc, and Narragansett against expanding New England settlements. Proportionally the deadliest war in American history, it destroyed dozens of towns but ended Native military power in southern New England.
cards.n: Pairs with Bacon's Rebellion, in the same years, as the twin land-hunger crises of the 1670s.

cards.q: Contrast the Pequot War and King Philip's War in scale and consequence.
cards.a: The Pequot War destroyed a single nation and opened the Connecticut valley early in settlement. King Philip's War was a pan-Native coalition four decades later, far bloodier for both sides, and it permanently ended Native military resistance in southern New England.
cards.n: Continuity of English land pressure; change in Native strategy from single nation to coalition.

cards.q: Identify the Quakers and their core beliefs.
cards.a: The Society of Friends believed in an 'inner light' of God in every person, which implied spiritual equality of men and women, no ordained clergy, refusal to swear oaths or defer to social superiors, pacifism, and early opposition to slavery.
cards.n: Their egalitarianism made them persecuted everywhere else - the context for Pennsylvania's toleration.

cards.q: Identify William Penn and the founding of Pennsylvania.
cards.a: A wealthy Quaker granted Pennsylvania in 1681 as a proprietary colony and 'holy experiment.' He guaranteed religious toleration and representative government, advertised widely in Europe, and initially purchased land from the Lenape rather than seizing it.
cards.n: Toleration plus fertile land made Philadelphia the fastest-growing and most ethnically diverse colonial city.

cards.q: Identify the defining economic and social features of the Middle Colonies.
cards.a: New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and Delaware exported wheat and grain as the 'breadbasket,' held the most ethnically and religiously diverse populations (Dutch, German, Scots-Irish, Quaker, Jewish), used a mix of family farms and some slave labor, and had thriving port cities.
cards.n: Their diversity is the standard contrast with homogeneous Puritan New England.

cards.q: Contrast New England and the Chesapeake in motive, labor, and demographics.
cards.a: New England was settled by Puritan families for religious community, with mixed farming, fishing, shipbuilding, long life expectancy, and balanced sex ratios. The Chesapeake was settled by young single men for profit, with tobacco monoculture, indentured then enslaved labor, high mortality, and few women.
cards.n: The single most tested P2 comparison; memorize both columns.

cards.q: Contrast the Middle Colonies with New England in society and religion.
cards.a: New England was ethnically English, religiously Puritan, town-centered, and intolerant of dissent. The Middle Colonies were ethnically and religiously plural, with dispersed commercial farms, larger landholdings, and legal toleration.
cards.n: Middle Colony pluralism is often cited as a root of American diversity in LEQs.

cards.q: Identify the economy and labor system of South Carolina and the British Caribbean.
cards.a: Rice and indigo in the Carolina lowcountry and sugar in Barbados and Jamaica used large plantations worked by enslaved Africans under brutal task and gang systems. Enslaved people formed a majority of the population, and West African rice-growing expertise was central to lowcountry success.
cards.n: Black majorities produced both the harshest slave codes and the strongest retention of African culture (Gullah).

cards.q: Contrast slavery in the Chesapeake with slavery in South Carolina and the West Indies.
cards.a: Chesapeake slavery centered on tobacco, smaller units, closer white supervision, and by the 1700s a self-reproducing enslaved population. Lowcountry and Caribbean slavery used larger sugar and rice gangs, had far higher death rates requiring constant importation, and left Black majorities greater cultural autonomy.
cards.n: Guards against treating 'slavery' as one uniform institution - a sophistication point.

cards.q: Define mercantilism.
cards.a: The economic theory that global wealth is fixed, so a nation grows powerful by exporting more than it imports and hoarding bullion. Colonies existed to supply cheap raw materials and to buy the mother country's manufactured goods exclusively.
cards.n: Theme WXT/WOR. Sets up the entire logic of imperial regulation and later colonial resentment.

cards.q: Identify the Navigation Acts.
cards.a: A series of English laws beginning in 1651 requiring that colonial trade travel in English or colonial ships, that 'enumerated' goods such as tobacco and sugar be shipped only to England, and that most European imports pass through England first.
cards.n: They were loosely enforced before 1763; strict enforcement afterward is what felt 'new' to colonists.

cards.q: Explain both the costs and the benefits of the Navigation Acts for the colonies.
cards.a: Costs: restricted markets, higher prices, and suppressed colonial manufacturing. Benefits: protected markets for tobacco and other staples, a booming colonial shipbuilding industry, and the protection of the Royal Navy. Widespread smuggling blunted the burden further.
cards.n: A balanced answer earns complexity credit; avoid claiming the Acts alone caused the Revolution.

cards.q: Define the triangular trade.
cards.a: The Atlantic trading pattern in which New England rum and manufactured goods went to West Africa, enslaved Africans were carried to the Caribbean and mainland colonies, and sugar, molasses, and staple crops returned to New England and Europe.
cards.n: A simplified model - real routes were messier - but it correctly ties New England's economy to slavery.

cards.q: Define the Middle Passage.
cards.a: The forced Atlantic voyage of enslaved Africans from West Africa to the Americas, lasting weeks to months in packed, unsanitary holds. Roughly 15 percent died en route; about 12.5 million Africans were embarked over the trade's history.
cards.n: Only about 4-5 percent of that total came to British North America; most went to Brazil and the Caribbean.

cards.q: Identify the Stono Rebellion and give its year.
cards.a: In 1739 about 20 enslaved people, many from Kongo and with military experience, seized weapons near the Stono River in South Carolina and marched toward Spanish Florida, which offered freedom. The largest slave uprising in the mainland colonies, it was crushed within days.
cards.n: Note the Spanish Florida pull factor - an imperial-rivalry angle graders like.

cards.q: Explain the consequences of the Stono Rebellion.
cards.a: South Carolina's Negro Act of 1740 banned enslaved people from assembling, growing food, earning money, and learning to read, tightened slave patrols, and temporarily taxed slave imports. Repression tightened precisely because a Black majority made planters fearful.
cards.n: Same pattern as Bacon's Rebellion: revolt from below produces harsher racial law from above.

cards.q: Identify the everyday forms of resistance used by enslaved people.
cards.a: Beyond open revolt: work slowdowns, feigned illness, breaking tools, theft, running away, maintaining African naming, music, language, and religious practice, and building family and kinship networks despite sale.
cards.n: Essential for arguing agency when open rebellion was suicidal; strong SOC/NAT evidence.

cards.q: Define salutary neglect.
cards.a: Britain's informal policy from roughly 1690 to 1763 of loosely enforcing trade laws and letting colonial assemblies govern themselves, on the theory that prosperous, unbothered colonies enriched the empire.
cards.n: The habit of self-rule it created is why post-1763 enforcement felt like tyranny rather than ordinary rule.

cards.q: Explain why salutary neglect matters for understanding the coming Revolution.
cards.a: Decades of light enforcement let colonial assemblies control taxation and pay governors' salaries, building genuine self-government and an expectation of autonomy. When Britain reversed course after 1763, colonists saw the change as stripping rights they already possessed.
cards.n: The best single bridge sentence from Period 2 into Period 3.

cards.q: Define the First Great Awakening.
cards.a: A wave of emotional Protestant revivals peaking in the 1730s and 1740s that stressed personal conversion, direct emotional experience of God, and individual judgment of preaching over deference to established, educated clergy.
cards.n: Theme SOC/PCE. The first genuinely intercolonial shared experience.

cards.q: Identify Jonathan Edwards and his most famous sermon.
cards.a: A Northampton, Massachusetts Congregational minister whose 1741 sermon 'Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God' used vivid imagery of damnation to provoke conversion, blending strict Calvinist theology with Enlightenment reasoning.
cards.n: Edwards is the intellectual pole of the Awakening; Whitefield is the popular pole.

cards.q: Identify George Whitefield.
cards.a: An English itinerant preacher who toured the colonies repeatedly from 1739, drawing outdoor crowds of thousands with a dramatic, theatrical style, advertising aggressively in newspapers, and preaching to enslaved people and poor colonists alike.
cards.n: The first true intercolonial celebrity - evidence of an emerging shared American public.

cards.q: Explain the political significance of the First Great Awakening.
cards.a: By encouraging ordinary people to judge ministers for themselves it undermined deference to established authority, split congregations into New Lights and Old Lights, spurred new colleges such as Princeton, spread across colonial borders, and rehearsed the questioning of authority later aimed at Britain.
cards.n: High-yield causation for LEQs on the ideological origins of the Revolution.

cards.q: Contrast New Lights and Old Lights.
cards.a: New Lights embraced revivalism, emotional conversion, and itinerant preaching, often without formal training. Old Lights defended educated, ordained clergy, settled congregations, and orderly worship, condemning revivals as emotional excess.
cards.n: The split itself matters: religious pluralism grew because neither side could suppress the other.

cards.q: Explain how Enlightenment ideas reached and influenced the colonies.
cards.a: Through print, colleges, and correspondence, colonists absorbed Locke's natural rights and social contract, Montesquieu's separation of powers, and a faith in reason and empirical science. Figures such as Benjamin Franklin embodied it, and these ideas supplied the vocabulary of the Declaration and the Constitution.
cards.n: Theme NAT/ARC. Name Locke specifically - graders reward the named source of 'consent of the governed.'

cards.q: Contrast the Enlightenment and the First Great Awakening as forces in colonial life.
cards.a: The Enlightenment appealed to reason, science, and natural law, mainly among educated elites. The Great Awakening appealed to emotion, personal revelation, and mass participation. Both, however, elevated individual judgment over inherited authority and so weakened deference.
cards.n: The shared effect is the sophistication move: opposite methods, converging political consequence.

cards.q: Identify the Salem witch trials and give the year.
cards.a: In 1692 accusations in Salem Village, Massachusetts led to the trials of over 150 people and the execution of 20, most of them women. Tensions between commercial Salem Town and farming Salem Village, frontier war anxiety, and Puritan gender expectations all fed the panic.
cards.n: Use it as evidence of social strain in a changing Puritan society, not merely superstition.

cards.q: Explain the Anglicization and consumer revolution of the eighteenth-century colonies.
cards.a: Rising prosperity let colonists buy British manufactured goods - tea, cloth, ceramics, furniture - on credit, while adopting British legal forms, print culture, and gentility. Colonists became more British in taste even as they governed themselves more independently.
cards.n: This paradox explains why boycotts of British goods later became such a potent political weapon.

cards.q: Place these Period 2 events in chronological order: Bacon's Rebellion, founding of Massachusetts Bay, Stono Rebellion, House of Burgesses, Salem witch trials.
cards.a: House of Burgesses 1619; Massachusetts Bay 1630; Bacon's Rebellion 1676; Salem witch trials 1692; Stono Rebellion 1739.
cards.n: Notice the 1670s cluster: Bacon's Rebellion and King Philip's War both erupt over land within a year.

cards.q: Place these colonial foundings in order with years: Pennsylvania, Plymouth, Massachusetts Bay, Jamestown.
cards.a: Jamestown 1607; Plymouth 1620; Massachusetts Bay 1630; Pennsylvania 1681.
cards.n: The 50-year gap before Pennsylvania explains why the Middle Colonies drew a later, more diverse migration.

cards.q: Contrast the Chesapeake labor force around 1650 with the labor force around 1720.
cards.a: Around 1650 most bound laborers were white English indentured servants on temporary contracts, with few Africans and no settled racial law. By 1720 the workforce was predominantly enslaved Africans held for life under hereditary, race-based slave codes, and indenture had faded.
cards.n: The cleanest CCOT card in P2: falling English migration, rising life expectancy, and Bacon's Rebellion all drove the shift.

cards.q: Identify New Netherland and New Amsterdam.
cards.a: A Dutch colony centered on the Hudson River, founded by the Dutch West India Company to control the fur trade, with its main port and capital at New Amsterdam on Manhattan Island. It was known for religious and ethnic diversity and the patroon system of large manorial land grants.
cards.n: Its diversity and commercial focus foreshadow New York's later character even after the English took over.

cards.q: Date the English seizure of New Netherland and its renaming as New York.
cards.a: 1664. English forces under the Duke of York took the colony from the Dutch without a fight and renamed New Amsterdam as New York City; the Dutch briefly recaptured it in 1673 before permanently ceding it in 1674.
cards.n: It closed the gap between New England and the Chesapeake and left New York with Dutch patroon estates and unusual ethnic diversity.

cards.q: Identify New France and its fur-trade-based economy.
cards.a: A French colony centered on the St. Lawrence River, founded at Quebec in 1608, that stayed thinly populated and built its economy around the fur trade rather than large-scale farming, relying on close alliances and intermarriage with Native peoples such as the Huron.
cards.n: Contrast with English land-hungry settler colonies, which needed Native land more than Native alliance.

cards.q: Identify James Oglethorpe and the founding of Georgia.
cards.a: A British philanthropist and soldier who founded Georgia in 1732-33 as a buffer colony against Spanish Florida and a haven for imprisoned debtors, funded by trustees rather than a profit-seeking company.
cards.n: Georgia was the last of the thirteen colonies founded and, unusually, was explicitly non-profit at first.

cards.q: Explain why Georgia's trustees originally banned slavery and hard liquor, and why the ban collapsed.
cards.a: Trustees wanted a colony of small, sober, self-sufficient farmer-soldiers who could defend the border, not planters competing with South Carolina's slave economy. Colonists agitated for slavery to compete economically, and the trustees lifted the ban in 1751.
cards.n: Shows that Georgia's slave society emerged by colonist demand, not original design.

cards.q: Identify the Dominion of New England and Sir Edmund Andros.
cards.a: A 1686 consolidation of Massachusetts, Connecticut, New York, and other northern colonies into a single royal province under Governor Edmund Andros, who abolished colonial assemblies and enforced the Navigation Acts, provoking deep colonial resentment.
cards.h: → consolidated colonies + governor + what he abolished
cards.n: The Glorious Revolution doomed it; Bostonians jailed Andros in 1689, a precedent colonists cited again in the 1760s.

cards.q: Explain how the Glorious Revolution of 1688-89 affected the American colonies.
cards.a: News of William and Mary's overthrow of James II let Bostonians arrest Andros and dissolve the hated Dominion of New England, while Jacob Leisler briefly seized control of New York in Leisler's Rebellion. Colonial assemblies and charters were largely restored.
cards.h: → England's revolution → colonial uprisings → assemblies restored
cards.n: Shows colonists invoking English constitutional rights against royal overreach, a rehearsal for 1776.

cards.q: Identify the Zenger trial of 1735 and its significance.
cards.a: New York printer John Peter Zenger was tried for seditious libel after criticizing the royal governor. His lawyer argued that true statements could not be libel, and the jury acquitted him, an early precedent for freedom of the press in the colonies.
cards.n: Not binding law, but a powerful precedent later cited in First Amendment debates.

cards.q: Define the Molasses Act of 1733.
cards.a: A British law placing a heavy duty on molasses imported into the colonies from non-British Caribbean islands, meant to protect British West Indian sugar planters. Colonial merchants evaded it so routinely through smuggling that it raised little revenue.
cards.n: Its widespread evasion previewed the smuggling culture Britain tried to crack down on after 1763.

cards.q: Differentiate the task system from the gang system of enslaved labor.
cards.a: Under the task system, common in South Carolina rice country, enslaved workers were assigned a daily quota and had time to themselves once it was done. Under the gang system, common in Chesapeake tobacco fields, enslaved workers labored in close-supervised groups for fixed hours all day.
cards.h: → quota + own time vs. supervised group + fixed hours
cards.n: The task system gave enslaved South Carolinians more autonomy to farm, trade, and sustain community life.

cards.q: Contrast Dutch and French colonization with English colonization in settler population and land use.
cards.a: The Dutch and French built small trading-post colonies focused on furs, with few settlers and dependence on Native alliances. The English, seeking farmland for large families, sent far more settlers and steadily displaced Native peoples from the land.
cards.n: This is why most Native nations sided with France in 1754: French traders wanted pelts, while English families wanted the land itself.

cards.q: Explain the 'Barbados connection' in South Carolina's founding.
cards.a: South Carolina was founded in 1670 partly by planters from the overcrowded sugar island of Barbados, who brought Caribbean-style slave codes and a Black-majority, profit-driven plantation model directly to the mainland.
cards.h: → Caribbean planters → harsh slave codes imported
cards.n: Explains why South Carolina's slave society more closely resembled the Caribbean than the Chesapeake.

cards.q: Define a redemptioner.
cards.a: An immigrant, often German, who received passage to the colonies on credit and had to work off the debt after arrival, similar to an indentured servant but sometimes allowed the family to negotiate terms once the ship docked.
cards.h: → debt for passage + who used it
cards.n: Common route for Pennsylvania's German ('Pennsylvania Dutch') settlers.

cards.q: Identify the German and Scots-Irish immigrants who settled the Middle Colonies and backcountry.
cards.a: Germans, fleeing war and religious persecution, settled heavily in Pennsylvania farmland, while Scots-Irish Presbyterians pushed into the Appalachian backcountry from Pennsylvania south into the Carolinas, making the Middle Colonies the most ethnically diverse region.
cards.n: Backcountry Scots-Irish settlement is the source of the Paxton Boys and Regulator conflicts and of lasting east versus west resentment.

cards.q: Identify Tisquantum (Squanto) and his role in the Plymouth colony's survival.
cards.a: A Patuxet man who had learned English after being kidnapped by an English sea captain years earlier. He taught the Plymouth Pilgrims to plant corn and fish, and served as interpreter with the Wampanoag sachem Massasoit in 1621.
cards.n: The 1621 harvest feast popularly called the 'First Thanksgiving' was a diplomatic event, not the origin of the national holiday, which dates to Lincoln's 1863 proclamation.

cards.q: Define feme covert and its effect on colonial women's legal status.
cards.a: The common-law doctrine that a married woman's legal identity merged into her husband's, so she could not own property, sign contracts, or sue in her own name. An unmarried woman, a feme sole, retained those legal rights.
cards.n: The Revolution left coverture untouched; married women's property acts only began chipping away at it in the 1830s and 1840s.

cards.q: Explain why most people accused of witchcraft at Salem in 1692 were women.
cards.a: Most accused were women, especially those who were widowed, unmarried, or held property outside male control, since they defied expectations of female subordination. Economic anxiety and family land disputes in Salem Village sharpened suspicion of such women.
cards.h: → women outside male control + land disputes
cards.n: Historian Carol Karlsen's research on Salem found accused women disproportionately stood to inherit property, undercutting purely religious explanations.

cards.q: Explain the push and pull factors that drew German and Scots-Irish migrants to the colonial backcountry in the early eighteenth century.
cards.a: Push factors included land scarcity, high rents, and religious persecution in the German Palatinate and Ulster. Pull factors included cheap Pennsylvania land, religious toleration, and reports from earlier migrants, drawing both groups down the Great Wagon Road into the backcountry.
cards.n: The Scots-Irish backcountry migration also intensified conflict with Native peoples already settled in the Appalachian foothills.

cards.q: Define the putting-out system of colonial household production.
cards.a: A system in which merchants supplied raw materials, such as wool or flax, to rural families who spun and wove them into cloth at home for a set fee, allowing manufacturing to happen outside any central workshop.
cards.n: The putting-out system persisted alongside factories well into the nineteenth century in trades like shoemaking.

cards.q: Identify Henry Hudson's 1609 voyage and the claim it gave the Dutch.
cards.a: Hudson, sailing for the Dutch East India Company, explored the river that bears his name in 1609, giving the Netherlands its claim to the region that became New Netherland.
cards.n: He was an Englishman hunting a Northwest Passage to Asia, so the Dutch claim was the by-product of a failed search.

cards.q: Identify the Covenant Chain linking the Iroquois Confederacy to the English colonies.
cards.a: A series of alliances beginning in the 1670s between the Iroquois Confederacy and English colonial governments, especially New York, coordinating trade and diplomacy and giving the Iroquois leverage as brokers between the English and other Native nations.
cards.n: Iroquois diplomatic leverage from the Covenant Chain declined sharply after their losses in the Revolution.

cards.q: Identify the Tuscarora War of 1711-1715 and its long-term result for the Iroquois Confederacy.
cards.a: A war between North Carolina settlers and the Tuscarora people that ended in Tuscarora defeat. Many survivors migrated north and were adopted into the Iroquois Confederacy around 1722, making it the Six Nations.
cards.n: The Yamasee War in South Carolina followed immediately, and both grew from trader abuses and the southern trade in enslaved Native people.

cards.q: Explain the economic importance of naval stores production in colonial North Carolina.
cards.a: Colonists tapped the region's pine forests for tar, pitch, and turpentine used to waterproof and maintain British naval ships. Parliament paid bounties for naval stores to reduce dependence on Baltic imports, tying North Carolina's economy to the Royal Navy's needs.
cards.n: A clean example of mercantilism steering a colonial economy; poor harbors still left North Carolina less wealthy than Virginia or South Carolina.

cards.q: Explain the economic role colonial women played as 'deputy husbands' managing farms and businesses.
cards.a: Wives routinely ran farms, shops, and even ships' business affairs when husbands traveled or died, despite lacking independent legal standing. This practical authority, though temporary and derivative of a husband's, gave many women real economic experience.
cards.h: → practical authority despite no legal standing
cards.n: The term comes from historian Laurel Thatcher Ulrich; the authority was borrowed and evaporated the moment a husband returned.

cards.q: Identify the Massachusetts School Law of 1647 (the 'Old Deluder Satan' Act).
cards.a: A law requiring Massachusetts towns of 50 or more families to hire a schoolteacher and towns of 100 or more to establish a grammar school, so children could read the Bible and resist Satan's deception through ignorance.
cards.n: This law is the direct ancestor of the American tradition of public, tax-funded education.

cards.q: Identify Eliza Lucas Pinckney and her development of indigo as a South Carolina cash crop.
cards.a: A young planter who, managing her father's South Carolina estates in the 1740s, experimented with West Indian indigo seed until she produced a marketable dye crop. Indigo became the colony's second staple alongside rice.
cards.n: Indigo depended on a British bounty, so the crop collapsed once independence cut South Carolina off from that subsidy.

cards.q: Date Jonathan Edwards's Northampton revival and George Whitefield's colonial preaching tour in sequence.
cards.a: Edwards's Northampton, Massachusetts revival began in 1734-1735; Whitefield's colony-wide preaching tour, which turned local revivals into a shared intercolonial movement, ran from 1739 to 1741.
cards.h: → Edwards local first, then Whitefield intercolonial
cards.n: The resulting Old Light and New Light split founded colleges such as Princeton and Dartmouth and taught colonists to question established authority.

cards.q: Identify the ship that brought the first documented Africans to English Virginia in 1619.
cards.a: The White Lion, an English privateer sailing under a Dutch flag, seized African captives from a Portuguese slave ship and sold about twenty of them at Point Comfort, Virginia, in 1619. The Dutch West India Company was not chartered until 1621, two years later.
cards.n: Their exact legal status in 1619, servant or slave, remains debated; Virginia's slave codes did not formalize hereditary racial slavery until decades later.

cards.q: Date the boundary years of AP Period 2 and name the event that marks each end.
cards.a: Period 2 runs from 1607, the founding of Jamestown, to 1754, the start of the French and Indian War, covering the growth of England's mainland colonies into distinct regional societies.
cards.n: Period 2 prompts are about regional difference and imperial neglect; the road to revolution belongs to Period 3, which opens in 1754.

cards.q: Identify John Locke and his theory of natural rights and government by consent.
cards.a: An English philosopher whose 'Two Treatises of Government' (1689) argued people possess natural rights to life, liberty, and property, and that legitimate government rests on the consent of the governed and may be overthrown if it violates that trust.
cards.h: → natural rights + consent + right to overthrow
cards.n: Locke's language is the direct source for Jefferson's 'life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.'

cards.q: State the approximate number of enslaved Africans brought to British North America specifically.
cards.a: Roughly 305,000 enslaved Africans arrived in British North America across the entire slave trade, a small share of the roughly 12.5 million taken from Africa, since most captives were sent to Brazil and the Caribbean instead.
cards.h: → ~305,000 to British North America, a small slice of the total
cards.n: Surprises students who assume most of the trade landed in the future United States.

cards.q: Identify the New York Conspiracy of 1741.
cards.a: A panic in which New York City authorities, fearing a plot by enslaved and poor white residents to burn the city and revolt, executed roughly 30 Black New Yorkers and 4 whites on often flimsy evidence extracted under threat.
cards.n: New York held the largest urban enslaved population outside Charleston, and the panic works as a northern parallel to Salem in 1692.

cards.q: Identify Maryland's Act of Toleration of 1649.
cards.a: A law granting religious freedom to all Christians, passed to protect Maryland's Catholic minority as Protestant settlement grew. It was among the earliest religious toleration laws in English America, though it did not extend to non-Christians.
cards.n: A frequent 'religion in the colonies' card; pairs with Rhode Island as America's two toleration pioneers.

cards.q: Identify Opechancanough's 1622 uprising against Jamestown.
cards.a: The Powhatan leader Opechancanough coordinated a surprise attack that killed roughly a quarter of Virginia's English settlers in a single day, ending hopes of peaceful coexistence and prompting a war of extermination against the Powhatan.
cards.n: He struck again in 1644, and the 1622 disaster is what moved the crown to revoke the Virginia Company charter in 1624.

cards.q: State the approximate population of Britain's mainland colonies by 1750.
cards.a: About 1.2 million people lived in the thirteen colonies by 1750, nearly five times the population of 1700 (about 250,000), driven by natural increase, the slave trade, and mounting immigration from Germany, Scotland, and Ireland.
cards.n: Franklin noticed the population doubling roughly every 25 years; New France, by contrast, held only about 70,000 settlers.

cards.q: Identify South Carolina's 1696 slave code and its origin.
cards.a: South Carolina adopted a slave code modeled directly on Barbados's harsh 1661 code, reflecting the direct migration of Barbadian planters and their labor system to the Carolina Lowcountry.
cards.n: The Stono Rebellion of 1739 then produced the harsher Negro Act of 1740, which banned literacy and assembly outright.

cards.q: Date when the enslaved population came to outnumber indentured servants as the Chesapeake's main labor force.
cards.a: By around 1700 enslaved Africans had become the dominant Chesapeake labor force, replacing indentured servants who had supplied most labor through the 1670s, as Virginia's enslaved population grew from a few hundred in 1650 to tens of thousands by 1700.
cards.n: Bacon's Rebellion in 1676 is the usual hinge, but rising English wages also dried up the supply of willing servants.

cards.q: State the approximate number of Puritans who migrated to New England during the Great Migration.
cards.a: Roughly 20,000 Puritans crossed to New England between 1630 and 1640, a single decade of migration that established most of the region's founding towns before English emigration slowed sharply.
cards.n: They came in whole families, so New England grew mainly by natural increase, unlike the young male servant flow into the Chesapeake.

cards.q: Identify William Penn's 'Holy Experiment.'
cards.a: Penn's design for Pennsylvania as a Quaker refuge combining religious toleration for all faiths, fair purchase of land from the Lenape, and representative government, intended to prove that peace and liberty could coexist with prosperity.
cards.h: → toleration + fair Native land deals + representative government
cards.n: Distinct from simply identifying Penn as founder; this is the philosophy behind the colony.

cards.q: Explain how tobacco monoculture affected Chesapeake soil and settlement patterns.
cards.a: Tobacco rapidly exhausted soil nutrients, forcing planters to clear new fields every few years and constantly push settlement westward onto Native land in search of fresh ground, tying the region's land hunger directly to its export crop.
cards.h: → tobacco depletes soil → constant westward expansion
cards.n: An environmental-history angle on Bacon's Rebellion-era land pressure.

cards.q: State the approximate share of South Carolina's Lowcountry population that was enslaved by the mid-1700s.
cards.a: Enslaved Africans made up roughly 60 percent of South Carolina's population by the mid-eighteenth century, giving the colony a Black majority unmatched elsewhere on the mainland and modeled on Caribbean sugar colonies.
cards.n: A Black majority let Gullah speech and West African rice knowledge survive, and it is also why white fear ran so high after Stono.

cards.q: Identify Benjamin Franklin's Poor Richard's Almanack.
cards.a: An annual publication Franklin printed from 1732 to 1758 under the pen name Richard Saunders, mixing weather predictions and practical advice with pithy maxims on thrift and hard work. It became colonial America's best-selling book after the Bible.
cards.h: → annual almanac + Franklin's pen name + maxims
cards.n: A print-culture entry point for Franklin as popularizer of practical Enlightenment values, distinct from his scientific and political roles.

cards.q: Identify the French and Indian War and give its dates.
cards.a: The 1754-1763 North American theater of the global Seven Years' War, fought between Britain with its colonial and Iroquois allies and France with most Algonquian-speaking allies, chiefly over control of the Ohio River valley.
cards.n: Theme WOR. Everything in the imperial crisis flows from how Britain paid for and administered this victory.

cards.q: Identify the Albany Plan of Union and its author.
cards.a: Benjamin Franklin's 1754 proposal at the Albany Congress for a unified colonial government with a president-general and a grand council to coordinate defense and Native diplomacy. Every colonial assembly rejected it, unwilling to surrender taxing power.
cards.n: First serious plan for colonial union; its rejection shows how weak intercolonial identity still was in 1754.

cards.q: Identify the terms of the Treaty of Paris of 1763.
cards.a: France surrendered Canada and all claims east of the Mississippi to Britain and ceded Louisiana west of the Mississippi to Spain; Spain gave Florida to Britain. France was effectively expelled from mainland North America.
cards.n: Do not confuse with the 1783 Treaty of Paris ending the Revolution - a very common slip.

cards.q: Explain the consequences of the French and Indian War for Britain and its colonies.
cards.a: Britain doubled its national debt and had to garrison vast new territory, prompting new colonial taxes and the end of salutary neglect. Colonists gained military experience and confidence, lost the French threat that had made British protection necessary, and pressed west onto Native land.
cards.n: The highest-yield causation card in Period 3; it launches the entire imperial crisis.

cards.q: Contrast French and British relations with Native peoples in North America.
cards.a: The French, few in number and focused on the fur trade, built alliances through trade, gift-giving, and intermarriage. The British came as settler-farmers who wanted land, so their expansion displaced Native peoples - which is why most Native nations sided with France.
cards.n: Explains Native alignment in 1754 and the collapse of Native leverage after France's defeat.

cards.q: Identify Pontiac's Rebellion.
cards.a: A 1763 pan-Native uprising in the Ohio valley and Great Lakes, inspired partly by the prophet Neolin and led by the Ottawa leader Pontiac, that captured most British western forts in response to settlement pressure and the end of French-style gift-giving.
cards.n: It directly triggered the Proclamation of 1763 - state that causal link explicitly.

cards.q: Define the Proclamation of 1763.
cards.a: A royal order barring colonial settlement west of the Appalachian crest, reserving that land for Native peoples in order to prevent costly frontier wars after Pontiac's Rebellion.
cards.n: Britain's motive was cost control, not Native rights; colonists read it as a betrayal of their war prize.

cards.q: Explain why colonists resented the Proclamation of 1763.
cards.a: They had fought partly to open the Ohio valley, land speculators held claims there, and settlers were already crossing the mountains. Being fenced in by a distant government that had just added new taxes looked like the empire treating them as subordinates rather than as Englishmen.
cards.n: Note the widespread defiance: the line was crossed almost immediately and proved unenforceable.

cards.q: Identify the Sugar Act of 1764.
cards.a: Grenville's act that actually lowered the molasses duty but enforced it strictly through vice-admiralty courts without juries, targeting the smuggling that had made the old tax meaningless. It was the first law explicitly intended to raise revenue from the colonies.
cards.h: → year + what it did + why it angered colonists
cards.n: Trap: it LOWERED the rate. The grievance was enforcement, jury-less courts, and revenue purpose.

cards.q: Identify the Stamp Act of 1765.
cards.a: A tax requiring an embossed stamp on all paper items in the colonies - newspapers, legal documents, licenses, playing cards. It was the first direct, internal tax Parliament levied on colonists and it hit the most vocal groups: lawyers, printers, and merchants.
cards.h: → year + what it taxed + why explosive
cards.n: Its choice of targets is why resistance became so loud so fast.

cards.q: Identify the Stamp Act Congress and its central claim.
cards.a: A 1765 meeting of delegates from nine colonies in New York that petitioned the king and Parliament, conceding Parliament's authority to regulate trade but denying its right to tax colonists who elected no members - 'no taxation without representation.'
cards.n: First major intercolonial political cooperation; note how limited and loyal the claim still was in 1765.

cards.q: Define virtual representation and state the colonial counterargument.
cards.a: Britain's claim that every member of Parliament represented the whole empire's interests, so colonists were represented even without electing anyone. Colonists insisted on actual representation - only a legislature they elected could tax them.
cards.n: Precise terminology here separates strong answers from vague ones on taxation questions.

cards.q: Identify the Sons of Liberty.
cards.a: Networks of colonial artisans, merchants, and laborers formed in 1765 to resist the Stamp Act, using boycotts, propaganda, crowd action, tarring and feathering, and intimidation of stamp distributors to make the law unenforceable.
cards.n: Shows ordinary people, not just elites, driving resistance - a key SOC/PCE point.

cards.q: Identify the Quartering Act of 1765.
cards.a: A law requiring colonial assemblies to provide barracks and supplies for British troops stationed in their colonies. New York's assembly resisted and was suspended by Parliament in 1767.
cards.n: It reads as a hidden tax and as evidence of a standing army in peacetime, a classic Whig fear.

cards.q: Identify the Declaratory Act of 1766.
cards.a: Passed the same day Parliament repealed the Stamp Act, it asserted Parliament's full authority to legislate for the colonies 'in all cases whatsoever,' conceding nothing in principle while retreating in practice.
cards.n: Colonists celebrated the repeal and largely ignored this - which is why the constitutional conflict stayed unresolved.

cards.q: Identify the Townshend Acts of 1767.
cards.a: Duties on imported glass, lead, paint, paper, and tea, designed as 'external' trade taxes whose revenue would pay royal governors' and judges' salaries, freeing them from colonial assemblies. They also expanded writs of assistance and customs enforcement.
cards.h: → what was taxed + the salary twist
cards.n: Paying officials directly attacked the assemblies' power of the purse - the deeper grievance beneath the duties.

cards.q: Explain how nonimportation agreements and the Daughters of Liberty worked as resistance.
cards.a: Merchants pledged not to import British goods while women organized spinning bees, produced homespun cloth, and boycotted British tea. Because colonial buying power mattered to British merchants, consumer refusal turned households into political instruments and drew women into public politics.
cards.n: Best P3 evidence for women's political participation before independence.

cards.q: Identify the Boston Massacre and give its date.
cards.a: On March 5, 1770, British soldiers guarding the Boston customs house, harassed by a crowd, fired and killed five colonists including Crispus Attucks. John Adams defended the soldiers at trial and most were acquitted.
cards.n: Sourcing gold: Revere's engraving is deliberate propaganda. Adams's defense shows Patriot commitment to rule of law.

cards.q: Identify the Committees of Correspondence.
cards.a: Networks begun in Massachusetts in 1772 under Samuel Adams and extended intercolonially by Virginia in 1773 to share news, coordinate protest, and circulate political arguments among the colonies.
cards.n: The communications infrastructure that made a unified Continental Congress possible in 1774.

cards.q: Identify the Tea Act of 1773 and explain the colonial objection.
cards.a: It let the failing East India Company sell tea directly in the colonies, making legal tea CHEAPER than smuggled Dutch tea while keeping the Townshend tea duty. Colonists objected that cheap taxed tea was a bribe to accept Parliament's right to tax, and it threatened colonial merchants.
cards.h: → what it did + why cheap tea angered them
cards.n: Trap: the tea got cheaper. The objection was principle plus monopoly, not price.

cards.q: Identify the Boston Tea Party and give its date.
cards.a: On December 16, 1773, Sons of Liberty disguised as Mohawks boarded three ships in Boston Harbor and destroyed 342 chests of East India Company tea worth roughly 10,000 pounds.
cards.n: Destruction of private property split colonial opinion; even Franklin urged repayment. That is why Britain responded so hard.

cards.q: Identify the Coercive (Intolerable) Acts of 1774.
cards.a: Britain's punishment of Massachusetts: the Boston Port Act closing the harbor until the tea was paid for, the Massachusetts Government Act gutting the charter and banning town meetings, the Administration of Justice Act moving trials of officials to Britain, and an expanded Quartering Act.
cards.n: Naming all four is a high-value specificity move on a DBQ.

cards.q: Identify the Quebec Act of 1774 and why colonists grouped it with the Intolerable Acts.
cards.a: It extended Quebec's boundary south to the Ohio River, granted Catholics religious freedom, and provided government without a representative assembly. Protestant colonists saw a Catholic, unrepresentative regime planted on land they claimed - a preview of their own possible future.
cards.n: Shows how religion and land hunger fused with constitutional argument.

cards.q: Place these British measures in chronological order: Townshend Acts, Sugar Act, Coercive Acts, Stamp Act, Tea Act, Declaratory Act.
cards.a: Sugar Act 1764; Stamp Act 1765; Declaratory Act 1766; Townshend Acts 1767; Tea Act 1773; Coercive Acts 1774.
cards.n: The escalating action-reaction sequence is itself the argument in most imperial-crisis LEQs.

cards.q: Contrast the colonial constitutional argument in 1765 with the argument by 1774.
cards.a: In 1765 colonists accepted Parliament's authority to regulate trade and objected only to internal taxes levied without representation. By 1774 many denied Parliament had any authority over them at all, claiming loyalty to the king alone and asserting rights as natural, not merely as English liberties.
cards.n: This radicalization arc is the best CCOT answer for the road to independence.

cards.q: Identify the First Continental Congress and its actions.
cards.a: Fifty-six delegates from twelve colonies met in Philadelphia in September 1774. They endorsed the Suffolk Resolves, issued a Declaration of Rights and Grievances, created the Continental Association to enforce a comprehensive boycott, and agreed to reconvene in 1775.
cards.n: Note it still sought redress within the empire - independence was not yet the goal.

cards.q: Identify the battles of Lexington and Concord and give the date.
cards.a: April 19, 1775. British troops marching to seize colonial arms at Concord met militia at Lexington; the resulting fighting and the bloody British retreat to Boston were the first military engagements of the Revolution - the 'shot heard round the world.'
cards.n: War begins more than a year before independence is declared; do not collapse the two.

cards.q: Identify the Second Continental Congress and its major decisions.
cards.a: Meeting from May 1775, it created the Continental Army under George Washington, printed money, conducted diplomacy, sent the Olive Branch Petition, and ultimately adopted the Declaration of Independence - functioning as a de facto national government without formal authority.
cards.n: It governed for years with no constitution, which is why the Articles later formalized a weak center.

cards.q: Identify Common Sense and its author.
cards.a: Thomas Paine's January 1776 pamphlet, written in blunt language for a mass audience, that attacked monarchy and hereditary rule as absurd, argued that an island could not rule a continent, and demanded immediate independence. It sold well over 100,000 copies within months.
cards.n: Paine shifts the target from Parliament to the KING - the last barrier to declaring independence.

cards.q: Explain why Common Sense was so influential.
cards.a: It reframed the conflict from a dispute over taxes within the empire into a rejection of monarchy itself, was written in plain speech accessible to ordinary readers rather than legal Latin, and made independence appear both morally necessary and practically achievable within weeks of publication.
cards.n: Feeds any prompt on how ideas mobilized ordinary colonists.

cards.q: Identify the Declaration of Independence and give its date and principal author.
cards.a: Adopted July 4, 1776, drafted chiefly by Thomas Jefferson. It declared the united colonies free and independent states, listed grievances against George III, and justified separation by appeal to natural rights.
cards.n: Congress voted for independence on July 2; July 4 is the adoption of the text.

cards.q: Explain the political theory underlying the Declaration of Independence.
cards.a: Drawing on Locke, it holds that people possess unalienable natural rights, that governments exist by consent to secure those rights, and that when a government becomes destructive of them the people may alter or abolish it. The grievance list is the evidence that the king breached that contract.
cards.n: Theme NAT/ARC. Its universal language later fuels abolitionists, Seneca Falls, and civil rights arguments.

cards.q: Contrast Patriots and Loyalists in numbers and motivation.
cards.a: Roughly 40-45 percent of colonists were Patriots, 15-20 percent active Loyalists, and the rest neutral. Loyalists included royal officials, Anglican clergy, some merchants, recent immigrants, backcountry settlers hostile to coastal elites, and many enslaved people and Native nations.
cards.n: The Revolution was also a civil war; naming Loyalist diversity earns complexity credit.

cards.q: Identify Dunmore's Proclamation.
cards.a: The 1775 offer by Virginia's royal governor Lord Dunmore of freedom to enslaved men who fled Patriot masters to fight for Britain. Thousands escaped, alarming planters and pushing many wavering southern slaveholders toward the Patriot cause.
cards.n: Crucial irony: British 'tyranny' offered enslaved people a liberty that Patriot liberty did not.

cards.q: Identify the Battle of Saratoga and give its year.
cards.a: In October 1777 American forces under Horatio Gates surrounded and forced the surrender of General Burgoyne's army in upstate New York, defeating Britain's plan to split New England from the other colonies.
cards.n: Always paired with the French alliance - state that causal link.

cards.q: Explain why Saratoga was the turning point of the Revolutionary War.
cards.a: The victory convinced France that the Americans could win, producing the 1778 Franco-American alliance that brought money, troops, officers, and above all a navy. Spain and the Dutch soon joined against Britain, turning a colonial rebellion into a global war Britain had to fight on many fronts.
cards.n: Highest-yield military causation card in Period 3.

cards.q: Identify the Battle of Yorktown and give its year.
cards.a: In October 1781 Washington's and Rochambeau's combined armies trapped Cornwallis on the Virginia peninsula while de Grasse's French fleet blocked escape by sea, forcing the surrender of about 8,000 British troops and effectively ending major fighting.
cards.n: Note the French navy - Yorktown is the clearest demonstration that the alliance won the war.

cards.q: Identify the terms of the Treaty of Paris of 1783.
cards.a: Britain recognized American independence, set boundaries at the Mississippi River in the west, Canada in the north, and Spanish Florida in the south, granted fishing rights off Newfoundland, and included promises to repay prewar debts and to recommend restoring Loyalist property.
cards.n: The unenforced debt and Loyalist clauses become British excuses for holding western forts - see Jay's Treaty.

cards.q: Explain how the Americans won the Revolutionary War despite British advantages.
cards.a: They fought a defensive war on home ground and only needed to avoid destruction, while Britain had to conquer and occupy a vast territory 3,000 miles from home. Washington preserved the army, popular support and militias controlled the countryside, and French intervention supplied money and naval power.
cards.h: → American advantages + British burdens + foreign aid
cards.n: Balanced multi-cause answers score highest; do not credit French help alone or American virtue alone.

cards.q: Place these Revolutionary events in order: Yorktown, Lexington and Concord, Declaration of Independence, Saratoga, Treaty of Paris.
cards.a: Lexington and Concord April 1775; Declaration of Independence July 1776; Saratoga October 1777; Yorktown October 1781; Treaty of Paris September 1783.
cards.n: Note the two-year gap between Yorktown and the treaty - fighting stopped long before peace was formalized.

cards.q: Explain how the Revolution affected Native American peoples.
cards.a: Most nations, including four of the six Iroquois, sided with Britain to halt settler expansion. Patriot campaigns devastated Iroquois towns, the 1783 treaty ceded their lands without consulting them, and the loss of a European counterweight left them facing an expansionist United States alone.
cards.n: Frequently the 'complexity' evidence in prompts asking who gained from the Revolution.

cards.q: Identify the Articles of Confederation and give the year of ratification.
cards.a: The first United States constitution, drafted in 1777 and ratified in 1781, creating a 'firm league of friendship' - a one-house Congress in which each state had one vote, with no executive and no national judiciary, and sovereignty retained by the states.
cards.n: Its weakness was deliberate: Americans had just fought a war against distant centralized power.

cards.q: State the major weaknesses of the Articles of Confederation.
cards.a: Congress could not tax or regulate interstate and foreign commerce, had no executive to enforce laws and no national courts, needed nine of thirteen states to pass major legislation and unanimity to amend, and could only request money and troops from the states.
cards.n: Each weakness maps to a specific fix in the Constitution - organize your answer that way.

cards.q: State the genuine achievements of the Articles of Confederation government.
cards.a: It won the Revolutionary War, negotiated the favorable Treaty of Paris of 1783, and established an orderly republican process for surveying western land and admitting new states through the Land Ordinance of 1785 and the Northwest Ordinance of 1787.
cards.n: Prompts often ask whether the Articles were a failure - a balanced answer needs these successes.

cards.q: Identify the Land Ordinance of 1785.
cards.a: A law creating a rectangular survey of western territory into townships of 36 sections of 640 acres each, to be sold to raise revenue for the government, with one section in each township reserved to support public schools.
cards.n: The school-section clause is an early federal commitment to public education - a favorite detail.

cards.q: Identify the Northwest Ordinance of 1787.
cards.a: It set the process by which territories north of the Ohio River would become states equal to the original thirteen, guaranteed civil liberties and support for education, and prohibited slavery in the territory.
cards.n: The most important act of the Confederation government; note it applied only NORTH of the Ohio.

cards.q: Explain the long-term significance of the Northwest Ordinance.
cards.a: It rejected a colonial model for the West by making territories future equal states, and by banning slavery north of the Ohio it drew the first federal line between free and slave territory - the precedent behind the Missouri Compromise and the later sectional crises.
cards.n: Strong continuity card that reaches forward into Periods 4 and 5.

cards.q: Identify Shays' Rebellion and give its dates.
cards.a: In 1786-1787 indebted western Massachusetts farmers led by Revolutionary veteran Daniel Shays shut down courts to stop foreclosures and attacked the Springfield arsenal. Congress could raise no force; a privately funded state militia suppressed them.
cards.h: → years + who + grievance + who stopped it
cards.n: The detail that Congress could not respond is the point - it dramatized the Articles' impotence.

cards.q: Explain why Shays' Rebellion led to the Constitutional Convention.
cards.a: It convinced nationalists such as Washington and Madison that the confederation could not protect property or keep order, and that unchecked state legislatures were themselves the danger. The alarm converted the limited Annapolis meeting into a full convention at Philadelphia in 1787.
cards.n: Classic causation prompt; note the fear was of too MUCH democracy in the states.

cards.q: Identify the Constitutional Convention of 1787.
cards.a: Fifty-five delegates from twelve states met in Philadelphia from May to September 1787, ostensibly to revise the Articles. Meeting in secret, they instead wrote an entirely new frame of government with a strong central authority, separation of powers, and federalism.
cards.h: → year + place + what it actually did
cards.n: Rhode Island sent no one. The secrecy itself became an Anti-Federalist grievance.

cards.q: Identify the Virginia Plan.
