cards.a: Madison's proposal for a strong national government with a bicameral legislature in which representation in BOTH houses was based on population, plus a national executive and judiciary chosen by the legislature. It favored large states.
cards.n: Pair with the New Jersey Plan; the clash between them produces the Great Compromise.

cards.q: Identify the New Jersey Plan.
cards.a: William Paterson's proposal to keep a single-house legislature with equal representation for each state, as under the Articles, while adding congressional power to tax and regulate commerce. It protected small states.
cards.n: Note it still expanded federal power - even small-state delegates agreed the Articles were too weak.

cards.q: Define the Great (Connecticut) Compromise.
cards.a: The agreement creating a bicameral Congress: a House of Representatives apportioned by population and elected directly, and a Senate with two members per state chosen by the state legislatures. It satisfied both large and small states.
cards.n: The most tested compromise; know that senators were NOT popularly elected until the 17th Amendment.

cards.q: Define the Three-Fifths Compromise.
cards.a: The agreement counting three-fifths of the enslaved population when apportioning both representation in the House and direct taxes among the states. It boosted southern political power without granting enslaved people any rights.
cards.n: Effect: the slaveholding South gained inflated House seats and electoral votes for decades.

cards.q: Define the Commerce Compromise and the slave trade clause.
cards.a: Congress received power to regulate interstate and foreign commerce but was barred from taxing exports, and it could not prohibit the international slave trade before 1808. Together these protected southern staple exports and the trade in enslaved people.
cards.h: → what Congress could and could not do
cards.n: The 1808 clause is a bargain with a deadline - Congress banned the trade the first year it was allowed to.

cards.q: Explain how the Constitution addressed slavery without naming it.
cards.a: The Three-Fifths clause inflated southern representation, the twenty-year protection of the slave trade delayed abolition of importation, and the fugitive slave clause required the return of escapees - all written in euphemism ('other persons') to secure southern ratification while avoiding the word.
cards.n: Frames the Constitution as a proslavery bargain, a standard sophistication argument.

cards.q: Define federalism, separation of powers, and checks and balances.
cards.a: Federalism divides authority between national and state governments. Separation of powers assigns legislative, executive, and judicial functions to distinct branches. Checks and balances give each branch tools - veto, override, confirmation, judicial review, impeachment - to restrain the others.
cards.n: All three reflect the Madisonian premise that power must be set against power because people are self-interested.

cards.q: Identify the Federalists and their main arguments.
cards.a: Supporters of ratification - Hamilton, Madison, Jay, Washington - who argued that a stronger union was necessary for defense, commerce, and order, that the structure itself checked tyranny, and that a large republic would dilute factions. They were generally urban, commercial, and coastal.
cards.n: Note the naming coup: they claimed the popular word 'federal' and left opponents defined negatively.

cards.q: Identify the Anti-Federalists and their main objections.
cards.a: Opponents of ratification - Patrick Henry, George Mason, Richard Henry Lee - who warned that a distant central government would swallow the states, that no bill of rights protected citizens, that republics could not survive over large territory, and that the presidency resembled a monarchy.
cards.n: Their demand produced the Bill of Rights - they lost the vote but shaped the result.

cards.q: Contrast Federalist and Anti-Federalist views of a large republic.
cards.a: Anti-Federalists followed Montesquieu in holding that republics survive only in small, homogeneous societies where citizens share interests and can watch their rulers. Madison argued in Federalist 10 that a large republic is SAFER because its many competing factions cannot easily combine into an oppressive majority.
cards.n: The inversion of conventional wisdom in Federalist 10 is the point graders look for.

cards.q: Identify the argument of Federalist No. 10.
cards.a: Madison argues that faction is rooted in human nature and unequal property, so it cannot be removed without destroying liberty and must instead be controlled. A large republic with representation filters popular passion and multiplies competing interests so that no majority faction can dominate.
cards.n: Frequently a stimulus document; know the distinction between removing the causes and controlling the effects.

cards.q: Identify the argument of Federalist No. 51.
cards.a: Madison argues that since 'men are not angels,' government must be structured so that ambition counteracts ambition. Separation of powers and checks and balances give each branch the means and motive to resist encroachment, and the federal system adds a 'double security' for rights.
cards.n: Pair 10 (size and faction) with 51 (structure) - they are the two halves of the Madisonian design.

cards.q: Identify the Bill of Rights and give the year of ratification.
cards.a: The first ten amendments, ratified in 1791 and drafted largely by Madison, guaranteeing freedoms of religion, speech, press, assembly, and petition, protections for the accused, and reserving unenumerated powers to the states and the people.
cards.n: It was the price of ratification in Virginia, New York, and Massachusetts - a concession, not an afterthought.

cards.q: Date the writing of the Constitution, its taking effect, and the Bill of Rights.
cards.a: Written at the Philadelphia Convention in 1787; ratified by the ninth state, New Hampshire, in June 1788 and in effect from 1789; Bill of Rights ratified 1791.
cards.n: Students routinely write 1776 for the Constitution - eleven years separate it from the Declaration.

cards.q: Identify the precedents set by Washington as president.
cards.a: He created a cabinet of department heads, accepted the title 'Mr. President' over royal alternatives, asserted executive control of foreign policy, used federal force to enforce law in the Whiskey Rebellion, and voluntarily retired after two terms.
cards.n: The two-term norm holds until FDR and is then written into the 22nd Amendment.

cards.q: Identify the four main parts of Hamilton's financial plan.
cards.a: Fund the national debt at full face value, assume the states' war debts, charter a Bank of the United States, and pass protective tariffs plus an excise tax to raise revenue and encourage domestic manufacturing.
cards.n: Theme WXT/PCE. The plan's real aim was tying wealthy creditors' interests to the new government's survival.

cards.q: Contrast loose and strict construction of the Constitution using the Bank debate.
cards.a: Hamilton argued loose construction: the necessary and proper clause implies powers, so a bank is constitutional as a means to enumerated fiscal ends. Jefferson argued strict construction: powers not expressly delegated are reserved to the states, and 'necessary' means indispensable, so the bank is unconstitutional.
cards.h: → two readings + the clause at issue
cards.n: The founding constitutional argument that recurs through McCulloch v. Maryland and beyond.

cards.q: Contrast Hamiltonian Federalists and Jeffersonian Democratic-Republicans.
cards.a: Federalists wanted a strong central government, commerce, manufacturing, banking, loose construction, and pro-British policy, and drew on New England merchants. Democratic-Republicans wanted limited federal power, an agrarian yeoman society, strict construction, and sympathy for France, drawing on the South and West.
cards.n: The most tested comparison of the 1790s; note both sides claimed to defend the Revolution's meaning.

cards.q: Explain why political parties emerged in the 1790s despite the Founders' hostility to them.
cards.a: Concrete disputes over Hamilton's program, the French Revolution, and treaties with Britain created durable coalitions. Once partisan newspapers, correspondence networks, and voter mobilization proved effective, each side accused the other of subverting the republic and organized permanently to win elections.
cards.n: Washington's Farewell warns against exactly what his own administration produced.

cards.q: Identify the Whiskey Rebellion and give its year.
cards.a: In 1794 western Pennsylvania farmers violently resisted Hamilton's excise tax on distilled spirits, which fell heavily on grain farmers who converted crops to whiskey for transport. Washington personally led roughly 13,000 militiamen and the resistance dissolved without a battle.
cards.n: Washington later pardoned the convicted leaders - firmness paired with leniency.

cards.q: Contrast the government's response to Shays' Rebellion and the Whiskey Rebellion.
cards.a: Under the Articles, Congress could raise no force against Shays and private funds paid a state militia. Under the Constitution, Washington federalized militia from several states and marched to enforce a federal tax - demonstrating that the new government could do what the old one could not.
cards.n: The cleanest available proof of the Constitution's practical effect; ideal for a change-over-time thesis.

cards.q: Identify the Proclamation of Neutrality of 1793.
cards.a: Washington's declaration that the United States would remain impartial in the war between revolutionary France and Britain, despite the 1778 alliance with France. Jeffersonians objected that it betrayed an ally and that neutrality was Congress's business.
cards.n: Establishes the precedent of executive control over foreign policy and of avoiding European wars.

cards.q: Identify Jay's Treaty and give its year.
cards.a: The 1794 treaty with Britain in which Britain agreed to evacuate its northwestern forts and submit some disputes to arbitration, but made no concessions on impressment or neutral shipping rights. It was widely denounced as a humiliating surrender and passed the Senate narrowly.
cards.h: → year + what was gained + what was not
cards.n: Its unpopularity supercharged party formation and drove France to attack American shipping.

cards.q: Identify Pinckney's Treaty and give its year.
cards.a: The 1795 Treaty of San Lorenzo with Spain, which granted Americans free navigation of the Mississippi River, the right of deposit at New Orleans, and acceptance of the 31st parallel as Florida's northern boundary.
cards.n: A genuine triumph, popular in the West; Spain conceded partly out of fear of Anglo-American cooperation after Jay's Treaty.

cards.q: State the main advice of Washington's Farewell Address.
cards.a: Avoid permanent foreign alliances and entanglement in European quarrels, beware the divisive 'baneful effects' of political parties and factions, and guard against sectionalism, since national unity underpins independence and prosperity.
cards.n: Published in newspapers in 1796; it anchors non-intervention arguments right through the 1930s.

cards.q: Identify the XYZ Affair.
cards.a: In 1797-1798 French agents identified only as X, Y, and Z demanded a bribe and a loan before negotiating with American diplomats. Publication of the insult produced an outburst of anti-French feeling and the undeclared naval Quasi-War of 1798-1800.
cards.n: Adams's refusal to seek a full declaration of war split his own party but kept the country out of a land war.

cards.q: Identify the Alien and Sedition Acts of 1798.
cards.a: Four Federalist laws that lengthened residency for naturalization from 5 to 14 years, allowed the president to deport or detain aliens from hostile nations, and criminalized 'false, scandalous and malicious' writing against the government - used to prosecute Republican editors.
cards.n: Aimed at immigrant voters and the opposition press; the Sedition Act expired the day before Jefferson took office.

cards.q: Identify the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions.
cards.a: Secretly written by Madison and Jefferson in 1798-1799, they argued that the states, as parties to the constitutional compact, could judge federal laws unconstitutional and interpose against or nullify them - the response to the Alien and Sedition Acts.
cards.n: The seed of nullification and states' rights arguments used by South Carolina in 1832 and by secessionists in 1860.

cards.q: Explain why the election of 1800 is called the 'Revolution of 1800.'
cards.a: It produced the first peaceful transfer of national power from one party to its bitter rival, with Federalists surrendering the presidency to Jefferson without force. An electoral tie with Aaron Burr was resolved in the House and led to the 12th Amendment.
cards.n: The peaceful transfer, not any policy shift, is the point - it proved the system could survive partisanship.

cards.q: Define republican motherhood.
cards.a: The postrevolutionary idea that women's civic role was to raise sons who would be virtuous, informed citizens. It justified expanded female education while confining women's influence to the household.
cards.n: Theme SOC. Always note both sides: real gains in literacy and schooling, no political rights.

cards.q: Identify gradual emancipation in the northern states.
cards.a: Between 1777 and 1804 every state north of Delaware abolished slavery, mostly through laws freeing children born to enslaved mothers only after they reached adulthood. Vermont's 1777 constitution and Massachusetts court rulings in the 1780s acted fastest; New Jersey acted last in 1804.
cards.n: 'Gradual' is the operative word: some people remained enslaved in the North into the 1840s.

cards.q: Contrast the Revolution's effects on slavery in the North and the South.
cards.a: In the North, revolutionary ideology plus limited economic dependence produced gradual abolition and growing free Black communities. In the South the same ideology prompted some manumissions, but staple agriculture and rising cotton demand entrenched slavery, and states tightened manumission laws after the 1790s.
cards.n: Sectional divergence begins here - essential context for Periods 4 and 5.

cards.q: Explain the limits of the American Revolution as a social revolution.
cards.a: It abolished titles of nobility, disestablished churches in most states, modestly broadened suffrage among white men, and spread republican ideology. But it left slavery intact in the South, women without political rights, property qualifications in place, and Native peoples dispossessed.
cards.n: The definitive 'how revolutionary was the Revolution' answer: real but bounded change.

cards.q: Contrast the arguments colonists made in 1776 with those Anti-Federalists made in 1787.
cards.a: Both feared distant, unaccountable power, standing armies, and taxation by a government the people could not effectively control. The difference is the target: in 1776 the enemy was Parliament and the Crown; in 1787 it was a proposed national government created by fellow Americans.
cards.n: Shows the continuity of revolutionary ideology into constitutional politics.

cards.q: Place these events of the 1790s in chronological order: Jay's Treaty, Whiskey Rebellion, Alien and Sedition Acts, Farewell Address, Pinckney's Treaty, XYZ Affair.
cards.a: Whiskey Rebellion 1794; Jay's Treaty 1794; Pinckney's Treaty 1795; Farewell Address 1796; XYZ Affair 1797-1798; Alien and Sedition Acts 1798.
cards.n: Jay's Treaty precedes and helps cause both Pinckney's Treaty and French retaliation - the sequence carries the causation.

cards.q: Place these founding documents in order and give each year: Constitution, Articles of Confederation ratified, Northwest Ordinance, Declaration of Independence, Bill of Rights.
cards.a: Declaration of Independence 1776; Articles of Confederation ratified 1781; Northwest Ordinance 1787; Constitution written 1787; Bill of Rights 1791.
cards.n: The Northwest Ordinance and the Constitution share 1787 but came from two different governments.

cards.q: Name the three developments of 1763 and put them in order.
cards.a: The Treaty of Paris ending the French and Indian War (February 1763); Pontiac's Rebellion (spring and summer 1763); the Proclamation of 1763 (October 1763).
cards.n: Compressing them into one year makes the causation obvious: peace, then Native revolt, then the settlement line.

cards.q: Date the First Continental Congress, the Second Continental Congress, and the Declaration of Independence.
cards.a: First Continental Congress September-October 1774; Second Continental Congress convened May 1775; Declaration of Independence adopted July 4, 1776.
cards.n: Almost two years pass from the first Congress to independence - proof that separation was not the original goal.

cards.q: Contrast the Articles of Confederation with the Constitution on taxation, commerce, executive power, and amendment.
cards.a: Articles: no power to tax, no power to regulate commerce, no executive or national courts, and unanimous consent to amend. Constitution: Congress taxes directly, regulates interstate and foreign commerce, a president enforces law with a federal judiciary, and amendment needs three-fourths of the states.
cards.n: Structure your Articles-to-Constitution essays on exactly these four fixes.

cards.q: Identify the Paxton Boys and their 1763 uprising.
cards.a: A group of Scots-Irish frontiersmen from Paxton, Pennsylvania, who massacred peaceful Christianized Native villagers in 1763 and marched on Philadelphia to demand the colonial government stop protecting Native peoples and better defend the frontier.
cards.n: Shows the deep east-west tension over Native policy that also fed the Regulator movement further south.

cards.q: Identify the Regulator movement in the North and South Carolina backcountry.
cards.a: Backcountry farmers in the Carolinas organized in the late 1760s to protest corrupt local officials, unfair taxes, and the lack of political representation for western settlers. North Carolina's Regulators were crushed by the colonial militia at the Battle of Alamance in 1771.
cards.h: → backcountry grievance + where it was crushed
cards.n: An internal east-west class conflict happening alongside, not because of, the imperial crisis with Britain.

cards.q: Explain what happened to Loyalists after the Revolutionary War.
cards.a: Many Loyalists had their property confiscated by state governments, and tens of thousands fled to Canada, Britain, or the Caribbean rather than live under the new republic. The 1783 Treaty of Paris only weakly urged states to restore their rights and property.
cards.n: About 60,000-100,000 Loyalists left, making it one of history's largest per-capita refugee crises at the time.

cards.q: Identify the Newburgh Conspiracy of 1783.
cards.a: A near-mutiny by unpaid Continental Army officers at Newburgh, New York, who considered military action against Congress over back pay. George Washington personally intervened, appealing to his officers' loyalty and defusing the crisis, preserving civilian control of the military.
cards.n: The underlying problem was that Congress could not tax under the Articles, so it could not pay; Washington's restraint set the civilian-control norm.

cards.q: Identify the Judiciary Act of 1789.
cards.a: A law passed by the first Congress establishing the federal court system called for but not detailed by the Constitution, creating a six-justice Supreme Court, federal district courts, and circuit courts, and the office of attorney general.
cards.h: → creates federal courts + Supreme Court size
cards.n: Section 13 of this act was the provision the Court struck down in Marbury v. Madison (1803).

cards.q: Identify the Battle of Fallen Timbers and the Treaty of Greenville.
cards.a: U.S. forces under Anthony Wayne defeated a Native confederacy in Ohio at Fallen Timbers in 1794. The resulting 1795 Treaty of Greenville forced Native nations to cede most of Ohio, opening the Northwest Territory to rapid American settlement.
cards.n: The British shut their fort's gates on the retreating warriors, and Jay's Treaty that year pulled British posts out, leaving Natives without an ally.

cards.q: Identify the election of 1796 and the flaw in the electoral system it exposed.
cards.a: Federalist John Adams narrowly defeated Democratic-Republican Thomas Jefferson, who then became vice president under the original rules awarding that office to the runner-up. It produced a president and vice president from rival parties, a problem the 12th Amendment later fixed.
cards.h: → Adams wins, Jefferson runner-up becomes VP
cards.n: Washington's Farewell Address had warned against parties only months before this first openly partisan contest.

cards.q: Identify the Democratic-Republican societies of the 1790s.
cards.a: Local political clubs, inspired by the French Revolution, that criticized Federalist policies such as Hamilton's financial program and the Jay Treaty. Washington blamed them for stirring up the Whiskey Rebellion, alarming Federalists about organized popular dissent.
cards.h: → clubs + inspiration + what Washington blamed them for
cards.n: They matter because no one yet accepted a loyal opposition: organized criticism still looked like conspiracy to Federalists.

cards.q: Identify the Quasi-War with France.
cards.a: An undeclared naval conflict between the United States and France from 1798 to 1800, sparked by French seizure of American merchant ships and the XYZ Affair, fought mostly at sea and ended by the Convention of 1800.
cards.n: Fed the political panic behind the Alien and Sedition Acts of the same years.

cards.q: Define the Necessary and Proper (elastic) Clause.
cards.a: Article I's grant of power to Congress to make all laws 'necessary and proper' for carrying out its enumerated powers. Hamilton used it to justify the Bank of the United States as an implied power; Jefferson read it far more narrowly.
cards.n: The textual battleground of the entire loose-versus-strict construction debate.

cards.q: Identify Federalist No. 78 and its argument.
cards.a: An essay by Alexander Hamilton arguing that an independent judiciary with life tenure was the 'least dangerous' branch, since it had neither the power of the purse nor the sword, and that courts must be able to strike down laws that conflict with the Constitution.
cards.h: → author + 'least dangerous branch' + judicial review preview
cards.n: Foreshadows judicial review a decade before Marbury v. Madison formally established it.

cards.q: Identify the first three new states admitted after the original thirteen.
cards.a: Vermont (1791), Kentucky (1792), and Tennessee (1796) were the first states admitted to the Union after the original thirteen, showing how quickly trans-Appalachian settlement was turning territories into states.
cards.n: Vermont free and Kentucky slave set the early habit of admitting states in pairs, the logic that later produced the Missouri Compromise.

cards.q: Explain the 'Massachusetts Compromise' that helped secure ratification of the Constitution.
cards.a: Facing a close vote, Massachusetts Federalists won over wavering delegates by promising that the first Congress would add a bill of rights as amendments once the Constitution took effect. Several other closely divided states adopted the same strategy.
cards.h: → promise a bill of rights → ratify now
cards.n: Explains why the Bill of Rights followed so quickly (1791) after ratification (1788).

cards.q: Identify Toussaint Louverture and the Haitian Revolution's effect on U.S. politics.
cards.a: Toussaint Louverture led the enslaved people's revolution in Saint-Domingue that destroyed slavery there in the 1790s and made him the colony's governor, still nominally under France. He was deported in 1802 and died in a French prison in 1803; Jean-Jacques Dessalines declared Haitian independence on 1 January 1804. The revolution terrified southern slaveholders, shaped the long U.S. refusal to recognize Haiti, and helped push Napoleon to sell Louisiana.
cards.h: → what he did, what he did not, and the U.S. reaction
cards.n: A direct link between the Haitian Revolution and the 1803 Louisiana Purchase — and a common trap: Louverture destroyed slavery, Dessalines declared independence.

cards.q: Contrast Hamilton's and Jefferson's visions of the ideal American economy.
cards.a: Hamilton favored a diversified economy of manufacturing, finance, and cities, funded by a national bank and tariffs, with wealthy creditors tied to the government's success. Jefferson favored a republic of independent farmers, distrusted banks and cities, and saw agriculture as the guarantor of civic virtue.
cards.n: This economic-vision contrast underlies nearly every First Party System fight, from the Bank to the Whiskey Rebellion to the Louisiana Purchase.

cards.q: Identify Hamilton's Report on Manufactures (1791) and its central argument.
cards.a: A report to Congress proposing federal tariffs and subsidies to encourage domestic manufacturing and reduce dependence on British imports. Congress rejected its subsidy proposals but later used protective tariffs to pursue similar goals.
cards.n: It is the third report after Public Credit and the Bank; Clay's American System later revived the same program under a new name.

cards.q: Identify the Compromise of 1790 (the 'dinner table bargain').
cards.a: An agreement, reportedly brokered over dinner by Jefferson, Madison, and Hamilton, in which southern representatives accepted federal assumption of state war debts in exchange for locating the new national capital on the Potomac River.
cards.n: Some historians doubt the dinner really settled the deal single-handedly, since both issues had separate momentum already.

cards.q: Define the compact theory of the Union laid out in the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions.
cards.a: The argument, written by Jefferson and Madison in 1798, that the Constitution was a compact among sovereign states, so a state could judge federal laws unconstitutional and refuse to enforce them, as Kentucky and Virginia proposed to do with the Alien and Sedition Acts.
cards.n: This is the direct ancestor of Calhoun's nullification theory in Period 4.

cards.q: State what the Naturalization Act of 1798 changed and why the Federalists wanted it.
cards.a: It extended the residency requirement for U.S. citizenship from five to fourteen years. Federalists, who saw recent immigrants as likely Democratic-Republican voters, hoped the longer wait would slow their path to the ballot box.
cards.n: Jefferson's Congress cut it back to five years in 1802, and five years remains the residency requirement today.

cards.q: Explain how the Iroquois Confederacy split during the American Revolution.
cards.a: The Confederacy's tradition of unanimous consent broke down as the Oneida and Tuscarora sided with the Patriots while the Mohawk, Seneca, Cayuga, and Onondaga sided with the British. The resulting civil war shattered two centuries of Confederacy unity.
cards.h: → Oneida/Tuscarora Patriot vs other four British
cards.n: Sullivan's 1779 campaign burned some forty Iroquois towns, and the 1783 peace ignored Native allies entirely, a pattern repeated after 1812.

cards.q: Identify Abigail Adams's 'Remember the Ladies' letter to John Adams.
cards.a: A March 1776 letter urging her husband and the Continental Congress to grant women legal protection against arbitrary treatment by husbands as they designed a new government, warning that women would 'foment a rebellion' if ignored.
cards.n: John Adams's dismissive reply shows how marginal even sympathetic Founders considered women's legal claims at the time.

cards.q: Identify Judith Sargent Murray and her argument in 'On the Equality of the Sexes.'
cards.a: An essayist who argued in 1790 that women's apparent intellectual inferiority resulted from unequal education, not innate ability, and called for expanded female schooling, an early Enlightenment-era feminist argument.
cards.n: She published as Constantia, two years before Wollstonecraft, and her case for schooling fed the republican motherhood argument.

cards.q: Explain why Virginia and other states without large war debts opposed Hamilton's assumption plan.
cards.a: States like Virginia had already paid off much of their Revolutionary War debt, so assuming other states' debts meant their taxpayers would help cover obligations they had already settled, a transfer they viewed as unfair.
cards.n: The deadlock broke at Jefferson's dinner table in 1790: Virginia accepted assumption in exchange for the capital on the Potomac.

cards.q: State what the Coinage Act of 1792 established.
cards.a: It created the U.S. Mint in Philadelphia and established a bimetallic dollar based on both gold and silver, giving the new nation its own standardized currency for the first time.
cards.n: The fixed gold-to-silver ratio it set is the root of the bimetallism quarrel that runs from Jackson's era to Bryan in 1896.

cards.q: Identify St. Clair's Defeat of 1791 and the Native leaders who won it.
cards.a: The Western Confederacy, led by Miami chief Little Turtle and Shawnee chief Blue Jacket, destroyed General Arthur St. Clair's army in the Ohio Country, the worst defeat the U.S. Army ever suffered against Native forces, before Fallen Timbers reversed the outcome in 1794.
cards.h: → Little Turtle + Blue Jacket, worst U.S. defeat
cards.n: It triggered the first congressional investigation of the executive branch and the first claim of what later became executive privilege.

cards.q: Explain how the Revolutionary War expanded colonial women's economic responsibilities.
cards.a: With men away fighting, women managed farms, shops, and finances, made decisions about planting and trade, and sometimes ran family businesses for years. This wartime necessity gave many women unaccustomed economic authority, though it rarely translated into lasting legal rights.
cards.h: → wartime necessity, not lasting legal change
cards.n: The same pattern repeats in the Civil War and both world wars: wartime work expands, then contracts once the men come home.

cards.q: Identify the 'Molly Pitcher' legend and the broader role of women who followed the Continental Army as camp followers.
cards.a: Molly Pitcher is a composite legend, often linked to Mary Ludwig Hays, symbolizing women who carried water and sometimes took up arms at battles like Monmouth. Thousands of women served armies as camp followers, cooking, nursing, and doing laundry.
cards.n: Most named 'camp follower' women were poor and enslaved, a fact the patriotic Molly Pitcher legend tends to obscure.

cards.q: Differentiate the funding of the national debt from the assumption of state debts in Hamilton's financial plan.
cards.a: Funding meant paying off federal Revolutionary War debt at full face value to establish government credit. Assumption meant the federal government additionally taking on the states' separate war debts, a distinct and more controversial step that shifted state obligations onto the nation.
cards.h: → federal debt paid vs state debts absorbed
cards.n: Speculators had bought soldiers' certificates cheaply, so Madison wanted to pay the original holders instead; Hamilton refused and won.

cards.q: Identify Charles Beard's 'An Economic Interpretation of the Constitution' (1913).
cards.a: Progressive historian Charles Beard argued the framers were propertied men who designed the Constitution to protect their own economic interests, especially creditors' investments in government bonds, rather than acting from purely disinterested principle. Later historians have challenged his evidence.
cards.n: The classic historiographical counterweight to a purely idealistic reading of the Constitutional Convention.

cards.q: State roughly how many specific grievances the Declaration of Independence levels against George III, and give two examples.
cards.a: The Declaration lists about 27 grievances, including 'he has dissolved Representative Houses' for opposing him and 'quartering large bodies of armed troops among us,' building a legal case for revolution before announcing independence.
cards.n: Congress cut Jefferson's grievance blaming the king for the slave trade, at the insistence of South Carolina and Georgia.

cards.q: Identify the rival partisan newspapers of the 1790s.
cards.a: John Fenno's Gazette of the United States backed Hamilton and the Federalists, while Philip Freneau's National Gazette, encouraged by Jefferson, attacked Hamilton's program. Their dueling coverage helped harden the era's first political parties.
cards.n: Shows the partisan press was built into party formation from the start, not a later development.

cards.q: Date the boundary years of AP Period 3 and name the event that marks each end.
cards.a: Period 3 runs from 1754, the start of the French and Indian War, to 1800, the election that peacefully transferred power to Jefferson's Democratic-Republicans.
cards.n: Note the period opens with a war for empire, not with the Revolution, so Period 3 prompts run from 1754 causes to 1800 consequences.

cards.q: Identify Jefferson's Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom (1786).
cards.a: A law Jefferson considered one of his three greatest achievements, it disestablished the Anglican Church in Virginia and guaranteed that no one could be compelled to support any religion, becoming a model for the First Amendment's religion clauses.
cards.h: → Jefferson's law + disestablishes church + models 1st Amendment
cards.n: Direct forerunner of the Establishment and Free Exercise Clauses ratified five years later.

cards.q: Define Jeffersonian democracy as a governing philosophy.
cards.a: Jefferson's vision of a limited federal government, strict construction of the Constitution, low taxes and debt, reduced military, and a republic anchored in independent yeoman farmers rather than merchants and financiers.
cards.h: → two-part: size of government + social base
cards.n: Watch the gap between theory and practice: Jefferson the strict constructionist bought Louisiana and kept the Bank running.

cards.q: Date the Revolution of 1800 and the constitutional fix it produced.
cards.a: Election of 1800; the Jefferson-Burr tie in the Electoral College was resolved by the House in 1801, and the 12th Amendment (1804) required separate ballots for president and vice president.
cards.n: The tie was between two Republicans, not between parties; Hamilton's lobbying for Jefferson over Burr led toward their 1804 duel.

cards.q: Identify the Louisiana Purchase and its terms.
cards.a: The 1803 purchase of roughly 828,000 square miles from France for about $15 million, doubling the size of the United States and giving the U.S. control of New Orleans and the Mississippi River outlet.
cards.n: Napoleon sold after the Haitian Revolution wrecked his plans for a New World empire.

cards.q: Date the Louisiana Purchase and the Lewis and Clark expedition.
cards.a: Louisiana Purchase 1803; the Lewis and Clark Corps of Discovery expedition ran 1804-1806.
cards.n: Jefferson the strict constructionist found no express power to buy land, so this is the standard example of principle yielding to opportunity.

cards.q: Explain the constitutional dilemma the Louisiana Purchase created for Jefferson.
cards.a: Jefferson was a strict constructionist, but the Constitution nowhere authorized buying territory. He accepted a loose-construction reading of the treaty power to close the deal, contradicting his own principles.
cards.n: A favorite irony question: the strict constructionist used implied powers when it served national interest.

cards.q: Identify the holding of Marbury v. Madison (1803).
cards.a: The Marshall Court held that Marbury was legally entitled to his commission, but that it could not order its delivery: the section of the Judiciary Act of 1789 that gave the Court original jurisdiction to issue such writs of mandamus conflicted with Article III and was unconstitutional. This established the Supreme Court's power of judicial review over acts of Congress.
cards.n: The Court gained power by declining a power; that paradox is the standard exam point.

cards.q: Define judicial review.
cards.a: The power of the federal courts to declare acts of Congress, the executive, or the states unconstitutional and therefore void. It is not written in the Constitution; it was asserted by the Court in Marbury v. Madison.
cards.n: Marbury (1803) voided part of the Judiciary Act of 1789; the Court struck down no other federal law until Dred Scott in 1857.

cards.q: Identify the holding of McCulloch v. Maryland (1819).
cards.a: Congress could charter the Bank of the United States under the necessary and proper clause (implied powers), and Maryland could not tax it because the power to tax involves the power to destroy. Federal law is supreme over state law.
cards.n: The strongest single case for expanded federal power in Period 4.

cards.q: Identify the holding of Gibbons v. Ogden (1824).
cards.a: The Court struck down a New York steamboat monopoly, holding that Congress alone regulates interstate commerce and defining commerce broadly to include navigation. State laws conflicting with federal commerce regulation are void.
cards.h: → which clause, which level of government
cards.n: The commerce clause reading here is the foundation for later federal economic regulation.

cards.q: Identify the holding of Fletcher v. Peck (1810).
cards.a: The Court voided a Georgia law rescinding a corrupt Yazoo land grant, ruling that the grant was a contract protected by the Constitution. It was the first time the Court struck down a state law as unconstitutional.
cards.h: → contract clause, first of its kind
cards.n: Pair with Dartmouth: both protect contracts and property against state legislatures.

cards.q: Identify the holding of Dartmouth College v. Woodward (1819).
cards.a: New Hampshire could not alter Dartmouth's colonial charter because a charter is a contract protected by the contract clause. The ruling shielded private corporations from state interference and encouraged corporate growth.
cards.n: Useful evidence that the Marshall Court favored a national business climate over state control.

cards.q: Identify the holding of Worcester v. Georgia (1832) and what followed.
cards.a: The Court ruled the Cherokee Nation a distinct political community over which Georgia law had no force, so removal was illegal. Jackson declined to enforce the decision and removal proceeded anyway.
cards.n: The classic example of the judiciary lacking enforcement power; do not confuse it with Cherokee Nation v. Georgia (1831).

cards.q: Explain the overall direction of the Marshall Court's decisions.
cards.a: The Court consistently strengthened the federal government against the states, protected contracts and property rights, and expanded the reach of the commerce clause, building a national legal framework for a market economy.
cards.n: Marshall was a Federalist appointee whose rulings outlasted the Federalist Party itself.

cards.q: Define the Embargo Act of 1807 and state its purpose.
cards.a: A law banning nearly all American exports to foreign ports, intended to force Britain and France to respect U.S. neutral shipping rights and stop impressment by depriving them of American goods.
cards.h: → what was banned, to pressure whom
cards.n: It wrecked New England shipping far more than Britain's trade, bred smuggling, and was replaced in 1809 by the Non-Intercourse Act.

cards.q: Explain why the Embargo Act backfired.
cards.a: Britain found other suppliers while the American economy, especially New England shipping, collapsed. Smuggling spread, Federalist opposition revived, and the embargo was repealed in 1809 without changing British policy.
cards.n: It ironically spurred domestic manufacturing, which supports arguments about the roots of the Market Revolution.

cards.q: Explain the causes of the War of 1812.
cards.a: British impressment of American sailors and seizure of neutral shipping, British support for Native resistance in the Northwest led by Tecumseh, and pressure from western and southern War Hawks such as Henry Clay and John C. Calhoun who wanted Canada and Florida.
cards.n: New England opposed the war it was supposedly fought to protect, a favorite contradiction on the exam.

cards.q: State the consequences of the War of 1812.
cards.a: Territorial boundaries were unchanged by the Treaty of Ghent, but American nationalism surged, the Federalist Party collapsed, domestic manufacturing grew, Native resistance east of the Mississippi was broken, and Andrew Jackson became a national hero after New Orleans.
cards.n: Called the Second War of Independence even though militarily it was roughly a draw.

cards.q: Date the War of 1812, the Treaty of Ghent, and the Battle of New Orleans.
cards.a: War declared June 1812; Treaty of Ghent signed December 1814; Battle of New Orleans fought January 1815, after the treaty was signed but before news reached America.
cards.n: The out-of-order sequence (treaty before the famous victory) is a common trap.

cards.q: Identify the Hartford Convention.
cards.a: An 1814-1815 meeting of New England Federalists who protested the War of 1812, proposed constitutional amendments limiting southern and western power, and discussed secession or a separate peace.
cards.n: It met just as news of New Orleans and peace arrived, making the delegates look disloyal.

cards.q: Explain how the Hartford Convention destroyed the Federalist Party.
cards.a: Its complaints and secession talk arrived at the exact moment of Jackson's victory at New Orleans and the peace treaty, so Federalists appeared unpatriotic and even treasonous. The party never won a national election again.
cards.n: Ironically Federalists used states-rights and nullification arguments they had long opposed.

cards.q: Define the Era of Good Feelings.
cards.a: The period roughly 1815-1825 under Monroe when the Federalist Party had collapsed and one-party rule created an appearance of political harmony, alongside surging nationalism after the War of 1812.
cards.n: The name is misleading: the Panic of 1819 and the Missouri crisis show deep sectional and economic conflict.

cards.q: Define Henry Clay's American System.
cards.a: A three-part nationalist economic program: a protective tariff to shield American manufacturing, a national bank to provide stable currency and credit, and federally funded internal improvements such as roads and canals.
cards.n: Southerners resisted the tariff and federally funded improvements, so it was only partly enacted.

cards.q: Identify the terms of the Missouri Compromise.
cards.a: Missouri entered as a slave state and Maine as a free state, keeping the Senate balanced, and slavery was banned in the rest of the Louisiana Territory north of latitude 36 degrees 30 minutes.
cards.n: The 36 30 line was later voided by Kansas-Nebraska (1854) and declared unconstitutional in Dred Scott (1857).

cards.q: Date the Missouri Compromise and the Panic that preceded it.
cards.a: Panic of 1819; Missouri Compromise 1820.
cards.n: Jefferson called the Missouri crisis a fire bell in the night; the 36 30 line it drew is exactly what Kansas-Nebraska repealed in 1854.

cards.q: Explain why Jefferson called the Missouri crisis a fire bell in the night.
cards.a: The debate exposed slavery as a permanent sectional dividing line that could break the Union. Jefferson saw that drawing a geographic line over slavery would define politics for generations rather than settle the question.
cards.n: Strong evidence for causation prompts tracing the long road to secession.

cards.q: State the Monroe Doctrine.
cards.a: Declared in 1823 that the Western Hemisphere was closed to further European colonization, that the U.S. would treat European intervention in the Americas as hostile, and that the U.S. would stay out of European affairs.
cards.h: → two rules, one for each hemisphere
cards.n: Britain's navy actually enforced it; the U.S. lacked the power to back it up in 1823.

cards.q: Date the Monroe Doctrine and the Adams-Onis Treaty.
cards.a: Adams-Onis Treaty (Florida ceded by Spain) 1819; Monroe Doctrine 1823.
cards.n: Britain proposed a joint declaration; Adams insisted the United States speak alone, though the Royal Navy did the actual enforcing.

cards.q: Define the Market Revolution.
cards.a: The early 1800s shift from local subsistence and barter economies to interconnected regional markets, driven by new transportation, factory production, wage labor, and cash crops grown for distant sale.
cards.h: → from what economy to what economy
cards.n: It made the North and West economically interdependent while the South specialized in cotton, deepening sectionalism.

cards.q: Identify the Erie Canal and its economic effect.
cards.a: Completed in 1825, the state-funded canal linked the Hudson River to Lake Erie, slashed shipping costs between the Midwest and New York City, made New York the nation's leading port, and triggered a canal-building boom.
cards.h: → what it linked, which city won
cards.n: It swung western produce away from New Orleans and the Mississippi, tying the Old Northwest to the Northeast rather than to the South.

cards.q: Explain how the transportation revolution reshaped sectional alignments.
cards.a: Canals and then railroads ran east-west, tying western farms to northeastern cities and markets instead of shipping goods down the Mississippi to New Orleans. This bound the North and West together and left the South comparatively isolated.
cards.n: A strong causation point for why the West sided with the Union in 1861.

cards.q: Define the Lowell system.
cards.a: A Massachusetts textile model that recruited young unmarried farm women to live in supervised company boardinghouses and work in mechanized mills that combined spinning and weaving under one roof.
cards.n: Lowell women organized some of the earliest labor protests in the U.S., including the 1834 and 1836 turnouts.

cards.q: Contrast the early Lowell workforce with the mill workforce by the 1840s-1850s.
cards.a: Early mills relied on native-born farm daughters working temporarily under paternalistic supervision. By the 1840s falling wages and speedups drove them out, and Irish immigrant families, including men and children, took the jobs at lower pay.
cards.n: Good continuity-and-change evidence on the degradation of factory labor.

cards.q: Contrast Irish and German immigration in the 1840s-1850s.
cards.a: Irish, driven by the potato famine after 1845, who were mostly poor, Catholic, and settled in northeastern cities as laborers and domestic servants; and Germans, fleeing the failed revolutions of 1848 and land pressure, who often had some capital and moved to midwestern farms and cities.
cards.n: The class difference explains why anti-Irish hostility was sharper than anti-German hostility.

cards.q: Define nativism and name its main political expression in the 1850s.
cards.a: Hostility toward immigrants and preference for native-born Protestants, driven by fear of Catholic influence and wage competition. Its political vehicle was the American Party, or Know-Nothings, which demanded longer naturalization periods and bans on immigrant officeholding.
cards.n: Nativism recurs in Period 6 and Period 7; use it for continuity-across-time prompts.

cards.q: Explain how the cotton gin expanded slavery.
cards.a: Whitney's 1793 gin made short-staple cotton profitable across the Deep South by mechanizing seed removal. Planters spread cotton cultivation west into Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, and Texas, and demand for enslaved field labor rose sharply.
cards.n: The domestic slave trade moved roughly a million people from the Upper to the Deep South after 1808.

cards.q: Differentiate the international slave trade from the domestic slave trade after 1808.
cards.a: Congress banned importing enslaved people from abroad in 1808. The domestic trade then supplied Deep South cotton lands by selling roughly one million people from the Upper South southwest, breaking apart families within the United States rather than across the Atlantic.
cards.n: A key MIG theme item: the largest forced internal migration in U.S. history.

cards.q: Define the Second Great Awakening.
cards.a: A wave of Protestant revivalism from the 1790s through the 1830s that emphasized emotional conversion, free will, and the idea that individuals could achieve salvation and perfect society. Charles Grandison Finney was its leading preacher.
cards.n: The doctrine of human perfectibility is the direct engine of antebellum reform.

cards.q: Explain the link between the Second Great Awakening and antebellum reform movements.
cards.a: Revivalists taught that people freely chose salvation and could perfect themselves and society, so believers, especially women, turned religious enthusiasm into organized campaigns against alcohol, slavery, illiteracy, and mistreatment of prisoners and the mentally ill.
cards.n: The single most reliable causation link in Period 4.

cards.q: Contrast the moral and the economic arguments for temperance.
cards.a: Moral reformers, drawing on the Second Great Awakening and led by groups such as the American Temperance Society founded in 1826, blamed drink for sin, poverty, and domestic violence. Employers backed temperance for practical reasons: sober workers meant fewer accidents and steadier factory output.
cards.n: Nativists tied drinking to Irish and German immigrants, entangling temperance with anti-immigrant politics.

cards.q: Identify William Lloyd Garrison and The Liberator.
cards.a: Garrison began publishing The Liberator in 1831, demanding immediate and uncompensated emancipation with no colonization, condemning the Constitution as a proslavery document, and founding the American Anti-Slavery Society in 1833.
cards.n: Immediatism marked a sharp break from earlier gradual emancipation and colonization schemes.

cards.q: Identify Frederick Douglass and his contribution to abolition.
cards.a: An escaped enslaved man who became the movement's most powerful speaker, published the Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass in 1845, and founded the North Star in 1847, arguing that the Constitution could be used as an antislavery weapon.
cards.n: His split with Garrison over the Constitution and political action is a classic comparison question.

cards.q: Identify David Walker's Appeal.
cards.a: Walker's Appeal to the Coloured Citizens of the World (1829) was a militant pamphlet by a free Black Bostonian that condemned slavery and racism and urged enslaved people to resist, by violence if necessary.
cards.n: Southern states banned it and blamed such writings for Nat Turner's 1831 rebellion.

cards.q: Contrast Garrison's and Douglass's strategies for ending slavery.
cards.a: Garrison rejected politics, burned the Constitution as a covenant with death, and urged moral suasion and northern disunion. Douglass came to argue that the Constitution was antislavery and that abolitionists should vote, organize parties, and use government power.
cards.h: → attitude toward the Constitution and voting
cards.n: Both are immediatists; the difference is means, not goals.

cards.q: Identify the Seneca Falls Convention.
cards.a: The first women's rights convention in the United States, held in New York in 1848 and organized by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott. It issued the Declaration of Sentiments demanding legal equality and, most controversially, suffrage.
cards.n: Many attendees came out of abolitionism, where women were barred from speaking.

cards.q: State what the Declaration of Sentiments argued and what document it imitated.
cards.a: Modeled on the Declaration of Independence, it declared that all men and women are created equal and listed the injuries of men toward women, including denial of the vote, property rights, education, and legal standing in marriage.
cards.n: Using the Declaration's form was a deliberate rhetorical claim to the Revolution's legacy.

cards.q: Date the Seneca Falls Convention and the founding of the American Anti-Slavery Society and its female auxiliaries.
cards.a: American Anti-Slavery Society founded 1833 with women organizing female auxiliaries from 1833-1837; Seneca Falls Convention 1848.
cards.n: The exam wants the causal link: exclusion from abolitionist podiums, especially at London in 1840, is what pushed women to organize separately.

cards.q: Identify Dorothea Dix and her reform campaign.
cards.a: A Massachusetts teacher who documented the confinement of the mentally ill in jails and almshouses and lobbied state legislatures from the 1840s to build publicly funded asylums offering treatment rather than punishment.
cards.n: Part of a broader shift toward state-run institutions, including penitentiaries designed to reform rather than merely punish.

cards.q: Identify Horace Mann and the common school movement.
cards.a: As Massachusetts secretary of education from 1837, Mann pushed for tax-supported public elementary schools, longer school years, standardized curricula, and teacher training in normal schools, arguing that education would make citizens and equalize opportunity.
cards.h: → what kind of school, funded how
cards.n: Teaching became a leading paid profession for women, which reformers justified as an extension of motherhood.

cards.q: Define utopian communities and name several examples.
cards.a: Experimental settlements that withdrew from mainstream society to model a perfected social order. Examples: the Shakers (celibacy and communal property), New Harmony (Owen's secular socialism), Oneida (complex marriage and communal child rearing), and Brook Farm (transcendentalist).
cards.n: Most grew out of Second Great Awakening perfectionism, though Owen's New Harmony was secular; nearly all collapsed within a generation.

cards.q: Define transcendentalism.
cards.a: A New England intellectual movement led by Ralph Waldo Emerson and Henry David Thoreau holding that truth comes from intuition and nature rather than from institutions or empirical reason, and celebrating self-reliance and individual conscience.
cards.n: Thoreau's Civil Disobedience, written against the Mexican-American War, later influenced Gandhi and King.

cards.q: Define the cult of domesticity.
cards.a: The middle-class ideal that emerged with the Market Revolution assigning women a separate private sphere of home, piety, purity, and child rearing, while men occupied the public world of work and politics.
cards.n: It applied mainly to white middle-class women; poor, immigrant, and enslaved women worked outside the home.

cards.q: Contrast the cult of domesticity with the women's rights movement of the 1840s.
cards.a: The cult of domesticity confined women to a moral private sphere; the women's rights movement demanded entry to the public sphere through suffrage, property rights, and legal standing. Yet reformers often used domesticity's claim of female moral superiority to justify public activism.
cards.n: The best answers note that domesticity both limited women and gave them a platform.

cards.q: Define Jacksonian democracy.
cards.a: The 1820s-1830s expansion of political participation through near-universal white male suffrage, popular election of presidential electors, nominating conventions, and rhetoric pitting the common man against entrenched elites and monopolies.
cards.h: → who gained the vote, who was excluded
cards.n: Expansion for white men coincided with the disfranchisement of free Black men in states like Pennsylvania and New York.

cards.q: Define the spoils system.
cards.a: Jackson's practice of replacing federal officeholders with loyal supporters, defended as rotation in office that prevented an entrenched bureaucracy and let ordinary citizens serve. Critics called it patronage that rewarded loyalty over competence.
cards.n: It is the target of civil service reform later, in the 1883 Pendleton Act.

cards.q: Identify the nullification crisis.
cards.a: South Carolina, guided by Calhoun's doctrine that a state could void federal law, declared the tariffs of 1828 and 1832 null in 1832. Jackson obtained a Force Bill authorizing military enforcement while Clay brokered a compromise tariff that lowered rates over ten years.
cards.h: → state, doctrine, and how it ended
cards.n: Jackson the states-rights Democrat defended federal supremacy here, which surprises students.

cards.q: Explain the long-term significance of the nullification crisis.
cards.a: It rehearsed the constitutional argument of secession: whether sovereignty rests with the states or the national government. Compromise deferred the fight, but South Carolina's willingness to defy federal law foreshadowed 1860.
cards.n: The tariff was the occasion; protecting slavery from federal power was the underlying stake.

cards.q: Identify the Indian Removal Act and the Trail of Tears.
cards.a: The 1830 act authorized the president to negotiate the exchange of eastern Native lands for territory west of the Mississippi. Enforcement drove the Cherokee, Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw, and Seminole west; the Cherokee march of 1838-1839 killed roughly 4,000 and is called the Trail of Tears.
cards.n: The Cherokee had adopted a written constitution, alphabet, and farms, so removal was not about assimilation.

cards.q: Date the Indian Removal Act, Worcester v. Georgia, and the Cherokee Trail of Tears.
cards.a: Indian Removal Act 1830; Worcester v. Georgia 1832; Cherokee Trail of Tears 1838-1839.
cards.n: The Court ruled against removal two years after the act and six years before the march.

cards.q: Identify the Bank War.
cards.a: Jackson's campaign against the Second Bank of the United States: he vetoed its early recharter in 1832 as an unconstitutional monopoly serving the rich, won reelection on the issue, and then removed federal deposits into state pet banks.
cards.n: The veto message is a key document for Jacksonian rhetoric about privilege and the common man.

cards.q: Explain how Jackson's financial policies contributed to the Panic of 1837.
cards.a: Moving deposits to pet banks fueled easy credit and land speculation, and the 1836 Specie Circular then required payment for public land in gold or silver. Credit collapsed, banks failed, and a depression lasting into the 1840s fell on Van Buren.
cards.n: Whigs blamed executive tyranny; the depression helped elect Harrison in 1840.

cards.q: Contrast the Whigs and the Jacksonian Democrats.
cards.a: Whigs backed Clay's American System, a national bank, protective tariffs, internal improvements, and moral reform, drawing business and evangelical support. Democrats wanted limited government, no national bank, low tariffs, expansion, and strong executive power, drawing farmers, workers, and immigrants.
cards.n: Both parties were national coalitions that avoided slavery to survive, which is why both fractured in the 1850s.

cards.q: Differentiate the First Party System from the Second Party System.
cards.a: The First System pitted Federalists against Democratic-Republicans in an era of limited suffrage and elite politics. The Second System pitted Whigs against Democrats with near-universal white male suffrage, nominating conventions, and mass campaigning, as in the 1840 log cabin campaign with about 80 percent turnout.
cards.n: Whigs won in 1840 by copying Jacksonian mass techniques rather than by arguing policy.

cards.q: Identify the Adams-Onis Treaty of 1819 and its terms.
cards.a: A treaty in which Spain ceded Florida to the United States and gave up its claim to the Pacific Northwest, in exchange for the U.S. dropping claims to Texas and assuming $5 million in American citizens' claims against Spain. It also fixed the western boundary of the Louisiana Purchase.
cards.h: → Spain gives up Florida + boundary line set
cards.n: Negotiated by Secretary of State John Quincy Adams; often paired with the Monroe Doctrine on the timeline.

cards.q: Identify the 'Corrupt Bargain' of 1824.
cards.a: When no candidate won an electoral majority in the four-way 1824 race, the House of Representatives chose John Quincy Adams over Andrew Jackson, who had won the most popular and electoral votes. Adams then named Henry Clay, who had also run, as secretary of state, and Jackson's furious supporters called it a corrupt bargain.
cards.h: → House picks Adams over Jackson + Clay's reward
cards.n: Fueled Jackson's 1828 campaign and the birth of the Democratic Party as a movement against elite manipulation.

cards.q: Explain why the election of 1828 is considered a turning point toward mass democracy.
cards.a: Nearly all states had dropped property requirements for white male voters, and turnout roughly tripled from 1824. Jackson's campaign used mass rallies, parades, and slogans to appeal directly to ordinary voters, a style of popular politics that defined the new Second Party System.
cards.h: → expanded suffrage + turnout surge + campaign style
cards.n: The gain in democracy was for white men only; it coincided with tightening restrictions on free Black voters in several states.

cards.q: Define the Tariff of Abominations of 1828.
cards.a: A high protective tariff on manufactured imports, passed to help northern industry, that Southerners condemned as favoring the North while raising the cost of goods and inviting British retaliation against southern cotton exports. It set off the nullification crisis.
cards.h: → high tariff + why South hated it
cards.n: Passed under John Quincy Adams, but Jackson inherited the fight; Calhoun answered it anonymously in the South Carolina Exposition and Protest.

cards.q: Define Calhoun's theory of nullification as laid out in the South Carolina Exposition and Protest.
cards.a: John C. Calhoun's 1828 argument that because states had created the Union, a state convention could declare a federal law unconstitutional and void within its borders, and even secede if overruled. South Carolina applied this theory to nullify the 1828 and 1832 tariffs.
cards.h: → author + core claim + which law it targeted
cards.n: A states' rights argument later echoed, in modified form, by secessionists in 1860-61.

cards.q: Explain how Jackson's Indian removal policy defied the Supreme Court's ruling in Worcester v. Georgia.
cards.a: The Court ruled that Georgia's laws did not apply within Cherokee territory, which fell under federal authority alone. Jackson refused to enforce the decision, reportedly saying Marshall could enforce it himself, and pushed forward with removal, leading to the Trail of Tears.
cards.h: → Court sides with Cherokee → Jackson ignores it
cards.n: A stark example of executive defiance of judicial authority, with no constitutional remedy available.

cards.q: Identify the American Colonization Society.
cards.a: An organization founded in 1816 that promoted resettling free Black Americans to Africa, founding the colony of Liberia in 1822. Many white members saw it as a moderate alternative to abolition; most free Black Americans and later abolitionists rejected it as racist.
cards.h: → goal + colony founded + why it was rejected
cards.n: A useful contrast to Garrison's later immediatist abolitionism, which explicitly repudiated colonization.

cards.q: Identify Nat Turner's Rebellion and give its year.
cards.a: In 1831, enslaved preacher Nat Turner led an uprising in Southampton County, Virginia, that killed about 55 white people before being suppressed. Turner and dozens of enslaved people, many uninvolved, were executed in the aftermath.
cards.n: Its aftermath closed off debate: Virginia rejected gradual emancipation in 1832 and southern states banned teaching enslaved people to read.

cards.q: Explain how Nat Turner's Rebellion changed the South's approach to slavery.
cards.a: Southern states passed much stricter slave codes banning Black literacy and independent Black churches, and southern legislatures largely abandoned public debate over gradual emancipation. It pushed proslavery writers toward defending slavery as a 'positive good' rather than a necessary evil.
cards.h: → stricter codes + end of emancipation debate
cards.n: The Virginia legislature had actually debated gradual emancipation in early 1832, its last such debate before the Civil War.

cards.q: Identify the Panic of 1819 and its main cause.
cards.a: The first major peacetime financial crisis in U.S. history, triggered when the Bank of the United States tightened credit after a land and cotton speculation boom collapsed. It caused widespread bank failures, unemployment, and debtor anger that fed both Missouri crisis tensions and Jacksonian politics.
cards.h: → first major panic + tight credit → collapse
cards.n: Deepened distrust of the national bank that Jackson later drew on in the Bank War.

cards.q: Identify Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott.
cards.a: Two abolitionist women who, after being barred from full participation at an 1840 world anti-slavery convention because of their sex, organized the 1848 Seneca Falls Convention and co-wrote the Declaration of Sentiments.
cards.h: → barred from abolition convention → organized Seneca Falls
cards.n: The suffrage demand was the only resolution that nearly failed at Seneca Falls; Frederick Douglass's support from the floor carried it.

cards.q: Identify Sojourner Truth.
cards.a: A formerly enslaved woman who became a powerful abolitionist and women's rights speaker, famous for challenging assumptions about race and gender in public addresses such as her 'Ain't I a Woman' speech.
cards.h: → formerly enslaved + dual cause + famous speech
cards.n: Her career links the abolition and women's rights movements, which drew heavily on shared activists.

cards.q: Identify the congressional gag rule of 1836-1844.
cards.a: A House rule automatically tabling all antislavery petitions without discussion, adopted to silence the flood of abolitionist petitions. Former president John Quincy Adams, then a congressman, led the fight to repeal it as a violation of the right to petition.
cards.h: → tables petitions + Adams leads repeal fight
cards.n: It turned abolition into a white northerner's free speech grievance, which won antislavery far more sympathy than moral arguments alone.

cards.q: Contrast the 'necessary evil' and 'positive good' defenses of slavery.
cards.a: Earlier southern leaders such as Jefferson called slavery a necessary evil, an unfortunate inherited system to be phased out eventually. After the 1830s, writers like Calhoun instead argued slavery was a positive good that civilized and cared for an inferior race better than northern wage labor did.
cards.h: → regrettable system vs. actively beneficial system
cards.n: The shift reflects Nat Turner's Rebellion, abolitionist pressure, and the booming cotton economy after the cotton gin.

cards.q: Identify Charles Grandison Finney and the 'burned-over district.'
cards.a: Finney was the leading revivalist preacher of the Second Great Awakening, known for emotional 'anxious bench' conversions. Upstate New York, swept so repeatedly by revivals that observers said no one was left unconverted, became known as the burned-over district.
cards.n: Finney's revivals drew heavily on women converts, who then carried reform energy into temperance and abolition societies.

cards.q: Identify John Humphrey Noyes and the Oneida Community's practice of 'complex marriage.'
cards.a: Noyes founded the Oneida Community in New York in 1848 on the belief that Christ's Second Coming had already occurred, freeing members from conventional sin. Complex marriage rejected monogamy, treating all adult members as married to one another under group oversight.
cards.n: Noyes fled to Canada in 1879 to avoid prosecution once outside pressure over complex marriage grew too strong.

cards.q: Identify Mother Ann Lee and the Shaker practice of celibacy.
cards.a: Lee founded the Shakers in America in the 1770s, teaching that celibacy and communal property ownership would perfect believers. Shaker communities practiced gender-equal leadership but relied on conversion and adoption, not birth, to survive.
cards.n: Their celibacy is the clean contrast with Oneida's complex marriage: opposite answers to the same perfectionist question about sex and family.

cards.q: Identify George Ripley and Brook Farm.
cards.a: Ripley, a transcendentalist minister, founded Brook Farm in Massachusetts in 1841 as a cooperative community where manual and intellectual labor were shared equally. Nathaniel Hawthorne briefly lived there before satirizing the experiment in The Blithedale Romance.
cards.n: It folded after a fire destroyed its uninsured new central building in 1846, one more experiment financed mostly on enthusiasm.

cards.q: Identify the Hudson River School and explain what its landscape paintings expressed.
cards.a: A group of painters led by Thomas Cole who depicted the American wilderness on a grand, romanticized scale. Their work expressed nationalist pride in a landscape untouched by Europe's history and reflected transcendentalist reverence for nature.
cards.n: Its second generation, Bierstadt and Church, moved west and gave Manifest Destiny its visual vocabulary of luminous open land.

cards.q: Identify Margaret Fuller and her contribution to transcendentalism and early feminist thought.
cards.a: Fuller edited the transcendentalist journal The Dial and wrote Woman in the Nineteenth Century (1845), arguing that women deserved the same access to self-development and intellectual independence that transcendentalism promised men.
cards.h: → The Dial editor + early feminist tract
cards.n: Fuller later became the first female foreign correspondent for a major U.S. newspaper, reporting on the 1848 Roman Republic.

cards.q: Define minstrelsy and its role in antebellum popular culture.
cards.a: A wildly popular stage entertainment in which white performers wore blackface makeup to mock and stereotype enslaved and free Black Americans. Figures like Thomas D. Rice, creator of 'Jump Jim Crow,' made minstrel shows the dominant form of American mass entertainment by the 1840s.
cards.n: Minstrelsy shaped white Americans' racial imagination well beyond the stage; the term 'Jim Crow' later named segregation laws.

cards.q: Contrast republican motherhood with the cult of domesticity.
cards.a: Republican motherhood, from the 1780s-90s, cast women's household role as civic: raising virtuous male citizens for the new republic. The cult of domesticity, emerging with the market revolution after 1830, cast the home as a private moral refuge from a competitive commercial world, disconnected from direct civic purpose.
cards.h: → civic child-rearing vs private moral refuge
cards.n: Both confined women to the home but justified it with different logic, one political, one economic.

cards.q: Date the sequence of transportation improvements in the market revolution: turnpikes, canals, and railroads.
cards.a: Private turnpikes spread from the 1790s through the 1820s; the Erie Canal, completed in 1825, triggered a canal-building boom through the 1830s; railroads then overtook canals as the dominant carrier from the 1830s through the 1850s.
cards.n: States financed most canals and many went broke after the Panic of 1837; railroads then ran on private capital plus federal land grants.

cards.q: Differentiate the putting-out system from the Lowell factory system.
cards.a: The putting-out system paid rural families to spin and weave cloth at home on their own schedule. The Lowell system gathered young unmarried women into centralized mills with power looms, company boardinghouses, and fixed factory hours under close supervision.
cards.h: → home-based, own pace vs mill, fixed hours
cards.n: Lowell operatives struck in 1834 and 1836, then were replaced by Irish immigrant families who could be paid less after the 1840s.

cards.q: Identify Tecumseh and Tenskwatawa (the Shawnee Prophet) and their pan-Indian resistance movement.
cards.a: Tecumseh organized a confederacy of Native nations to resist U.S. expansion by refusing to recognize land cessions made by individual tribes, while his brother Tenskwatawa provided religious inspiration urging rejection of white culture and alcohol. William Henry Harrison broke the movement at Tippecanoe in 1811.
cards.n: Tecumseh's death fighting for the British at the Battle of the Thames (1813) effectively ended organized pan-Indian resistance east of the Mississippi.

cards.q: Identify the Treaty of New Echota (1835) and why it was considered fraudulent.
cards.a: A treaty ceding all Cherokee land east of the Mississippi in exchange for western land and payment, signed by a small unauthorized 'Treaty Party' faction rather than the elected Cherokee government under Chief John Ross. The Senate ratified it anyway, providing the legal basis for the Trail of Tears.
cards.n: John Ross petitioned Congress against the treaty with thousands of Cherokee signatures, but removal proceeded regardless.

cards.q: Identify the Maine Law of 1851.
cards.a: The first statewide prohibition law in the United States, banning the manufacture and sale of alcohol except for medicinal and industrial purposes. A dozen other states copied it within a few years before most repealed or weakened their versions by the Civil War.
cards.n: Temperance laws often aimed at Irish and German drinkers, which is why nativism and reform overlap; this is the ancestor of the 18th Amendment.

cards.q: Identify Harriet Tubman and the Underground Railroad.
cards.a: An escaped enslaved woman who returned to the South roughly thirteen times to guide about seventy enslaved people to freedom via the Underground Railroad, a loose network of secret routes and safe houses. She later served the Union Army during the Civil War.
cards.h: → escaped conductor + network of safe houses
cards.n: The 1850 Fugitive Slave Act pushed the routes all the way to Canada, and most escapes were self-directed rather than led by any conductor.

cards.q: Identify the penny press and Benjamin Day's New York Sun.
cards.a: Starting with Day's Sun in 1833, penny newspapers sold for a cent instead of six, funded by advertising rather than subscriptions, and covered crime and human interest alongside politics, building the first true mass-circulation press.
cards.h: → Day's Sun 1833 + cheap + ad-funded + mass readership
cards.n: The direct ancestor of the yellow journalism the deck covers in Period 7.

cards.q: Explain how the cotton gin's success reshaped the geography of American slavery.
cards.a: By making short-staple cotton profitable everywhere, the gin pushed planters to exhaust Upper South soil quickly and then buy land in the fresh Deep South 'Cotton Belt' of Alabama, Mississippi, and Louisiana, driving the massive forced migration of enslaved people sold south by the domestic slave trade.
cards.h: → gin → soil exhaustion → westward Cotton Belt → forced migration
cards.n: An ecological angle on the domestic slave trade card already in the deck.

cards.q: Identify Joseph Smith and the founding of Mormonism.
cards.a: Joseph Smith founded the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints in 1830 after publishing the Book of Mormon. Persecution and his 1844 murder in Illinois drove Brigham Young to lead the Mormons on a trek to the Great Salt Lake valley in Utah by 1847.
cards.h: → Smith founds church 1830 + Young leads trek to Utah 1847
cards.n: One of Period 4's most tested new religious movements alongside the Second Great Awakening.

cards.q: Explain how the Market Revolution deepened regional economic specialization.
cards.a: Cheap transportation let each region specialize: the Northeast industrialized and shifted to wage labor, the Old Northwest grew grain and livestock for eastern markets, and the South intensified cotton for northern and British mills, binding the regions economically even as slavery divided them politically.
cards.h: → North industry, West grain, South cotton, linked by trade
cards.n: This is why the Old Northwest stayed with the Union in 1861: its grain moved east by canal and rail, not south down the Mississippi.

cards.q: State the approximate volume of Irish and German immigration in the 1840s-1850s.
cards.a: Roughly 1.5 million Irish and 1 million Germans arrived in this period, driven out by the Irish potato famine and German crop failures and political upheaval, making these the two largest immigrant streams before the Civil War.
cards.n: The Know Nothing party grew directly out of this influx; Germans arrived with more capital and moved west, while the Irish stayed in port cities.

cards.q: Explain southern opposition to Henry Clay's American System.
cards.a: Southerners, who exported cotton and imported manufactured goods, saw the protective tariff as raising their costs to benefit northern factories, and viewed federally funded internal improvements and a national bank as unconstitutional expansions of federal power that could later be turned against slavery.
cards.h: → tariff hurts cotton exporters + fears federal power
cards.n: Calhoun himself backed the tariff and the Bank in 1816 before reversing, which shows sectional interest driving the constitutional argument.

cards.q: Identify Robert Fulton's steamboat, the Clermont (1807).
cards.a: Fulton's Clermont made the first commercially successful steamboat voyage, traveling up New York's Hudson River in 1807. Steamboats let cargo and passengers move upstream quickly for the first time, transforming river trade well before canals or railroads.
cards.n: The monopoly his backers held on the Hudson is exactly what the Supreme Court struck down in Gibbons v. Ogden in 1824.

cards.q: Identify George Fitzhugh's paternalist defense of slavery.
cards.a: In 'Sociology for the South' (1854), Fitzhugh argued that enslaved people were better cared for than northern wage workers, whom he called 'free laborers' abandoned to market forces, making slavery a more humane system than capitalism itself.
cards.h: → Fitzhugh + slavery kinder than wage labor
cards.n: Pairs with the necessary evil/positive good contrast already in the deck as a third, more radical strand of proslavery thought.

cards.q: State the price and size of the Louisiana Purchase.
cards.a: The United States paid France about $15 million, roughly three cents an acre, for 828,000 square miles stretching from the Mississippi River to the Rocky Mountains, doubling the nation's size overnight.
cards.n: Napoleon sold because Haitian revolutionaries and yellow fever had destroyed his army, leaving Louisiana worth little to him without Saint-Domingue.

cards.q: Explain the human and economic toll of the Panic of 1837.
cards.a: Hundreds of banks failed, unemployment in some cities reached one in three workers, and the depression dragged on for roughly six years, making it the worst economic crisis Americans had experienced up to that point.
cards.n: Voters blamed Van Buren and turned him out in 1840, though the roots lay in Jackson's bank war and the Specie Circular of 1836.

cards.q: Explain the criticism leveled against Jackson's spoils system.
cards.a: Critics charged that rewarding political supporters with government jobs regardless of competence bred incompetence and corruption in federal offices, a complaint that grew louder after the Civil War and eventually produced the civil service reform movement.
cards.n: Forward-links to the Pendleton Civil Service Act the deck covers in Period 6.

cards.q: Explain how Jefferson's actions as president stretched his own strict-constructionist philosophy.
