cards.q: Identify Coney Island as a symbol of Gilded Age commercialized leisure.
cards.a: A Brooklyn beachfront resort that grew into a massive amusement district by the 1890s, with roller coasters, sideshows, and dance halls drawing millions of working- and middle-class New Yorkers seeking affordable escape from crowded, industrial city life.
cards.n: Cheap streetcar and later subway fares made it possible; mass leisure needed transit and a little free time as much as it needed money.

cards.q: Identify the founding of professional baseball's National League in 1876.
cards.a: The National League organized professional baseball into a stable business with standardized rules and franchises, turning the sport into the era's leading spectator pastime and a shared cultural touchstone across growing industrial cities.
cards.n: The reserve clause bound players to one team for life, and a color line drawn in the 1880s kept Black players out until 1947.

cards.q: Identify the Woman's Christian Temperance Union and Frances Willard's 'Do Everything' policy.
cards.a: Founded in 1874, the WCTU was the largest women's organization of the era, campaigning against alcohol. Under Frances Willard it adopted a 'Do Everything' policy linking temperance to broader reforms, including woman suffrage, labor rights, and prison reform.
cards.n: The WCTU shows how a 'respectable' women's cause became a training ground for wider political organizing, including suffrage.

cards.q: Contrast the Greenback Party's currency demands with the postwar push to resume specie payments.
cards.a: The Greenback Party, active from 1874 into the 1880s, demanded keeping and expanding paper currency to inflate prices and ease farmers' debt burdens. Conservative 'hard money' advocates pushed the Resumption Act of 1875, which returned greenbacks to gold convertibility by 1879, favoring creditors over debtors.
cards.h: → more paper money vs return to gold
cards.n: After 1878 silver replaced paper as the inflationists' demand, which is how this fight becomes the free silver issue of the 1890s.

cards.q: Name the main nativist organizations in order from the 1850s through the 1920s: Know-Nothings, APA, Immigration Restriction League, and the second Klan.
cards.a: The Know-Nothings (American Party) targeted Irish and German Catholics in the 1850s; the American Protective Association targeted Catholics from 1887; the Immigration Restriction League pushed a literacy test from 1894; the revived Ku Klux Klan of the 1920s targeted Catholics, Jews, and immigrants nationwide.
cards.n: Notice the escalation: from party politics (Know-Nothings) to lobbying (APA, IRL) to a mass paramilitary-adjacent fraternal order (1920s Klan).

cards.q: Identify the Immigration Restriction League and its proposed literacy test.
cards.a: Founded by Boston elites in 1894, the League lobbied for a federal literacy test to exclude illiterate immigrants, aiming disproportionately at the 'new immigrants' from southern and eastern Europe. Congress passed a literacy test in 1917 over Wilson's veto.
cards.n: Three presidents vetoed literacy tests before one finally passed in 1917, and the real closing came with the quota acts of 1921 and 1924.

cards.q: Identify the Chautauqua movement.
cards.a: A traveling and later stationary adult education movement, founded in New York in 1874, that brought lectures, concerts, and religious instruction to small towns, giving the rural middle class access to culture and self-improvement outside formal schooling.
cards.h: → traveling adult education for rural towns
cards.n: Theodore Roosevelt called it the most American thing in America; radio and the automobile killed off the traveling circuits in the 1920s.

cards.q: Identify the Carlisle Indian Industrial School and Richard Henry Pratt's assimilationist motto.
cards.a: Founded in 1879 by Richard Henry Pratt, Carlisle was the model for federal boarding schools that removed Native children from their families to force assimilation, cutting their hair and banning Native languages under Pratt's motto to 'Kill the Indian, and save the man.'
cards.h: → Pratt's boarding school + forced assimilation motto
cards.n: The schools backfired in one respect: gathering children from many nations together produced the first pan-Indian generation of activists.

cards.q: Identify Susan B. Anthony's 1872 arrest for voting.
cards.a: Anthony voted illegally in the 1872 presidential election to test whether the 14th Amendment's citizenship guarantee implied a right to vote for women. She was arrested, tried, and fined, refusing to pay, but the courts rejected her constitutional argument.
cards.n: The judge directed the verdict and never let her testify; Minor v. Happersett in 1875 shut the door by ruling citizenship did not include voting.

cards.q: Identify Lillian Wald and the Henry Street Settlement.
cards.a: Wald founded the Henry Street Settlement on New York's Lower East Side in 1893, pioneering public health nursing for immigrant families and helping launch the visiting nurse movement alongside her settlement work.
cards.h: → Lower East Side + public health nursing
cards.n: She coined the term public health nurse and campaigned for the federal Children's Bureau that Congress created in 1912.

cards.q: Explain how the Dawes Act and boarding schools like Carlisle pursued the same assimilationist goal by different means.
cards.a: The Dawes Act broke up communally held reservation land into individual allotments to replace tribal identity with individual landowning citizens. Boarding schools pursued the same end culturally, stripping Native children of language, dress, and religion to remake them as assimilated Americans.
cards.h: → land allotment + cultural stripping, same goal
cards.n: Both assumed Native cultures had to vanish; the 1934 Indian Reorganization Act reversed the land half while the boarding schools lingered on.

cards.q: Define the company town model of industrial paternalism practiced at Pullman, Illinois.
cards.a: George Pullman built a planned town where employees rented company-owned housing and bought from company stores, with rent deducted directly from wages. When wages fell in the 1894 depression but rents did not, workers' resentment fueled the Pullman Strike.
cards.n: The strike ended with a federal injunction under the Sherman Act, upheld in In re Debs, and Cleveland offered Labor Day as consolation.

cards.q: Date the founding of the WCTU and the merger that created the National American Woman Suffrage Association.
cards.a: The Woman's Christian Temperance Union was founded in 1874. The rival National and American woman suffrage associations reunited in 1890 to form the National American Woman Suffrage Association (NAWSA).
cards.n: Frances Willard's do-everything policy tied temperance to suffrage, and the WCTU was far larger than any suffrage organization of its day.

cards.q: Identify Thomas Edison's electric light and Alexander Graham Bell's telephone as symbols of Gilded Age technological change.
cards.a: Bell patented the telephone in 1876 and Edison introduced a practical incandescent light bulb in 1879, both transforming daily communication and urban life and symbolizing the era's rapid pace of technological innovation.
cards.n: Edison's deeper innovation was the Menlo Park research lab and an entire power distribution system, not the bulb by itself.

cards.q: Identify Gustavus Swift's refrigerated railcar and its effect on the meatpacking industry.
cards.a: Swift financed practical refrigerated railcars in the 1880s, letting Chicago packers slaughter cattle centrally and ship dressed beef nationwide instead of shipping live animals to local butchers. It centralized meatpacking and cut costs, though local butchers and some railroads resisted the change.
cards.h: → refrigerated cars + centralized Chicago packing + cheaper beef
cards.n: The centralized Chicago plants this made possible are exactly the ones Upton Sinclair exposed in The Jungle two decades later.

cards.q: Identify Dwight L. Moody and his urban revival campaigns.
cards.a: A former shoe salesman turned evangelist, Moody held massive urban revival meetings across American and British cities from the 1870s through the 1890s, using businesslike organization, popular hymns, and simple appeals to reach city dwellers unmoved by traditional church life.
cards.n: Shows evangelical religion adapting to, rather than fleeing, industrial urban life.

cards.q: Identify Nellie Bly and her stunt journalism.
cards.a: Reporter Elizabeth Cochrane, writing as Nellie Bly, went undercover in a New York asylum for her 1887 expose 'Ten Days in a Mad-House' and in 1889-90 circled the globe in 72 days to beat the fictional record from 'Around the World in Eighty Days,' pioneering sensational, self-promoting 'stunt journalism.'
cards.n: A forerunner of the yellow journalism the deck covers under 7.3.

cards.q: Identify Walter Rauschenbusch and the Social Gospel movement.
cards.a: A Baptist minister in New York's Hell's Kitchen, Rauschenbusch argued in works like 'Christianity and the Social Crisis' (1907) that Christians had a duty to fight poverty, unsafe factories, and slums as structural sins, not just save individual souls, inspiring settlement houses and Progressive reform.
cards.n: Set it against Carnegie's Gospel of Wealth: the same Protestant culture produced both a defense of great wealth and an attack on it.

cards.q: State the approximate volume of immigration to the United States between 1880 and 1920.
cards.a: Roughly 20 to 25 million immigrants arrived in this four-decade span, the largest sustained wave in American history, overwhelmingly from southern and eastern Europe and processed mainly through Ellis Island after 1892.
cards.n: Perhaps a third of them eventually returned home, and the flow was cut off by the war and then by the quota laws of 1921 and 1924.

cards.q: State how the urban share of the U.S. population changed between 1860 and 1900.
cards.a: The urban population share roughly doubled, rising from about 20 percent in 1860 to about 40 percent by 1900, as industrial jobs and immigration concentrated Americans in cities faster than at any earlier point in the nation's history.
cards.n: Sets up the 1920 census milestone (majority urban) that Period 7 continues.

cards.q: Explain historians' main criticism of Turner's Frontier Thesis.
cards.a: Critics, especially the 'New Western History' school led by Patricia Nelson Limerick, argue Turner ignored the West's Native peoples, Mexican Americans, and women, treated conquest as empty land waiting to be settled, and overstated the frontier's role in shaping democracy compared to industrial and urban forces.
cards.h: → ignores Native/Mexican/women's West + overstates frontier's role
cards.n: A useful historiography pairing with the Frontier Thesis identification card already in the deck.

cards.q: Identify the Comstock Lode.
cards.a: A massive silver deposit discovered in Nevada in 1859 that touched off a mining rush and boomtowns like Virginia City, financing western development and helping fuel the free-silver movement decades later when mine owners wanted the metal coined.
cards.h: → Nevada silver 1859 + boomtowns + fuels later free-silver push
cards.n: Deep-rock mining needed corporate capital within a few years, so the lone prospector with a pan is mostly myth.

cards.q: Identify the Oklahoma Land Rush of 1889.
cards.a: The federal government opened two million acres of former Native land in Indian Territory to white settlement, and tens of thousands of homesteaders raced to claim plots at a starting gunshot; some 'Sooners' had already sneaked in early, giving Oklahoma its nickname.
cards.h: → 2 million acres opened + settlers race to claim + 'Sooners'
cards.n: The land had been promised in perpetuity to nations removed there in the 1830s, and Indian Territory vanished entirely at statehood in 1907.

cards.q: Identify the Buffalo Soldiers.
cards.a: Black cavalry and infantry regiments, including the 9th and 10th Cavalry, formed after the Civil War and stationed across the West, where they fought in the Indian Wars, built roads, and protected settlers, earning a nickname reportedly given by Native peoples who fought them.
cards.h: → Black army regiments + western frontier duty
cards.n: They fought at San Juan Hill in 1898 as well, and the hard irony is Black soldiers enforcing the dispossession of another people.

cards.q: Identify the technologies that made large-scale Great Plains farming possible.
cards.a: John Deere's steel plow (1837) could cut tough prairie sod, mechanical reapers sped harvesting, windmills pumped groundwater to the surface, and barbed wire, patented by Joseph Glidden in 1874, let farmers fence land on a treeless landscape with no natural material for fences.
cards.n: Complements the barbed wire and closing-the-open-range cards already in the deck with the crop-farming side of Plains technology.

cards.q: Identify the Geary Act of 1892.
cards.a: Congress extended the 1882 Chinese Exclusion Act for another ten years and additionally required Chinese residents to carry a certificate of residence at all times or face deportation, tightening surveillance of Chinese immigrants already in the country.
cards.h: → extends exclusion 10 years + requires residence certificates
cards.n: The Court upheld it in Fong Yue Ting (1893), and Chinese exclusion stayed law until the wartime alliance with China ended it in 1943.

cards.q: Identify the convict lease system.
cards.a: Southern states leased mostly Black prisoners, often convicted of minor or fabricated offenses under new vagrancy laws, to plantations, mines, and railroads as forced laborers, letting planters replace slavery's coerced labor within a nominally free legal system.
cards.h: → prisoners leased as forced labor + replaces slave labor loophole
cards.n: The concrete mechanism behind the gap between New South rhetoric and reality already noted in the deck.

cards.q: Define muckrakers and name several of them with their targets.
cards.a: Investigative journalists of the early 1900s who exposed corruption and abuse to spur reform. Upton Sinclair (meatpacking, The Jungle), Ida Tarbell (Standard Oil), Jacob Riis (tenement poverty, How the Other Half Lives), Lincoln Steffens (city machines).
cards.n: Muckrakers are the classic DBQ example of press pressure producing federal regulation.

cards.q: Identify the two 1906 laws that followed publication of The Jungle.
cards.a: The Pure Food and Drug Act (banned mislabeled and adulterated food and medicine, basis of the FDA) and the Meat Inspection Act (federal inspection of meatpacking plants).
cards.n: Sinclair aimed at workers and hit consumers instead: he said he aimed at the public's heart and hit its stomach.

cards.q: Define Theodore Roosevelt's Square Deal and list its three C's.
cards.a: TR's domestic program promising fairness to labor, business, and consumers. The three C's: control of corporations (trust-busting bad trusts), consumer protection, and conservation of natural resources.
cards.n: TR distinguished good trusts from bad trusts; he regulated far more than he broke up.
x: control of corporations, consumer protection, conservation

cards.q: Name the direct-democracy reforms Progressives used to weaken party machines.
cards.a: The initiative (voters propose laws), the referendum (voters approve or reject laws), the recall (voters remove officials), the secret ballot, direct primaries, and the direct election of senators.
cards.n: Pioneered at the state level, especially Wisconsin under Robert La Follette (the Wisconsin Idea).

cards.q: Identify the Federal Reserve Act (1913) and its purpose.
cards.a: Wilson-era law creating a central banking system of twelve regional Federal Reserve banks under a national board, empowered to set interest rates and issue currency to stabilize the money supply and prevent panics.
cards.n: The most durable New Freedom reform; it answers the long Populist demand for a flexible currency.

cards.q: Identify the Clayton Antitrust Act (1914).
cards.a: It strengthened the Sherman Act by banning price discrimination and interlocking directorates, and exempted labor unions and farm organizations from antitrust prosecution, legalizing strikes, boycotts, and peaceful picketing.
cards.n: Samuel Gompers called it labor's Magna Carta, though the courts later narrowed the exemption.

cards.q: Identify the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire and its consequence.
cards.a: A 1911 New York factory fire that killed 146 workers, mostly young immigrant women, who were trapped behind locked exit doors. It produced state fire-safety codes, factory inspection laws, and stronger workers' compensation rules.
cards.n: Prime evidence that much Progressive labor reform happened at the state, not the federal, level.

cards.q: State what the 16th Amendment (1913) established.
cards.a: It authorized Congress to levy a federal income tax without apportioning it among the states by population.
cards.n: The income tax made a large federal state financially possible, from the New Deal to WWII mobilization.

cards.q: State what the 17th Amendment (1913) changed.
cards.a: It provided for the direct popular election of U.S. senators, who had previously been chosen by state legislatures.
cards.n: Textbook Progressive answer to machine politics and to a Senate mocked as the millionaires' club.

cards.q: State what the 18th Amendment (1919) did and what enforced it.
cards.a: It prohibited the manufacture, sale, and transportation of intoxicating liquors nationwide. The Volstead Act supplied the enforcement machinery. The 21st Amendment repealed it in 1933.
cards.n: Prohibition bridges Progressive moral reform and 1920s cultural conflict, and it fed organized crime.

cards.q: State what the 19th Amendment (1920) guaranteed.
cards.a: It barred the states and the federal government from denying the right to vote on account of sex, granting women nationwide suffrage.
cards.n: Capstone of a movement running from Seneca Falls in 1848; wartime service gave the final push.

cards.q: Define yellow journalism and name its two leading practitioners.
cards.a: Sensational, exaggerated reporting designed to sell newspapers. William Randolph Hearst (New York Journal) and Joseph Pulitzer (New York World) inflamed public anger over Spanish rule in Cuba before 1898.
cards.n: Classic sourcing question: yellow-press coverage shows how purpose and audience shape evidence.

cards.q: Identify the Teller Amendment and the Platt Amendment.
cards.a: The Teller Amendment (1898) pledged that the U.S. would not annex Cuba. The Platt Amendment (1901) then forced Cuba to permit U.S. intervention, to limit its treaty-making and debt, and to lease Guantanamo Bay to the United States.
cards.n: The pair is the sharpest evidence of the gap between anti-imperialist rhetoric and imperial practice.

cards.q: Identify the Philippine-American War and the Anti-Imperialist League.
cards.a: After annexation in 1898, Emilio Aguinaldo's forces fought a brutal U.S. counterinsurgency (1899-1902) that killed hundreds of thousands of Filipinos. The Anti-Imperialist League (Twain, Carnegie, Bryan, Addams) opposed annexation as a betrayal of self-government.
cards.n: Shows that empire was contested at home; the war undercut the civilizing-mission justification.

cards.q: Define the Open Door Policy.
cards.a: Secretary of State John Hay's 1899-1900 notes asking the imperial powers to keep equal trading access to all of China and to preserve Chinese territorial integrity, protecting U.S. commercial opportunity without colonies.
cards.n: The economic model of U.S. expansion: markets and access rather than territory.

cards.q: State the Roosevelt Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine (1904).
cards.a: TR asserted that chronic wrongdoing or instability in Latin America could compel the United States to act as an international police power, intervening to preempt European debt collection in the hemisphere.
cards.n: It turns Monroe's defensive warning into a claimed right to intervene; cite it for Big Stick diplomacy.

cards.q: Identify the Zimmermann Telegram.
cards.a: A secret 1917 German message, intercepted by the British, offering Mexico an alliance and the recovery of Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona if the U.S. entered the war. Its publication enraged American opinion.
cards.n: Combined with unrestricted submarine warfare, it is the standard proximate cause of U.S. entry.

cards.q: Identify the Espionage Act (1917) and the Sedition Act (1918).
cards.a: Wartime laws criminalizing interference with the draft or military operations (Espionage) and disloyal, profane, or abusive speech about the government, flag, or armed forces (Sedition). Socialist Eugene Debs was imprisoned under them.
cards.n: The best evidence for wartime contraction of civil liberties; pair them with Schenck.

cards.q: Identify Schenck v. United States (1919) and its legal test.
cards.a: The Supreme Court unanimously upheld an Espionage Act conviction for anti-draft leaflets. Justice Holmes held that speech creating a clear and present danger of substantive evils Congress may prevent is unprotected, especially in wartime.
cards.n: Holmes's falsely shouting fire in a theater line comes from this case; the test stood until Brandenburg (1969).

cards.q: Identify the Committee on Public Information.
cards.a: The federal propaganda agency under George Creel that mobilized opinion for WWI through posters, films, press releases, and Four Minute Men speakers, promoting patriotism and anti-German sentiment.
cards.n: It fed the wave of anti-German hysteria and pressure for conformity on the home front.

cards.q: Define the Great Migration.
cards.a: The movement of roughly one and a half million African Americans out of the rural South to Northern and Midwestern cities from about 1910 to 1940, driven by wartime industrial jobs, boll weevil crop failures, and escape from Jim Crow and lynching.
cards.n: Push-pull migration card: it reshaped Northern politics, produced the Harlem Renaissance, and sparked race riots.

cards.q: State the purpose and key elements of Wilson's Fourteen Points.
cards.a: Wilson's 1918 peace program: open diplomacy, freedom of the seas, free trade, arms reduction, national self-determination, adjustment of colonial claims, and above all Point 14, a general association of nations, the League.
cards.n: Only self-determination and the League survived at Versailles; the rest lost out to Allied demands for reparations.

cards.q: Define the First Red Scare and identify the Palmer Raids.
cards.a: The 1919-1920 panic over communism, anarchism, and labor radicalism after the Bolshevik Revolution and a wave of strikes and bombings. Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer's raids arrested thousands of suspected radicals and deported hundreds without due process.
cards.n: Sacco and Vanzetti's 1921 trial and 1927 execution is the standard illustration of nativist and anti-radical bias.

cards.q: Identify the Emergency Quota Act (1921) and the National Origins Act (1924).
cards.a: Immigration laws that imposed national-origins quotas pegged to earlier census counts, sharply restricting southern and eastern Europeans, and barring most Asian immigration entirely. Western Hemisphere migration was left unrestricted.
cards.n: The 1924 quotas used the 1890 census on purpose, to favor northern and western Europeans; repealed in 1965.

cards.q: Identify the Scopes Trial (1925) and what it symbolized.
cards.a: The Tennessee prosecution of teacher John Scopes for teaching evolution. William Jennings Bryan argued for the state and Clarence Darrow for the defense. Scopes was convicted, but the trial dramatized the clash between fundamentalism and modern science.
cards.n: Use it as evidence of the urban-rural, modernist-fundamentalist divide of the 1920s.

cards.q: Define the Harlem Renaissance and name several figures.
cards.a: The 1920s flowering of African American literature, art, and music centered in Harlem, asserting racial pride and a distinct Black cultural identity. Figures: Langston Hughes, Zora Neale Hurston, Claude McKay, Duke Ellington, Louis Armstrong.
cards.n: Direct product of the Great Migration; connect culture to demographic change on the exam.

cards.q: Define the Lost Generation.
cards.a: Postwar American writers disillusioned by WWI and by 1920s materialism and conformity, many of them expatriates in Paris. Key figures: Ernest Hemingway, F. Scott Fitzgerald, Gertrude Stein, T.S. Eliot.
cards.n: Cultural evidence that WWI shattered Progressive confidence in reform and progress.

cards.q: Define 1920s consumer culture and the credit practice that fueled it.
cards.a: Mass production (Ford's assembly line), national advertising, radio, and chain stores created a market for cars, appliances, and radios. Installment buying let consumers purchase on credit, sustaining demand but building household debt.
cards.n: Buying on the installment plan and stock buying on margin are the two debt habits that made 1929 worse.

cards.q: Identify the Dust Bowl and its human consequence.
cards.a: Severe drought plus deep-plow farming stripped the southern Plains of topsoil in the 1930s, creating enormous dust storms. Hundreds of thousands of displaced farm families, called Okies, migrated west to California as farm laborers.
cards.n: Steinbeck's The Grapes of Wrath is the classic source; links environment, migration, and the Depression.

cards.q: Name the three R's that organize the New Deal and give one program for each.
cards.a: Relief (immediate aid: CCC, WPA, FERA), Recovery (restart the economy: AAA, NRA, TVA), Reform (prevent recurrence: FDIC, SEC, Social Security, Wagner Act).
cards.n: The fastest way to sort alphabet agencies on an MC question or in an LEQ paragraph.

cards.q: Identify the AAA, the NRA, and the TVA.
cards.a: AAA (1933) paid farmers to cut production to raise prices. NRA set industry codes on prices, wages, and hours under the Blue Eagle. TVA built dams in the Tennessee Valley for flood control, public power, and regional development.
cards.n: All First New Deal recovery programs; the Court struck down the NRA (Schechter, 1935) and the original AAA (1936).

cards.q: Identify the CCC and the WPA.
cards.a: The Civilian Conservation Corps put young unmarried men to work on reforestation, parks, and erosion control, sending most of their pay home. The Works Progress Administration (1935) employed millions on roads, schools, and public buildings, and paid artists, writers, and musicians.
cards.n: Work relief, not a dole: FDR insisted on jobs, and WPA murals and guidebooks are common stimulus documents.

cards.q: Identify the FDIC, the Glass-Steagall Act, and the SEC.
cards.a: Glass-Steagall (1933) separated commercial from investment banking and created the FDIC to insure bank deposits. The Securities and Exchange Commission (1934) regulates the stock market, requiring disclosure and policing fraud and margin abuse.
cards.n: These are the Reform pillar and the New Deal's most lasting structural legacy in finance.

cards.q: Identify the Social Security Act (1935) and its major provisions.
cards.a: It created old-age pensions funded by payroll taxes on workers and employers, unemployment insurance, and aid to dependent children and the disabled. Farm and domestic workers were excluded, leaving out most African Americans and many women.
cards.n: The exclusion of agricultural and domestic labor is the standard limits-of-the-New-Deal evidence.

cards.q: Identify the Wagner Act (1935).
cards.a: The National Labor Relations Act guaranteed workers the right to organize and bargain collectively, banned unfair employer labor practices, and created the NLRB to supervise union elections. Union membership surged, especially through the CIO.
cards.n: The single most important pro-labor law in U.S. history; explains labor's place in the New Deal coalition.

cards.q: Name the three leading popular critics who pushed FDR from the left and state each one's demand.
cards.a: Huey Long (Share Our Wealth: confiscatory taxes on the rich and a guaranteed family income), Father Charles Coughlin (radio priest demanding nationalized banking and currency inflation), and Dr. Francis Townsend (a monthly pension for the elderly).
cards.n: Their pressure helps explain the more redistributive Second New Deal, especially Social Security.

cards.q: Identify the Lend-Lease Act (1941) and the Atlantic Charter.
cards.a: Lend-Lease let the U.S. lend or lease war material to Britain and later the USSR without payment, making America the arsenal of democracy. The Atlantic Charter (FDR and Churchill, 1941) stated shared war aims: self-determination, free trade, and collective security.
cards.n: Both show the U.S. abandoning neutrality before Pearl Harbor; the Charter previews the UN.

cards.q: Identify Executive Order 9066 and its effect.
cards.a: FDR's 1942 order authorizing the military to designate exclusion zones, used to remove about 110,000 people of Japanese ancestry, two-thirds of them U.S. citizens, from the West Coast into inland internment camps. Redress and an apology came in 1988.
cards.n: Contrast with the far milder treatment of German and Italian Americans to make a race-based argument.

cards.q: Identify Korematsu v. United States (1944) and its holding.
cards.a: The Supreme Court upheld Japanese American exclusion as a wartime military necessity, ruling 6-3 that national security justified the order. The dissents called it the legalization of racism; the Court repudiated the decision in 2018.
cards.n: The wartime bookend to Schenck: rights contract under claimed military necessity.

cards.q: Define the Double V campaign and identify A. Philip Randolph's achievement.
cards.a: Double V was the Black wartime demand for victory over fascism abroad and over racism at home. Randolph's threatened 1941 March on Washington pushed FDR to issue Executive Order 8802, banning discrimination in defense industries and creating the FEPC.
cards.n: This is the direct seedbed of the postwar civil rights movement, and Randolph's tactic returns in 1963.

cards.q: Define the Bracero Program.
cards.a: A 1942 agreement with Mexico admitting temporary Mexican farm and rail workers to fill wartime labor shortages. It brought hundreds of thousands of laborers, often into low pay and poor conditions, and ran until 1964.
cards.n: Pair with the 1943 Zoot Suit Riots in Los Angeles to show demand for Mexican labor alongside hostility to Mexican Americans.

cards.q: Identify the Manhattan Project.
cards.a: The secret U.S. program (1942-1945), directed by J. Robert Oppenheimer at Los Alamos under General Leslie Groves, that built the first atomic bombs, tested at Trinity in July 1945.
cards.n: Also the model for the permanent federal-scientific partnership that defines the Cold War state.

cards.q: Explain the main causes of American overseas expansion in the 1890s.
cards.a: Industrial overproduction demanded foreign markets; Alfred Thayer Mahan's The Influence of Sea Power argued for a large navy, coaling stations, and colonies; Social Darwinism and missionary duty supplied racial and religious justification; and the 1890 census closing of the frontier prompted a search for new frontiers.
cards.n: Economic, strategic, and ideological causes together; a one-cause answer loses points on the LEQ.

cards.q: Explain the immediate causes of the Spanish-American War.
cards.a: Cuban revolt against Spain and Spanish reconcentration camps drew U.S. sympathy; yellow journalism amplified atrocity stories; the de Lome letter insulted President McKinley; and the explosion of the USS Maine in Havana harbor was blamed on Spain, producing the cry Remember the Maine.
cards.n: John Hay called it a splendid little war: ten weeks that produced Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines.

cards.q: Explain why the United States entered World War I in 1917.
cards.a: German unrestricted submarine warfare (Lusitania, then the 1917 resumption), the Zimmermann Telegram, deep economic ties and loans to the Allies, cultural and press sympathy for Britain, and Wilson's ideological aim of making the world safe for democracy.
cards.n: Note the timing: the immediate triggers are 1917, but economic entanglement began in 1914.

cards.q: Explain why the Senate rejected the Treaty of Versailles.
cards.a: Article X of the League Covenant appeared to commit the U.S. to defend member states, which critics said surrendered Congress's war power. Henry Cabot Lodge's reservationists demanded amendments; the irreconcilables opposed any League; and Wilson refused all compromise after his stroke.
cards.n: The U.S. never joined the League it invented, a favorite example of the limits of Wilsonian idealism.

cards.q: Explain the main causes of the Great Depression.
cards.a: Speculation and buying stock on margin, an overextended banking system with no deposit insurance, farm overproduction and debt, industrial overproduction against stagnant wages and deep inequality, weak purchasing power propped up by installment credit, and the 1930 Hawley-Smoot Tariff, which choked world trade.
cards.n: The crash was a trigger, not the cause; graders want structural weaknesses in the 1920s economy.

cards.q: Explain why FDR proposed the court-packing plan and why it backfired.
cards.a: After the Court struck down the NRA and AAA, FDR proposed adding a justice for every one over seventy, up to six. Congress and the public saw a threat to separation of powers; the plan died, split the Democratic coalition, and emboldened a conservative bloc, though the Court soon began upholding New Deal laws.
cards.n: The switch in time that saved nine: FDR lost the battle but won the constitutional war.

cards.q: Explain how World War II ended the Great Depression and transformed the economy.
cards.a: Massive deficit-financed war spending, the draft, and conversion of industry to war production erased unemployment, doubled GDP, drew women and rural migrants into wage work, expanded union membership, and created a permanent federal role in the economy through taxes, contracts, and research funding.
cards.n: The best evidence that spending, not New Deal programs alone, ended the Depression.

cards.q: Explain the arguments for and against the use of atomic bombs on Japan.
cards.a: For: it would end the war quickly, avoid a projected invasion of the home islands with heavy casualties, and answer Pearl Harbor. Against: Japan was near collapse, a demonstration or modified surrender terms were possible, the targets were civilian, and a motive was to intimidate the Soviet Union.
cards.n: Truman's decision is a standard DBQ; give both the military-necessity and atomic-diplomacy interpretations.

cards.q: Explain the U.S. response to the Holocaust and its limits.
cards.a: The State Department restricted refugee admissions under existing quotas, the SS St. Louis was turned away in 1939, and the Allies rejected proposals to bomb the rail lines to Auschwitz. Only in 1944 did FDR create the War Refugee Board, which helped save perhaps 200,000 lives.
cards.n: Antisemitism, nativist quotas, and a win-the-war-first strategy all explain the delay.

cards.q: Contrast New Nationalism and New Freedom in the election of 1912.
cards.a: Roosevelt's New Nationalism (Progressive Bull Moose) accepted big business but demanded a strong federal regulatory state and social welfare legislation. Wilson's New Freedom promised to break up trusts, cut tariffs, and restore competition through smaller government.
cards.n: Four-way race: Wilson won with 42 percent because Taft and TR split Republicans; Debs took 6 percent.

cards.q: Contrast the imperialist and anti-imperialist arguments over annexing the Philippines.
cards.a: Imperialists cited naval bases, Asian markets, national prestige, and a duty to uplift and Christianize. Anti-imperialists argued annexation violated consent of the governed, would entangle the U.S. in war, would admit non-white peoples and cheap labor, and betrayed the Declaration of Independence.
cards.n: Note that some anti-imperialism was itself racist; both sides used racial reasoning.

cards.q: Contrast Big Stick diplomacy, dollar diplomacy, and moral diplomacy.
cards.a: Roosevelt's Big Stick used naval power and intervention (Panama, the Roosevelt Corollary). Taft's dollar diplomacy substituted American loans and investment for bullets. Wilson's moral diplomacy promised to back only democratic, legitimate governments, yet he intervened in Mexico, Haiti, and the Caribbean.
cards.n: All three produced intervention; the continuity is U.S. dominance in the Caribbean, not the rhetoric.

cards.q: Contrast the suffrage strategies of Carrie Chapman Catt and Alice Paul.
cards.a: Catt's NAWSA pursued a Winning Plan of state-by-state campaigns plus a federal amendment, stressing respectability and wartime patriotic service. Paul's National Woman's Party picketed the White House, went on hunger strikes, and held the party in power responsible.
cards.n: Both mattered: Paul's confrontation raised urgency while Catt's lobbying delivered the votes.

cards.q: Compare 1920s nativism with earlier nineteenth-century nativism.
cards.a: Both cast recent immigrants as racially and religiously unassimilable, and both surged in economic stress. The 1850s Know-Nothings attacked Irish and German Catholics through party politics; 1920s nativism targeted southern and eastern Europeans, Catholics, and Jews, winning federal quota laws and reviving the Klan.
cards.n: Change over time: 1920s nativism succeeded in writing racial preference into federal immigration law.

cards.q: Contrast Marcus Garvey's program with that of the NAACP.
cards.a: Garvey's UNIA preached Black separatism, racial pride, and economic self-sufficiency, with a Back to Africa vision and the Black Star Line. The NAACP under Du Bois pursued integration and equal citizenship through litigation, lobbying, and publicity in The Crisis.
cards.n: This split anticipates the later King versus Malcolm X and Black Power debate.

cards.q: Contrast Hoover's and Roosevelt's responses to the Depression.
cards.a: Hoover relied on voluntarism, local relief, and confidence, then moved to limited federal action through the Reconstruction Finance Corporation, which lent to banks and businesses; he opposed direct federal relief. FDR embraced direct relief, work programs, deficit spending, and permanent social insurance.
cards.n: The difference is scale and direct aid, not a total break: Hoover began federal intervention, FDR expanded it.

cards.q: Contrast the First New Deal with the Second New Deal.
cards.a: The First (1933-1934) focused on emergency relief and recovery through business-government cooperation: banking holiday, CCC, AAA, NRA, TVA. The Second (1935-1938), pushed by populist critics and labor unrest, was more redistributive and pro-labor: WPA, Social Security, Wagner Act, and wealth taxes.
cards.n: Second New Deal reforms are the ones that survive; they build the modern welfare state.

cards.q: Date the Spanish-American War and name the treaty that ended it.
cards.a: 1898. The Treaty of Paris gave the U.S. Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines (for 20 million dollars) and independence in name for Cuba.
cards.n: 1898 marks the pivot from continental to overseas empire.

cards.q: Date the opening of the Panama Canal.
cards.a: 1914. The U.S. backed Panama's 1903 revolt against Colombia and secured the Canal Zone by the Hay-Bunau-Varilla Treaty.
cards.n: The canal is the strategic payoff of the Roosevelt Corollary and Mahan's naval doctrine.

cards.q: Date the U.S. declaration of war on Germany in World War I.
cards.a: April 1917, nearly three years after the war began in Europe in August 1914; U.S. troops arrived in force in 1918.
cards.n: The long delay is why arguments about neutrality and economic ties matter.

cards.q: Date the ratification of the 19th Amendment.
cards.a: 1920, seventy-two years after the Seneca Falls Convention of 1848.
cards.n: Chronology trap: the 19th comes after the 18th (1919), not before.

cards.q: Date the stock market crash that opened the Great Depression.
cards.a: October 1929 (Black Thursday, October 24 and Black Tuesday, October 29). Unemployment peaked near 25 percent by 1933.
cards.n: Hoover was seven months into his term; FDR did not take office until March 1933.

cards.q: Date the attack on Pearl Harbor.
cards.a: December 7, 1941. Congress declared war on Japan the next day; Germany and Italy declared war on the U.S. on December 11.
cards.n: Note that Germany declared war on the U.S., which is what made it a two-front American war.

cards.q: Date D-Day and the atomic bombings of Japan.
cards.a: D-Day, the Allied landing at Normandy, was June 6, 1944. Hiroshima was bombed on August 6, 1945 and Nagasaki on August 9; Japan surrendered on August 15 (V-J Day).
cards.n: V-E Day is May 8, 1945, three months before the Pacific war ends.

cards.q: Explain how the sinking of the USS Maine helped push the U.S. into the Spanish-American War.
cards.a: A U.S. battleship exploded and sank in Havana harbor in February 1898, killing over 260 sailors. Yellow press outlets blamed Spanish sabotage without proof, and 'Remember the Maine' became the rallying cry that pushed Congress toward war.
cards.h: → ship explodes + press blames Spain + slogan → war fever
cards.n: The explosion's actual cause (likely an internal coal-bunker fire) remains disputed; the point for APUSH is how the press used it.

cards.q: Explain why the United States annexed Hawaii in 1898.
cards.a: American sugar planters had already overthrown Hawaii's monarchy, Queen Liliuokalani, in 1893 with the help of U.S. Marines. Congress annexed the islands in 1898 to secure a coaling and naval station supporting American power in the Pacific during the Spanish-American War.
cards.n: Cleveland blocked annexation in 1893 as illegitimate; McKinley finally got it through by joint resolution because a treaty lacked two-thirds.

cards.q: Identify the holding of Lochner v. New York (1905).
cards.a: The Supreme Court struck down a New York law limiting bakers' work hours, ruling it violated employers' and workers' 'freedom of contract' protected by the 14th Amendment's due process clause. It became the symbol of the Court blocking Progressive economic regulation.
cards.h: → strikes down hours law + freedom of contract
cards.n: The 'Lochner era' (roughly 1905-37) describes decades of the Court using this reasoning against labor and welfare laws.

cards.q: Contrast the holdings of Lochner v. New York (1905) and Muller v. Oregon (1908).
cards.a: Lochner struck down a law limiting men's bakery hours as violating freedom of contract. Muller upheld a law limiting women's work hours, reasoning that women's health and childbearing role justified special protection, revealing the Court's gendered double standard on labor regulation.
cards.h: → men's hours struck down vs. women's hours upheld
cards.n: Muller's protective reasoning was later criticized by feminists for reinforcing women's unequal legal status.

cards.q: Identify the founding of the NAACP and give its year.
cards.a: The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People was founded in 1909 by a coalition including W.E.B. Du Bois and white progressive reformers, in response to ongoing lynching and the 1908 Springfield race riot, to pursue Black civil rights through legal action and lobbying.
cards.n: Its legal strategy eventually produced Brown v. Board of Education decades later.

cards.q: Identify the Niagara Movement.
cards.a: A civil rights organization founded by W.E.B. Du Bois and William Monroe Trotter in 1905 that demanded full political, civil, and social rights for Black Americans, rejecting Booker T. Washington's accommodationist approach. It was a direct forerunner of the NAACP.
cards.n: The NAACP that grew out of it in 1909 was founded interracially, with Du Bois the only Black officer among its first leaders.

cards.q: Identify the sinking of the Lusitania and give its year.
cards.a: A German U-boat sank the British passenger liner Lusitania in 1915, killing nearly 1,200 people including 128 Americans. It turned American public opinion against Germany, though the U.S. did not enter the war for two more years.
cards.n: Germany's pledge to limit submarine warfare after this sinking broke down by 1917, directly triggering U.S. entry.

cards.q: Identify the Selective Service Act of 1917.
cards.a: A law requiring young American men to register for the military draft, ultimately registering over 24 million men and inducting nearly 3 million into the armed forces for World War I, after volunteer enlistment proved far too slow.
cards.n: Local civilian boards ran it to avoid Civil War draft-riot resentment; opposing it is what produced Schenck v. United States in 1919.

cards.q: Identify Henry Ford and his contribution to 1920s mass production.
cards.a: Automaker Henry Ford perfected the moving assembly line for the Model T, drastically cutting production costs and prices. His 1914 'five-dollar day' wage also let his own workers afford the cars they built, fueling the era's consumer culture.
cards.h: → assembly line + Model T + five-dollar day
cards.n: The five-dollar day was welfare capitalism, meant to cut brutal assembly-line turnover and keep unions out, not simple generosity.

cards.q: Define welfare capitalism as practiced by 1920s employers.
cards.a: A strategy in which large companies offered workers benefits such as paid vacations, pensions, stock options, and recreational facilities, in order to build loyalty and discourage unionization without raising wages or accepting collective bargaining.
cards.n: It weakened union membership through the 1920s, right before the Depression exposed its limits.

cards.q: Identify the Bonus Army of 1932.
cards.a: Thousands of unemployed World War I veterans marched on Washington, D.C., in 1932 demanding early payment of a bonus promised for 1945. Army troops under General Douglas MacArthur forcibly dispersed their camp on Hoover's orders, badly damaging Hoover's already weak public image.
cards.h: → WWI vets demand bonus + violent dispersal → Hoover's image ruined
cards.n: A second march in 1933 was met with coffee and Eleanor Roosevelt instead of troops, and Congress finally paid the bonus in 1936 over FDR's veto.

cards.q: Explain why the election of 1932 marked a political realignment.
cards.a: Franklin Roosevelt's landslide victory over Hoover built a durable New Deal Coalition of urban workers, immigrants, Catholics, Jews, Black voters outside the South, and white southerners, uniting behind an activist federal government that would dominate American politics for decades.
cards.h: → FDR wins big → New Deal Coalition forms
cards.n: This coalition, not the specific 1932 platform (which was still fairly cautious), is the lasting significance.

cards.q: Identify the Good Neighbor Policy.
cards.a: Franklin Roosevelt's 1933 policy formally renouncing U.S. military intervention in Latin America, replacing the Roosevelt Corollary's interventionism with diplomatic and economic engagement, including withdrawing Marines from Haiti and Nicaragua.
cards.n: A direct reversal of the Roosevelt Corollary (1904); a useful contrast pair across Period 7.

cards.q: Explain why Congress passed the Neutrality Acts of the 1930s.
cards.a: Disillusionment with U.S. entry into World War I, documented by the Nye Committee's claims that arms manufacturers had pushed the country into war for profit, drove Congress starting in 1935 to ban arms sales and loans to nations at war, in hopes of avoiding another European conflict.
cards.h: → WWI disillusionment + Nye Committee → ban arms sales
cards.n: FDR gradually chipped away at these laws (cash-and-carry, then Lend-Lease) as the Axis threat grew.

cards.q: Identify Rosie the Riveter and women's World War II workforce mobilization.
cards.a: A cultural icon representing the roughly six million American women who took factory and defense-industry jobs during World War II, filling labor shortages as men went to fight, alongside women who served in uniform through the WACs and WAVES.
cards.h: → icon + wartime factory work + military auxiliaries
cards.n: Most women left or were pushed out of these jobs after the war, though the experience shaped later feminist demands.

cards.q: Identify the Yalta Conference and give its year.
cards.a: A February 1945 meeting of Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin near the end of World War II that planned Germany's occupation into zones, Soviet entry against Japan, and free elections in liberated Eastern Europe, promises the Soviets soon broke.
cards.h: → 1945 + Big Three + broken promises on Eastern Europe
cards.n: Its broken promises are a standard opening cause cited for the Cold War.

cards.q: Identify the Nuremberg Trials.
cards.a: A series of military tribunals held in Nuremberg, Germany, from 1945 to 1946 that prosecuted top Nazi leaders for war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide, establishing the precedent that following orders was not a valid legal defense.
cards.n: Justice Robert Jackson led the prosecution and parallel Tokyo tribunals tried Japanese leaders; the Holocaust's full scale became public here.

cards.q: Identify Zora Neale Hurston's contribution to the Harlem Renaissance.
cards.a: Hurston combined anthropological fieldwork on southern Black folklore with fiction, most famously the novel Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937), celebrating Black vernacular culture rather than presenting it for white approval.
cards.h: → folklore + Their Eyes Were Watching God
cards.n: Richard Wright panned the novel as apolitical, and Hurston died in obscurity before Alice Walker revived her reputation in the 1970s.

cards.q: Identify Duke Ellington's residency at the Cotton Club and its significance.
cards.a: Ellington led his orchestra at Harlem's Cotton Club from 1927 to 1931, broadcasting nationally over radio. The club excluded Black patrons even as it showcased Black performers, exposing white audiences nationwide to jazz while illustrating the era's persistent segregation.
cards.n: Radio wires running from the club carried Harlem's sound nationwide, a reminder that the Great Migration moved culture as well as people.

cards.q: Identify Langston Hughes's essay 'The Negro Artist and the Racial Mountain.'
cards.a: A 1926 manifesto in which Hughes argued Black artists should express authentic Black experience without regard to whether it pleased white or Black middle-class audiences, resisting pressure toward respectability.
cards.n: Hughes wrote it as a direct reply to George Schuyler, who had argued in the same magazine that there was no distinctly Black art.

cards.q: Contrast the 1920s flapper with the Victorian ideal of womanhood she rejected.
cards.a: The Victorian ideal prized modesty, domesticity, and deference. The flapper cut her hair short, wore short skirts and makeup, smoked and drank in public, and pursued paid work and sexual freedom, symbolizing a new, more independent version of young womanhood.
cards.n: The flapper was a mostly urban, young, white media image; for most American women the 1920s changed housework more than it changed freedom.

cards.q: Explain why the Panic of 1907 led directly to the creation of the Federal Reserve System.
cards.a: When the 1907 panic hit, only J.P. Morgan's private intervention prevented a full banking collapse, exposing the danger of relying on one banker to manage a national crisis. Congress created the Federal Reserve in 1913 to give the government its own tool to stabilize banks and currency.
cards.h: → Morgan's private bailout exposed the gap
cards.n: The Fed's founders deliberately built a decentralized system of regional reserve banks, a compromise between fear of Wall Street control and fear of pure government control.

cards.q: State the specific quota formulas of the Emergency Quota Act of 1921 and the National Origins Act of 1924.
cards.a: The 1921 act capped immigration from each nation at 3 percent of that nationality's U.S. population as of the 1910 census. The 1924 act tightened this to 2 percent based on the 1890 census, a baseline chosen specifically to shrink quotas for southern and eastern Europeans.
cards.n: The 1890 baseline is the tested detail: choosing an earlier census before the 'new immigration' surge was a deliberate way to favor northern and western Europeans.

cards.q: Explain how New Deal deficit spending anticipated Keynesian economics before Keynesian theory was fully adopted.
cards.a: John Maynard Keynes argued government spending could revive demand during a depression, and New Deal relief and public works programs put this logic into practice even before Keynes's General Theory (1936) was widely accepted, though FDR's own deficits remained too small to end the Depression fully.
cards.n: Full-scale Keynesian deficit spending during World War II, not the New Deal itself, is what actually ended the Depression.

cards.q: Identify the Bretton Woods Conference of 1944 and the international monetary system it created.
cards.a: Forty-four Allied nations met in New Hampshire in 1944 to design a postwar monetary order pegging currencies to the U.S. dollar, itself convertible to gold, and creating the International Monetary Fund and World Bank to stabilize global trade and finance.
cards.n: The system lasted until Nixon ended dollar-to-gold convertibility in 1971; the Soviets attended the conference but never joined the institutions.

cards.q: Explain how the 'Brandeis Brief' shaped the Supreme Court's reasoning in Muller v. Oregon (1908).
cards.a: Louis Brandeis's brief relied mainly on sociological and medical data about the physical toll of long working hours on women, rather than legal precedent, persuading the Court to uphold Oregon's maximum-hours law for women as protecting maternal health.
cards.n: This 'sociological jurisprudence' approach became a model for later reform litigation, though it also cemented the sexist premise that women alone needed such protection.

cards.q: Explain what happened to Rosie the Riveter's wartime factory jobs after 1945.
cards.a: As veterans returned seeking work, employers laid off or reassigned millions of women from wartime industrial jobs, and postwar culture pushed a return to domesticity. Many working-class and Black women, who had worked out of necessity, quietly stayed in the paid workforce.
cards.h: → postwar layoffs + push back to domesticity
cards.n: Government propaganda that had urged women into factories in 1942 flipped almost overnight in 1945 to urge them back into the home.

cards.q: Identify the Zoot Suit Riots of 1943.
cards.a: White servicemen stationed in Los Angeles attacked Mexican American youths wearing zoot suits, seen as unpatriotic given wartime fabric rationing. The violence lasted several days before military authorities intervened, exposing wartime racial and ethnic tension.
cards.h: → LA 1943 + servicemen attack Mexican American youth
cards.n: Police arrested the beaten youths rather than the sailors, and Detroit's deadly race riot came only weeks later that same summer.

cards.q: State the effect of the Smoot-Hawley Tariff of 1930 on the Great Depression.
cards.a: The act raised tariffs on thousands of imported goods to record levels, provoking retaliatory tariffs from other nations that collapsed international trade and deepened the global depression, despite over a thousand economists petitioning Hoover against it.
cards.n: It did not cause the Depression, only deepened it; Congress reversed course with the Reciprocal Trade Agreements Act in 1934.

cards.q: Identify the War Production Board.
cards.a: A federal agency created in 1942 to convert civilian industry to wartime production, allocating scarce materials and coordinating output that helped make the United States the 'arsenal of democracy' and pulled the economy fully out of the Depression.
cards.n: The exam's favorite point sits here: this wartime deficit spending, not the New Deal, is what finally ended mass unemployment.

cards.q: Identify the Reconstruction Finance Corporation.
cards.a: A 1932 agency created under Hoover that made emergency loans to banks, railroads, and other large businesses to prevent collapse. Critics called it relief for institutions rather than for unemployed individuals directly.
cards.n: It shows Hoover was not pure laissez faire, and the agency survived to lend far more aggressively under the New Deal.

cards.q: Identify the Kellogg-Briand Pact of 1928.
cards.a: An international agreement, eventually signed by over 60 nations, renouncing war as an instrument of national policy. It had no enforcement mechanism and did nothing to prevent World War II, but reflected 1920s hopes for peace through diplomacy.
cards.n: Japan, a signer, invaded Manchuria in 1931; the pact still supplied the legal basis for the Nuremberg charge of waging aggressive war.

cards.q: Identify the Indian Reorganization Act of 1934.
cards.a: Also called the Wheeler-Howard Act, this centerpiece of the 'Indian New Deal' ended further land allotment under the Dawes Act, restored some tribal self-government, and encouraged tribes to write their own constitutions, reversing decades of forced assimilation policy.
cards.n: John Collier pushed it through, some tribes voted it down as one more imposed model, and 1950s termination policy reversed its direction.

cards.q: Differentiate contextualization from the complexity point on the AP History rubrics.
cards.a: Contextualization is its own row worth 1 point: it situates the argument in the broader events, trends or processes before, during or after the prompt’s time frame. Complexity sits inside the Analysis and Reasoning row and is earned across the whole essay — by qualifying the argument, holding two things in tension, or connecting to another period, region or field.
cards.h: → contextualization = its own point; complexity = inside Analysis and Reasoning
cards.n: Synthesis was its own rubric point until the 2017-18 revision removed it from both the DBQ and the LEQ. Cross-period connections now count toward complexity instead.

cards.q: Explain how to write a contextualization sentence connecting Gilded Age industrial capitalism to Progressive Era reform.
cards.a: A strong contextualization sentence would note that unregulated industrial growth after the Civil War produced immense wealth alongside monopoly power, urban poverty, and unsafe workplaces, conditions that by the 1900s convinced a rising middle class that government activism was needed to correct capitalism's excesses.
cards.h: → name the prior trend, then the condition it created
cards.n: A worked example students can adapt as a template for any period-transition contextualization paragraph.

cards.q: Identify the Potsdam Conference of 1945.
cards.a: Truman, Churchill (replaced mid-conference by Attlee), and Stalin met in occupied Germany in July-August 1945 to plan Germany's postwar administration and reparations. Truman used the meeting to hint to Stalin about the atomic bomb, and rising distrust there foreshadowed the Cold War.
cards.h: → Truman/Churchill-Attlee/Stalin + Germany's postwar plan + bomb hint
cards.n: Every Yalta face but Stalin's had changed, and the conference issued the surrender ultimatum to Japan that preceded Hiroshima.

cards.q: Identify the founding of the United Nations in 1945.
cards.a: Fifty nations drafted the UN Charter at the San Francisco Conference in spring 1945, creating a General Assembly for all members and a Security Council with five permanent members holding veto power, intended to prevent the League of Nations' failures from recurring.
cards.h: → San Francisco 1945 + General Assembly + Security Council veto
cards.n: A direct answer to interwar-period criticism of the League of Nations' weakness, already covered elsewhere in the deck.

cards.q: Identify the Teapot Dome scandal (1923).
cards.a: Interior Secretary Albert Fall secretly leased federal oil reserves at Teapot Dome, Wyoming, to private companies in exchange for personal bribes during the Harding administration. Fall became the first Cabinet officer convicted of a crime committed in office.
cards.h: → Fall + secret oil leases + bribes + first Cabinet officer convicted
cards.n: The signature scandal of Harding's presidency, essential for any 1920s political-corruption prompt.

cards.q: Identify the Boxer Rebellion (1900) and the U.S. response.
cards.a: Chinese nationalists known as Boxers attacked foreigners and Chinese Christians to expel foreign influence. The United States joined a multinational force to crush the rebellion and then reaffirmed the Open Door Policy to keep China's markets open rather than let the powers carve it into colonies.
cards.h: → anti-foreign uprising in China + US joins force + reaffirms Open Door
cards.n: The Open Door was an assertion with no enforcement behind it; the United States put part of its indemnity into scholarships for Chinese students.

cards.q: Identify General John J. Pershing and the American Expeditionary Force.
cards.a: Pershing commanded the roughly two million American troops of the American Expeditionary Force sent to France in 1917-1918, insisting U.S. soldiers fight as an independent army under American command rather than being folded into depleted British and French units.
cards.h: → Pershing commands AEF + insists on independent US command
cards.n: American numbers told mostly in 1918, and Black units such as the Harlem Hellfighters were handed to the French rather than kept in the AEF.

cards.q: Identify the Washington Naval Conference (1921-1922).
cards.a: The United States hosted major powers to negotiate the Five-Power Treaty, which set ratios limiting battleship tonnage among the U.S., Britain, Japan, France, and Italy, an early attempt at arms control and cost-cutting after World War I's expense.
cards.h: → US hosts + battleship tonnage ratios + arms control
cards.n: Japan resented its smaller ratio as a mark of inferiority and walked away from naval limits altogether in the 1930s.

cards.q: Identify Frances Perkins.
cards.a: As FDR's secretary of labor from 1933 to 1945, Perkins became the first woman to serve in a presidential Cabinet and helped design the Social Security Act, the Fair Labor Standards Act, and other core New Deal labor reforms.
cards.h: → first female Cabinet member + designs Social Security/FLSA
cards.n: Social Security as passed excluded farm and domestic labor, leaving most Black workers and many women outside the system she built.

cards.q: Explain the strategic significance of D-Day (June 6, 1944).
cards.a: The Normandy landings were the largest amphibious invasion in history, opening a second front in Western Europe that forced Germany to fight the Allies on two sides simultaneously and began the drive that liberated France within months.
cards.h: → largest amphibious invasion + opens second front
cards.n: Stalin had demanded a second front since 1942, and the two-year delay fed the distrust that shows up in Cold War origins arguments.

cards.q: Define containment and identify the diplomat who formulated it.
cards.a: The U.S. strategy of blocking any further expansion of Soviet influence without direct war. George Kennan set it out in the 1946 Long Telegram and the 1947 Mr. X article, arguing that patient, firm resistance would eventually force Soviet mellowing.
cards.n: Containment is the organizing idea of Period 8: every Cold War policy question can be sorted by it.

cards.q: Identify the Truman Doctrine (1947).
cards.a: Truman's pledge to support free peoples resisting armed subjugation, made when asking Congress for 400 million dollars in aid to Greece and Turkey. It committed the U.S. to global anticommunist intervention.
cards.n: The rhetorical template reused for Korea, Vietnam, and beyond: a local crisis framed in global terms.

cards.q: Identify the Marshall Plan (1948).
cards.a: The European Recovery Program, roughly 13 billion dollars in U.S. aid to rebuild Western European economies. It aimed to restore trading partners and to make communism less attractive by removing the poverty it fed on.
cards.n: Economic containment: humanitarian and strategic at once. The USSR barred its satellites from joining.

cards.q: Identify NATO and the Warsaw Pact.
cards.a: NATO (1949) is a mutual-defense alliance of the U.S., Canada, and Western European states in which an attack on one is an attack on all. The Warsaw Pact (1955) was the Soviet counter-alliance of Eastern European satellites.
cards.n: NATO was the first peacetime military alliance in U.S. history, a break from the no entangling alliances tradition.

cards.q: Identify the Korean War and its outcome.
cards.a: After North Korea invaded the South in 1950, Truman sent U.S. forces under a UN mandate. MacArthur's Inchon landing pushed north, China intervened, and Truman fired MacArthur for insubordination. The 1953 armistice restored a divided Korea near the 38th parallel.
cards.n: First hot war of containment: it tripled defense spending, militarized NSC-68, and set the limited-war pattern.

cards.q: Define McCarthyism and identify HUAC.
cards.a: McCarthyism is making sweeping accusations of communist disloyalty without evidence, named for Senator Joseph McCarthy. The House Un-American Activities Committee investigated alleged subversion, blacklisting the Hollywood Ten and probing Alger Hiss; the Rosenbergs were executed for atomic espionage in 1953.
cards.n: McCarthy fell after the televised 1954 Army-McCarthy hearings and Senate censure; television undid him.

cards.q: Identify the military-industrial complex and who warned against it.
cards.a: The permanent alliance of the armed forces, defense contractors, and Congress created by sustained Cold War spending. President Eisenhower warned in his 1961 Farewell Address that its unwarranted influence threatened liberty and democratic process.
cards.n: Striking sourcing document: the warning comes from a five-star general and Republican president.

cards.q: Identify the Bay of Pigs invasion and the Cuban Missile Crisis.
cards.a: The 1961 Bay of Pigs was a failed CIA-backed invasion by Cuban exiles. In October 1962 U-2 photos revealed Soviet missiles in Cuba; Kennedy imposed a naval quarantine, and Khrushchev withdrew the missiles in exchange for a U.S. pledge not to invade Cuba and the quiet removal of U.S. missiles from Turkey.
cards.n: Closest approach to nuclear war; it produced the Moscow-Washington hotline and the 1963 Test Ban Treaty.

cards.q: Identify the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (1964).
cards.a: After reported North Vietnamese attacks on U.S. destroyers, Congress authorized the president to take all necessary measures to repel attack and prevent further aggression, effectively a blank check for war without a declaration.
cards.n: Only two senators voted no; the reported second attack probably never happened, which fuels the credibility gap.

cards.q: Identify the Tet Offensive (1968).
cards.a: A coordinated North Vietnamese and Viet Cong surprise assault on more than 100 South Vietnamese cities during the lunar new year. U.S. forces repelled it with heavy communist losses, but the scale of the attack contradicted official claims that victory was near.
cards.n: Military win, political defeat: Johnson's approval collapsed and he declined to run again.

cards.q: Define Vietnamization and the Nixon Doctrine.
cards.a: Vietnamization was Nixon's policy of withdrawing U.S. ground troops while training and equipping South Vietnamese forces to fight, backed by intensified bombing and the invasion of Cambodia. The Nixon Doctrine generalized it: allies would supply the manpower, the U.S. the aid and air power.
cards.n: The 1970 Cambodia incursion triggered campus protests and the Kent State shootings.

cards.q: Identify the Pentagon Papers and the War Powers Act.
cards.a: The Pentagon Papers (1971) were a leaked classified history showing that administrations had misled the public about Vietnam; the Court allowed publication. The War Powers Act (1973) required the president to notify Congress within 48 hours and to end deployments within 60 days absent authorization.
cards.n: Both are the institutional aftershock of the credibility gap; Congress reclaiming war power from the presidency.

cards.q: Define detente and give three examples of it.
cards.a: The 1970s easing of Cold War tensions through negotiation. Examples: Nixon's 1972 visit to China, opening relations and splitting the communist bloc; the 1972 Moscow summit and SALT I limiting missiles and the ABM Treaty; and the 1975 Helsinki Accords on borders and human rights.
cards.n: Only a committed anticommunist like Nixon could open China: the political-cover argument.

cards.q: Identify the GI Bill (1944) and its effects.
cards.a: The Servicemen's Readjustment Act gave veterans tuition and stipends for college, low-interest home and business loans, and unemployment pay. It expanded higher education, built a mass middle class, and fueled suburban homeownership.
cards.n: Its benefits ran through segregated institutions and banks, so white veterans gained far more, widening the wealth gap.

cards.q: Identify Levittown and describe postwar suburbanization.
cards.a: Levittown was a mass-produced Long Island subdivision built with standardized assembly-line methods and sold cheaply to veterans. Backed by FHA and VA mortgages, the baby boom, and new highways, suburbs grew explosively; their deeds and lending practices excluded African Americans.
cards.n: White flight plus redlining creates de facto segregation in the North, which is why Brown did not desegregate Northern schools.

cards.q: Identify the Interstate Highway Act (1956) and its stated justification.
cards.a: Eisenhower's National Interstate and Defense Highways Act funded over 40,000 miles of interstate highway, justified as national defense for evacuating cities and moving military traffic. It was the largest public works project in U.S. history.
cards.n: Effects: suburban sprawl, decline of railroads and inner cities, Sunbelt growth, and highways cutting through Black neighborhoods.

cards.q: Identify Brown v. Board of Education (1954) and its holding.
cards.a: A unanimous Warren Court held that separate educational facilities are inherently unequal, overturning the Plessy v. Ferguson separate but equal doctrine in public schools. Thurgood Marshall argued the case for the NAACP Legal Defense Fund.
cards.n: Brown II (1955) ordered desegregation with all deliberate speed, the vague phrase that licensed massive resistance.

cards.q: Identify the Montgomery Bus Boycott and its outcome.
cards.a: Sparked by Rosa Parks's arrest in December 1955, African Americans in Montgomery boycotted city buses for 381 days under the Montgomery Improvement Association led by Martin Luther King Jr. The Supreme Court ruled bus segregation unconstitutional in 1956.
cards.n: It launched King nationally and proved mass nonviolent economic pressure could work; the SCLC followed in 1957.

cards.q: Identify the Greensboro sit-ins, the Freedom Rides, and SNCC.
cards.a: In 1960 four Black college students sat in at a Greensboro Woolworth lunch counter, sparking sit-ins across the South and the founding of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. CORE's 1961 Freedom Rides tested desegregation of interstate bus travel and met mob violence in Alabama.
cards.n: Student-led direct action forced a reluctant Kennedy administration to enforce federal desegregation rulings.

cards.q: Identify the Birmingham campaign and the Letter from Birmingham Jail.
cards.a: King's 1963 SCLC campaign in Birmingham used marches and boycotts; Bull Connor's police dogs and fire hoses, televised nationally, produced national outrage. King's Letter from Birmingham Jail answered white moderate clergy, defending nonviolent direct action and the duty to disobey unjust laws.
cards.n: Deliberate media strategy: provoke visible repression to force federal action. It pushed Kennedy to propose the civil rights bill.

cards.q: Identify the March on Washington (1963).
cards.a: A quarter of a million people rallied for Jobs and Freedom at the Lincoln Memorial, where King delivered the I Have a Dream speech. Organized by A. Philip Randolph and Bayard Rustin, it pressed Congress to pass the pending civil rights bill.
cards.n: Note the full name: it demanded economic justice as well as legal rights, a point often missed.

cards.q: Identify the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
cards.a: It outlawed discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin in public accommodations and employment, allowed the federal government to withhold funds from segregated programs, and created the EEOC.
cards.n: Title VII's sex clause, added by an opponent hoping to kill the bill, became a foundation of the women's movement.

cards.q: Identify the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
cards.a: Passed after the violence at Selma's Edmund Pettus Bridge, it suspended literacy tests and sent federal examiners to register voters in districts with a history of discrimination, requiring federal preclearance of changes to election rules.
cards.n: Black registration in the South rose dramatically within a few years; the 24th Amendment (1964) had already banned poll taxes in federal elections.

cards.q: Identify Black Power, the Watts riot, and the Kerner Commission.
cards.a: Black Power, popularized by Stokely Carmichael and SNCC after 1966, stressed racial pride, self-determination, and self-defense; the Black Panthers added armed patrols and social programs. After the Watts and Detroit uprisings, the Kerner Commission found the nation moving toward two societies, separate and unequal.
cards.n: The Kerner Report blamed white racism and de facto inequality, not agitators, and is a standard DBQ document.

cards.q: Identify the Great Society and the War on Poverty.
cards.a: Lyndon Johnson's domestic program aiming to end poverty and racial injustice. It included the Economic Opportunity Act, Head Start, Job Corps, VISTA, food stamps, federal aid to education, housing and urban development, the NEA and NEH, and public broadcasting.
cards.n: The most sweeping liberal legislation since the New Deal; poverty fell sharply, but Vietnam spending starved it.

cards.q: Identify Medicare and Medicaid (1965).
cards.a: Medicare provides federal health insurance for Americans 65 and older through Social Security; Medicaid is a joint federal-state program covering health care for low-income people.
cards.n: The largest expansion of the welfare state since Social Security and the direct ancestor of debates over the ACA.

cards.q: Identify the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965.
cards.a: The Hart-Celler Act abolished the 1924 national-origins quotas, replacing them with hemispheric caps and preferences for family reunification and needed skills. It opened large-scale immigration from Asia, Latin America, Africa, and the Caribbean.
cards.n: The single most important cause of late-twentieth-century demographic change; connects Period 7 quotas to Period 9 debates.

cards.q: Define the counterculture of the 1960s.
cards.a: A youth movement rejecting middle-class conformity, materialism, and sexual restraint in favor of communal living, rock music, drug experimentation, and personal liberation. Landmarks include the Free Speech Movement at Berkeley, SDS and the Port Huron Statement, and Woodstock (1969).
cards.n: Distinguish the cultural counterculture from the political New Left, though they overlapped on Vietnam.

cards.q: Identify Betty Friedan, The Feminine Mystique, and NOW.
cards.a: Friedan's 1963 book named the problem that has no name, the frustration of educated suburban housewives confined to domestic roles, and helped launch second-wave feminism. In 1966 she co-founded the National Organization for Women to press for equal pay, equal employment enforcement, and legal equality.
cards.n: Second-wave feminism borrowed the civil rights model: Title VII gave NOW its legal lever.

cards.q: Identify the Equal Rights Amendment and the campaign against it.
cards.a: The ERA, passed by Congress in 1972, would have barred denial of rights on account of sex. Phyllis Schlafly's STOP ERA campaign argued it would end protective laws, alimony, and single-sex facilities and would draft women; ratification fell three states short by 1982.
cards.n: The ERA fight is the clearest evidence that grassroots conservatism was mobilizing before Reagan.

cards.q: Identify Roe v. Wade (1973) and its reasoning.
cards.a: The Supreme Court struck down most state abortion bans, holding that a right to privacy implied by the Fourteenth Amendment covers a woman's decision to end a pregnancy, subject to increasing state regulation by trimester.
cards.n: It built on Griswold's privacy right and became the central mobilizing issue of the religious right; overturned in 2022.

cards.q: Identify the Chicano movement and Cesar Chavez.
cards.a: Mexican American activism for labor rights, bilingual education, and political power. Chavez and Dolores Huerta built the United Farm Workers, using nonviolent strikes and the national grape boycott (1965-1970) to win contracts; younger activists formed La Raza Unida and Brown Berets.
cards.n: Chavez consciously adopted King's and Gandhi's nonviolent methods, including fasts, to gain moral leverage.

cards.q: Identify the American Indian Movement.
cards.a: AIM, founded in 1968, demanded tribal sovereignty, treaty enforcement, and an end to termination policy, drawing attention through the occupation of Alcatraz (1969-1971) and the standoff at Wounded Knee (1973). It won the Indian Self-Determination Act of 1975.
cards.n: Red Power parallels Black Power: from integration and assimilation toward self-determination.

cards.q: Identify the Stonewall riots (1969).
cards.a: Patrons of the Stonewall Inn, a gay bar in Greenwich Village, fought back against a police raid over several nights. The uprising catalyzed the gay liberation movement, the first pride marches, and organizations demanding an end to legal and medical persecution.
cards.n: Fits the pattern of rights movements expanding after 1965 by adapting civil rights tactics.

cards.q: Identify Silent Spring, Earth Day, and the EPA.
cards.a: Rachel Carson's Silent Spring (1962) exposed the ecological damage of DDT and launched modern environmentalism. The first Earth Day came in 1970, and Nixon created the Environmental Protection Agency that year; the Clean Air and Clean Water Acts followed.
cards.n: Environmental regulation is bipartisan in this era: Nixon signs it, and the Three Mile Island accident (1979) hardens antinuclear feeling.

cards.q: Identify Gideon v. Wainwright and Miranda v. Arizona.
cards.a: Gideon (1963) required states to provide counsel to defendants who cannot afford a lawyer. Miranda (1966) required police to inform suspects of the rights to silence and to an attorney before custodial interrogation.
cards.n: Warren Court criminal-procedure revolution: it applied Bill of Rights protections to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment.

cards.q: Identify Engel v. Vitale and Griswold v. Connecticut.
cards.a: Engel (1962) barred official prayer in public schools as an establishment of religion. Griswold (1965) struck down a ban on contraceptives for married couples, finding a right to privacy in the penumbras of the Bill of Rights.
cards.n: Engel energized religious conservatives; Griswold's privacy right leads directly to Roe.

cards.q: Identify the Watergate scandal and its outcome.
