cards.a: The 1972 break-in at Democratic headquarters, ordered by operatives tied to Nixon's reelection committee, and the cover-up that followed. Senate hearings revealed secret tapes; United States v. Nixon (1974) forced their release, and Nixon resigned in August 1974 facing impeachment.
cards.n: US v. Nixon limited executive privilege: no president is above the judicial process. Congress then passed FOIA and campaign-finance reforms.

cards.q: Define stagflation and identify the 1973 OPEC oil embargo.
cards.a: Stagflation is simultaneous high inflation, high unemployment, and stagnant growth, which Keynesian policy could not explain or cure. OPEC's 1973 embargo, retaliating for U.S. support of Israel in the Yom Kippur War, quadrupled oil prices and produced gas lines and rationing.
cards.n: Deficit spending on Vietnam and the Great Society, plus the 1971 end of the gold standard, set the inflation up; the embargo lit it.

cards.q: Identify the Camp David Accords and the Iran hostage crisis.
cards.a: Carter brokered the 1978 Camp David Accords, in which Egypt's Sadat and Israel's Begin agreed to the first Arab-Israeli peace treaty. In November 1979 Iranian revolutionaries seized the U.S. embassy in Tehran and held 52 Americans for 444 days, released the day Reagan took office.
cards.n: The pairing is the standard framing of Carter: a diplomatic triumph swamped by a humiliation he could not end.

cards.q: State what the 22nd and 25th Amendments provide.
cards.a: The 22nd (1951) limits a president to two elected terms, a reaction to FDR's four. The 25th (1967) sets presidential succession and disability procedures and lets the president nominate a vice president confirmed by Congress.
cards.n: The 25th made Gerald Ford president in 1974 without ever being elected to either office.

cards.q: State what the 24th and 26th Amendments provide.
cards.a: The 24th (1964) abolished poll taxes in federal elections. The 26th (1971) lowered the voting age to 18, driven by the argument that those old enough to be drafted for Vietnam were old enough to vote.
cards.n: Both extend the franchise; the 26th ties directly to Vietnam-era protest.

cards.q: Explain the origins of the Cold War.
cards.a: Wartime cooperation broke down over Eastern Europe: Stalin demanded a buffer zone and imposed communist regimes despite Yalta pledges of free elections. Add ideological hostility between capitalism and communism, the U.S. atomic monopoly, Soviet resentment of the delayed second front, and the iron curtain descending.
cards.n: Traditional, revisionist, and post-revisionist interpretations argue over blame; the exam wants mutual misperception plus real conflicts of interest.

cards.q: Explain NSC-68 and how it changed containment.
cards.a: The 1950 National Security Council report, written after the Soviet atomic test and the communist victory in China, portrayed a global struggle and called for a massive permanent military buildup and a quadrupled defense budget. Korea provided the justification to implement it.
cards.n: It converts Kennan's selective, largely political containment into militarized, global containment.

cards.q: Explain the significance of the Berlin blockade and airlift.
cards.a: When Stalin cut off ground access to West Berlin in 1948, Truman refused to withdraw or force the issue and instead supplied the city by air for eleven months. The USSR backed down, Germany was permanently divided into two states, and NATO was created the next year.
cards.n: It showed containment could work without war and made West Berlin a symbol reused through the 1961 Wall.

cards.q: Explain why the Second Red Scare gained such force after 1949.
cards.a: The fall of China, the Soviet atomic bomb, the Hiss and Rosenberg spy cases, and the Korean War made subversion look plausible. Truman's own loyalty program legitimized the hunt, and politicians found accusations electorally profitable. It collapsed once McCarthy attacked the Army on live television.
cards.n: Compare with the First Red Scare of 1919-1920: fear of foreign ideology plus domestic political payoff.

cards.q: Explain the significance of Sputnik (1957) for U.S. policy.
cards.a: The first Soviet satellite implied missiles that could reach America and shattered assumptions of U.S. technological superiority. Congress responded with NASA (1958) and the National Defense Education Act, funding science, math, and foreign language instruction; talk of a missile gap shaped the 1960 election.
cards.n: Neat example of Cold War competition reshaping domestic institutions, especially schools.

cards.q: Explain why the United States escalated its involvement in Vietnam.
cards.a: Containment logic and the domino theory held that losing Vietnam would topple Southeast Asia; leaders feared looking weak after China and Korea; commitments piled up from Truman's aid to France through Kennedy's buildup; and the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution let Johnson escalate without a declaration of war.
cards.n: Emphasize incrementalism: no single decision, but a chain each president found harder to reverse.

cards.q: Explain why the Tet Offensive was a turning point despite being a military failure for the communists.
cards.a: It contradicted official assurances that the enemy was nearly beaten, widening the credibility gap. Walter Cronkite declared the war a stalemate, Johnson's approval fell, he halted bombing and withdrew from the 1968 race, and majority opinion turned against the war.
cards.n: Media and public opinion as a factor of war: the classic causation prompt for Period 8.

cards.q: Explain the significance of Brown v. Board of Education and the limits of its enforcement.
cards.a: Brown destroyed the legal foundation of Jim Crow. But Brown II's all deliberate speed invited delay: Southern officials signed the Southern Manifesto and closed schools, Eisenhower had to send troops to Little Rock in 1957, and most Southern Black students remained in segregated schools a decade later.
cards.n: Court victories need executive enforcement and mass pressure; that argument organizes many civil rights essays.

cards.q: Explain why nonviolent direct action was effective from 1955 to 1965.
cards.a: Boycotts imposed economic costs, and disciplined nonviolence in the face of dogs, hoses, and beatings created televised images that shocked national opinion, isolated segregationists, and generated pressure on presidents and Congress to act. It also claimed moral and religious authority that opponents could not match.
cards.n: The tactic depended on television and on federal willingness to intervene; it worked poorly against Northern de facto segregation.

cards.q: Explain why the civil rights movement fragmented after 1965.
cards.a: Once legal segregation and voting barriers fell, the remaining problems were economic and structural: poverty and Northern housing and school segregation, which laws did not reach. Younger activists rejected nonviolence, urban uprisings frightened white allies, Vietnam split the coalition, and King was killed in 1968.
cards.n: Change over time: from legal equality to economic justice, a far harder goal with far less white support.

cards.q: Explain the causes of 1970s stagflation.
cards.a: Deficit spending on Vietnam and the Great Society without tax increases fed inflation; the 1971 abandonment of the gold standard weakened the dollar; the 1973 and 1979 oil shocks raised prices across the economy; and rising foreign competition plus deindustrialization slowed growth and cut manufacturing jobs.
cards.n: Stagflation discredited Great Society liberalism and opened the door to supply-side conservatism.

cards.q: Explain the significance of Watergate for American politics.
cards.a: It forced the first presidential resignation, confirmed that the president is subject to judicial process, and produced reforms in campaign finance, war powers, and government transparency. Combined with Vietnam, it drove a lasting collapse of public trust in the federal government.
cards.n: The distrust Watergate created is a key precondition for Reagan's argument that government is the problem.

cards.q: Contrast containment with rollback.
cards.a: Containment sought to hold the line against further Soviet expansion through aid, alliances, and limited war, accepting the existing communist sphere. Rollback, urged by critics such as MacArthur and by 1952 Republican rhetoric about liberation, meant actively freeing territory already under communist control.
cards.n: Truman's firing of MacArthur is the moment containment beats rollback and civilian control is affirmed.

cards.q: Contrast the Truman Doctrine with the Marshall Plan.
cards.a: The Truman Doctrine was a military and political commitment to aid governments resisting communist takeover, framed in urgent ideological terms. The Marshall Plan was economic reconstruction aid designed to make Western Europe prosperous, and thus resistant to communism, while creating markets for U.S. goods.
cards.n: Both are containment; the difference is the instrument, hard commitment versus economic prevention.

cards.q: Contrast massive retaliation with flexible response.
cards.a: Eisenhower's massive retaliation threatened overwhelming nuclear reprisal for aggression, cheaper than large conventional forces (more bang for the buck) but credible only against major threats. Kennedy's flexible response built conventional and counterinsurgency forces for limited wars, making intervention easier.
cards.n: The shift helps explain escalation in Vietnam: more usable options meant more temptation to use them.

cards.q: Contrast the approaches of Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X.
cards.a: King preached nonviolent direct action, integration, and appeals to Christian conscience and federal power. Malcolm X, in his Nation of Islam years, rejected integration and nonviolence, urging Black separatism, self-defense by any means necessary, and racial pride; after Mecca he sought broader alliances.
cards.n: Both diagnosed the same injustice; the difference is over means, and Malcolm X spoke more directly to Northern urban conditions.

cards.q: Contrast the strategies of the NAACP, SCLC, and SNCC.
cards.a: The NAACP litigated for legal change through the courts. King's SCLC mobilized Black churches for staged nonviolent campaigns aimed at national media and federal action. SNCC organized students for grassroots direct action and voter registration, and moved after 1966 toward Black Power.
cards.n: Movement, not monolith: knowing the division of labor prevents a vague one-leader essay.

cards.q: Contrast the Civil Rights Act of 1964 with the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
cards.a: The 1964 act attacked segregation and discrimination in public accommodations and employment, using federal funding leverage and the EEOC. The 1965 act targeted political exclusion, suspending literacy tests and placing federal registrars and preclearance requirements over states with histories of disfranchisement.
cards.n: 1964 addresses access to public life, 1965 addresses power; Selma is the event that produces the second.

cards.q: Contrast de jure and de facto segregation.
cards.a: De jure segregation is separation required by law, as in the Jim Crow South, and can be struck down by courts and statutes. De facto segregation arises from private practice and policy, including redlining, restrictive covenants, and white flight, and persisted in Northern cities after the laws changed.
cards.n: This distinction explains why the movement's Northern campaigns after 1965 largely failed.

cards.q: Compare the New Deal and the Great Society.
cards.a: Both expanded federal responsibility for economic security under liberal Democrats with large majorities. The New Deal answered mass unemployment with relief, jobs, and social insurance for workers; the Great Society, in a time of prosperity, targeted poverty, health care, education, civil rights, and quality of life.
cards.n: Great Society is New Deal liberalism extended to groups the New Deal excluded, especially African Americans.

cards.q: Compare first-wave and second-wave feminism.
cards.a: The first wave, from Seneca Falls to 1920, concentrated on legal rights, above all suffrage. The second wave, after 1963, targeted workplace discrimination, equal pay, reproductive rights, and cultural and domestic roles, arguing that legal equality alone left women subordinate.
cards.n: Both drew organizers and tactics from contemporaneous reform movements: abolition then, civil rights now.

cards.q: Compare U.S. Cold War policy in the late 1940s with policy in the early 1970s.
cards.a: Late 1940s: confrontation, refusal to recognize communist China, alliance building, and a rapid arms buildup. Early 1970s: detente, arms control through SALT I, recognition of the Soviet sphere at Helsinki, and Nixon's opening to China, exploiting the Sino-Soviet split.
cards.n: The continuity is the goal, containing Soviet power; the change is negotiation replacing confrontation as the method.

cards.q: Contrast 1950s mainstream culture with the 1960s counterculture.
cards.a: 1950s culture stressed suburban domesticity, corporate conformity, religious observance, and consumer abundance, with dissent confined to figures like the Beats. The 1960s counterculture rejected those norms for personal authenticity, communal living, sexual freedom, and open political protest.
cards.n: Note the continuity: both rest on postwar affluence, which gave youth the leisure and means to opt out.

cards.q: Date the Truman Doctrine and the Marshall Plan.
cards.a: The Truman Doctrine was announced in March 1947; the Marshall Plan was proposed in June 1947 and funded in 1948.
cards.n: 1947 is the standard start date for open Cold War in most exam framings.

cards.q: Date the Berlin airlift, the founding of NATO, the Soviet atomic test, and the communist victory in China.
cards.a: The Berlin airlift ran from June 1948 to May 1949. NATO was founded in April 1949, the USSR tested an atomic bomb in August 1949, and Mao's communists won China in October 1949.
cards.n: 1949 is the hinge: the loss of the atomic monopoly and of China drives NSC-68 and the Second Red Scare.

cards.q: Date the Korean War.
cards.a: 1950 to 1953. It began with the North Korean invasion in June 1950 and ended with an armistice, not a peace treaty, in July 1953.
cards.n: No formal peace treaty exists; the war explains the permanent U.S. military presence in Asia.

cards.q: Date Brown v. Board of Education and the Montgomery Bus Boycott.
cards.a: Brown was decided in May 1954. The Montgomery Bus Boycott ran from December 1955 to December 1956.
cards.n: Chronology trap: Brown comes first and helps make the boycott legally plausible.

cards.q: Date the Cuban Missile Crisis.
cards.a: October 1962, thirteen days of confrontation resolved by the Soviet withdrawal of missiles from Cuba.
cards.n: It follows the failed Bay of Pigs (1961) and the building of the Berlin Wall (1961).

cards.q: Date the Civil Rights Act and the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution.
cards.a: Both came in 1964, the Civil Rights Act in July and the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution in August, months before Johnson's landslide election.
cards.n: Same president, same summer: the Great Society and Vietnam escalation start together and then compete for money.

cards.q: Date the Tet Offensive, the assassinations of King and Robert Kennedy, and Nixon's election.
cards.a: All in 1968: Tet in January and February, King in April, Robert Kennedy in June, and Nixon's victory in November on a law-and-order and peace-with-honor platform.
cards.n: 1968 is the pivot of Period 8: liberal coalition fractures and conservative realignment begins.

cards.q: Date Nixon's resignation and the fall of Saigon.
cards.a: Nixon resigned in August 1974; Saigon fell to North Vietnamese forces in April 1975, ending the war.
cards.n: Within nine months the U.S. loses both a president to scandal and the war, deepening the crisis of confidence.

cards.q: Identify Executive Order 9981 and give its year.
cards.a: President Truman's 1948 order declaring equal treatment and opportunity in the U.S. armed forces regardless of race, which led to the desegregation of military units over the following several years, ahead of most civilian institutions.
cards.n: An early Cold War civil rights move: Truman worried segregation embarrassed the U.S. in its propaganda contest with the Soviets.

cards.q: Identify the Little Rock Nine and the 1957 crisis at Central High School.
cards.a: Nine Black students who integrated Little Rock Central High School in Arkansas in 1957 despite Governor Orval Faubus using the National Guard to block them. President Eisenhower federalized the Guard and sent Army troops to enforce the integration order.
cards.h: → 9 students + governor blocks + Eisenhower sends troops
cards.n: Shows the federal government's willingness, if reluctantly, to enforce Brown with military force.

cards.q: Identify the Eisenhower Doctrine and give its year.
cards.a: A 1957 policy pledging U.S. military and economic aid to any Middle Eastern nation resisting communist aggression or subversion, extending containment into a region destabilized by the Suez Crisis and declining British and French influence.
cards.n: It grew out of the 1956 Suez Crisis and was invoked once, to land Marines in Lebanon in 1958.

cards.q: Identify the U-2 incident of 1960.
cards.a: The Soviet Union shot down an American U-2 spy plane over its territory and captured pilot Francis Gary Powers. Eisenhower's initial denial was embarrassed by Soviet proof, and the incident wrecked a planned Paris summit and worsened Cold War tensions.
cards.h: → spy plane shot down + failed cover story
cards.n: Eisenhower's denial collapsed because the Soviets had Powers alive; he was later swapped for Soviet spy Rudolf Abel in 1962.

cards.q: Explain why East Germany built the Berlin Wall in 1961.
cards.a: Hundreds of thousands of East Germans were fleeing to the West through Berlin's open border each year, draining the East German economy of skilled workers. East Germany, backed by the Soviet Union, built a concrete wall in 1961 to seal the border and stop the exodus.
cards.h: → mass exodus west → wall seals the border
cards.n: It became the Cold War's most visible physical symbol of a divided Europe.

cards.q: Identify the Peace Corps.
cards.a: A federal volunteer program created by President Kennedy in 1961 that sent young Americans abroad to work on education, agriculture, and health projects in developing nations, combining humanitarian goals with a soft-power effort to counter Soviet influence.
cards.n: Pair it with the Alliance for Progress in Latin America: both are the soft-power half of Kennedy's flexible response strategy.

cards.q: Identify the Taft-Hartley Act of 1947.
cards.a: A law passed over Truman's veto that curbed union power gained under the Wagner Act, banning the closed shop, allowing states to pass 'right-to-work' laws, and letting the president order an 80-day cooling-off period to delay strikes threatening national health or safety.
cards.n: Labor called it the 'slave labor act'; it marked the start of organized labor's postwar decline.

cards.q: Identify Truman's Fair Deal.
cards.a: Truman's postwar domestic program proposing an extension of New Deal liberalism, including national health insurance, an increased minimum wage, and civil rights legislation. A conservative coalition in Congress blocked most of its ambitious elements.
cards.h: → New Deal extension + what passed vs. blocked
cards.n: A higher minimum wage, expanded Social Security, and the 1949 Housing Act did pass; the blocking coalition had formed against FDR back in 1938.

cards.q: Explain why Congress passed the National Defense Education Act in 1958.
cards.a: The Soviet Union's 1957 Sputnik launch convinced American leaders the U.S. was falling behind in science and technology. The 1958 act funneled federal funding into science, math, and foreign language education and student loans to close the perceived gap.
cards.h: → Sputnik shock → federal funding for STEM education
cards.n: It broke the taboo on federal money for schools, the precedent Johnson's 1965 education act expanded far beyond science and languages.

cards.q: Identify the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965.
cards.a: A Great Society law providing the first major federal funding for K-12 public education, targeted especially at schools serving low-income students, greatly expanding the federal government's role in a policy area traditionally left to states and localities.
cards.n: Aid followed low-income students rather than schools, which is how Johnson got past the church-state fight that had killed earlier school bills.

cards.q: Identify the Clean Air Act of 1970.
cards.a: A federal law, strengthened during the environmental movement's peak, that set national air quality standards and required states to reduce industrial and vehicle pollution, enforced by the newly created Environmental Protection Agency.
cards.h: → 1970 + national air standards + enforced by EPA
cards.n: Nixon, no environmentalist, signed it and created the EPA because the first Earth Day in 1970 made the issue too popular to resist.

cards.q: Identify the holding of United States v. Nixon (1974).
cards.a: The Supreme Court unanimously ruled that executive privilege was not absolute and ordered President Nixon to turn over White House tape recordings sought in the Watergate investigation, a decision that led directly to his resignation.
cards.h: → rejects absolute executive privilege → tapes released
cards.n: A landmark check on executive power, decided unanimously even by Nixon's own appointees.

cards.q: Explain why Nixon's 1972 visit to China mattered for Cold War diplomacy.
cards.a: By opening relations with Communist China after more than two decades of hostility, Nixon exploited the growing Sino-Soviet split to gain diplomatic leverage over the Soviet Union, a striking example of detente-era pragmatism from a longtime anticommunist.
cards.h: → opens China relations + exploits Sino-Soviet split → leverage over USSR
cards.n: A striking reversal from the anticommunist Nixon of the 1950s Red Scare era.

cards.q: Identify Title IX and give its year.
cards.a: A 1972 federal law banning sex discrimination in any education program receiving federal funding, which dramatically expanded women's and girls' access to school athletics and professional and graduate programs over the following decades.
cards.h: → 1972 + bans sex discrimination in education + athletics impact
cards.n: It came in the Education Amendments the same year Congress sent the ERA to the states, and athletics was not what its drafters had in mind.

cards.q: Contrast the legislative fate of Truman's Fair Deal with Lyndon Johnson's Great Society.
cards.a: A conservative coalition of Republicans and southern Democrats blocked most of the Fair Deal in a closely divided Congress. Johnson, with huge Democratic majorities after 1964 and the political momentum from JFK's assassination, pushed most of the Great Society into law.
cards.h: → mostly blocked vs. mostly enacted + why (majorities)
cards.n: The window was short: the 1966 midterms cut those majorities back and Vietnam spending crowded out the rest of Johnson's domestic agenda.

cards.q: Explain why Eisenhower relied on covert CIA operations as a Cold War tool.
cards.a: Covert action, such as CIA-backed coups that overthrew elected governments in Iran (1953) and Guatemala (1954), let the U.S. remove leaders viewed as pro-Soviet without the cost, casualties, or diplomatic fallout of open military intervention.
cards.n: Both coups had long-term backlash: Iran's 1979 revolution and decades of anti-U.S. sentiment in Latin America.

cards.q: Date Executive Order 9981, Brown v. Board of Education, and the Little Rock crisis in order.
cards.a: Executive Order 9981 desegregated the armed forces in 1948, Brown v. Board of Education struck down school segregation in 1954, and the Little Rock Nine integrated Central High School amid federal troop enforcement in 1957.
cards.n: Eisenhower privately disliked Brown but sent the 101st Airborne to Little Rock; the issue for him was federal authority, not civil rights.

cards.q: Identify Jack Kerouac's On the Road and Allen Ginsberg's Howl as Beat critiques of 1950s conformity.
cards.a: Kerouac's 1957 novel On the Road celebrated spontaneous cross-country travel over stable careers, while Ginsberg's 1956 poem Howl attacked consumerism and conformity in raw, confrontational language. Both defined the Beat movement's rejection of mainstream 1950s values.
cards.h: → Kerouac's travel novel + Ginsberg's confrontational poem
cards.n: Howl's 1957 obscenity trial ended in an acquittal that widened literary free speech, and the Beats prefigure the 1960s counterculture.

cards.q: State the central argument of Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique (1963).
cards.a: Friedan argued that postwar culture trapped educated, middle-class suburban women in an idealized housewife role that left many secretly unfulfilled, a feeling she called 'the problem that has no name,' and urged women to seek identity and work outside the home.
cards.h: → 'problem that has no name' + suburban housewife
cards.n: Friedan's book focused almost entirely on white, educated, suburban women; critics note it largely ignored working-class and Black women, who were rarely full-time homemakers by choice.

cards.q: Explain how rock and roll emerged from Black rhythm and blues to become a symbol of 1950s youth culture.
cards.a: Rock and roll fused Black rhythm-and-blues traditions with country music, popularized by artists like Chuck Berry and by white performers such as Elvis Presley who brought Black musical styles to segregated white audiences, alarming parents and giving teenagers a distinct identity through music.
cards.h: → R&B roots + Presley crossover to white teens
cards.n: Presley's crossover success also raised uncomfortable questions about who profited from Black musical innovation.

cards.q: Identify David Riesman's The Lonely Crowd and William Whyte's The Organization Man.
cards.a: Both 1950s bestsellers criticized suburban conformity: Riesman's 1950 book argued Americans had become 'other-directed,' anxiously conforming to peer approval, while Whyte's 1956 book warned that corporate bureaucracy was replacing individualism with team-player conformity.
cards.n: Pair them with Harrington's The Other America (1962), which attacked invisible poverty rather than conformity in the same affluent decade.

cards.q: Identify the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act of 1975.
cards.a: A law that formally ended termination policy, allowing tribes to administer their own federal programs, such as schools and health services, under contracts with the government, marking a shift toward tribal self-governance.
cards.n: It followed a decade of activism: the Alcatraz occupation of 1969 and the AIM standoff at Wounded Knee in 1973.

cards.q: Define termination policy of the 1950s.
cards.a: A federal policy ending recognition of certain tribes as sovereign nations, withdrawing reservation trust status and federal services, and relocating Native people to cities, all aimed at ending tribal identity by dissolving tribes' legal existence.
cards.n: Around a hundred tribes lost recognition, and the urban relocation it pushed created the city communities that later produced AIM.

cards.q: Identify the 1973 occupation at Wounded Knee.
cards.a: Members of the American Indian Movement occupied the town of Wounded Knee, South Dakota, for 71 days in 1973 to protest corrupt tribal leadership and demand treaty rights, drawing national attention back to the site of the 1890 massacre.
cards.n: Do not confuse with the 1890 Wounded Knee massacre; this is a Red Power protest eighty-three years later at the same site.

cards.q: Differentiate the counterculture from the New Left.
cards.a: The counterculture rejected mainstream values through lifestyle, drugs, music, and communal living, largely apolitical in its goals. The New Left, centered on groups like Students for a Democratic Society, pursued explicit political change through campus activism, civil rights work, and opposition to the Vietnam War.
cards.h: → lifestyle rebellion vs organized political activism
cards.n: AP exam essays often wrongly treat the counterculture and New Left as one movement; graders reward students who separate them.

cards.q: Identify the Port Huron Statement and Students for a Democratic Society.
cards.a: SDS, founded in 1960, issued the Port Huron Statement in 1962, a manifesto calling for 'participatory democracy' and criticizing Cold War liberalism, corporate power, and racial injustice. It became the New Left's founding document.
cards.n: The group split apart by 1969, when the Weather Underground turned to bombings, ending the New Left's mass-organizing phase.

cards.q: Explain the demographic consequences of the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965.
cards.a: By abolishing the national-origins quota system and prioritizing family reunification and job skills, the act shifted the source of immigration away from Europe toward Latin America and Asia, reshaping U.S. demographics far more than Congress anticipated.
cards.h: → ends quotas, shifts source to Latin America/Asia
cards.n: Its sponsors promised the ethnic mix would not change, and the law also imposed the first numerical cap on Western Hemisphere migration.

cards.q: Identify Jerry Falwell and the rise of televangelism in the late 1970s.
cards.a: Falwell built a national following through his televised Old-Time Gospel Hour and founded the Moral Majority in 1979, using cable and satellite broadcasting to mobilize evangelical Christians into a conservative political voting bloc.
cards.n: Its organizing spark was as much federal pressure on segregated Christian academies as abortion, though abortion became the public issue.

cards.q: Explain the immediate effect of Title IX (1972) on women's college athletics.
cards.a: By barring sex discrimination in any federally funded education program, Title IX forced colleges to fund women's sports comparably to men's, producing a rapid multi-fold increase in female collegiate athletic participation over the following decade.
cards.n: One unintended effect: as women's programs merged into men's athletic departments, the share of women coaching those teams fell sharply.

cards.q: Name the major antipoverty programs created under the Economic Opportunity Act of 1964.
cards.a: The act created Head Start (early childhood education), the Job Corps (job training for youth), and VISTA (Volunteers in Service to America, a domestic counterpart to the Peace Corps), among other community action programs.
cards.n: Its maximum feasible participation rule let poor residents run local programs, which enraged big-city Democratic mayors and doomed community action.

cards.q: Explain the United Farm Workers' use of consumer boycotts under Cesar Chavez.
cards.a: Chavez and the UFW organized a nationwide boycott of California table grapes during the Delano strike beginning in 1965, pressuring growers by turning ordinary consumers into economic allies rather than relying on strikes alone, winning contracts by 1970.
cards.n: Farm workers were excluded from the 1935 Wagner Act, so they had no legal right to bargain; the boycott was a way around that gap.

cards.q: Identify Phyllis Schlafly's STOP ERA campaign.
cards.a: Schlafly led a grassroots campaign arguing the Equal Rights Amendment would strip women of protections like alimony and exemption from the military draft while undermining traditional family roles, helping stall ratification three states short of the required 38.
cards.n: The amendment had passed Congress overwhelmingly in 1972 and looked certain, which makes her campaign the standard example of backlash politics.

cards.q: Identify court-ordered busing as a tool for school desegregation in the 1970s.
cards.a: Federal courts ordered busing students across district lines to integrate schools after Brown's slow enforcement, most controversially in Boston starting in 1974, provoking violent white resistance and accelerating white flight to suburbs.
cards.n: Swann approved busing in 1971, but Milliken v. Bradley in 1974 barred crossing city-suburb lines, which locked segregation in by district.

cards.q: Explain how a complexity move could connect Cold War containment to earlier American foreign policy.
cards.a: You might note that containment's premise — that the U.S. must actively counter a rival ideology beyond its own hemisphere — echoed and extended Wilson's post-war vision of American-led collective security, showing continuity of ambition even as alliances and foreign aid were new tools.
cards.h: → link containment's logic back to Wilsonian internationalism
cards.n: This earns complexity inside Analysis and Reasoning. There is no separate synthesis row: it was removed from both rubrics in 2017-18, so a dedicated "synthesis paragraph" chases a point that does not exist.

cards.q: State the developments the College Board identifies as central to Period 8.
cards.a: The Cold War's domestic and international effects, the growth of federal power and the welfare state, and the postwar struggle to extend civil rights and equality to groups still excluded from full citizenship.
cards.h: → Cold War + federal power/welfare state + civil rights struggle
cards.n: Treat these three as the contextualization menu for any Period 8 essay: open with the Cold War frame and narrow from there.

cards.q: Identify Billy Graham and postwar religious revival.
cards.a: Evangelist Billy Graham drew huge crowds to his 'crusades,' broadcast on radio and television starting in the late 1940s, becoming an informal spiritual adviser to Cold War presidents. Congress added 'under God' to the Pledge of Allegiance in 1954 amid the era's civic religious revival.
cards.h: → Graham's crusades + adviser to presidents + 'under God' 1954
cards.n: Ties Cold War anti-communism to a religious revival, since atheism was closely associated with communism.

cards.q: Identify the 1960 Kennedy-Nixon televised debates.
cards.a: The first televised presidential debates let a young, telegenic Kennedy outshine a pale, sweating Nixon on screen, even though radio listeners judged the debate closer. It marked television's arrival as the dominant force in American political campaigns.
cards.h: → first TV debate + Kennedy looks better on screen + TV era begins
cards.n: The claim that radio listeners preferred Nixon rests on one small survey, so use it carefully; the safe point is that image became a campaign asset.

cards.q: Explain how highway construction and urban renewal affected Black urban neighborhoods after 1956.
cards.a: Interstate highways and 'slum clearance' projects were often routed directly through thriving Black neighborhoods, demolishing homes and businesses, displacing residents, and cutting off communities from downtown jobs, while the new highways simultaneously enabled white flight to the suburbs.
cards.h: → highways/renewal demolish Black neighborhoods + fuel white flight
cards.n: Complements the Interstate Highway Act and Levittown cards already in the deck with the era's environmental-justice cost.

cards.q: Identify the Army-McCarthy hearings of 1954.
cards.a: Televised Senate hearings into Joseph McCarthy's accusations against the U.S. Army let millions of Americans watch his bullying tactics firsthand. Army counsel Joseph Welch's rebuke, 'Have you no sense of decency,' helped turn public opinion against McCarthy, who was censured by the Senate that December.
cards.h: → televised hearings + Welch's rebuke + Senate censure
cards.n: McCarthy fell, but the machinery outlived him: loyalty boards and HUAC kept working for years after his censure.

cards.q: Identify the Three Mile Island accident (1979).
cards.a: A partial nuclear reactor meltdown at a Pennsylvania power plant released small amounts of radioactive gas and triggered a mass evacuation scare. It became the worst commercial nuclear accident in U.S. history and stalled new nuclear plant construction for decades.
cards.h: → PA nuclear plant + partial meltdown 1979 + halts new construction
cards.n: The film The China Syndrome had opened twelve days earlier, so the public already had a script in mind for what it was hearing.

cards.q: Identify the Clean Water Act of 1972.
cards.a: Passed over Nixon's veto, the act set national goals for eliminating water pollution and required permits for discharging pollutants into waterways, extending the regulatory reach the Clean Air Act had established for air two years earlier.
cards.h: → passed over veto + regulates water pollutant discharge
cards.n: The Cuyahoga River catching fire in 1969 gave the cause its image; Nixon signed other environmental laws but balked at this one's cost.

cards.q: Identify the New Right coalition that elected Reagan in 1980.
cards.a: A coalition of economic conservatives seeking tax cuts and deregulation, religious conservatives mobilized by abortion, school prayer, and the ERA, Cold War hawks demanding rearmament, and Southern and Sunbelt whites who had left the Democratic party, joined by blue-collar Reagan Democrats.
cards.n: Reagan's win rests on the collapse of the New Deal coalition; explain both the pull of conservatism and the push of stagflation.

cards.q: Define supply-side economics and identify Reagan's core domestic policies.
cards.a: Supply-side, or Reaganomics, held that cutting taxes on high incomes and business would spur investment, growth, and ultimately higher revenue. Reagan cut top marginal rates sharply (1981 and 1986), deregulated industries, cut domestic social spending, and broke the 1981 PATCO air traffic controllers strike.
cards.n: The Laffer curve is the theory; the results were growth with tripled national debt, weakened unions, and rising inequality.

cards.q: Identify the Reagan Doctrine and the Strategic Defense Initiative.
cards.a: The Reagan Doctrine supported anticommunist insurgents against Soviet-backed governments, as in Afghanistan, Nicaragua, and Angola. SDI, nicknamed Star Wars, proposed a space-based missile shield; never built, it pressured the USSR into an arms race it could not afford.
cards.n: Reagan's first term revives confrontation and the evil empire rhetoric before he turns to negotiation with Gorbachev.

cards.q: Identify the Iran-Contra affair.
cards.a: Reagan administration officials secretly sold arms to Iran to free American hostages and diverted the proceeds to fund Nicaraguan Contra rebels, in defiance of the Boland Amendment banning such aid. The scandal produced hearings and convictions but did not implicate Reagan directly.
cards.n: A constitutional issue like Watergate: executive action to evade an explicit congressional prohibition.

cards.q: Identify Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms.
cards.a: Glasnost (openness) permitted criticism and loosened censorship, and perestroika (restructuring) introduced limited market mechanisms into a stagnant Soviet economy. Gorbachev also cut military spending, negotiated the INF Treaty (1987), and refused to use force to hold Eastern Europe.
cards.n: His refusal to intervene in 1989 is the immediate reason Eastern Europe's revolutions succeeded.

cards.q: Identify the fall of the Berlin Wall and the dissolution of the Soviet Union.
cards.a: In 1989 Eastern European communist regimes fell in rapid succession and the Berlin Wall was opened in November; Germany reunified in 1990. After a failed hardline coup, the USSR dissolved into fifteen independent republics in December 1991, ending the Cold War.
cards.n: The result is a unipolar moment: the U.S. as sole superpower, which frames 1990s foreign policy debates.

cards.q: Identify the Moral Majority and the culture wars.
cards.a: Jerry Falwell's Moral Majority (1979) organized evangelical Christians into a Republican voting bloc against abortion, gay rights, feminism, and secular public schools. The resulting culture wars pitted traditionalist against progressive views of family, religion, sexuality, and national identity.
cards.n: Religion becomes a stable predictor of party alignment, a major cause of later polarization.

cards.q: Identify the AIDS crisis and the activist response.
cards.a: AIDS spread in the U.S. from 1981, killing tens of thousands amid stigma and federal inaction; Reagan did not address it publicly for years. ACT UP and other groups used direct action to demand research funding, faster drug approval, and treatment access, winning major changes by the 1990s.
cards.n: It shows public health as a political question and pushed gay rights into national visibility.

cards.q: Identify the Persian Gulf War (1991).
cards.a: After Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990, George H. W. Bush assembled a broad UN-backed coalition; Operation Desert Storm expelled Iraqi forces in about six weeks with few U.S. casualties. Saddam Hussein was left in power.
cards.n: Bush called it the end of the Vietnam syndrome; leaving Saddam in power sets up the 2003 war.

cards.q: Identify NAFTA and the digital revolution as forces of globalization.
cards.a: NAFTA (1994) created a free trade zone among the U.S., Canada, and Mexico, cutting prices and expanding trade while accelerating Rust Belt manufacturing job losses. Personal computers, the internet, and mobile technology reorganized work and commerce, fueling the 1990s boom and the dot-com bubble.
cards.n: Globalization is the WXT engine of Period 9: growth and cheap goods alongside deindustrialization and inequality.

cards.q: Identify the Contract with America and the domestic politics of the Clinton years.
cards.a: Newt Gingrich's 1994 Contract with America won Republicans control of Congress on balanced budgets, tax cuts, term limits, and welfare reform. Clinton triangulated, declared the era of big government over, and signed welfare reform in 1996; the House impeached him in 1998 and the Senate acquitted.
cards.n: Divided government plus impeachment: evidence that partisan polarization was hardening well before 2000.

cards.q: Identify Bush v. Gore (2000).
cards.a: In an election decided by Florida's disputed count, the Supreme Court halted the recount 5-4 on equal protection grounds, effectively awarding the presidency to George W. Bush. Gore had won the national popular vote.
cards.n: One of only a handful of elections where the popular-vote winner lost; it fed distrust of both the Court and the process.

cards.q: Identify the September 11 attacks and the War on Terror.
cards.a: Al-Qaeda hijackers flew planes into the World Trade Center and Pentagon on September 11, 2001, killing nearly 3,000 people. The U.S. invaded Afghanistan to destroy al-Qaeda and topple the Taliban, and declared a global campaign against terrorist networks and states supporting them.
cards.n: The defining rupture of Period 9: it reorients foreign policy and reopens the security-versus-liberty debate.

cards.q: Identify the USA PATRIOT Act and the Department of Homeland Security.
cards.a: The PATRIOT Act (2001) expanded federal surveillance of communications, records, and finances and eased information sharing among agencies. DHS (2002) merged more than twenty agencies. Critics cited warrantless surveillance, indefinite detention at Guantanamo, and profiling of Muslim Americans.
cards.n: Put it in the wartime civil liberties series with the Sedition Acts, Schenck, and Korematsu.

cards.q: Identify the Iraq War (2003).
cards.a: The U.S. and a small coalition invaded Iraq to remove Saddam Hussein, justified by claims of weapons of mass destruction and ties to terrorism. No such weapons were found; the fast conventional victory gave way to years of insurgency, sectarian civil war, and a costly occupation.
cards.n: Preemptive war under the Bush Doctrine; the intelligence failure deepened distrust of government claims.

cards.q: Identify the 2008 financial crisis and the government response.
cards.a: The collapse of a housing bubble built on subprime mortgages and mortgage-backed securities brought down major financial firms, froze credit, and produced the Great Recession with unemployment near ten percent. Congress passed the 700 billion dollar TARP bailout, then a 2009 stimulus and the Dodd-Frank law.
cards.n: The bailouts spawned both the Tea Party and Occupy Wall Street, populist reactions from right and left.

cards.q: Identify Barack Obama's presidency and the Affordable Care Act.
cards.a: Obama was elected in 2008 as the first African American president amid crisis and war. The ACA (2010) expanded coverage through insurance exchanges, subsidies, Medicaid expansion, and a ban on denial for preexisting conditions, and became a central partisan battle.
cards.n: Trace the line from Social Security to Medicare to the ACA when a prompt asks about the federal role in welfare.

cards.q: Identify the demographic changes and immigration debates of the 1990s and 2000s.
cards.a: Immigration after the 1965 act, largely from Latin America and Asia, made the U.S. far more diverse, with Latinos becoming the largest minority group and growth concentrated in the Sunbelt. Debate centered on undocumented migration, enforcement, guest workers, and a path to citizenship (IRCA 1986, DACA 2012).
cards.n: MIG and NAT themes: arguments over national identity and assimilation echo the 1850s and the 1920s.

cards.q: Explain the rise of modern conservatism by 1980.
cards.a: Stagflation and tax revolts discredited liberal economic management; Vietnam and Watergate destroyed trust in government; backlash against the counterculture, busing, crime, and Roe mobilized religious voters; Sunbelt growth shifted electoral power; and think tanks, direct mail, and evangelical media built a movement.
cards.n: Answer both halves: what liberalism lost and what conservatives built, since the shift is not just reaction.

cards.q: Explain why the Cold War ended.
cards.a: The Soviet command economy stagnated under military spending, the Afghan war, and falling oil prices; Gorbachev's reforms loosened control and he refused to defend satellite regimes by force; U.S. rearmament and SDI raised the cost of competition; and movements from Solidarity onward dissolved the bloc from within.
cards.n: Historians argue over how much credit Reagan deserves versus Soviet internal collapse; acknowledge both.

cards.q: Explain the economic effects of Reagan's policies.
cards.a: Recession and tight money broke inflation by 1983, and the 1980s brought long expansion and financial deregulation. But defense spending with tax cuts tripled the national debt, union membership and manufacturing jobs fell, inequality widened sharply, and social program cuts hit the poor hardest.
cards.n: Balanced evaluation earns the point; note that the deficit outcome contradicted supply-side predictions.

cards.q: Explain how the September 11 attacks changed American government and society.
cards.a: They produced a permanent domestic security apparatus (DHS, TSA, expanded surveillance), two long wars, a doctrine of preemptive war, and fights over torture and indefinite detention. At home came a surge of unity, then lasting debate over security versus liberty and rising anti-Muslim discrimination.
cards.n: The strongest continuity argument on the exam: every major war narrows civil liberties, then the courts and public push back.

cards.q: Explain the causes of the 2008 financial crisis.
cards.a: Low interest rates and lax lending fueled a housing bubble; subprime mortgages were bundled into securities that ratings agencies mispriced; deregulation and the repeal of Glass-Steagall let banks take enormous leveraged risks; when housing prices fell, defaults spread through the financial system and credit froze.
cards.n: Compare with 1929: speculation, leverage, and thin regulation, but this time the federal response was immediate.

cards.q: Explain the causes of increased political polarization since 1990.
cards.a: Partisan realignment sorted conservatives into the Republican party and liberals into the Democratic, aligning region, religion, and race with party; cable news and social media created separate information worlds; gerrymandering and primaries rewarded ideological purity; and inequality hardened the divide.
cards.n: Useful for a Period 9 causation LEQ, which usually asks about political or social change since 1980.

cards.q: Contrast New Deal liberalism with Reagan-era conservatism.
cards.a: New Deal liberalism treated federal power as the cure for insecurity, favoring regulation, social insurance, progressive taxation, and unions. Reagan conservatism treated government as the problem, favoring tax cuts, deregulation, lower domestic spending, and traditional moral order, while expanding the military.
cards.n: Note the continuity: Reagan did not dismantle Social Security or Medicare, so the New Deal core survived.

cards.q: Compare U.S. foreign policy during the Cold War with policy after 1991.
cards.a: Cold War policy centered on containing one superpower rival through alliances, deterrence, and proxy conflicts. After 1991 the U.S. acted as sole superpower, intervening in the Balkans and Somalia, then after 2001 reorienting around terrorism, preemption, and nonstate enemies.
cards.n: Continuity: global military presence and intervention. Change: the enemy shifts from a state rival to networks.

cards.q: Compare the federal response to the Great Depression with the response to the 2008 recession.
cards.a: Both used federal money to stabilize a collapsing financial system: bank holiday, FDIC, SEC, and jobs programs in the 1930s; TARP, Federal Reserve action, the 2009 stimulus, and Dodd-Frank after 2008. The New Deal response was larger and created lasting jobs programs; the 2008 response was faster and bank-centered.
cards.n: Excellent continuity-and-change prompt: the New Deal precedent is exactly what made rapid 2008 intervention thinkable.

cards.q: Compare immigration debates of the 1920s with those of the 2000s.
cards.a: Both featured claims that newcomers threatened jobs, culture, and national identity, and both produced calls for restriction. The 1920s brought racial national-origins quotas aimed at southern and eastern Europeans and Asians; the 2000s focused on undocumented migration, border enforcement, and legal status.
cards.n: Nativism recurs in every period of heavy migration; note that current restrictionism cannot use explicit racial categories.

cards.q: Date the fall of the Berlin Wall and the dissolution of the Soviet Union.
cards.a: The Berlin Wall opened in November 1989; the Soviet Union formally dissolved in December 1991.
cards.n: Two years separate them: the East European revolutions come first, the USSR's own collapse second.

cards.q: Date the September 11 attacks and the invasion of Iraq.
cards.a: The attacks came on September 11, 2001; the U.S. invaded Afghanistan in October 2001 and Iraq in March 2003.
cards.n: Keep the order straight: Afghanistan is the direct response, Iraq is a separate decision eighteen months later.

cards.q: Date the financial crisis, Obama's election, and the Affordable Care Act.
cards.a: The financial crisis broke in September 2008, Obama was elected in November 2008, and the Affordable Care Act was signed in March 2010.
cards.n: The crisis makes the election, and the election makes the law: a tight causal chain for a short-answer question.

cards.q: Identify the PATCO strike of 1981.
cards.a: When the Professional Air Traffic Controllers Organization struck illegally for better pay and conditions, President Reagan fired over 11,000 striking controllers and banned them from federal service for life, signaling a new era of hostility toward organized labor.
cards.n: Often cited as the symbolic start of organized labor's steep decline in the 1980s.

cards.q: Explain why the election of 1980 is considered a realigning election.
cards.a: Ronald Reagan's decisive win over Jimmy Carter, amid stagflation and the Iran hostage crisis, brought together economic conservatives, evangelical Christians, and 'Reagan Democrats' disillusioned with liberalism into a durable New Right coalition that reshaped American politics for decades.
cards.h: → Reagan wins + coalition forms + why (economic/cultural discontent)
cards.n: Reagan took just under 51 percent with John Anderson running third, so the realignment shows up in the coalition, not in the popular-vote margin.

cards.q: Identify the World Trade Organization and give its founding year.
cards.a: An international body created in 1995 to replace the older GATT system, setting rules for global trade and resolving disputes between member nations. Its founding reflected and accelerated the rapid economic globalization of the 1990s.
cards.n: Critics on both left and right blamed it for job losses to overseas competition, fueling later anti-globalization protests.

cards.q: Explain why the United States invaded Afghanistan in October 2001.
cards.a: The Taliban government ruling Afghanistan refused to hand over al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden after the September 11 attacks. The U.S. invaded to topple the Taliban and destroy al-Qaeda's base of operations, opening what became America's longest war.
cards.h: → Taliban shelters al-Qaeda → invasion → longest war
cards.n: Congress's 2001 authorization passed with a single dissenting vote and was later stretched to justify operations far beyond Afghanistan.

cards.q: Identify the Family and Medical Leave Act of 1993.
cards.a: A federal law, one of Bill Clinton's first major signed bills, guaranteeing eligible employees up to twelve weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave for childbirth, adoption, or family medical emergencies.
cards.h: → 1993 + unpaid job-protected leave + first Clinton bill
cards.n: George H. W. Bush had vetoed the same bill twice, and the leave stayed unpaid, leaving the United States unusual among wealthy nations.

cards.q: Identify the 'Don't Ask, Don't Tell' policy and give its year.
cards.a: A 1993 Clinton administration compromise policy that let gay and lesbian Americans serve in the military only if they concealed their sexual orientation, banning the military from asking about it but also barring service members from disclosing it. It was repealed in 2011.
cards.n: It was a retreat from Clinton's promise of open service, and discharges of gay service members actually rose in the years right after it took effect.

cards.q: Identify the Defense of Marriage Act and give its year.
cards.a: A 1996 federal law defining marriage as between one man and one woman for federal purposes and letting states refuse to recognize same-sex marriages performed elsewhere. The Supreme Court struck down its federal-recognition provision in United States v. Windsor (2013).
cards.n: Clinton signed it during his reelection campaign and years later publicly urged its repeal, a neat measure of how fast opinion moved.

cards.q: Explain the rise and collapse of the dot-com bubble.
cards.a: Investors poured money into internet startups in the late 1990s on hopes of explosive future growth, driving stock prices far above the companies' actual earnings. When many of these unprofitable firms failed in 2000-2001, the bubble burst, wiping out trillions in market value.
cards.n: The crash came before 9/11, not after, and the low interest rates used to cushion it helped inflate the housing bubble that burst in 2008.

cards.q: Identify Citizens United v. FEC (2010) and its holding.
cards.a: The Supreme Court ruled that restricting independent political spending by corporations and unions violated the First Amendment's free speech protections, opening the door to unlimited outside spending in elections through super PACs.
cards.n: A frequently cited turning point in debates over money's role in modern American politics.

cards.q: Identify the Tea Party movement.
cards.a: A grassroots conservative movement that emerged in 2009 opposing federal bailouts, the Affordable Care Act, and government spending, pushing the Republican Party rightward on fiscal and constitutional issues and helping fuel major Republican gains in the 2010 midterms.
cards.n: It began with anger at bailouts started under Bush, and its main weapon was primary challenges against sitting Republicans, not general elections.

cards.q: Contrast the Tea Party and Occupy Wall Street movements.
cards.a: The Tea Party, emerging in 2009, blamed government spending and bailouts and pushed politics rightward through electoral organizing. Occupy Wall Street, emerging in 2011, blamed corporate greed and economic inequality, organizing through decentralized protest camps rather than electoral politics.
cards.n: Both arose from the same 2008 financial crisis but diagnosed the cause, and proposed opposite solutions, to it.

cards.q: Identify Obergefell v. Hodges and give its year.
cards.a: A 2015 Supreme Court decision holding that the 14th Amendment guarantees same-sex couples the right to marry, legalizing same-sex marriage nationwide and overturning remaining state bans.
cards.n: Kennedy wrote the 5 to 4 opinion on due process and equal protection grounds, and Dobbs in 2022 insisted that reasoning did not carry over.

cards.q: Identify the Black Lives Matter movement.
cards.a: A decentralized civil rights movement that emerged in 2013 after the acquittal of George Zimmerman in the shooting of Trayvon Martin, growing into nationwide protests against police violence and racial injustice, especially after the 2014 killing of Michael Brown in Ferguson, Missouri.
cards.n: Often framed as a continuation of the long civil rights movement using social media organizing tools unavailable in the 1960s.

cards.q: Date the founding of the WTO, NAFTA's implementation, and the 2008 financial crisis in order.
cards.a: NAFTA took effect in January 1994, the World Trade Organization was founded in 1995, and the global financial crisis struck in 2008, tracing the arc from accelerating globalization to its most severe modern economic shock.
cards.n: NAFTA was negotiated under the first Bush and pushed through by Clinton against his own party's unions; the WTO replaced the older GATT.

cards.q: Identify the Mariel Boatlift of 1980.
cards.a: Fidel Castro allowed roughly 125,000 Cubans to leave for the United States by boat from the port of Mariel in 1980, including some released prisoners and psychiatric patients, straining Florida's resources and reshaping Miami's Cuban American community.
cards.n: Earlier Cuban arrivals had been welcomed as Cold War refugees, so the hostile reception marks a shift, and it damaged Carter in 1980.

cards.q: Contrast supply-side economics with Keynesian demand-side economics.
cards.a: Keynesian policy uses government spending to boost demand during downturns. Supply-side economics, embraced by Reagan, argued cutting taxes on high earners and businesses would spur investment and production, with benefits 'trickling down,' following the Laffer Curve's claim that lower rates could even raise total revenue.
cards.h: → boost demand vs cut taxes to boost supply
cards.n: Critics point to the 1980s deficits as evidence the Laffer Curve's revenue claim failed in practice, even as marginal rates fell sharply.

cards.q: Explain the debate over NAFTA's effects on American manufacturing jobs.
cards.a: Critics, including Ross Perot, warned of a 'giant sucking sound' as factories relocated to lower-wage Mexico, costing American manufacturing jobs. Supporters argued the 1994 agreement would lower consumer prices and grow trade, and economists still dispute its net effect on wages and employment.
cards.h: → Perot's warning vs free-trade growth argument
cards.n: Perot's line came in the 1992 debates, and Clinton needed more Republican than Democratic votes in Congress to get the treaty through.

cards.q: Identify the 1992 'Year of the Woman' in Congress.
cards.a: A record number of women won congressional seats in the 1992 elections, a surge widely attributed to public anger over the all-male Senate Judiciary Committee's treatment of Anita Hill during Clarence Thomas's 1991 confirmation hearings.
cards.n: The Senate went from two women to six, and Carol Moseley Braun became the first Black woman ever elected to it.

cards.q: Identify California's Proposition 187 (1994).
cards.a: A state ballot initiative barring undocumented immigrants from public schools, non-emergency healthcare, and other state services. Voters approved it, but federal courts struck down most provisions, and the backlash helped shift California's Latino electorate toward the Democratic Party.
cards.h: → 1994 CA measure + court struck it down
cards.n: Governor Pete Wilson rode the measure to reelection, and the 1996 federal welfare law achieved some of what the courts had blocked.

cards.q: Explain how the Christian Coalition extended the religious right's political influence after the Moral Majority.
cards.a: Founded by Pat Robertson after his 1988 presidential run, the Christian Coalition built grassroots organizing and voter guides distributed through churches, sustaining evangelical political mobilization into the 1990s after the Moral Majority disbanded in 1989.
cards.n: Ralph Reed ran its day-to-day operations, and it faded after 1999 as evangelical organizing moved inside the Republican Party itself.

cards.q: Identify the Immigration Act of 1990.
cards.a: It raised the overall annual ceiling on legal immigration, expanded employment-based visas, and created the diversity visa lottery to admit immigrants from countries with historically low rates of immigration to the United States.
cards.n: It followed the 1986 reform that paired amnesty for about three million people with employer sanctions that were barely enforced.

cards.q: Identify the savings and loan crisis of the late 1980s.
cards.a: Deregulation and risky lending drove hundreds of savings and loan institutions to insolvency, forcing a federal bailout costing taxpayers over 100 billion dollars, one of the costliest financial crises before 2008.
cards.n: Deregulation in 1982 had let thrifts chase risky loans with federally insured deposits, the same moral hazard that returned in 2008.

cards.q: Identify Sandra Day O'Connor's 1981 Supreme Court appointment.
cards.a: Reagan appointed O'Connor as the first woman to serve on the U.S. Supreme Court, fulfilling a 1980 campaign promise and often positioning her as a moderate swing vote on the increasingly conservative Court.
cards.n: Her swing vote saved Roe's core in Casey (1992), and her replacement by Samuel Alito in 2006 moved the Court sharply right.

cards.q: Identify the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act of 1988.
cards.a: A federal law establishing legal and regulatory ground rules for casino gambling on tribal land, which became a major source of independent revenue and economic development for many, though not all, Native nations in the following decades.
cards.n: Congress wrote it after California v. Cabazon Band (1987) held that states could not regulate gaming on sovereign tribal land.

cards.q: Identify MTV's 1981 launch and its effect on youth and music culture.
cards.a: MTV began broadcasting music videos around the clock in 1981, turning visual image into a central part of a musical artist's success and giving advertisers a powerful new channel to reach a national youth audience.
cards.n: It largely excluded Black artists until Michael Jackson's videos broke the format open in 1983, a small case study in gatekeeping.

cards.q: Explain the push and pull factors behind Latin American and Asian immigration after the 1965 Hart-Celler Act.
cards.a: Push factors included civil wars and economic instability in Central America and political upheaval in Southeast Asia and elsewhere in Asia. Pull factors included family reunification preferences under the 1965 act, labor demand, and refugee resettlement programs.
cards.n: US Cold War policy created some of that push itself, from Vietnam after 1975 to the Central American wars Washington funded in the 1980s.

cards.q: Identify the Telecommunications Act of 1996.
cards.a: A sweeping deregulation of the telecommunications industry that eased restrictions on media ownership and cross-industry competition among phone, cable, and broadcast companies, accelerating consolidation and the buildout of internet infrastructure.
cards.n: Radio ownership consolidated fast afterward, and the act's Section 230 became the legal shield for the entire modern internet.

cards.q: Contrast the abortion-rights battle in Planned Parenthood v. Casey (1992) with the marriage-equality battle resolved in Obergefell v. Hodges (2015).
cards.a: Casey narrowly upheld Roe's core right to abortion while allowing states to impose restrictions that did not create an 'undue burden.' Obergefell went further, establishing a nationwide constitutional right to same-sex marriage and striking down all state bans outright.
cards.h: → Casey narrows/preserves vs Obergefell establishes right
cards.n: Casey's undue burden standard governed abortion law until Dobbs discarded both Roe and Casey in 2022, while Obergefell was left standing.

cards.q: Explain the specific controversy behind the Bush v. Gore (2000) Florida recount.
cards.a: With the presidency hinging on a few hundred Florida votes, disputes arose over 'hanging chad' punch-card ballots and inconsistent county recount standards. The Supreme Court halted the recount, ruling 5-4 that inconsistent standards violated equal protection, effectively deciding the election for Bush.
cards.n: Critics on both sides still debate whether the ruling reflected genuine constitutional reasoning or a results-driven decision; it remains the Court's most contested modern intervention in an election.

cards.q: Differentiate a complexity move from a contextualization paragraph, using Reagan-era conservatism as the example.
cards.a: Contextualizing Reagan's rise describes the immediate 1970s backdrop — inflation, the Iran hostage crisis, busing — that fuelled voter anger; that earns the 1-point Contextualization row. Connecting his small-government, pro-business rhetoric back to Gilded Age laissez-faire is a complexity move inside Analysis and Reasoning, not a separate point.
cards.h: → context = 1970s backdrop; complexity = the link to the Gilded Age
cards.n: Contextualization needs a few sentences reaching before the prompt's window; complexity scores only if you sustain it, not with one clever line.

cards.q: State the developments the College Board identifies as central to Period 9.
cards.a: The end of the Cold War and America's search for a new global role, a technology-driven economy increasingly tied to globalization, and battles over the size of government and the nation's changing racial, religious, and demographic makeup.
cards.h: → post-Cold War role + globalization/tech economy + government-size and demographic debates
cards.n: Period 9 carries the smallest weight on the exam and almost never anchors the DBQ, so learn it for context and multiple choice.

cards.q: Identify the impeachment of Bill Clinton (1998).
cards.a: The House impeached Clinton on charges of perjury and obstruction of justice stemming from his false testimony about an affair with intern Monica Lewinsky. The Senate acquitted him in February 1999, and he served out his term with high approval ratings.
cards.h: → perjury/obstruction charges + Lewinsky affair + Senate acquits
cards.n: Only the second impeachment to that point, after Andrew Johnson in 1868, and like every other one it ended without a Senate conviction.

cards.q: Identify the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Act (welfare reform, 1996).
cards.a: Signed by Clinton after negotiating with the Republican Congress, the law replaced the open-ended Aid to Families with Dependent Children program with time-limited block grants (TANF) to states, added work requirements, and fulfilled Clinton's pledge to 'end welfare as we know it.'
cards.h: → AFDC replaced by time-limited TANF + work requirements
cards.n: Clinton vetoed two earlier versions before signing this one, the clearest instance of his triangulation after the 1994 Republican sweep.

cards.q: Identify the Rodney King beating and the 1992 Los Angeles riots.
cards.a: Amateur video captured Los Angeles police officers beating Black motorist Rodney King in 1991. When a jury acquitted the officers in April 1992, six days of rioting, arson, and looting killed over 50 people, exposing deep anger over police brutality and urban poverty.
cards.h: → King beating caught on video + officers acquitted + 6 days of rioting
cards.n: The trial had been moved to suburban Simi Valley, and Korean American shop owners bore much of the destruction, complicating any simple framing.

cards.q: Identify the Oklahoma City bombing (1995).
cards.a: Timothy McVeigh, an anti-government militia sympathizer angry over the Waco siege, detonated a truck bomb outside a federal building in Oklahoma City, killing 168 people. It was the deadliest act of domestic terrorism in U.S. history and spotlighted the era's armed militia movement.
cards.h: → McVeigh + federal building + 168 dead + deadliest domestic terror attack
cards.n: Early news coverage wrongly blamed Middle Eastern terrorists, a useful reminder about assumptions in the decade before 9/11.

cards.q: Identify the National Voter Registration Act ('Motor Voter' Act, 1993).
cards.a: The law required states to let citizens register to vote when applying for a driver's license or at public assistance offices, aiming to raise turnout by removing registration barriers, though its effect on actual turnout proved modest.
cards.h: → register to vote via DMV/public assistance offices
cards.n: Several states fought it in court, and it opens the modern argument over ballot access versus fraud that runs on through voter ID laws.

cards.q: Identify the U.S. invasion of Panama (1989).
cards.a: George H.W. Bush ordered troops to remove Panamanian dictator Manuel Noriega, who had been indicted on U.S. drug-trafficking charges. Noriega surrendered, was flown to the U.S., and was convicted, in one of the first major post-Cold War uses of American military force.
cards.h: → Bush removes Noriega + drug charges + early post-Cold War intervention
cards.n: Noriega had been on the CIA payroll for years, which makes this a tidy example of a Cold War asset becoming a liability.

cards.q: Identify the 1992-93 U.S. intervention in Somalia.
cards.a: American troops joined a UN humanitarian mission to secure food aid during a famine and civil war, but the mission grew into a manhunt for a warlord that ended in the deadly Battle of Mogadishu in October 1993, prompting Clinton to withdraw U.S. forces.
cards.h: → humanitarian mission → Battle of Mogadishu → withdrawal
cards.n: Widely cited as making Clinton reluctant to intervene quickly in Rwanda a year later.

cards.q: Identify U.S. intervention in the Balkans during the 1990s.
cards.a: Clinton used NATO airstrikes and the 1995 Dayton Accords to end the Bosnian war, then led a 1999 NATO bombing campaign to stop Serbian ethnic cleansing in Kosovo, marking a new post-Cold War pattern of humanitarian military intervention in Europe.
cards.n: The Kosovo campaign went ahead without UN Security Council authorization, the precedent critics raised again over Iraq in 2003.

cards.q: Explain the connection between the 1994 Crime Bill and the rise of mass incarceration.
cards.a: The Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act funded 100,000 new police officers and prison construction, expanded the federal death penalty, and encouraged tougher state sentencing, contributing to a prison population that roughly quadrupled between 1980 and 2000.
cards.h: → 1994 bill funds police/prisons → prison population quadruples
cards.n: Many Black mayors and members of Congress backed it amid the crack epidemic, so the later criticism was not the view of 1994.

cards.q: Identify the Kyoto Protocol (1997).
cards.a: An international treaty committing industrialized nations to binding greenhouse gas emission cuts. The Clinton administration signed it, but the Senate never ratified it, and George W. Bush withdrew U.S. support in 2001, citing economic costs and the exclusion of developing nations like China.
cards.h: → binding emissions cuts + signed but never ratified + Bush withdraws
cards.n: The Senate had already voted 95 to 0 on the Byrd-Hagel resolution against any treaty exempting developing nations, so ratification was hopeless.

cards.q: Identify the Paris Agreement (2015).
cards.a: Nearly every nation pledged voluntary targets to limit global warming under this climate accord negotiated during Obama's presidency. Trump withdrew the United States in 2017, and Biden rejoined on his first day in office in 2021.
cards.h: → voluntary targets + Obama joins, Trump exits, Biden rejoins
cards.n: Unlike Kyoto its targets are voluntary, which is precisely how it avoided needing Senate ratification as a formal treaty.

cards.q: Identify Massachusetts's 2004 legalization of same-sex marriage.
cards.a: Following the state supreme court's ruling in Goodridge v. Department of Public Health (2003), Massachusetts became the first state to issue same-sex marriage licenses in May 2004, launching a state-by-state expansion that culminated in nationwide legalization under Obergefell v. Hodges (2015).
cards.h: → Goodridge ruling + first state, 2004 + leads to Obergefell
cards.n: The backlash was immediate: eleven states passed constitutional bans that November, and the issue helped drive turnout for Bush.
x: Goodridge v. Department of Public Health

cards.q: Identify the killing of Osama bin Laden (2011).
cards.a: U.S. Navy SEALs killed al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden in a raid on his compound in Abbottabad, Pakistan, in May 2011, under Operation Neptune Spear, nearly a decade after the September 11 attacks he had orchestrated.
cards.n: The raid went ahead without telling Pakistan, straining that alliance, and the war in Afghanistan still ran on for another ten years.

cards.q: Identify Edward Snowden and the 2013 NSA surveillance revelations.
cards.a: Former NSA contractor Edward Snowden leaked classified documents revealing the National Security Agency's mass collection of Americans' phone and internet data, sparking a national debate over the balance between security and privacy in the post-9/11 surveillance state.
cards.h: → Snowden leaks + NSA mass data collection exposed
cards.n: Congress ended bulk phone metadata collection in the 2015 USA Freedom Act, while Snowden himself took asylum in Russia.

cards.q: Identify Hurricane Katrina (2005) and its political fallout.
cards.a: Katrina flooded most of New Orleans after levees failed, killing over 1,800 people, disproportionately Black and poor residents unable to evacuate. The slow federal response under FEMA severely damaged public confidence in George W. Bush's administration.
cards.h: → levee failure floods New Orleans + slow FEMA response + Bush's approval falls
cards.n: New Orleans never regained much of its Black population, and the disaster was an engineering failure as much as a storm, since federal levees gave way.

cards.q: Identify the opioid crisis.
cards.a: Beginning in the late 1990s, aggressive marketing of prescription painkillers like Purdue Pharma's OxyContin fueled widespread addiction that shifted toward heroin and illicit fentanyl, contributing to tens of thousands of overdose deaths annually by the 2010s and prompting lawsuits against drug manufacturers.
cards.h: → OxyContin/Purdue Pharma + shifts to heroin/fentanyl + mass overdose deaths
cards.n: The response leaned toward treatment rather than prison, a contrast with the crack era of the 1980s that students are often asked to explain.

cards.q: Identify the #MeToo movement (2017).
cards.a: Sparked by allegations against film producer Harvey Weinstein and spread through the hashtag #MeToo, the movement encouraged widespread public disclosure of sexual harassment and assault, leading to the removal of prominent figures in media, politics, and business.
cards.h: → Weinstein allegations + #MeToo hashtag spreads + accountability wave
cards.n: Tarana Burke had coined the phrase back in 2006, so the exam can use it as a case of older organizing suddenly going viral.

cards.q: Identify the 2016 presidential election.
cards.a: Republican Donald Trump, a political outsider running on immigration restriction and economic nationalism, defeated Democrat Hillary Clinton despite losing the popular vote, winning the Electoral College by carrying traditionally Democratic Rust Belt states.
cards.h: → Trump defeats Clinton + loses popular vote, wins Electoral College
cards.n: It was the fifth time a winner lost the popular vote, after 1824, 1876, 1888, and 2000, so Electoral College reform is the usual follow-up.

cards.q: Identify Shelby County v. Holder (2013).
cards.a: The Supreme Court struck down the Voting Rights Act's coverage formula that required certain states with histories of discrimination to get federal approval (preclearance) before changing voting laws, effectively ending federal preclearance and prompting several states to adopt new voting restrictions.
cards.h: → strikes preclearance formula + states pass new voting restrictions
cards.n: Directly reverses the enforcement mechanism behind the Voting Rights Act of 1965, elsewhere in the deck.

cards.q: Explain how the internet and social media reshaped American news consumption after 2000.
cards.a: Free online news and platforms like Facebook and Twitter drained advertising revenue from print newspapers, hundreds of which closed or shrank, while algorithm-driven feeds let readers curate sources that confirmed existing views, a shift historians link to rising political polarization.
cards.h: → ad revenue shifts online → newspapers shrink → feeds sort readers into echo chambers
cards.n: A direct extension of the print-culture thread running from the penny press through yellow journalism to today.

cards.q: State how the size of the U.S. immigrant population changed between 1970 and 2010.
cards.a: The foreign-born share of the U.S. population roughly tripled, rising from under 5 percent in 1970 to about 13 percent by 2010, as immigration after the 1965 Hart-Celler Act shifted its sources from Europe toward Latin America and Asia.
cards.n: The 1970 figure was the lowest foreign-born share in American history, and the all-time peak of about 15 percent came around 1890.

cards.q: State the overall time and structure of the AP US History exam.
cards.a: Section I: 55 multiple-choice questions in 55 minutes (40%) plus 3 short-answer questions in 40 minutes (20%). Section II: 1 document-based question in 60 minutes (25%) plus 1 long essay in 40 minutes (15%). Total: 3 hours 15 minutes.
cards.h: → two sections, four question types, times and weights
cards.n: MC is the single biggest chunk of the score, but the three essay-based tasks together outweigh it, 60% to 40%.

cards.q: State the format of Section I, Part A.
cards.a: 55 multiple-choice questions in 55 minutes, worth 40% of the total score. Questions are grouped into stimulus sets of roughly 2 to 5 questions sharing one image, map, chart, or text excerpt.
cards.n: About one minute per question, but budget by set: read the stimulus once, then answer every question tied to it before moving on.

cards.q: State the format of Section I, Part B.
cards.a: 3 short-answer questions in 40 minutes, worth 20% of the total score. All three questions are required - there is no choice and no fourth question.
cards.h: → count, time, weight, all three required
