cards.n: Roughly 13 minutes per question, but each SAQ is really three small tasks - pace by part, not by question.

cards.q: Identify the stimulus attached to SAQ Question 1.
cards.a: One or more secondary sources: short excerpts from historians' writing, presenting an argument or interpretation for you to engage with.
cards.h: → secondary source(s), possibly more than one
cards.n: You are not asked whether the historian is right - you are asked to explain historical evidence connected to the claim.

cards.q: Identify the stimulus attached to SAQ Question 2.
cards.a: A primary source: a short primary text excerpt produced during the period being asked about.
cards.n: Primary-source SAQs often ask you to read the source itself for one part, then reach beyond it for another.

cards.q: State what stimulus SAQ Question 3 carries, and whether Question 4 still exists.
cards.a: SAQ 3 carries a primary or secondary non-text source - an image, map, chart, or cartoon. There is no Question 4: all three SAQs are required, and none are optional.
cards.h: → non-text source (image/map/chart/cartoon); no Q4, no choice
cards.n: The old choice between Q3 and Q4 is gone starting with the May 2027 redesign - every SAQ is now mandatory.

cards.q: State the format of Section II, Part A, the document-based question.
cards.a: One question, 60 minutes total (including a suggested 15-minute reading period), worth 25% of the total score. You are given seven documents to use as evidence.
cards.h: → time incl. reading period, weight, doc count
cards.n: 25% from a single question - the DBQ is worth more than the entire short-answer section.

cards.q: State the format of Section II, Part B, the long essay question.
cards.a: One question - a single broad prompt every student answers - 40 minutes total, worth 15% of the total score. No documents are provided; the prompt's introductory statement names two or three historical themes as valid areas of analysis, and you choose your own line of reasoning, evidence, and reasoning process.
cards.h: → one shared prompt, time, weight, no sources, choice moves inside the question
cards.n: 15% is the smallest single-task weight on the exam, but it is still worth more than 8 multiple-choice questions.

cards.q: Explain what the LEQ's introductory statement gives you, and what choice remains within the question.
cards.a: The prompt comes with an introductory statement naming two or three historical themes or processes as valid areas of analysis - it does not tell you which argument to make. The choice now lives inside the question: which line of reasoning to build, which evidence to use, and which reasoning process to apply.
cards.h: → one prompt; themes named, argument and reasoning process are your choice
cards.n: Before 2027 you chose among three prompts covering different periods; from May 2027 everyone answers the same prompt and the choice is in how you argue it.

cards.q: State what materials are and are not allowed on the AP US History exam.
cards.a: No calculator, no periodic table, and no outside notes or sources - this is a humanities exam. The exam is fully digital, taken in the Bluebook app: every document and stimulus you need appears on screen, and you type and submit all responses in the app.
cards.h: → nothing brought in; fully digital in Bluebook, all typed
cards.n: Everything you analyze is on the screen in front of you, not a paper booklet; the exam tests reading and writing about it, not recall of a textbook page number.

cards.q: Recall the nine chronological periods the AP US History course is divided into.
cards.h: → nine ranges, roughly 50-60 years each, overlapping at the edges
cards.n: Periods overlap on purpose - a single event, like the Civil War, can appear in two adjacent periods' evidence pools.

cards.q: Contrast what the SAQs test against what the DBQ and LEQ test.
cards.a: The SAQs reward short, accurate factual recall and brief explanation with no argument required. The DBQ and LEQ reward building and supporting an extended, defensible argument across a whole essay.
cards.h: → short factual recall vs sustained argument
cards.n: Do not try to write a thesis for an SAQ, and do not answer an LEQ with a bare list of facts - each task rewards a different kind of writing.

cards.q: State how the four AP US History task weights add up.
cards.a: Multiple choice 40%, short answer 20%, document-based question 25%, long essay question 15%. These four numbers sum to 100% of the composite score.
cards.n: No task type can be skipped without a real cost - even the smallest, the LEQ at 15%, outweighs a third of the SAQ section.

cards.q: Explain why the DBQ's 60 minutes and the LEQ's 40 minutes are not directly comparable in difficulty.
cards.a: The DBQ's 60 minutes include a 15-minute reading period for seven documents, leaving about 45 minutes to write; the LEQ's 40 minutes are pure planning-and-writing time with no documents to read first.
cards.h: → subtract the DBQ's reading period first
cards.n: Effective writing time is closer to 45 versus 40 minutes - much closer than the raw 60-vs-40 split suggests.

cards.q: Explain how to read a multiple-choice stimulus set.
cards.a: Read the stimulus first - note its date, author, and main point - then read every question in the set before answering any of them, since later questions can clarify what the set is testing. Answer using only what the stimulus and your outside knowledge support.
cards.h: → stimulus first, then all questions in the set, then answer
cards.n: Jumping straight to question 1 without previewing the set wastes the fact that one stimulus was built to support several questions at once.

cards.q: Identify the most common way students lose points on stimulus-based multiple choice.
cards.a: Picking an answer that is factually true on its own but is not actually supported by, or relevant to, the specific stimulus given - the question asks what the source shows, not everything you know about the topic.
cards.h: → true in general is not the same as supported by this source
cards.n: AP MC questions are open-book in a sense: the stimulus is the evidence, and the correct answer must trace back to it.

cards.q: Explain the a/b/c structure of a short-answer question.
cards.a: Each SAQ has three parts, worth one point each and scored independently - you can earn point (c) even if you missed (a) and (b). Parts typically move from describing evidence, to explaining a cause or effect, to explaining a comparison or another cause or effect.
cards.n: Never skip a part because an earlier part went badly - the parts are graded separately, not as a package.

cards.q: Explain what briefly explain actually demands in an SAQ answer.
cards.a: One specific, accurate piece of historical evidence, plus a sentence connecting that evidence to the claim the question asks about. Naming a fact alone, with no connection made, does not earn the point.
cards.h: → specific evidence plus one linking sentence
cards.n: A vague answer like farming changed a lot fails; naming what changed and why it answers the question succeeds.

cards.q: Explain what the DBQ asks you to do with its seven documents.
cards.a: Build and support a historical argument about the prompt, using the documents as evidence - not summarize each document in turn. You choose which documents support which parts of your argument.
cards.h: → argument using documents as evidence, not a document-by-document summary
cards.n: A DBQ organized as Document 1 says this, Document 2 says that rarely earns full evidence or complexity credit.

cards.q: Explain what the LEQ asks you to do without any documents provided.
cards.a: Construct an argument from your own knowledge of the period, using specific historical evidence you recall. The prompt's introductory statement names two or three valid themes but does not assign a reasoning process - you choose whether to build the argument through comparison, causation, or continuity and change.
cards.h: → argument from memory; you choose the reasoning process yourself
cards.n: With no source to lean on, evidence quality depends entirely on how specific your recalled examples are.

cards.q: Explain what earns the DBQ thesis point.
cards.a: A historically defensible claim that directly responds to the prompt and establishes a line of reasoning - usually by naming the categories or factors your essay will argue through.
cards.h: → defensible claim plus a line of reasoning
cards.n: Restating the prompt as a sentence does not earn this point; the thesis must take a position and preview how you will argue it.

cards.q: Decide: does merely restating the prompt as a claim earn the DBQ thesis point?
cards.a: No. A thesis must go beyond the prompt's wording to state a specific, arguable position with a line of reasoning - restatement alone has no line of reasoning to score.
cards.h: → no, restatement has no line of reasoning
cards.n: This is the single most common way strong writers still lose the thesis point: confident prose, no actual claim.

cards.q: Explain what earns the DBQ contextualization point.
cards.a: A description of broader historical context relevant to the prompt - situating the argument in events, trends, or processes before, during, or after the prompt's time frame, in more than a phrase.
cards.n: Contextualization must connect to the specific prompt, not just narrate general background.

cards.q: Decide: does a single sentence naming one prior event, with no elaboration, earn DBQ contextualization?
cards.a: No. The rubric requires describing the broader context, not just referencing it - one bare mention without explanation of how it connects is too thin to score.
cards.h: → no, a reference alone is too thin
cards.n: Aim for two to three sentences building outward before narrowing to your thesis.

cards.q: Explain the two tiers of the DBQ evidence-from-documents point.
cards.a: One point for using the content of at least three documents accurately to address the topic. A second point requires using the content of at least six documents, and using that content to actually support your argument, not just describe it.
cards.h: → 3 docs described = 1 pt; 6 docs used as support = 2 pts
cards.n: The second point needs both more documents and a higher bar - support, not summary.

cards.q: Explain what earns the DBQ evidence-beyond-the-documents point.
cards.a: One specific piece of historical evidence, not found in any of the seven documents, that is relevant to your argument and explained - not just named.
cards.h: → one specific outside fact, explained, relevant to the argument
cards.n: A vague outside reference to other events at the time does not count - it must be a real, specific piece of evidence.

cards.q: Explain what earns the DBQ sourcing point.
cards.a: For at least three documents, explaining how or why the document's point of view, purpose, historical situation, or audience is relevant to your argument - not just identifying which HIPP category applies.
cards.h: → 3 documents, explain relevance to argument, not just label HIPP
cards.n: Naming purpose with no explanation of why that purpose matters to your argument earns nothing.

cards.q: Decide: does writing that a source is biased because the author had a point of view earn a DBQ sourcing point?
cards.a: No. Every source has a point of view; the point requires explaining what that point of view was and how it connects to the specific argument being made, not a generic claim of bias.
cards.h: → no, biased alone is not an explanation
cards.n: Replace biased with the specific stake the author had, and what that stake predicts about the document's content.

cards.q: Explain what earns the DBQ complexity point.
cards.a: Demonstrating a complex understanding of the historical development in the prompt - for example by corroborating multiple documents, qualifying an argument, explaining multiple variables, or connecting the argument across periods.
cards.h: → corroboration, qualification, or connecting across periods
cards.n: This point is earned through the essay as a whole; it cannot be scored from one isolated sentence.

cards.q: Decide: does using content from all seven documents automatically earn the DBQ complexity point?
cards.a: No. Complexity is about the sophistication of the argument's reasoning, not the count of documents cited - an essay can use all seven and still argue in a flat, single-dimension way.
cards.h: → no, document count is not complexity
cards.n: A three-cause causation essay that ranks its causes by importance shows more complexity than a seven-document list.

cards.q: Explain what earns the LEQ thesis point.
cards.a: A historically defensible claim responding directly to the prompt, with a line of reasoning - the same bar as the DBQ thesis, but built from your own knowledge instead of documents.
cards.h: → same bar as DBQ thesis, no documents needed
cards.n: An LEQ thesis is scored identically to a DBQ thesis; practicing one sharpens the other.

cards.q: Explain what earns the LEQ contextualization point.
cards.a: Describing broader historical context relevant to the prompt, connecting it to events, developments, or processes before, during, or after the prompt's time frame - same standard as DBQ contextualization.
cards.h: → same standard as DBQ, no documents needed
cards.n: Because there is no document set to distract you, contextualization is often easier to place cleanly in an LEQ.

cards.q: Explain the two tiers of the LEQ evidence point.
cards.a: One point for providing specific historical examples relevant to the topic. A second point requires using that evidence to actually support an argument responding to the prompt, not just listing it.
cards.h: → specific examples = 1 pt; examples used to argue = 2 pts
cards.n: Two vague examples earn less than one specific example explained and put to work.

cards.q: Explain what earns the LEQ reasoning point.
cards.a: Using the historical reasoning process named or implied by the prompt - comparison, causation, or continuity and change - to structure the argument throughout the essay, not just to describe events chronologically.
cards.h: → structure the whole essay around the named reasoning process
cards.n: A causation prompt answered as a narrative timeline, with no causal language, misses this point even with good facts.

cards.q: Explain what earns the LEQ complexity point.
cards.a: The same standard as the DBQ: a complex understanding shown through qualification, corroboration, explaining multiple variables, or connecting the argument to other periods or contexts, sustained across the essay.
cards.h: → same complexity standard as the DBQ
cards.n: Complexity is the point most essays leave unearned - it demands more than accurate facts.

cards.q: Contrast the DBQ and LEQ rubrics point for point.
cards.a: Both score thesis (1) and contextualization (1) identically. The DBQ splits evidence into documents (1-2) plus outside evidence (1) for 3 possible points; the LEQ has one evidence category worth up to 2. Both end with reasoning/complexity worth up to 2.
cards.h: → same thesis/context; DBQ evidence split 3 ways, LEQ 2 ways
cards.n: DBQ tops out at 7 points, LEQ at 6 - matching their 25% vs 15% weights.

cards.q: State how SAQ points are awarded across the three parts.
cards.a: Each SAQ is worth 3 points total, one per part (a, b, c). Parts are scored independently - a wrong or missing answer on one part does not affect scoring on the others.
cards.n: Always attempt every part, even a weak guess - there is no penalty tying parts together.

cards.q: Identify the most common way students lose an SAQ point despite writing something relevant.
cards.a: Naming a general trend or topic without a specific, accurate piece of evidence - for example writing that the economy grew instead of naming what grew and how that answers the specific question asked.
cards.h: → specificity, not just relevance, earns the point
cards.n: Readers score for a concrete example plus explanation, not for evidence that the topic was studied.

cards.q: Contrast what briefly explain rewards versus what identify or describe reward alone.
cards.a: Identify or describe rewards naming an accurate fact. Briefly explain requires that same fact plus a sentence of reasoning connecting it to the question - cause, effect, similarity, or significance.
cards.n: Most SAQ verbs on the real exam are explain, so plan for two sentences per part, not one.

cards.q: Explain what a causation essay must do that a narrative essay does not.
cards.a: A causation essay identifies specific causes (or effects), explains the mechanism connecting cause to effect, and often weighs which causes mattered most - a narrative retelling of what happened in order is not causation.
cards.h: → name causes, explain the mechanism, weigh importance
cards.n: Causal language matters: words like because, led to, and as a result signal the reasoning readers are scoring for.

cards.q: Explain what a comparison essay must do.
cards.a: Identify specific similarities and differences between two developments, groups, or time periods, and explain the significance of those similarities and differences - not just describe each side separately.
cards.h: → similarities and differences, plus why they matter
cards.n: Two back-to-back paragraphs that never touch each other rarely earn full comparison credit - the essay must actually compare.

cards.q: Explain what a continuity-and-change-over-time (CCOT) essay must do.
cards.a: Identify specific elements that changed and specific elements that stayed the same across a given time span, and explain why - not simply list a start state and an end state.
cards.h: → what changed, what continued, and why
cards.n: CCOT essays that only describe the end point and skip the why lose their strongest reasoning credit.

cards.q: Name the three historical reasoning processes tested on the LEQ.
cards.a: Comparison, causation, and continuity and change over time.
cards.n: Under the 2027 format there is one LEQ prompt for everyone; you choose which of the three processes to structure your argument around, rather than the exam assigning one for that testing year.

cards.q: Define the acronym HIPP as used for sourcing a document.
cards.a: Historical situation, Intended audience, Purpose, and Point of view - the four angles used to explain why a document says what it says.
cards.h: → Historical situation, Intended audience, Purpose, Point of view
cards.n: You rarely need all four for one document - pick whichever angle actually explains the content, then argue it.

cards.q: Explain the difference between a document's purpose and its point of view for sourcing.
cards.a: Purpose is what the author was trying to accomplish by creating the document - persuade, record, warn. Point of view is the perspective or stake shaping what the author included or left out.
cards.h: → purpose = goal of writing it; point of view = the stake behind it
cards.n: They often overlap, but naming both precisely reads as stronger sourcing than blending them into one vague sentence.

cards.q: Explain what corroboration means as a way to earn DBQ or LEQ complexity.
cards.a: Showing that multiple independent pieces of evidence, from different documents or different outside facts, point to the same conclusion - strengthening the argument by cross-checking it.
cards.h: → multiple independent sources agreeing on the same point
cards.n: Corroboration is easiest to show explicitly, by naming two sources and stating that both confirm the same point.

cards.q: Explain what qualification means as a way to earn DBQ or LEQ complexity.
cards.a: Acknowledging a limit, exception, or counterpoint to your own argument, and explaining why the main argument still holds despite it - not abandoning the thesis, but showing its edges.
cards.h: → acknowledge a limit or exception, then explain why the thesis still stands
cards.n: A qualifying sentence often starts with while or although and ends by reaffirming the thesis.

cards.q: Explain what it means to connect an argument across periods for complexity credit.
cards.a: Showing how the development discussed relates to a cause, effect, or parallel in a different time period than the one named in the prompt - linking it to a broader arc of change.
cards.h: → tie the argument to a different period's cause, effect, or parallel
cards.n: This is often the fastest complexity move: one sentence linking the prompt's period to an earlier or later one.

cards.q: Contrast contextualization as a scored row versus contextualization as a historical thinking skill.
cards.a: As a scored row, it is one point earned by a specific paragraph early in the essay. As a thinking skill, it is a habit applied throughout - reading every document and building every paragraph with an eye to the surrounding context.
cards.h: → one row up front vs a habit throughout
cards.n: Strong essays keep placing evidence in context past the opening paragraph, even though only the opening earns the point.

cards.q: Explain how to spend the first two minutes of Section I, Part A.
cards.a: Do not start answering yet - glance at how many stimulus sets there are and confirm your pace target, then read the first stimulus fully before touching its questions.
cards.h: → pace check, then read the first stimulus
cards.n: 55 questions in 55 minutes leaves no time for a slow start; setting pace expectations up front prevents a late-exam scramble.

cards.q: Explain how to spend the first two minutes of an SAQ.
cards.a: Read all three parts before writing anything, underline the command term in each (explain, identify, describe), and note whether the part points you to the source, to outside knowledge, or either.
cards.h: → read all 3 parts first, underline command terms
cards.n: Writing a great answer to part (a) that also accidentally answers part (b) wastes time better spent on a genuinely new point.

cards.q: Explain how to spend the first two minutes of the DBQ reading period.
cards.a: Skim all seven documents for date and author only, sorting them by rough grouping or stance, before rereading any of them closely - this builds a map of the document set before you commit to a thesis.
cards.h: → skim all 7 for date/author first, then commit to a thesis
cards.n: Committing to a thesis after reading only the first two documents often produces an argument the later documents contradict.

cards.q: Explain a workable order for writing the DBQ within its 60 minutes.
cards.a: About 15 minutes reading and planning, then write contextualization and thesis, then body paragraphs weaving in documents and outside evidence, saving one complexity move for the final paragraph or a closing sentence.
cards.h: → 15 min plan, then context+thesis, then body, then complexity
cards.n: Writing the thesis last, after seeing what the documents actually support, often produces a stronger line of reasoning than committing to one first.

cards.q: Decide when to abandon trying to use a difficult DBQ document.
cards.a: As soon as it costs more time than one more document is worth - the DBQ only requires three documents (or six for full credit), not all seven, so a document you cannot make sense of can simply be dropped.
cards.h: → drop it once it costs more time than it is worth, you do not need all 7
cards.n: Chasing a full sweep of all seven documents to the point of running out of time is a worse trade than skipping one.

cards.q: Explain how to spend the first two minutes planning the LEQ.
cards.a: Read the prompt's introductory statement and identify the themes it names, then pick whichever reasoning process - causation, comparison, or continuity and change - fits your strongest evidence, and jot three specific points before writing a word of prose.
cards.h: → read the named themes, pick your reasoning process, then outline 3 points
cards.n: There is no longer a prompt to choose - the only choice left is which reasoning process and evidence you build the one prompt around.

cards.q: Decide which multiple-choice questions to leave for a second pass.
cards.a: Any question where you cannot rule out at least two answer choices on a first read - mark it, move on, and return only after finishing every question you can answer confidently.
cards.h: → skip and mark anything you can't narrow to 2 choices
cards.n: A stuck 90-second question costs the same time as three easy ones answered elsewhere.

cards.q: State a rough time budget for a 40-minute SAQ section across three questions.
cards.a: About 13 minutes per question, but spend unevenly within it: less time on a straightforward identify-type part, more time on a part that requires connecting evidence to reasoning.
cards.h: → about 13 min per question, distributed by part difficulty
cards.n: Do not divide time evenly by part - divide it by how much thinking each part actually needs.

cards.q: Explain why writing the DBQ thesis last, after planning, often outperforms writing it first.
cards.a: A thesis written before reading the documents risks a line of reasoning the evidence does not actually support; a thesis written after sorting the documents can commit to categories you have already confirmed you can support.
cards.h: → plan from evidence, then commit to a thesis that fits it
cards.n: This costs a few minutes of restraint but avoids the common trap of forcing evidence to fit an early guess.

cards.q: State the closing-minutes check worth running before time is called on any essay task.
cards.a: Confirm the thesis is still on the page, at least one contextualization sentence exists, and at least one sentence explicitly explains a document's HIPP or explicitly states a qualification - the cheapest points to recover.
cards.h: → check thesis, contextualization, and one sourcing/complexity sentence exist
cards.n: These checks recover points fastest in the last two minutes, when there is no time left to add new evidence.

cards.q: SAQ source: an excerpt where Franklin (1751) praises the Iroquois Confederacy's unity as a model for the colonies. (a) Briefly explain ONE Enlightenment idea reflected in the excerpt.
cards.a: Model: the excerpt reflects the Enlightenment idea that government derives legitimacy from a rational, agreed-upon structure uniting separate parts - Franklin points to the Iroquois' confederated unity as evidence such structures could work for the colonies too.
cards.h: → name the idea, then tie it to the excerpt's content
cards.n: The point is earned by connecting a named idea to the specific content of the excerpt, not by defining Enlightenment in general.

cards.q: Same source as above. (b) Briefly explain ONE development, not in the excerpt, that pushed colonists to rethink political authority before 1776.
cards.a: Model: Britain's post-1763 turn away from salutary neglect - taxes like the Stamp Act and Townshend Acts, passed without colonial representation, led colonists to question Parliament's authority over them.
cards.h: → pick a specific post-1763 policy and its effect on colonial thinking
cards.n: Must be a development the excerpt does not mention - repeating Franklin's point again earns nothing here.

cards.q: Same source. (c) Briefly explain ONE effect of colonists' rethinking of political authority in the period 1776-1800.
cards.a: Model: state constitutions written after 1776, such as Pennsylvania's, expanded voting rights and legislative power, applying the idea that authority should rest on the consent of the governed.
cards.h: → name a specific post-1776 outcome and connect it to the cause
cards.n: Vague effects like they became more independent-minded, with no concrete example, fail this part.

cards.q: SAQ content-knowledge practice (imagine no stimulus). (a) Briefly explain ONE way the market revolution changed the Northern household economy before 1848.
cards.a: Model: as factories took over cloth production, many Northern households shifted from home-based textile production to wage labor or purchasing manufactured goods, weakening the household as a self-sufficient economic unit.
cards.h: → name a specific economic shift with a before/after
cards.n: The point wants a specific change in economic activity, not a general statement that things got more industrial.

cards.q: Same SAQ. (b) Briefly explain ONE cause of the reform movements (temperance, abolition, women's rights) of 1820-1860.
cards.a: Model: the Second Great Awakening's emphasis on personal moral responsibility and the possibility of a perfected society pushed converts to organize against social sins such as drinking and slavery.
cards.h: → tie a specific cause to a specific reform reaction
cards.n: Naming the reforms without naming what caused them does not answer a briefly explain a cause prompt.

cards.q: Same SAQ. (c) Briefly explain ONE way Southern development in this period differed from the North's.
cards.a: Model: the South's economy remained centered on plantation agriculture and enslaved labor, investing far less in factories, railroads, and cities than the North did in the same decades.
cards.h: → name the contrast, anchored in a concrete economic feature
cards.n: A comparison part is scored on the difference stated, not on describing the South alone.

cards.q: SAQ content-knowledge practice (imagine no stimulus). (a) Briefly explain ONE way big business practices changed the US economy, 1865-1900.
cards.a: Model: horizontal and vertical integration, as practiced by firms like Standard Oil, let a few large corporations dominate entire industries, replacing the many small competing firms typical of the antebellum economy.
cards.h: → name the business practice and its structural effect
cards.n: Naming a company alone is not enough - explain the practice and what it changed.

cards.q: Same SAQ. (b) Briefly explain ONE Progressive Era reform that responded to problems of industrialization.
cards.a: Model: the Pure Food and Drug Act (1906) responded to public alarm, sharpened by muckraking journalism, over unsafe and mislabeled products from unregulated manufacturers.
cards.h: → name a reform and the problem it directly answered
cards.n: The link between the specific problem and the specific reform earns the point, not just naming a Progressive law.

cards.q: Same SAQ. (c) Briefly explain ONE way the federal government's economic role in 1900 differed from 1850.
cards.a: Model: by 1900 the federal government had begun regulating interstate business directly, as with the Interstate Commerce Act (1887) and Sherman Antitrust Act (1890), a level of economic oversight absent in 1850's minimal federal role.
cards.h: → contrast a specific 1900 policy with the near-absence of one in 1850
cards.n: Cite an actual law or agency, not just the claim that the government got bigger.

cards.q: SAQ content-knowledge practice (imagine no stimulus). (a) Briefly explain ONE cause of the growth of the civil rights movement after 1945.
cards.a: Model: Black veterans returning from fighting fascism abroad, having experienced less rigid segregation while stationed overseas, were newly unwilling to accept Jim Crow at home, fueling postwar organizing.
cards.h: → name a specific postwar cause and its effect on organizing
cards.n: Double V style reasoning (victory abroad, victory at home) is a well-evidenced, specific cause readers recognize.

cards.q: Same SAQ. (b) Briefly explain ONE way Cold War goals shaped US domestic policy, 1945-1980.
cards.a: Model: competing with Soviet claims about racial equality, the federal government had new incentive to support civil rights reforms, since segregation embarrassed the US in front of newly independent nations it hoped to court.
cards.h: → connect an external Cold War pressure to a domestic policy motive
cards.n: This is a causation part - name the international pressure and the domestic response it motivated.

cards.q: Same SAQ. (c) Briefly explain ONE way post-1980 conservative politics responded to developments of the 1960s-70s.
cards.a: Model: Reagan-era tax cuts and deregulation responded to the stagflation and expanded federal spending of the 1970s, arguing that shrinking government's economic role would restore growth.
cards.h: → name a specific 1980s policy and the prior decade's problem it answered
cards.n: Answers that just say people wanted change skip the required specific policy and specific prior problem.

cards.q: SAQ content-knowledge practice (imagine no stimulus). (a) Briefly explain ONE similarity between the goals of Populists (1890s) and Progressives (1900s-1910s).
cards.a: Model: both movements sought to check the political and economic power of large corporations and concentrated wealth on behalf of ordinary citizens, though through different coalitions.
cards.n: A similarity part fails if it only describes one movement and assumes the reader infers the overlap.

cards.q: Same SAQ. (b) Briefly explain ONE difference between Populist and Progressive methods.
cards.a: Model: Populists organized primarily as a rural third party seeking direct political power, while Progressives worked mainly through existing parties and government agencies, often led by urban, middle-class reformers.
cards.h: → contrast the base and the method of pursuing change
cards.n: Naming who (rural vs. urban, party vs. agency) turns a vague difference into a scorable one.

cards.q: You used to be able to pick SAQ3 or SAQ4 by content strength. Decide: does that choice still exist?
cards.a: No. All three SAQs are required in the May 2027 format - there is no SAQ4 and no choice. You can no longer dodge a weak period by picking the other question, so solid knowledge across the full course timeline now matters for every SAQ.
cards.h: → no, the choice is gone - all three SAQs are mandatory
cards.n: Practice books written before the 2027 redesign will still describe this choice - it no longer applies to your exam.

cards.q: DBQ prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the American Revolution changed American society, 1775-1800. Write a thesis.
cards.a: Model: The Revolution produced substantial political change - more democratic state constitutions and republican rhetoric of equality - but left deeper social structures, including slavery and gender roles, largely intact.
cards.h: → take a position (extent), then name 2-3 categories your essay will argue
cards.n: Extent to which prompts want you to weigh, not just list - this thesis picks political change as greater than social change.

cards.q: DBQ thesis to judge: The Civil War changed the United States in many ways. Does it earn the thesis point?
cards.a: No. It restates the prompt's topic without taking a specific position or naming a line of reasoning; simply saying it changed in many ways is not a defensible, arguable claim.
cards.h: → no, no position taken, no line of reasoning
cards.n: A fix like specifically politically, economically, and socially still needs a real claim about which mattered most or how.

cards.q: DBQ prompt: Evaluate the extent to which industrialization transformed American society, 1865-1900. Write a thesis.
cards.a: Model: Industrialization transformed the nation's economic and social landscape through mass immigration and urban growth, but its transformation of political power was limited, as the same elite economic interests retained control.
cards.h: → pick categories (economic, social, political) and rank their extent
cards.n: Naming which category changed least is often the strongest, most arguable part of a thesis like this.

cards.q: DBQ thesis to judge: While the New Deal relieved suffering, its greatest impact was expanding the federal government's economic role, a change reinforced by WWII mobilization. Earn the point?
cards.a: Yes. It takes a specific position (greatest impact = expanded federal role), acknowledges a counterpoint (relief), and previews a line of reasoning extending into WWII.
cards.h: → yes, specific claim, counterpoint, and forward-looking line of reasoning
cards.n: Notice the thesis does more than the minimum: it also sets up complexity by reaching past 1939 into the war.

cards.q: DBQ prompt: Evaluate the extent to which Reconstruction transformed the political and social status of African Americans, 1863-1877. Write a thesis.
cards.a: Model: Reconstruction produced real but incomplete transformation - sweeping political gains like Black male suffrage and officeholding, undercut by social and economic structures, such as sharecropping, that preserved much of the prewar racial hierarchy.
cards.h: → split political gains from social/economic limits, then weigh them
cards.n: This is a strong extent to which answer because it grants real change while still taking a clear position on its limits.

cards.q: DBQ thesis to judge: The Cold War caused the US government to grow, and this had many effects on American life. Earn the point?
cards.a: No, borderline at best. It gestures at causation but many effects names no actual line of reasoning - which effects, and how do they connect to the claim?
cards.h: → no/borderline, many effects is not a line of reasoning
cards.n: Compare to the New Deal thesis above: naming the specific categories is what turns a vague claim into a scorable thesis.

cards.q: LEQ prompt (causation): Evaluate the extent to which economic factors caused the American Revolution. Write a thesis.
cards.a: Model: Economic factors were the primary cause of the Revolution - Parliament's postwar taxes and trade restrictions after 1763 directly provoked colonial resistance, though ideological objections to taxation without representation sharpened that resistance into rebellion.
cards.h: → take a position on economic vs. other causes, then connect them
cards.n: A strong causation thesis often ranks causes rather than just listing several side by side.

cards.q: LEQ thesis to judge (comparison, Northern vs. Southern colonies): Northern and Southern colonies developed differently due to geography, religion, and economy. Earn the point?
cards.a: Borderline/no. It names categories but states no actual claim about what the differences were or which mattered most - a comparison thesis needs to specify the difference, not just gesture at causes of one.
cards.h: → borderline, names categories but no actual comparative claim
cards.n: Fix: state one specific difference in each category, such as cash-crop plantation labor versus subsistence farming and trade.

cards.q: LEQ prompt (continuity and change): Evaluate the extent to which the federal government's role in the economy changed, 1865-1945.
cards.a: Model: The federal government's economic role expanded dramatically by 1945, moving from the largely hands-off Gilded Age approach to direct regulation and spending under the Progressive Era and New Deal, though private industry remained the dominant economic force throughout.
cards.h: → name the start state, end state, and what stayed constant
cards.n: Noting what did not change (private industry's dominance) is what earns this thesis complexity potential too.

cards.q: LEQ thesis to judge (causation, US entry into WWII): Pearl Harbor caused the United States to enter World War II. Earn the point?
cards.a: No. It is accurate but too narrow - a single-sentence restatement of one event with no broader line of reasoning about the causes leading up to entry does not meet the bar.
cards.h: → no, accurate fact, but not a line of reasoning
cards.n: A stronger version would add prior causes, such as economic ties to the Allies or rising tensions with Japan over Asia-Pacific expansion.

cards.q: LEQ prompt (comparison): Compare the goals and methods of the civil rights movement and the women's rights movement, 1945-1980.
cards.a: Model: Both movements pursued legal equality through federal action, but the civil rights movement relied more heavily on mass nonviolent protest and litigation, while the women's movement leaned more on legislative lobbying and workplace-focused organizing.
cards.h: → one shared goal, one method difference, stated specifically
cards.n: Comparison theses score best when they name a similarity and a difference, not just one or the other.

cards.q: LEQ thesis to judge (causation, origins of the Cold War): Differing ideologies and mutual distrust between the US and USSR caused the Cold War to begin after 1945. Earn the point?
cards.a: Yes. It states a specific, defensible position (ideology and distrust as causes) and previews a line of reasoning the essay can build on with specific postwar events.
cards.h: → yes, specific causes named, arguable, and expandable with evidence
cards.n: This thesis works because ideology and distrust are concrete enough to be supported with named events like the Iron Curtain or containment.

cards.q: Document: Las Casas, A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies (1542), addressed to the Spanish crown. Write a sourcing sentence linking his purpose to an argument about colonization.
cards.a: Model: Because Las Casas wrote to persuade the crown to reform its colonial policy, his account emphasizes atrocities in order to shock his royal audience into action, which suggests his numbers may be inflated for that persuasive purpose.
cards.h: → name the purpose, then explain what it predicts about the document's content
cards.n: The strongest sourcing sentences end by saying what the purpose implies about reliability or emphasis, not just naming the purpose.

cards.q: Document: an anonymous 1775 loyalist pamphlet addressed to fellow colonists. Write a sourcing sentence using audience to support an argument about divided colonial opinion.
cards.a: Model: Because the pamphlet was written for a colonial audience still weighing loyalty to the crown, its anonymous author likely feared reprisal from patriot neighbors, which itself is evidence that colonial opinion in 1775 was genuinely split, not united behind independence.
cards.h: → tie the audience to the risk or motive it created for the author
cards.n: Anonymity plus audience is a strong sourcing combination - explain what the anonymity itself reveals.

cards.q: Document: Douglass's 1852 speech What to the Slave is the Fourth of July?, delivered to a Rochester abolitionist audience. Write a sourcing sentence for an argument about sectional tension.
cards.a: Model: Speaking to a sympathetic abolitionist audience, Douglass could use direct, confrontational language about slavery's hypocrisy that he might have softened for a mixed or Southern audience, showing how polarized public rhetoric on slavery had become by 1852.
cards.h: → connect the sympathetic audience to the boldness of the rhetoric
cards.n: Note how the sourcing sentence uses the audience to explain the tone, not just to restate who was in the room.

cards.q: Document: the Populist Party's 1892 Omaha Platform, addressed to American voters amid a farm crisis. Write a sourcing sentence using historical situation.
cards.a: Model: Written during a period of falling crop prices, high railroad shipping rates, and mounting farm debt, the platform's demands for currency reform and railroad regulation directly reflect the economic distress farmers were experiencing in 1892.
cards.h: → tie the document's demands to the crisis it was written during
cards.n: Historical situation works best when you name the specific conditions, not just economic hardship in general.

cards.q: Document: a 1917 Committee on Public Information poster urging enlistment. Write a sourcing sentence using purpose.
cards.a: Model: As a government-produced wartime poster meant to build public support for the war effort, it uses emotional appeals and simplified imagery rather than balanced argument, since its purpose was persuasion and mobilization, not neutral information.
cards.h: → government propaganda purpose predicts emotional, one-sided content
cards.n: Government-produced plus wartime is enough historical situation to justify calling the content persuasive rather than neutral.

cards.q: Document: Barry Goldwater's 1964 GOP nomination acceptance speech, addressed to convention delegates. Write a sourcing sentence using point of view.
cards.a: Model: Speaking as the standard-bearer of the conservative wing of his party to delegates who had just nominated him over moderate rivals, Goldwater's point of view led him to sharply reject compromise, reflecting the rising influence of conservative activism within the GOP by 1964.
cards.h: → connect his political position to the sharpness of his stance
cards.n: Point of view sourcing works by explaining why this speaker, in this role, would say this rather than something more moderate.

cards.q: Essay prompt: causes of the American Revolution. Write a contextualization opener.
cards.a: Model: For decades before 1763, Britain governed its colonies under salutary neglect, loosely enforcing trade laws and leaving colonial assemblies to manage most local affairs. Britain's massive war debt after the French and Indian War ended that approach, setting the stage for new taxes.
cards.h: → describe the prior norm, then the shift that triggered the prompt's topic
cards.n: This opener earns the point by describing, not just naming, the shift from neglect to new taxation.

cards.q: Essay prompt: effects of the market revolution. Write a contextualization opener.
cards.a: Model: Before 1800, most American households produced goods for their own use or local trade, with limited transportation connecting distant markets. Improvements in roads, canals, and later railroads after the War of 1812 began knitting the country into a single national market.
cards.h: → describe the pre-1800 baseline, then the change that enables the prompt's topic
cards.n: Naming specific infrastructure (roads, canals, railroads) makes this more than a vague claim that things got more connected.

cards.q: Essay prompt: causes of the Civil War. Write a contextualization opener.
cards.a: Model: Through the early 1800s, sectional disputes over slavery's expansion were repeatedly managed through compromise, including the Missouri Compromise of 1820 and the Compromise of 1850. By the mid-1850s, events like the Kansas-Nebraska Act had shattered that pattern of compromise.
cards.h: → describe the compromise pattern, then how it broke down
cards.n: Contextualization for causation topics often works by describing a prior equilibrium and then the strain that broke it.

cards.q: Essay prompt: Populist and Progressive responses to industrialization. Write a contextualization opener.
cards.a: Model: In the decades after the Civil War, rapid industrial growth, immigration, and urbanization transformed the American economy, concentrating enormous wealth and power in a small number of corporations while creating harsh conditions for farmers and factory workers alike.
cards.h: → describe the industrial transformation that both movements were reacting to
cards.n: This single context paragraph can set up either a Populist-only or a Populist-and-Progressive essay.

cards.q: Essay prompt: origins of the Cold War. Write a contextualization opener.
cards.a: Model: During World War II, the United States and the Soviet Union cooperated as allies against Nazi Germany despite deep ideological differences between capitalism and communism. As victory approached, that wartime alliance began to fracture over the postwar fate of Eastern Europe.
cards.h: → describe the wartime alliance, then the strain that ended it
cards.n: Framing the alliance as already strained before 1945 sets up causation evidence about Yalta and Potsdam cleanly.

cards.q: Essay prompt: conservative resurgence after 1980. Write a contextualization opener.
cards.a: Model: Through the 1960s and 1970s, expanding federal programs, the unpopular Vietnam War, the Watergate scandal, and economic stagflation eroded public confidence in an activist federal government, creating an opening for a political movement promising smaller government and lower taxes.
cards.h: → list what eroded confidence in government before naming the reaction to it
cards.n: Four concrete grievances (spending, Vietnam, Watergate, stagflation) is stronger contextualization than a vague claim of 1970s troubles.

cards.q: State what changed about AP US History Section I, Part B (SAQ) for May 2027.
cards.a: All three SAQs are now required in 40 minutes - the old choice between Question 3 and Question 4 is gone, and there is no fourth question. Every SAQ now comes with a source: SAQ1 has one or more secondary sources, SAQ2 a primary text, SAQ3 a primary or secondary non-text source (image, map, chart, or cartoon).
cards.h: → 3 required SAQs, no more Q3/Q4 choice, every one has a source
cards.n: Most SAQ prep material written before 2027 still describes Q1+Q2 required plus a choice of Q3 or Q4 - that choice no longer exists on your exam.

cards.q: State what changed about the AP US History LEQ for May 2027.
cards.a: There is now one broad LEQ prompt that every student answers - the old choice among three prompts is gone. The prompt's introductory statement names two or three valid historical themes, but you choose your own line of reasoning, evidence, and reasoning process (causation, comparison, or continuity and change).
cards.h: → one prompt for everyone; choice moved inside the question
cards.n: Older LEQ guides describing picking the best of three prompts by period or reasoning type no longer apply - there is only one prompt to answer.

cards.q: Explain which parts of an older AP US History prep book are still safe to use for the May 2027 exam.
cards.a: Every DBQ and LEQ rubric criterion is unchanged in the May 2027 redesign, and the DBQ prompt still comes from Periods 3-8, so rubric explanations and content review from older material stay valid. Two things did change: the SAQ’s question count and choice, and the LEQ’s prompt choice.
cards.h: → rubrics and DBQ untouched; SAQ structure and LEQ choice changed
cards.n: If a book or website is silent about its edition, check whether it describes choosing SAQ3 or SAQ4, or choosing among three LEQ prompts - either flags outdated material.

cards.q: State the College Board's stated purpose for the 2027 SAQ and LEQ redesign.
cards.a: To give students time back, reposition choice so it lives within the question rather than between whole prompts, and improve focus and transparency about what each task is testing.
cards.h: → time back, choice moves inside the question, more focus and transparency
cards.n: Knowing the rationale helps you recognize the pattern: fewer competing options, more structure around one shared task.

cards.q: State how the AP US History exam is administered for May 2027, and what that changes about your workflow.
cards.a: The exam is fully digital, taken in the Bluebook app - you read every stimulus on screen and type and submit all SAQ, DBQ, and LEQ responses in the app, rather than writing in a paper booklet.
cards.h: → fully digital, Bluebook app, typed responses
cards.n: Practice typing full-length timed responses, not just handwriting them, since your actual submission method has changed.
